The Coming Fight—And Two Others in the

Up to this, the excitement has been constantly in-

enemy to disable him, and render him unfit

erry. Bill Ryall, we regret to learn, was so very

title: The Prize Fight - A Brief but Exciting Mill
text:
i THE PRIZE FIGHT.

A Brief but Exciling Mill.

Charlie Gallagher Whips Tom Allen in Two
Rounds and in Three Minutes. -

Gne Terrific Blow Settles the Business.

The “Fancy” Surprised—Incidents of
the Day—The Betting, &c.

Yesterday, amid the snow and chilly breezes of
the mornmg, the lovers of pugilism turned outin
considerable force for attendance at the fight to take
place between Charles C. Gallagher and Thomas
Allen, both of Cleveland, Ohio.

The men and their condition and position have
already been described in these columns. Charlie
Gallagher is a mere boy of 23 years of age, 6 feet 1}
inches in height, and a comparative novico in the
plize-ring. Tom Allen is about 30 years of age. 5
teet 10 inches in height, and claims to be the Fagiish
ehampion of the prize-ring.

THE START.

At nine o'clock, at the foot of Washington avenue,
the “Gem” was receiving passengers for an excursion
trip to the scene of battle. Within a aquare or two,
be “Galatea” was receiving the friends and backers
ef Tom Allen, and seemed to run m opposition to
tke “Gem.” The “Gem” was specially crowded
with the lovers of the *‘manly art.” The “Galatea”

had a very small and, no doubt, select carzo.

Among the notabilities of the sporting fraternity
Present were the tollowmg, whose names we give
ter the enlightenment of posterity:

Mike McCoole, Johan Looney, Tom Kehoe, J.
Hickey, Patsey Curtin, Dan Stevens, Pat Wall,
Pete Brooks, Pat Hanlon, Mike Ryan, Geo. Looney,

Cir.; Joe Ferry, Cin.; Barney Frain, Covington,

_Ky.; and many other lesser lights.

it waa about 10 o'clock when the Gem, with hor

“precious” cargo, toddled up the stream to Bis-
--Bell’s Point, where the Galatea took Tom Alicw on
board, to the sound of some shouting. The boats
then wended their way down the stream, for the

scene of action. McCoole and a few others Icft the
beat at Blsseil’s Point, in what many on board
would call “disgust.” ibe beat remained at the

“Point” a long time, and, at an adjacent store, the

boys belped themselves to beer, crackers, cheese,

end @ variety of other creature comforts, on which
the proprietor made slim profita.

On board the boat were a variety of gawea of
ebance—called chuck-luck, red-and-black, reven-up,
dice and five or six others thatare Known oniy to
the mitiated.

Itjwould be a rich subject fora novelist ora philoso-
pher to study the crowd gathered on the lazy boards
of the “Gem.” There were fighters trom all parts
of the continent, and persons of all classes of
Society. A motley throng suimated by the spirit of

the barbaric amusement in prospect.

_ At Carondelet the “Gem” took Chartie Gallagher
on board, and he was cordially received by his
| friends.

THE SCENE OF THE FIGHT,

The project was to go dewn the river te some

| spotoffering a suitable scene for the contest. Car-

--Foil’s Island was selected as the scene of the en-
counter. It is situated about one mile below

| Quarantine, and is well wooded, and enlivened by

a tew shanties and log cabins.

On this island, in a clearing in the woods, a “ Ting”
was improvised, according to the regulations of the
British prize-ring. The ground was a little uneven
and had to be leveHed. The snow lay thick and heayy
all around, but the genial sun shene out as brightly
as if on a camp meeting.

PRELIMINARY MATTERS.

Tom Allen chose for his umptre Daa Ryan. Char-
lie Gallagher chose for his Jimmie McDonnell; but
the great difficulty was the selection of a reteree.

Chatlie Gallagher was the first in the ring,
and shied his castor to .intimate that he
was “on hand.” soonafier Tom Alien arrived, and
the fightists were comfortably wrapt in blankets.
Beth of them looked tresh, physically and mentally.

Aftera hundred names were proposed and dis-
cussed for referee 1t was—at or near 5 P. M.—agreed
that Messrs. Kearney and Judd should act in the
capacity.

Charlie Gallagher flourished a “C” that Allen
| promptly took up, and then Allen tried to bluff the
triends of Gallagher by offering $10) even, 100 to
90, 100 to 80, and he hallooed very loudly for 100 to

70, which was ultimately returned to Mr. Walker,

the treasurer for the occasion.

On a “toss wp” for a choice ot corners, Gallagher
happened to be the lucky man, and turned his back
to the setting sup. The fighters were ready—only
to divest them of their toggery and prepare for the
inner ring. The ring was neatly prepared, the ar-
rangements being conducted by the following com-
mittee: Frank Curry, Barney Frayne, Mike Sulli-
van, Wm. Fitzgibbons, fom Riley, Pat Hanley, Pat
Reilly, the “dead boxer,” Bob Collins, J:m Hotlor-
an, Fd. Robinson, Josh Shaw, Billy Dago, Mike

Frank Curry deserves credit for instituting the

chairs, and everything dune to facilitate their opera-

ors.

THE FIGHT,

Patsy Reardon and Jack Looney were the seconds
ot Tom Allen; Patsy Curtin and “Dabiin Tricks’,
manipulated Charlie Gallagher. Pete Brooks acted
as ring-muster.

It was nearly five o’cluck when the referees were
chosen, and the “men” declared themselves ready
for the “tun.”

Round 1—Betting ran high and seemed to be in
favor of Allen, who looked confident of an easy vic-
tory. The men came to the call of ‘time’ with
much determination. Gallagher was more cool
than we couid inaglie be woula be. Allen hida
gay cardonic smile on his handsome Enghsh phiz as
he reassured his opponent. They played arounda
little, and a right-bander from Gallagher drew first
bleed trom Alien’s upper lip. Soon after a clincher
from Alien’s right mauler sent the ruby flowing
trom Gallagher’s proboscis. There were several
“handsome” right and lett thrusts on both sides,
and a clip trom Allen, aided by a slip, brought Gal-
lagher tothe surface of the earth. First knock
down claimed for Allen.

Round 2 and last—The men came to the call of
time with great promptitude. Allen dealt Galiagher
a tip.on the nozzle that sent the carmme over Gal-
lagher’s frontispicce and inspired him to exert
himself. Then Gallagher, quick a3 lightning,
give Allen a left-hander on the chest, and,
as Allen dodged bis head, a right-hander
bebind the ear that knocked the champion senseless
beyond the ropes. His head lay eutside the ring,
and the first impression was that Alien was killed.
He bad to be carried to his corner, and was com-
pletely knocked out ot time and tune. Eestoratives
had to be applied with some energy m order to re.
store him, and his greatest opponents were glad to
ree Signs of Peturning life.

This ended the fight, and Charlie Gallagher
was declared the victor, and his chosen
color, the green, was flaunted amid deafening cheers-

After Tom Allen’s revival there was some talk of
his rechallenging Gallagher for $5,000 a side, but
nothing definite transpired.

THE RETURN.

Tke trip heme was very animated—iiscussing
the merits ot the fight anc C. A. Donaldson's
refresbments, which the party did with mack en-
thusiam.

There isno doubt but the sporting fraternity
were much surprised at the issue of the fight. All
expected Allen to be the victor, but the blow which
might be called a *‘chance” blow, and might not uc-
cur ia a hundred fights sent Allen out of time, and
almost out ot the world. Allen isa man of firmly

knot frame, while Gallagher is what may be consid-
dered a mere boy as yet, and certamily not Allen’s
equal in strength.

he fight was even looked upon ima national
sense. Allen isan Englishman, and a member of
the Queen's own,” while Gallagher is a genuine
Fenian and bere the **Green” as if the fate of Ire-

title: Boxiana - St Louis the Fistic Centre - The Night Before the Battle - A Visit to the Haunts of 'the Fancy'
text:
St. Louis the Fistic Centre.

The Night Before the Battle—A Visit to the
Haunts of “the Fancy.”

Whether St. Louis shall or shall not be the gov-
ernmental centre of ‘*the universal Yankee nation”
remains tobe decided hereafter by the force of
events and the wisdom of the great American peo-
ple; but she enjoys one position already, which
none of her rivals dare dispute. St. Louis is the fistic
centre of the Republic, beyond all question. Here
are gathered the creme de la creme of pugilistic soci-
ety; the pick and flower of modern gladiators; the
bright, particular stars, whose orbit is in the twenty-
four-foot ring; the best illustrators of “the manly
art of self-defence;” the men who “go in on their
muscle” as a profession, and hammer one another
into bloody jelly purely asa matter of business—in
short, the chiefs of the noble army of “buffers” are
within our borders. St. Louis has an almost exclu-
sive monopoly of these unblushing honors, and wears
them as gracefully asshe can under the circum-
stances.

John Morrissey, once the pet and pride of the New
York “fancy,” has fallen from his high estate, and
dwindled into a mere member of Congress; Heenan,
the gallant youth from Benicia, strikes no more from
the shoulder, but bets judiciously, and wins tre-
quently on trotting horses and voracious “tigers;
Joe Coburn has departed into unknown regions,
and the rest of the illustrious ex-pounders
are so entirely forgotteh that we need not
announce theirnames or whereabouts. But while
the remainder of the country cannot boast ofa single
champion, we have no less than three of them—each
ready and willing to wear the belt, or to
“belt” one another at the slightest provocation.
Allen, Gallagher and McCoole are permanent resi-
depts and permanent attractions; they mix with or-
dinary mortals on terms of perfect equality, and dis-
pense facial and liquid “smiles” over their respect-
ive bars ata low price for cash, or approved secu-
rity.

The presence of these burning and shining lights
draws a multitude of the smaller fry, who flutter
around the champions like moths around a candle.

And each champion has his own particular set of
retainers, men who pat him onthe back, shout his
praises, drink his whiskey and make themselves use-
ful and ornamental generally.

The “chaffing” and “blowing” of these fellows
furnish the electric atmosphere h generates
matches—for all matches are not in heaven,”
while those we allude to emanate frum an en-
tirely different locality.

Allen’s friend tells Gallagher's friend that the for-
mer can whip the latter. Gallagher hears of it, de-
nies the soft impeachment, &c., &c., until both
having screwed their courage to the fighting
point, a challenge is offered and accepted, the pre-
liminaries are arranged, the money put up, the box-
ers go inte training, and at the appointed time the
whole culminates in “a merry miil,”’ like the one ex-
pected to-day.

When the fight is thoroughly cooked and ready to
be served up hot, the distinguished guests from
abroad begin to arrive; never standing on etiquetie,
or waiting for an invitation, but just stepping in
“like one of the family,” and making themselves
entirely at home. Consequently the twelve or
twenty-four hours previous to a battle is apt to be
somewhat exciting and brilliant. There is a sort of
Ireemasonry among prize-fighters, ani they all
seem to know each other by “grips”’ as well as pass-
words. No introduction is ever needed; one o/ these
game-cocks walks into a saloon where game-cocks
congregate, gives a preliminary crow, asks the crowd
up to drink, and the thing is done without ceremony
or cards. aces,

Every train yesterday brought in a delega‘ion of
the P. R. fraternity. They area curious breed, and
the student of human nature who has never studied
their habits has yet very much learn if riot to enjoy.
What quantities of active, belligerent, original sia is
wrapped up in these unregenerate bodies we do not
care to inquire, but the bodies certainly are models
for asculptor. Strip yonder swaggering ruffian of his
clothes, and he would show like the Apollo Belvi-
dere. If he be in good condition, or ‘‘in fighting
trim,” as it is called, not an ounce of superfluous
flesh encumbers his bones. The massive neck sits
firm and strong upon the broad shoulders; the limbs
taper toward the extremities as cleanly and perfectly
as those of a thorough-bred horse, and beneath
the marble skin the net-work of muscle: rise
and falls like a piece of superb machinery. What
splendid antmals they are! But their beauty ends
where their heads begin. Naturally enough they al;
have striking countenances, but they are not pretty,
and, we presume, do not want to be considered so.
There is a large preponderance of brain behind the

ears, a scanty development where the organs of ven-
eration and conscientiousness are supposed to re-
side; suspicious scars are scattered here and there;
the nose bridges bear painful evidence of having
been travelled over too often, and the ivory crop is
usually short—likewise the hair. Giving the devi,
his due, prize fighters are seldom quarrelsome, and
their behavior on the street is rather subdued than
otherwise. To see them in their glory, one must go
to their haunts—as we did last night. But even then
he must be more fortunate than we were, else his
stock of knowledge will not be materially increased.
Our first call was at

TOM ALLEN’S. e

This establishment is on Fitth, between Biddle and
O’Falion streets, and the sign announces it asa
a “Concert Saloon.” The usual drinking par apher-
nalia occupy the front, and through a narrow door
in a low partition the visitor passes into a narrow
apartment dedicated to the worship of Bacchus
and Calliope. A range of round tables and
chairs are provided for the devotees of the
former, and a piano perched upon a platform serves
for those of the latter. Thus the twin deities of
wine and music, by a convenient and satisfactory
arrangement, receive their offerings at the same al-
tar. The bar was lmed by a thirsty and enthusias-
tie crowd, and the tables were also liberally patron-
ized, two or three servitors being engaged in dealing
outthe potables, and rushing hither and thither in
the most frantic manner. A young manu with bright
auburn bair presiged at the instrument and execut-
ed a terrific accompaniment to a gentleman in his
shirt sleeves who sang a terrific song in praise of

lager beer. At certain intervals another gentleman
rapped on the table and the whole company burst
forth in a tremendous chorus which made the very
rafters tremble. The audience could not be consid-
ered strictly select, in fact it was miscellaneous and
variegated. Men with soft hats, men with beavers;
men with good clothes on and men whose clothes
were not so good; men sober as they could be, and
men not so sober as they might be; but among them
all there were very few of boxiana’s upper crust.
The nationality of those present was English, in-
tensely English, and the broai cockney dialect had a
Jvbn Bull-ish flavor which tasted strongly of the
mother country.

There was not much said about the fight, but if we
might judge of the popular feeling a perfect confi-

dence Was entertained in the prowess of Allen, and
his friends were too sanguine to discuss the chances.
So we swung round to

CHARLIE GALLAGHER’S,

on Broadway. This is more spacious than its rival,
but got up on the same principles and dedicated to
the same purpose. A piano and a violin blended
their discords for the benefit of the patrons, but no
vocal harmonies disturbed the serenities of the
time and place. Square, steady drinking appeared
to constitute the order of exercises, but no noise or
boistercus conduct was observed. Here England
was lost sight of, and we were to all intents and pur-
poses in the heart of Ireland. Natives of ** the gem
of the ocean” circulated about promiscuously, in ex-
cellent humor with themselves and everybody else,
but the approaching battle did not enter into the
conversation to as great an extent as might be im-
agined. Gallagher’s adherents evidently preferred
to await the issue of the combat, and not to spoil the
victory, or intensify the defeat by any preliminary
beasting.

title: M'Coole - A visit to his Training Quarters
text:
.
MCOGLE.
A Visit to his Training Quarters.

Hiow the Giant Leeks, Acts and Feeis.

The approaching fight between Mike McCoole and
Tom Allen, to come off within fifty miles of Cincin-
nati, on the 10thof next month, is already attract-
ing the usual amount of conjectures, scrmises and
attention at the hands of the devotees of the P. R.
Judging from the tone of the Cincianati press Allen
has numerous friends there, but concerning the fistic
giant McCoole but little has been said. Being an ad-
Yocate of fair play, we yesterday paida visit to the
chieftain at his headquarters at the Fairfield House,
about four miles out on Grand avenue, near the
Fair Ground, arriving in time to find him Just
emerging from his customary bath after his morn-

ing’s exercise. The Fairfield House, by the way, is
somewhat noted as the rendezvous of profeesional
shoulder hitters, and is kept by Mr. Frank Curry.
It was here McCoole trained for the Ooburn “mill,”
and its remoteness from the bustle of the city and
healthy location are admirably adapted to the work
of developing muscle fur the contests of the ring.

THE INTERVIEW.

Approaching frem Grand avenue we had no trouble
in finding the place, for above it floated a large
American flag, and across it in ample letiers was
painted ‘“ McCoole’s Headquarters—Training
Ground.” We walked mto the bar and sitting-
room, and made known our business toa consumptive
looking gentleman, and were informed that McCoole

and giving all information possible upon the subject
oi training, bealth, &c. He is evidently used to an-

and to the point.

HIS TRAINING.

McCoole is in charze, so to speak, of

James Haley, a somewhat formidable knight

ot the P. KR. by the wey, and _ considered
one of the best trainers in the country,

and Mr. Thomas Kelly, mentioned before. McCoole
bes now been in preparatory exercise for the
“mili” some two months. When he commenced
his weight was 24817 pounds, and, as he stands full
#ix feet in his stockings, the reader who never saw
Lim can form some adequate idea of his appearance.
His weight now, of course, is a secret, probably
known to pone but himself. He admits, however,
that it is very hard work to reduce himself to the
requisite pot for work in the ring, but he is being
reduced, and yesterday he looked in admirable com-
ition. His skin has that healthy rosiness about it
which betokens excellent health and no dissipation.
| Taudeed, be informed us that when he got ready w
fight Coburn he was in as good condition as he ever
was iu bis life, and now he felt full as well as then.
His trainers told us also that he was m splendid
Plight and daily improving.

He sleeps on a goud mattress, with plenty of warm
covering, rises promptly at five o’clock in the morn-
ing, rain or shine, and immeiiately proceeds
to a thed room on the rear of the lot,
about 10x12, where ke exercises with the
dumb-bells, a suspended sand bag weighing
about four hundred pounds, cannon balls and
two heavy bags attached to cords running over a
pully. This exercise is continued for about a half
hour, and is done to develop the muscles of the arm,
the flesh on which now feels like buckskin stretched
over marble. After this he wraps himself up as
warm as possible, and mufties ap his face so es to be
hardly dis¢ernible—for the purpose of producing
profuse perspiration, and starts out on his four
mile walk—two in and two out. Returning he takes
a salt water bath, and undergoes a pretty severe
scrubbing and rubbing process, sufficiently rough,
indeed, to take the skin off almost any other man
but him. After the bath he dresses warmly again
and restsawhile, and then breakfasts moderately
on beef or mutton, with trimmings—the meat, of
course, always are. His diet is substantial, and
varies but little from that of a laboring man, al-
though, probably, he does not eat as much. After
breakfast comes rest of an hour or s0, or until
one o'clock, when he dons his walking
shoes, each weighing about five pounds,
and, accempanied by ene or both of his trainers,
and well muffied up, be starts out on a walk of
from thirteen to sixteen miles—and as a walkist he
is a decided success. A day or so ago, when the
Natural Bridge road, and, indeed, ali the roads
_ about the suburbs of the city were in a muddy, slip-
pery condition, he walked fourteen miles in one
bour and fifty-tive minutes, loaded down as he was
with the heaviest of clothing, and said he felt so
little fatigued that he could have repeated it in the
same time. His powers of endurance are astonish-
ing. On bis return from the walk he enjoys a short
rest, then eats supper, and a short time after supper
comes another walk of two or three miles. He never
ventures out after the dampness of evening sets in,
and is in bed promptly at 8 o’clock. These are his
every-day exercises, rain or shine.

MEMORASDA.

For a short time after he went out to the Fairfield
House the training was pretty severe for him. It
was hard to get used to the systematized work of
reducmg weight, and at the same time develop the
muscles; besides, it was a difficult matter to wean
himself trom the inactivity of a city life; but he soon

| “came down to the work,” so to speak, and when we
saw him be was the personification of health and
strength. McCoole of the city, and McUoole of the
ring, are two cifferent individuals. He speaks con-
fidently of “getting away” with Allen, bat alluded
to his antagovist in complimentary terms. There
is, however, in the coming mill, on the part of both

out victorious. ride and ambition are doing more
toward making it one of the hottest contested fights
ever known on the continent than the amount of
money now up; and with ro interveamy sickn +s 1;—
m ingas a drawback on McCoole, he will mak
lively work for Allen. As we parted with the fisti

and kindly invited us to accompany him—we de-
clined. Couldn’t make the time in two hours as he
pemoeet doing. Our pedal extremities were not
ended for such time. We are no: training for the

GALLAGER IN DURANCE.

Gallagher, .bo was arrested at Carondelet in the

= ccmments about bis being sick, and unfit for the

HOW HE WAS ARRESTED.
He related the manner of his arrest as follows :
ras after getting off the train at Carondelet and
bout one hundred rods from the train when I
was arrested. I was gingto the ferry to take the

fought twice before on Carroll Island; I am no

i never was arrested betore.

CONFIDENT.

drink when training; Lam astone cutter by trade;
Iden’t Lke St. Lonis; don’t like the climate as

tend to go back there as seon as I fight Allen; I have
lost a great opportunity to-day.

Gallagher was finally released about half past
3 o'clock, no charge having been made against him.

THE LAW AND THE CHIEF OF POLICE.

The intention of the chief of police in causing the
arrests of Allen and Gallagher was not so much to
have the pugilists punished as to break off the tight.
Under the existing laws it is a difficult thing to insti-
lute prosceutions with any success against prize
fighters. The law psssed in 1569 is as follows: It
| provides for the punishment of parties engaged in a

prize fight, but is inoperative to prevent the arrange-

ments ting made and the departure of a prizetight-
ing expedition, which in this city is the best way to
put an end to such affairs:

An act for tbe suppression of prize- fighting.

D act suppr o! ti

Section 1. That every person who be engiged
— it or combat with tists, commonly denomi-
pated p fighting, whether such fight or combat be
for money or = valuable thing, or merely to
test the skill or bodily powers of the pugilists or cOm-
batants, and every person who shallbe aiding, as-
sisting or abetting, by their presence or otherwise, in
any such fight or combat, shall be guilty of a high
misdemeanor, and on conviction thereof shall be pan-
ished by imprisonment at hard laber not exceeding
two years, or by fine net exceeding $1,000, or both.

Approved February 18, 169.

The law unser which the arrests were made yes-
terday reads as follows:

Chapter 205, section 6, General Statutes:

Srcrion 6. If two or more persons shall, in any pab-
lic place, voluntarily or by agreement, engage in any
tight, or use any blows or violence toward each other,
in avy angry or quarrelsome manner, or do each
other any willful mischief, or if any person shail
assault another and strike him, in any public place,
to the terror or disturbance of others, the persen or
perscns to offending sball be deemed guilty of an
afiray, and, on conviction, shall be punished by im-
prisopment in the county jail for a term not exceed-
ing three months, or by fine not exceeding one hun-
dred dollars, or by both such fine and imprisonment

Src. 7. If three or more persons shall assemble
together with the intent, or, being assembled, shall
agree mutually to assist one another to do any un-
lawful act, with force or violence, against the person
er property of another, or against the peace, or to
the terror of the people, such persons se assembling,
and each of them. shall be deemed guilty of an un-
lawful assembly, and, on conviction thereof, shall be
punished by imprisonment in the county jail for a
term not exceeding six months, or by tine not ex-
ceeding five hundred dotlars, or by both such fine and
impr onment.

AN ATIEMPT TO GET UP OTHER FIGHTS.

After the exit of Allen, and the premature depar-
ture of Barney Aaron, the crowd that remained on
board became tbhir+ty for a fight. In order to ailay
the exci ment an altempt was made to get = sev-
eral ninor matches, but allto no purpose. Feehan
would not fight Madden, stating as # reason that he
did noi have the requisite amount of the “necessary "
O'Connor, alias Red Hand Mike, would not fight

cressed on one of the ferry boatsto meet Barney
Asron on his arrival in _ Illinois. The
object of the are it is stated, was
to demand the three dollars which Henneberry
bad paid to witness the fight. The meeting, it was re-
ported, terminated satisfactorily to the donator, and
Herneberry had his money returned. Barney was in
town last night. and together with Roach, Looney
and others, enjoyed themselves after a general fash -

ion.
NO FIGHT.

Tom Allen, and also Tom Kelly, assert that the
fight will not take place, as there was a clause in the
agreement that in the case of magisterial interference
the stakes would not be forfeited. The money still
remains in the hands of the stakeholders. Tom Kel-
ly was accused of causing the arrest of Allen and
Gallagher, but denies all complicity in the matter.
He moreover generously states that he hopes every
man who paid will get his money back. The menof the
fancy necd aye mee among themselves about the
arrests. No nt caused them. The chief

keep on arresting prize-fighters bound for a fight,
whenever be gets a chance, and he will generally be

“MUCH ADO ABOUT NOTHING,” OR A LUDICROUS MIS-

At a smali town where I “put up” «a
few days ago, I witnessed an excitement

and people in groups of two or three walking around

quired the cause that had so snddenly broken the
quiet of the little village. “Have you not heard the
news?" said one ortwo. “No,” I replied, and in-
quired as to what it was. “Tom Allen, the prize
fighter, is in town, and you bet our sheriff will get
him.” It was also supposed that be was accom-
panied by Jem Mace, and the citizens had no idea of
allowing them to remain or depart in peace.
The sheriff with two or three as-

positive evidence of bis being in town. for he made
a call at the newspaper office and left his card with

plied that I was not aware “ of being
a = fugitive from justice. that the sheriff
ef this or any other county should be  re-
quired to be looking after me. Is pot that your card,

title: Chinning the Champion
text:
“CHINNING THE CHAMPION.

TOM ALLEN AT HOME-

The Knife and the
|

Hite Views of the Bill Abolishing Prize-
Fighting in the State—Is Spar-
ring Against the Law ?

—<———

Walking along the classic banks of the tunnel
on Washington avenue, yesterday, we came to
che well-known hostelry of Sir Thomas de Al-
len, whereot he calieth himself the champion of
the twenty-four-foot-roped pugilistic ring of
these United States.

We thought we would blow one of the cham-
pion’s cigars, and as we entered the conqueror
of the McCoole was coming forward with a gen-
tle swile rippling on his Spartacussian brow
and informing a gentieman in acap that if he
eawe round there fooling, and couldu’t be
quiet, that he’d serve him as he had MecCoole,
aud then pitch him ito the street to refresh
himself.

**How are you, Tom ?”

**How are you, sir? Extraordinary what a
fool a man will make of himself when he’s got it
up his nose.”

‘Have a good deal of annoyance of that
kind, we suppose {”

**f should say so. Because I’m Tom Allen
any fool thinks he has the right tocome in
aud shoot off Lis mouth at me.”

**What’s youropinion about the law agamst
prize-fighting !”

**I think it’s unnecessary and uncalled for in
this state.”

“Why ?”

**‘Why ? Because they never fought in the
state. They always went out of the state, either
into Tlinois or Louisiana. Ithink it a mistake
to putit down. It’s a@ manly exercise and a
interest to the people of the city to keepit up.
Why, there’s the members of the legislature
that passed the bili; don’t they carry a bloody
battery around with them? Isn’t that worse
than fightiug with the fist ?””

We suggested to the champion that fighting
didn’t seem to equalize matters so well as the
pistolor the knife, although, of course, we
Gidn’t advocate either. Between a
large man and au small man
equally scienced and with equal courage we
could’nt detect the equality between them.
Superior brute strength must decide in favor of
the large man.

**In England,” continued Allen, ‘‘tle; don’t
@ght with the knife, and thousands tight with
their tists every day. You don’t hear of mur-
ders there as you do here. Why! Because boys
are brought upto put up their hunds and defend
themselves, and they don’t murder one another
Because they quarrel.”

**Society is differently constituted here,
Tow, and men don’tend « fight with a knock-
down.”

**Yes, and look at the fellows that do draw
pistols. Why, I’ve scen ’em turn as pale as

|
1

ghosts when they doit. Do you call that pluck?
Brave men don’t turn pale when they’re going
into a fight.”

**Let us ask you what youthink of pugilism as
it exists now in this country?”

**As it stands now it’s quite time it was done
away with. There’s nothing in the manly art
asitisnow. No honest man has a chance; not
auless he’s associated with gamblers and pimps,
and thieves. Then he’s hunkydory aud can car-
ry the crowd with him. The bigger the loafer
the better man he is with them.”

**The opinion of men who are friendly toa fair
fight on its merits, Allen, is that you can not be
permitted to run aftight here. The McCoole
fight stands for nothing. He was a big traud as
@ fightist.”

**The man’s in trouble, I’ve got nothing to
Say against him. Asto this law, can’t men
QOght in Canada or in York stuie ? The law
don’t prevent that. One law can’t make laws
Tor another state can they!”

*‘Clearly not. But the law may read, and
certainly does, that no watch can be made
bere to fight elsewhere.”

**What does that watter? The match can be
be made in Canuda or New York or somewhere-
tise iu the East. In this bill I’m made to suf-
ter for others. Why, they put my name in It to
mark me, aud the Times had wn editorial about
me that I was # refugee.”

**What did they mean {”

**I don’t know. I’m no refugee; I can go
back whenever [ want to go. I’m a prize-
tghter, and they can’t say any more agin me
than that. No man can ever say I’ve done wrong
against him. I came here to live, and I’m
going to stay here. When men come here from
all parts to see me—some miners came here
to-day, two huudred miles out of their way, to
tee the tunnel and me. One of ’em madea
speech about me. He said he’d heard tell of
fom Allen, and he wanted to see him.”

“Quite complimentary. And, now, don’t
you think you've got a beiter thing here, at-
tending toyour business, than wearing your-
self out by training and then to get robbed out
the stakes ?””

‘*Iside with the legislature about this bill
against prize-tightine. If it’s got so that there
can’t be a fair tight, why, stopit. A man who
wants afair tight on its merits hasn’t got no
chauce. It’s not the fighting meu that’s to blame
and that break up the contidence. Its the gang
that follow the ring.”

**‘That [ believe tobe true. The fight with
McCoole proved it. So longas tbe gentlemen
were protected, and the roughs were limited to
numbers, all went smooth enough.”

**Tellme. They don’t mean to bar sparring,
do they ¢”

**f believe it is included in the prohibition of
public exhibitions.”

**Well, but it’s a play—the Tom and Jerry
seene—and [ don’t see why Deagle can’t engage
two sparrers just a3 well as he can two trapeze
men and clog and dance men ?”’

**There’s some logic in that.”

‘*Arthur Chambers and Billy Edwards are
cowing on here about the 7th of March and they
Want to give some exhibitions; in fact, Deagle
haus got them, or will have them for a week, ana
Idon’t believe Mudd’s bill can preventit. At
allevents, we mean to test it.”

**Billy Edwards has never been here ?”’

**No; he’s the little mau that fought Sam Coll-
yer aud Barney Aaron. As for Chambers—
you remember him seconding me—he’s a Man-
shester miu, and the best I ever saw of bis size.
He stands over ’em all!”

**Good night, Tom, I'll call in again.”

**Do, sir; glad to see the REPUBLICAN always.
You’ve always been fair and honest with me,
end that’s vil as J want from anybody.”

Tom Allen looks well, but 1s much fatted and
grosser, of course, than when iu a state of pre-
Paration for his recent fights. There
is also—as secn yesterday—a marked
improvement in his manner. There is a larger
and pleasing absence of sauguinary and profane
adjectives than ue was wont to interlard his
very Englisn style of conversation with a few
mouths ago. Tomisa perfect specimen of the
blunt, rough, hard-toiling, middle county
Englishman, and don’t pick his words either for
friend or foe, and would just as soon fight as
eat, and a little sooner ata pinch. He reminds
usstrougly of one of poor Leach’s admirable
Punch sketches of life in the black country (coal
counties) of England. A rough ‘‘navvy’’ is
leaning ugainst a post, and a girl—his wife—has
jJustcomeup. It is three o’clock in the after
noon, and he wants to be ganging homewards.
Bhe says:

**Bill, hast thee had thee foight, lad? If thee
hasn't, thee’d better get thee foight over, and
let us get aloug whoame.”

It being impossible to come to town without
baving a fight.

ANenshas never been known to **wesken,”

Tom Allen returned from Chicago this

THE PRIZE RING.

Jalks Sy the Bruisers of New York
and Elsewhere.
From the Chicago Times.]

New York, January 27.—The prize.
fight between Johnny Dwyer and Steve
Taylor, of Jersey City, for $590 and the

“championship of the heavy weights, is
still the subject of discussion among the
sporting circles of Brooklyn and this
city. It is certain that Taylor, on last
Monday, was no match for Dwyer, and
the latter’s chances of winning were
never in doubt after the second round.
It has often been proved, and is beyond

‘doubt, that aman must be well trained
and in condition, to successfully
participate in any competition, especial-
ly a contest like that on Monday. It
was the same as a prize-tight, ex-
cept that the principals had gloves on.
Both men knew they had to win by hard
blows and endurance. Taylor was not
in condition, and he wore shoes without
spikes aud was unable to keep his feet.
Taylor, mn arecent contest with Prof.
Win. Miller, broke the small bone of his
right arm, and the bone had not time to
knit firmly. Taylor knew this all along,

-- and stopped his friends from betting that
he would win. Taylor did go through a
course of what he called training—that
is, he reduced himself from 214 to 194
pounds, but he did not harden and
strengthen his muscles as he should have
doue. Therefore, with these obstacles to
overcome, he had no chance of standing
up against the sledge-hammer blows of

. such an experienced pugilist as Dwyer,
but with a strict course of training and
his arm as strong as it used to be, Taylor
could enter the arena against Dwyer,
and the contest would be an obstinate
and protracted struggle. Dwyer went
into the match with Taylor witha deter-
ination to do all he could to win. He
Jooked upon Taylor as a determined,
thorough boxer, and knew he had no
easy inatch without he trained and
worked hard. He trained into condi-
tion, and he was, on last Monday night,
capable of disputing the right of any-
body aspiriag for the championship.
lie wore spiked shoes, which gave hima
ereat advantage over Taylor, as the lat-
ter would slip at every blow he
would make. To-day, Joe Coburn,
in a dispute with Taylor, © said:
“You cannot fight; neither can Johnny
Dwyer. I can whip you, and I can whip
Dwyer. Neither he nor yeu are any
ood, and both of you have a heap to
learn if you ever fight in the ring.” Tay-
lor replied that he was ready to fight

\ dnybody, and he would declare himself
after he saw his friends. It is probable
the affair will end in a regular match for
$1,000 a side, being arranged between
the rivals, Joe Coburn, Johnny Dwyer
ant Steve Taylor, Brooklyn sporting
men are almost frantic over Dwyer’s
pericrinances, anil they oifer t> match
him, now that he has enteretl the arena,
to fight any man in the world for $1,000

g 2 side and upward. Joe Coburn can get
matched to iight anybody fer any amount
as soon as he is ready to fight.

George Rooke is qiuetly awaiting to

get ona raatch with some one, while
Tom Allen of St. Louis, who holds the
title of champion of America, is anxious
ly awaiting the arrival of Jem Mace, and
if that noted bruiser dues not soon come
over, Allen will be looking for a match
to sain fresh laurels. Johnny Dwyer
beat Tom Allen several years ago in a
contest in Central hall, Bowery. Allen
‘has not forgotten that event, and it
would just suit Allen to arrange a mateh
With the Brooklyn giant to try and rub
out that reverse. In the meantime,
Taylor, notat all satisfied with the result
on. Monday night, states that he is ready
to arrange a match against any man in
America bunt Tom Allen, to fight at
catch weight, according to the rules of
the London prize ring, for 31,000 a side,
the tight to take place within 500 miles
of New York next April. No doubt
either Jolinny Dwyer, Joe Colburn, or
George Rooke may accept the challenge,
From present indications, there prom-
ises to be a lively time in pugilistic cir-
cles.

A communication has been received
by The News from Boston, which reads
as follows:

“HakvVarnpD STREET, Bostox, Jan.
25.—Waving witne=sed the glove contest
between John Dwyer and Steve Taylor,
in your city, on Monday, oblige me by
publishing the following inthe spotting
eolumn of The Daily News: 1 will
match Prot. Tom Denny, of this city, to
a glove contest upon the same condi-
tions as the recent contest between Tay-
lor and Dwyer, except that the contest
is to jast one hour iustead of thirty mi-
nutes. The stakes are to be $250 or
2500 aside. The contest is to take

“place at this city or in New York in four
vor six weeks. A reply will be promptly
attended to. Acdress ‘Glovist,’ in care

title: Tom Allen’s Statement
text:
TOM ALLEN’S STATEMENT.

What he says of Donnelly, Coburn an?
Others—A Challenge to Cobura and
his Friends,

This morning Tom Allen the pugilist,
called at the DISPATCH office and asked that
he be set right as to the libelous reports
in circulation against him the past few
days to the _ effect that he was

going tojump the town and goto England.
Tom's statement is as follows: “After my
engagement at the Theatre Comique, I
made a similar engagement for one week

with the manager of the Adelphi Theater.
to go with Donnelly and give sparring exhi-
bitions. and I was prepared to fultill my
engagement until Tuesday morning
last, when I had trouble’ with
Donnelly. Donnelly, whose real name
is George Bruer, I took from the streets
some months since where he was getting
but $1 25 aday asa laborer, clothe 1 him and
puthim in training. <Aiter continuous lIa-
bor I made a clever boxer of him—provid-
ed him with money wh never he wante1 it,
lodged and boarded him and treated him as
a gentleman. On Tuesday morning he
came down stairs from over my late saloon
on Wash'ngton avenue. where he slept, and
got money from behind the bar and went to
breakfast. Returning he left a note for me
saying,

“I HAVE PLAYED IRISHMAN LONG ENOUGH.’

I asked him what he meant; he told me
he had something better in view. I asked
him if he was going to go back on his engage-
ment with me to goto Chicago after all I had
done for him, when he sneered at me and
I knocked him down, and he lay where he
tell and cried like a woman. He got up
when he found I was not going to tap him
vgain; went off and had my trunks attach-
ed for $125. This was done you see to get
my traps,so I could not fulfill my engage-
ment at Chicago. But after some trouble I
got everything fixed all right and will go to
Chicago, fill my engagement, and return
here on the 2sth.

How about going to England?

Well, thatis a bloody lie, for I hadno
more intention than yeu have of going to
the old country. Doyou think I would go
irom St. Louis, where I have lived seven
vears’ No; Il intendtolive in St. Louis.
That story was gotten up by Brurer alias
Donnelly and Billy Allen, of the St.
Louis Adelphi. You see Allen wanted
me to go to his theater and spar with Joe
Coburn, but I wouldn’t spar with

THAT DIRTY BLACKGUARD,

for when I was in New York he refused to
spar with me, and I couldn’t get a New
Yorker to ‘put up” befere me. When Billy
Allen found I wouldn’t have anything to do
with Coburn, he got around Burer alias
Donnelly, and prevailed upon him to break
with me. You see that’s what caused the
trouble, and Billy Allen has been keeping it
up as an advertisement for his place.

But Tom, acorrespondent in the Globe-
Democrat, this morning intimates that you
are skipping out to aveid meeting Coburn.
How’s that?

Why should I skip out to avoid Coburn?
Joe Coburn has no more intention of fizht-
ing me than I have of jumping off the Court
House. I have given Coburn every chance
a man could give but he won’t fight me, and
{ authorize the Dispatcn to state that while
[am gone to Chicago, I have made ar-
rangements with Fred Watkins, my backer,
of 720 Main street, to accept any challenge
Coburn or his frienas may offer for $500 a
side or more, and if they mean business.
the money will be up in two hours. I
wouldn’t want any better sport than to get
Joe. Coburn out of the bounds of the law in
the Indian Territory, ter instance, where a
“om 8 > fight a week without being mo-
ested.

There is a statement to the effect that the
constable closed you up?

Well that too,

IS A BLOODY LIE.

The lease on the place I had expired and as
they are going to tear down the old house,
and re-build of course I had to get out, but
I am looking for another place. My goods
were not sold as stated, but are stored at
1222 Collins street. This scoundrel Brurer
and my enemies got up these stories out of
-pite against me. They won't fight me and
take this means of doing me hurt.

Tom’s bartender, James Garvin, corrobo-
rated this statement, and said he never
heard the champion say he was going to
England. Tom expressed his thanks to the
reporter, and said any messages sent to the
DI:PATCH would be recognized by him.

title: Another Victory
text:
ANOTHER VICTORY.

|The Invincible Bauer Wins the Wrest-
ling Match with Schroeder.

| The Burly German Proves a Powerful
Man, But Lacks Skill.

The much talked, of wrestling match be-
tween Prof. Thiebaud Bauer, the champion
of America, and Herr Julius Schroeder, pro-
prietor of the saloon known as ‘ ‘Section 11°”
of this city, came off last night according to
announcement at the Temple, before a well-
filled house, Both men were in good condi-
tion, Bauer weighing 176 pounds, and
Schroeder 243; the former confident and the
latter hopeful.

At half-past eight o’clock Tom Allen made
his appearance on the stage, accompanied by
Arthur Chambers and Billy Edwards, the
light-weight champions, whom he introduced
to the audience. They arrived in the city
yesterday morning, and are billed for a ben-
efit at the Adelphi theatre on Thursday even-
ing next.

‘The pugilists then retired and the wrestlers
eame forward, Bauer first and Schroeder
next, accompanied by their umpires, Mr.
Frank Printz for Schroeder and
Billy Edwards for Bauer. They were
greeted with cheers. Tom Allenthen stated
that he had been chosen referee, and would
fill the position to the best of his ability. He
then called ‘*Time,’’ and the men advanced
towards each other and began the struggle.

The first bout, by agreement, was accord-
ing to the German style. which permits of no
back holds and no neck locks. This bout
lasted 14 minutes and was won by Bauer,
who showed throughout his thorough mastery
of his profession, taking matters as coolly
and as easily as his burly antagonist would
let him, and yet being always on the alert
whenever he saw an _ advantage to be
gained. Schroeder, after a few minutes work,
began to puff and blow, and the perspiration
rolled from his face. He found that he had
before him no plaything, and that, with all
his giant strength, he had to exert himself to
the utmost if he hoped to win. After
several ineffectual efforts he managed
to get his right arm round Bauer’s
waist, and then his left, when both
men struggled fiercely for a few _ mo-
ments -towards the right wings. Bauer
broke the grip, but was soon afterwards
seized in the same manner and forced to_ his
knees, when Schroeder secured the best hold
of the bout, grasping Bauer around
the waist sideways and lifting
him off the stage; but in doing so, the latter,
with a good deal of strategy and no less ac-
tivity. broke loose from him, amid the ap-
plause of the audience. Bauer then got a
waist grip on Schroeder, raised him from the
ground, and fcllowed up his advantage by
throwing him on his knees. It looked to the
audience as if he ought to have still wrestled
with him, but the rules of the German style
require that when one man is on his knees the
other shall allow him to arise. This Bauer
did. He then allowed Schroeder to get
a good shoulder grip, rested a
few seconds, and then, exerting
allhis strength, turned Schroeder over his
shoulder to the ground, where he threw his
weight on him and forced both of his shoul-
ders to touch the carpet. There was consid-
erable cheering at this display.

A fifteen minutes’ recess was then taken to
allow the men to cool off. Bauer stated toa
REPUBLICAN A ceil during the intermis-
sion that Schroeder was a much stronger man
than Heygster, but that strength alone could
not win in such an encounter.

The second bout, which was according to
Greco-Roman _ rules, lasted only = six
minutes, and was quite hotly contested.
Schroeder, acting under the advice of his
friends, who told him to work quickly and
force the fun, went at Bauer impetuously at
first: but the latter seemed to play with him,
and the audience, seeing this, enjoyed the
‘sport. Bauer permitted Schroeder to sieze
‘him almost any way he pleased, and just as
‘he was aboutto throw him, Bauer would
quickly force himself free. As this was too
‘monotonous, however, Bauer putin a little
work. He got a savage neck lock on Schroed-
er and squeezed his head under his left arm
until the latter groaned with pain, but could
not break the lock. With this hold Bauer
raised him in his arms and swung
shim around the stage, finally throwing him
from him. Schroeder seemed annoyed at
‘this and the laughter which the audience in-
duiged in, added to his discomfort. He
fought desperately for a <ood hold, but could
‘not obtain one. Suddenly Bauer terminated
‘the bout by raising Schroeder in his arms by
a waist grip from behind, throwing him on
the carpet and falling on his chest, so that
‘both shoulders touched. Time. six minutes
and a half.

This terminated the match in favor of
Bauer, who was called out twice and raptur-
ously applauded.

title: The Great Prize Fight
text:
THE GREAT PRIZE FIGHT.

Seven Rounds Fought with Allen
Ahead.

After Which the Kentucky Militia
Appear.

Ard Scatter the Crowd of Pugilisis and|
Spectators-

fhe Fight Renewed Again in|
Another Place.

Goss Winning on a Foul at the
Twenty-Third Round.

Details of the Fight by Rounds—Scenes
and Incidents—Record of the Men.

Arrest of Allen After the Fight in
Covington.

—_——_

[Special to the St. Louis Republican,]

Watton, Ky., Sept. 7.—The fight between
Tom Alien of St. Louis and Joe Goss of Lon-
don, announced for to-day, was besun this
morning about 7:35 at «a voint near
Walton, Ky., on the Louisville Short Line rail-
road, 18 miles from Cincinnati. Some six or
seven hundred persons were in attendance
incIuding the prominent fighting men and
roughs from all the large cities of the Union,
mixed with a sprinkling of sporting men,
afew merchants and professional men from
Cincinnati, St. Louis, Louisville and the |
West.

it was noticeable how !

FEW FRIENDS

Allen seemed to have—even those from St.
Louis appeared to be against him; and, in-
deed, the only men, with few exceptions, who
chose or dared to express opinions in his favor
were in great part those notin any way con-
nected with the ring or sporting life. Particu-
larly was this to be remarked among the
roughs from New York and the East. Allen’s
wordy contests with Coburn, Rooke, O’Bald-
Win and others have made him irreconcilable
enemies who are as dangerous as they are
noisy. aad

The English fighting men with few
exceptions are against him. A man
never went into a ring with more
enemies, and a man less game
than Allen would never have dared to do so.
His nonchalance isremarkable. It is almost
fatalism, and while there is very little doubt
that he is good enough to

BEAT TWO GOSSES,
In the same ring, it is more than doubtful if
he will be permitted by the New York school
of roughs to do so.

Despite this feeling a general under-current
of admiration of the man’s pluck is manifest-
ed. Very few expect Goss to win, but there is
& confidence that he will be able to makea
strong rough fight of it for an hour, trusting
to the chapter of accidents fora chance blow
like that which Gallacher gave
to Allen and defeated himor toafoul blow
andihe decision of the referee, or as last re-
source toa general break-up of the ring and
stealing the fight out of Allen’s hands in this
way.

This is not openly spoken of course, but it is
asclearly the determination of certain men
here that Allen

SHALL NOT WIN.
The fight as that the sun has risen ona des-
perate mob of high-toned roughs, eager for
blood. If all other ruses fail to stop the fight,
in the event of its going in favor of the St.
Louis man, acry of police or militia will be
raised, and then will come a stampede.

The ring is pitched ina smooth

PATCH OF CLOVER
And allis promising as could well befor a
fight or a fvot-race—on the outside. It would
be agood.place for a camp-meeting. Tuais
isn’t a camp-meeting by alarge majority. At
~ 2
THE MEN ENTERED THE RING.

The roar for Goss was like the going-off ofa
small park of artillery, as he shied his castor
inside the ropes. Allen also received a share
of applause, but there was comparatively lit-
tie heartinit. Both men smiled pleasantly
and retired to corners, where the process of
the toilet was commenced.

THE TOSS FOR CORNERS
Having been decided, the business of the
day was tairly in order. At
7:35 the men with their seconds
advanced to the centre ofthe ring. This part
of a fight is imposing, and hasin it a certain
air of.chivalry which, however, is dispelled
the next moment. The principals grasp hands,
and the four seconds shake hands across their
extended arms. The seconds then retire to
their respective corners and the men are left
standing facing each other eager for the fray.

APPEARANCE OF THE MEN.

Both men have paid fair attention to their
training—as Alien always does—but Goss looks
seedy and aged toa keen observer, notwith-
Standing all that has been done for him. The
marks of a rough life are visible on his battle
worn face, bat there is a cCare-devil force
about the man that inspires a confidence
in his backers. He is serious
and perhaps a little nervous, for it is his first
fight in America, and he has a desperate con-
tract before him. Allenisin fine form, clear
of skin and eyes, and like a rock on his finely
rounded legs, which are models for a sculp-
tor. Altogether the comparison isin favor of
Allen.

ROUND ONE.

The men, left to themselves, eye each other
eagerly and watchfuliy. The positions
of both men are good, that of Goss being per-
haps the more artistic of the two, in a pugil-
istic sense. He reminds some of the old ring
goers of Tom Sayersin position, but the com-
parison ends there. Both men sparred cau-
tiously and worked round for an opening.
Tiresome for the crowd. At last Allen led off
andclinched. They fell in Allen’s corner with
Goss on top. First blood ailowed for Allen.
Time seven minutes.

ROUND SECOND.

Both men came up quickly and smiling.
Goss evidently serious and Allen anxious to
get to work and bustle his man. Tom spars
quickly and cross counters on Goss’ lip slightly
in reply to one or two heaviiy on his ribs from
Goss’ left. Goss staggers and bleeds, and in
the wrestle fails under.

ROUND THIRD.

Close in-fighting, all in Allen’s favor, and
Goss under atthe finish. The Gossites roar-
ing.

= ROUND FOURTH.

Both men getto work at once. Exchanges
are fast and furious. Allen gets in a terrible
blow on Goss’ neck, which knocks him clean
off hislegs. Time three minutes. Good fight-
ing, but all in favor of the champion.

ROUND FIFTH.

The pace is telling on both. Sparring for
wind. Allen, as usual, leads off at Goss’
face, but fails short, andin return receives a
terrific blowinthe stomach, which ought to
have sickened him. Tom grins horribly and
looks wickedly green about the eyes. He
Stexdies himself for a moment and
then delivers his left heavily on
the body, and his right by a cross hit
on Goss’ damaged eye, which exhibits signs of
the early closing movement. Goss wont be
denied, bores his way in, gets in one ortwo
lightly on Allen’s body and then they get to
Sharp half-arm hitting, in which Allen has ali
the best of it. His blows have more steam in
them and the condition of the men is telling.
Goss goes down to avoid punishment. ©

ROUND SIXTH.

Both come up quickly and active. No posi-
tive damage done yet, but the fignt all for
Alen, barring a ioul which the crowd is eager-
ly looking for. Allen gets in viciously on
Goss’ head, which he repents, being countered
glightly on the cheek. Allen repeats, and
again sends in another hot one on the damaged
optic. A desperate rally and in-
fighting, and Goss is finally fought
down. This was the best round in the fight.
Nothing can save the fight to Goss except a
Stroke of lightning, the police or the roughs.

ROUND SEVENTH.

On time being called the men stood up in
their corners, but the Covington Light Guard
made their appearance at the ring Saye" and

the fight was eee. A hasty flight is in |
progress, and itis believed that the fight will |
be renewed as soon as a place of safety can be |
reached.

{Assoctated Press Report. ;
The Goss-Allen Prize Fight.

CINCINNATI, Sept. 7.—The point chosen for
the fight between Allen and Gos sa clover
fieid near Walton, Ky., on the Louisville Short
Line railroad, 18 miles froin Cincinnati. A
crowd of some 500 arein attendance. Goss
and Allen take their place sin the ring at seven |
o’clock; the fight begins at 7:35. |

Goss first steps to the middle of the ring.
Fikst Rounp.—Both men spar cautiously—
Goss falling into Allen's corner. The sparring |
| is rather tiresome for the crowd. Yirst blood |
for Allen and a clinch and a fall, Goss on top.

Time: 7 minutes.

SECOND ROUND.—Allen strikes Goss on the
| lips and slightly staggers him; Goss has given }
Allen some heavy body blows; Goss’ mouth
| bieeding; a fall for Allen. H
THizp Rotup.—Close fighting. Allen win-
ning.

At this point

THE MILITIA
Appeared, but fighting still goes on.
Capt. Frank Wood with the Covington
Light Guards reached a  poiat north
ot Walton at seven o'clock, having been car-
ried past the tighting-grounds by the con-
ductor. Capt. Wood stopped the train three
miles past the point, and the militia
marched back, arriving at eight
o'clock. W.G. Lobban, aid to the governor,
sent for Eph. Holland, and advised that the

fight immediately cease. Holland
Stated that he was a law-abid-
ing man opposed to blood

shed and accordingly stopped the fight atter
seven rounds had been fought. Holland de-
clares he will make the men fight out the fight
before they reach Cincinnati to-night.
Neither of the men are much punished.

FourtTuH RounD.—Excbange of fast and heavy
blows; Allen by a terrible blow on Goss’ neck
knocked hint dow. Time three minutes.

FirtH Rounp.—After considerable sparring
Allen struck out and feli short on Goss’ face;
| in return he received a blow
in the stomach. This did not
appear to worry Allen and he
returned heavily on Goss’ body, and gave him
afearfulone on his damaged eye. Goss re-
taliated, and after sharp half-arm fighting
Goss went down to avoid punishment.

SixTH Rocunp.—Both men promptly to the
seratch, Allen leading off getting in on Goss’
face. He repeated this, getting in another
blow on Goss’ dainaged right eye. Alien
finaily fights Goss down.

SEVENTH RouND.—When time was called the
| Coving gton Light Guards appeared and the
fight ceased.

Second Dispatch—The Fight Resumed.
CixcrynaTi, Sept. 7.-—After being dispersed
by the militia a second ring formed a short

distance below Walton, in Boone county. The
sheriff was present, but hadn’t a sufficient
posse to interfere.

EIGHTH Rounp.—Goss threw Allen, though
the former was severely punished.

NINTH RounD.—Goss forced the fighting. Al-

len finisied the round for himself with; heavy
blows on Goss’ face.

TENTH RoOUND.—Heavy blows exchanged;
Goss forced on the ropes; the fighters were
parted by seconds.

ELEVENTH RotunD.—Goss ieads the fighting;
hardest fighting in this round.

‘TWELFTH RotND.—Both Goss’ eyes badly
swollen; Allen knocks Goss down.

| THIRTEENTH RounbD.—Terrific blow on Goss’

| mouth. Goss on his knees.

| FOURTEENTH ROUND.—Goss threw Allen by a

clinch ; foul claimed but not allowed.

| FIFTEENTH RounD.—Heavy, close fighting;

both badly punished.

| SIXTEENTH RounpD.—In chasing Allen about
the ring Goss slips and falls.

SEVENTEENTH ROUND.—Goss knocked over
the ropes.

EIGHTEENTH ROUND.—Goss plants a stinger
on Allen’s body; close fighting: a foul claimed
by Goss but rot allowed.

NINETEENTH ROUND.—Goss slips and falls;
close fighting.

TWENTIETH RouND.—Both fall.

TWENTY-FizstT RouND.—In close fighting,
Goss falls andis struck by Allen while on his
knees. A foul claimed and allowed. Fight
decided in favor of Goss at 11:50 a. M.

Allen shows little or no injury aboutthe face.
Goss terribly beaten—almost blind. Time of
fight, 1 hour and 52 minutes.

Arrest of Tom Alien.

CINCINNATI, O., Sept. 7.—Two trains from
the fight to-day, arrived at Newport at 2:40,
were stopped by the authorities and Tom Allen
arrested.

The law on the subject in Kentncky pro-
vides:

For engaging in a prize fight the penalty is a
fine of $250 to $1,000 and imprisonment three
to twelve months. The seconds are liable to a
fine of $100 to $500 and imprisonment two to
six months. Any person present at the fight
or betting on the same is liable to a fine of $: 20
to $100. The person on wiiose land tne fight
is permitted to take place is liable to a fine of
$100 to $500. Any person training in the
state can be fined $20 for each day in which he
is so engaged.

If etther of the combatants is killed, or dies
from the effect of his injuries within three
months froin the time of the fight,the survivor
and the assistants of both parties are deemed
guilty of manslaughter, and the penaity is im-
prisonment in the. penitentiary for from two to
ten vears. Itismadethe duty of all judges,
justices, mayors, trustees of towns and other
conservators of the peace, all sheriffs, consta-
bles, marshals and police officers having rea-
son to suspect such fight, to suppress the same
and arrest all the parties engaged.

——
Going to tne Fight.
{From Yesterday's Cincinnati Commercial. ]

12:30 a. M.—It has been determined that
Sheriff Percival, accompanied by City Marshal
Bolan, Capt. Frank Wood and ten ot his com-
pany, shall go to Walton, on the Short line,
near which piaceit is supposed the fight is to
come off. An extra engine and car containing
the party will start from the depot at Newport t
in about anbour. Itis expected that detach-
ments of militia from other portions of the
state will rendezvous atthat point, who wiil
give their aid to the civil authorities in arrest-
ing the principals, seconds and abettors of the
fight.

Se: :45.—A dispatch just received from the

overnor orders the full company to leave

or Waiton on the first convenient train. Asit
is now discovered that an extra train is not to
be had, and no regular train leaves until six
o "clock, two hours behind the time appointed
for the excursion train to start, it seems prob-
aa that the fight will be over before the Coy-

on party can get to the spot.

70Sss and Alien slept in Cincinnati at the Gib-
son house last night, and were to
take the four o’clock train (the last
one) with their seconds, Tom Kelly and
Artitur Chambers for Allen and Barney Aaron
and John Dwyer for Goss. On this train were
to go the managers, the reporters and ail who
had purchased seven-dollar tickets.

DEPARTUEE OF THE FIRST TRAIN.

At an early hour this morning two trsins
were put into the Little Miami depot. One con-
sisted ot nine passenger cars and a caboose,
most of the coaches being short, bunty arranze-
ments, belonging to the Louisvilie ‘and Indi-
anapolis company, and tbe others venerable
affairs, with dingy paint and of a nondescript
character.

At 2 o'clock alarge and motley crowd had

thered into the depot, the large majority

eing young fellows belonging to the ‘*boys,
and not possessing tickets, but depending on
their chances of getting to the fight.

A littie after 2 o’clock an attempt was made
to ioad the train with ticket-holders. But as
soon as the first car was opened the roughs
crowded in and jammed it full. About fifty
climbed in at the windows after the car was
already overcrowded, and a large number
scrambled to the roof. It was then announced
that tickets would be collected after the train
had reached Newport; and the cars were
thrown open. Not ail were filed when, ata
quarter past 2,the train was puiled out. li wes
not known where it would = stop, but
knowing ones asserted that it
would not reach the place of the
fight, and that those init holding tickets, as
wellas those without, wouid ‘be fooled in
boarding it. Most of the ticket-holders quiet-
ly remained behind, seeming to understand
that the ,arst train went out to carry off the
**bums

There was no disturbance at the depot upto
the starting oi the first train, though many
had begun to pull freely on their whiskey
flasks, and were getting pretty drunk. A
strong force of police were in attenaance. The
officers. however, were ordered to keep back
out of the depot, and notto interfere with the
crowd except in case of a serious trouble.

Record of the Men.

The record of each of the principals in to-
day’s fight isa somewhat extended one, and,
in connection with the account of tue inter:
‘rupted battle oa above, may prove of in-
terest. The llowing ccendenused history of
the men was lately prepared by the Cincinnati

Enquirer:
TOM ALLEN
Comes from a fighting family and a fighting

‘ee ee en een
lidwn_Biaminehan. in merrv England. When!
a youth he learned the trade of gan-making.
During the Crimean wir he entered the
army, and it was Liss good luck in a
number of ‘‘turn-ups’’ that he had in
front of Sevastopol that convinced him that he
had the stuffin him out of which che umpions t
are made. On his return to England he tested
the matter with Jack White tor £5 a side. The
result was s factory to Alle n, so he next
tackled Mor Conner for £10 aside. He got
the best of Morris in twen ty-two rounds and
fifty minutes.

In September, 1861, he beat Jack Gould for
£15 a side in fifty-one rounds and
one hour and twenty-two minutes.
Hali of Portsmouth was his next
opponent. The match was for £25 a side, and
was won by the conquering Ailen in fifteen
rounds and forty-two minutes. Tom's next
| vis-a-vis in the ring was Goss’ old opponent,
2 Price. The fight was for £10 a side, and
: won by Price i “two rounds and
flity-five minute a. Sse next lowered
his colors to Alien for £25 a side im ten rounds
and twenty-two minutes
i Allen next met the Americ an darky Beb
i Smiths w ho was 2 thoroughbr he was a
} ‘*‘nagur. They fe a side, and the

battle was we zh one hunared and
eight rounds, cupying three hours and fifty-
seven minutes, at the end of which time Ailén
was defeated.

Jack Parkison and Tom next hed a ‘‘zo’’ at
each other for £25 a side. After fighting
eleven rounds in twenty minutes, Jack con-
cluded that he had had enough of Tom’s terri-!
ble ‘‘left,”’ and he gave in-

Allen now tried his old congueror Posh
Price, this time for £50a side, and after mill-
ing forty-five rounds in two hours and iive
minutes, Tom was proclaimed the victor.

George Lies, who fought O’Baldwin, the
Irish Giant, was Alien’s next customer. They
met for £100 aside, and after fifteen rounds
and fifty-two mintues had been consumed, Les
was deteated.

Joe Goss was Allen’s next competitor, with
result above stated. After fighting Go s, Allen,
in company with the celebrated feather-weight,
Pever Morris, came to this country, arriving
herein 1567. His first fight in America was
with Old Bill Davis for $1,000 aside. It oc-
eurred in January, 1869, and was won with
ease by Allen in forty rounds and 40 minutes.

Charley Gallagher of Cleveland was Allen’s
next opponent. They fought for $1,000
aside in 1569. Allen thought he
had a soft thing, and in ‘‘kidding’’ Gal-
lagher gave hiniself away, and Chariey
put him to sleep in two rounds and three min-
utes.

Mike McCoole and Tom next fought for$1,000
in June ot 1869. Ailen had the best of the
fight ali through, but the crowd cut the ring
to pieces and the fight was‘drawn after seven
rounds, in fourteen minutes, had been fought.
Tom's fourth fightin 1869 was wih Charley
Gallagher for $1,000 aside. This time he
turned the tables on Gallagher and whipped
him in seventeen rounds and  twen-
ty-two minutes. He next fought
Jem Mace near New Orleans
for $1,500 a side. Mace won in ten
rounds and forty-four minutes. Jim Gallagher
thought at this time that he was Tom’s mas-
ter, and he matched himself against him for |
$500 a side. He wasn’t common amusement |
to Alien, however, for he thumped him to a
stand-still without half trying in fiftecn
rounds and twenty-two minutes. In December
of 1870 Mike McCoole, who had again been
matched against Ajlen, forfeited $1,000 and
the match was off. A fresh match for $2,500 was
made between the parties in 1873, and in Sep-
tember of that yearthey met near St. Lonis
and fought eight rounds in nineteen minutes,
when Mike was beaten. Ben Hogan next had
thetemerity to meet Ailen for $1,000 aside,
butin three rounds, occupying but six min-
utes, he was done for. George Rooke of New-
ark, last year matched himseif to tight Tom for
21.500 aside, but at the last moment his heart
faiied him and he did not put in an appear-
ance. After considerable wrangling it was at
last agreed to draw the stakes.

JOE GOSS

Was bornin Northampton, in England, No-
vember 6, 1836. He is consequently in his
fortieth year, though, but fora slight baid-
ness, he would notlook his age by five years.
His father kept a large shoe-making estublish-
ment, and atthe proper age he learned cord-
waining. It was this experience, perhaps,
that hus enabled himto das¢ so weil in his
fights, and to welt the larger portion of his op-
ponents, causing them to peg out well basted.
In his youth he proved a tongh bit of stuff, as
many of his townsmen have cause to know,
and, early deveiopiug a decided predilection
for the ring, he found friends without trouble
to back him for £5 against George Ayers of
Long Berkley. He was then but nineteen
years of age, but he beat Ayers to a stand-stili
in one hour and thirty ininutes.

He next met Jem Rickerson for £10 a side.
Just when victory was within his grasp the
police interfered and stopped the mill. Goss
received £17 of the stake money the next day
to consent to make the match a draw.

Joe was next matched against Jack Rooke,
and fought him inthe same ring where Tom
Savers put the ‘‘comether’’ on poor
Bob Brettle. This battle was for
£25 a side, and was won cleverly by Joe.
Tom Price of Bilson now intimated that he
was ready to match Joe if the iatter would
stake £10 to £8. Joe had no objections. They
met, und Joe again walked off the victor.
Charis, Patchet of Wolverhampton thougit
lhe pocs_ssed the ability to take the shine out
of Sir Joseph, and a match for £20 was the
result. It didn’t take Joe long to
convince Charley that he was mis-
taken. Goss had now made quite a repu-
tation as a quick game fighter, and his
friends matched him against the celebrated
Bodger Crutchley for £100 aside. This was
a terrible battle, lasting over three hours, but
victory again perched on Goss’ brow. Joe
was soon thought good enough to fight any
mun in Englanu, and he next met Bill Riali, a
**big un,’’ who had fought for the champion-
ship. Thestakes were £50 a side, and Goss
won in two hours and fifty minutes. Riall was
not satisfied with his defeat,and a fresh maich
for £100 wastheresult. In the third round
Goss broke the ‘‘scuifie’’ bone of his right
shoulder. The police then interfered, and an
adjournment had to be made to unother coun-
ty. Here they fought for an hour and twenty
minntes, when they were again chased by the
peelers, who ran themintotheriver. They
got away, however, and met tne third time.
After fighting until dark came on the match
was made a draw.

Posh Price, one of the best men who ever
puiled off asbirt in Engiand, was Joe’s next
opponent. They tougut for "€2 5 aside, and,
though punished feariully, Joe’ s pluck and
Stamina pulled him through successfully. He
had now so much contidence in himseif that he
bantered the renowned Jem Mace for a
match, only asking that the Gypsy give him
the Odds of six to four on the stakes.
Mace,nothing loth, assented, and staked £600
to £400 and the chanipionship. Joe at last hud
gone too far, and ior the firsttime in his ca
reer he was compelled to cry peccari, and ac-
knowledge himself beat. Ike Baker at this
time thought that Joe’s star had bezan to de-
cline, and hetackled him for £100 a side.
Goss convinced him to iris heart’s content that
his cake was dough, and the doughty Baker
was glad to cry, ‘‘Hold, enough!’’

Goss now came to the conclusion
that if he pursued other tac-
tics with Mace than those he had
udopted before, he might be able to get the
best of him, and asecond match for £200a
side and the championship, was made be-
tween Mace and he. After fighting over an
hour this battle was declared adraw. Joe
naturally felt consideraly eluted over his last
match, and when bantered tomeet Macein a
sixteen-toot ring, he toolishly assented, and a
third match was ade between them for £106
aside. Joe had no opportunity to
**get away’’ from Mace’s attacks in these cir-
cumscribed limits. And the result was that he
was again licked.

His next match was for £100 a side, and his
opponent wasTorm Allen. Goss had been sent
to jail tor thirty days for seconding a manina
prize-tight, and only got out the day before he
met Alien. The fight was a good one, end
lasted until night came on, when a Craw
was made of it. Jose seemed to
like fighting the Alien tamily
so well that he next matched himseli with
Tom's brother Harry for £1°9 aside, but the
police apprehended Harry,and the figit never

TOM. ALLEN, THE PUGILIST.

The Champion of America in Lon-
don—His Forthcoming Mili with
Gilbert.

Tom. Allen, the pugilist, who resided in
St. Louis for over ten years, during which
time he gained the title of Champion of
America by his prowess in the squared cir-
cle, has recently turned up in London,
and, according to newspaper reports, is
full asready now to face an opponent as
he was some years siice when he met and
conquerred Davis, McCoo!e. Jones, Galla-
gherand other dougthy knights of the
ring. Though Allen left this region under
somewhat of a cioud, owing most-
ly to unfortunate business ven-
tures, he left behind him a host
of warm friends and ardent
admirers whose interest in the champion
and his movements is still deep-felt and
anxious. Knowing that everything ap-
pertaining to him would be of more than
ordinary interest, a DISPATCH reporter
has taken some psins to investigate the
facts in regard to the reported forthcom-
ing mill between Allen and Tompkins
Guibert, who is styled the champion of
England.

Tom Kelly being considered the most
orthodex authority in matters of this kind,
our reporter called upon him at his saison,
No. 11 North Sixth street, where he found
Kelly amusing himself with three fine bull
terrier dogs. which had just been received
from New York, and at once inquired
what he knew about Gilbert and nis rec-
ord in the ring.

Kelly—Well, I don’t believe that fellow
has any record. You see, it’s been some
time since I was overin the old country,
and that man wasn’t known in my time;
and though I keepa pretty good run of
such matters, I’ve never heard of Gilbert
putting up his hands before any manin a
regular fight. ;

tep.—‘**But, Tom, a New Yorker says
that—’’

Kelly—‘ ‘How much does it say Gilbert
weighs?”

Rep.— ‘Eleven sione, and he is over six
feet high.’’

Kelly—(After s moment’s reflection) —
Eleven stone, eh? Well, Tom Allen can
whip him. Butsee here, tnat match for
£50 a side is not for a regular out-and-out
fight in the ring.

Rep.—‘*No! What fs it then?’?’

Kelly—* Why, Tomkins Gilbert is said
to be the champion sparrer of Eagiand,
and this mutch is to be a sparring match.
Both men have their bhauds viachened, so
that every blow given leaves its mark, and
at the expiration of the agreed time, say
balf an hour, or an bour, the one wko has
delivered the most blows upon his adver-
sary is declared the winner.’’

Rep.—‘*Then it ain’t a fair stand up
take and give fight?’’

Kelly—*‘Ol, no. But it’s almost as hard
on the men, for it tests their skillandisa
severe strain upon their powers of endus
rance.’”?

Rer.—‘*Well, Tom, to change the
subject a little, thoseare mighty ferocious
looking dogs. Going to have some work
for the brutes, eh?’’

Kelly—‘*Ohb, no; nothing of that kind.
They belong tosome New York parties
who are goipg to open a school shortly
where terriers can be taught to catch rats.
Thst’s all. Good day. Come again and
see the pups.’’
