The publicis avery sensitive body, and
whatever maybe urged against any crooked
transactions and want of fair play in sporting
matters, itis generally known when “‘eyents”
are to be conduced on a square basis. It is
not easily fooled, and only a yery short period
of double dealing and bad faithis necessary
to break up patronage bestowed onsport of any
kind. That the fight at New Orleans yester-
day was conducted on honest principles
there is no reason to doubt, and however re-.
pulsiye the spectacle may be, of two men |
beating each other out of shape, there can be

no doubt but that the general interest taken
in the affuir has been of more than passing
mportance.

Yesterday Mr. Sullivan, of Boston, knocked
Mr. Ryan, of Troy, into a state of insensibil-
ity in twenty-six minutes, after one of the
‘“‘vamest’’ contests on record; thus carrying
outthe predictions of the Post-DispaTcH
sporting editor, that the battle would be
short and decisive. A retrospect is exceed-
ingly timely, and there are
some very interesting reminiscences
to be recd#iled regarding pugilism
in America. Perhapsring fighting had no
incentive inthe country until the National
American movemeut sprang up and then the
**native’’ element was in the field for ag-
gressive movement on every point. Cath-
olie churches were riddied, engines and hose
carts run bv Americans, such as the Vigi
lance and Shiffler in Philadelphia attacked
the Hibernia and Mavamensing companies,
mounted by fire‘nen of Celtic origin. Th:
streets of Baltimore ran with blood, the Dead
Rabbits and Bowerv Bovs fought for days
and nights in New York streets; Macready,
the English actor,was driven from the boards
of the Axtor Place Opera House, New York,
and the militia badto be called ovt to sup-
Press one of the bloodiest riots on re
cord. Bill Poole and his confreres were
held up as models for emulation for our
youth, and when the former was shot by
Lewis Baker—living seven days with a ball in
his brea~t—the Government took enough in-
terest ip the matter to senda man of-war af-
ter 'h+ aggressor and ca ture him in the An-
tipodes. Those were indeed stirring times:
dsys of a riotous family strife, which had no
Place in history, but in which no man had s

fe place outside of his own doors. **Pau-

esa? was murdered; John Morrissey, a

ighting stevedore, was held ona hot stove,
until pain made him exert himself and seat-
ter his dozen or s0 antagonists like as many
chips. i

Iu these mild, poetical and cheerful day-

such men as Frank Ambrose—known to his-.

tory as Yankee  Sullivan—and Tom

Hyer came to the front as national
aniagonists. Their friends made a mates
and on February 7, 1849, they fought for tne
large=t stake ever put up, $10,060. The bat-
tle was at Rock Pvint, Maryland, and Hver,
Who represented the American faction, was
the winner after a vicious battle. About thi
period Chris Lilly, Hammer Lane, Orville
Gardner, Lar Buieral and scores of others
were note! fortheir exploits in the ring and
battles were numerons and hard fought.
ANEW ERA
was thatin which Morrisey, who had long
ranked as a good fighter in any shape, rough
and tumble or according tothe ring rules,
and John C. Heenan tigured. Heenan wa-
known as the “‘Benicia B»y,”’ and despite hi-
Hibernian origin ranked as the repre-
sentative of the Americin element. Hi-
nick-name was derived from the place of his
birth, Benicia, Cal., where he worked
as a blacksmith and laid the foundation for
one of the gr ndest physiques ever given to
mortalman. A mateh was made beiween
them, the stakes being $5,000. The battle
took place at Long Poiut, Canada, on
October 20, 1858, and the excitement at the
time Was most intense and puisated through
the nation. Heenan was trained too fine, and
the reduction was such that a terrible boil
showed on his neck. He made no complain:
but fought with thenerve and strength tnat
only a patnral gladiator could bave exhibited
under the circumstances. He punished
Morrissey terribly, but the hard head of the
‘Hon. John” received the biows as though it
was made of rock. The fight was a short
one, and although Heenan was whipped
he showed such stuff that it was
virtually regarded as a victory for him Dur
ing their famous match Heenan had the good
services of Aaron Jones, an ex-Eavlish
ehampion. Morrissey retired after this, but
inthe subsequent battle between Heenan
and Sayers, fought at Farnborough, England,
in 1860, he was notable from the fact that he
sided with the Evglishman against his old
antagonist, which created avery bitter feel-
ing against him, and the impression of which
he was many vears erajicating in New York.
The Farnborough fizzie,in which Heenan
ewhipped Sayers almost toa standstill—at
which point a mop brokein and robbed the
American of his laurels, is a matter of pugi-
listic record. Heenan afterwards fought
Tom King, the Euglish champion afterwards,
but was defeated. by him. Hee-
nan was out of condition and
although he never ‘‘squealed’’ it was openly
asserted that he was given “painted’’ food
the morning of the fight. About this period
Edmund Price and “Australian” Kelly
fought, the former beating the latter and
breaking a couple of his ribs. Price is now
a rather prominent legal practitioner in
Washington courts. On dit one of the
greatest ovations ever offered to mortal man
Was given to Heenan in July, 1860, after his
return from England after his Savers fizht.
This was at Jones Wvods, New York, and
upon a raised stage be sparred with Prof.
Ottignon in presence of a multitude, so
large that only a simal! portion of it could
possilby see the exhibition. From morn al-
most to dewy eve, the street cars struggled
along under the burden of bumanity
which crowded not oniv the interiors
and platforms, but the very roofs, and scores
clung to the windows from the outside.
Henry Bergh’s siar had not then arisen.
Heenan died about eleven years ago, and, it
must be said, m: ch regretted by those who
knew him. He bad many manly qualities,
and was in private a quiet and inoffensive
man. At the time of his death he was a suc-
cessful gambler in New York, he and his old
adversary, Morrissey, having fallen into the
same line of business. Morrissey’s political
life was well known, and he was noted for
bis fidelity to his friends, to his faith in his
own word and for owning the most brilliant
mbling house ever instituted in America.
e Was a great poker player,and there is a

his brother Mickey being a splendid light-

Mace made a match with Goss and knocked

THERE WAS A RESPITE
in the interest taken in prize ring matters
for along time, the war being in progress.
Dunn and Davis, two fighters of the second
grade, hada meeting néar Port Jarvis, N. J.,
1865, Dunn winning. The influx of English
pugs to this country became something
notabie. Dooney Harris, a scienced fighter,

Peter Morris,English light weight champion,

one invoice and they were followed

made and failures to meet were demonstra-
tive of cowardice or ‘*‘skins.’? In 1868 there
was some little stir overa challenge from
John C. Heenan to fight McCoole; this was

Tom Allen whipped Bill Davis, Charlie Gal-

JEM MACE,
perhaps the greatest of fistic notabilities since
Heenan, had come to America. He was of
zipsy origin, a sparrer withont a rival and
who could use defense with the quickest hit-
ters without putting up his bands, His head
movements and ducking were something
which took the average boxers’ breath away,

this great battle Heenan

Chicago Tribune,

“How many belts have you won?”

“Five.”

“What do they represent?”

“One isthe champion belt of the world,

the twelve best men. All are silver belts,

“What else have you been presented

“Gold medals and cups too numerous

“How mush money have you won?”

“7 have taken more money from Bell's
saat any other man—forfeits and for bat-

“How much—$100,000.”

“T guess so; but I couldn't say.”

“How much have you got now?”

“That is asking a little too much.”

“Ts it all gone?”

“T never talk about my private affairs.”

“Do you think prize-tighting pays?”

“Tt has paid me. Ihave made two or
three fortunes. That is doing pretty
well.”

“How many men are engaged in the
business now?”

“T have no idea.”

“Hundreds?”

_ “Without doubt.”

“What are the qualifications for the
business?”

“A man must be strong-minded, very
confident, perfectly well and healthy,
take good care of himself, and let whisky
alone. And he must study the business
to be a tip-top one.”

TP as has a great doal to do with
it?”

“Science and health mixed. I am 52,

as strong as a lion, and healthy.”
“Were you ever seriously injured?”
- “Oh, Thad my jaw broken once, and
my nose two or three times,”

“Who do you think is the best man in
the world to-day?”

“Tt is hard to say, but I guess Sullivan
is thechampion. He is the best onenow,
according to what T hear,”

“Does your heart ever trouble you?”

“Tt runs like a clock.”

“But isn’t heart disease the curse of a
great many prize fighters?”

“Yes, it kills four-fifths of them. It
killed Tom Sayers. It killed Tom Hyer.
It killed Heenan, but they said it was
his lungs, and it killed John Morrissey.
‘The heavy pounding over the heart did
the work for lots of them. I could name
yon. Bie fifty fighers who have died of heart

“Do you drink much now?”

“Not much. Mostly ale, There is no
more pure claret, leastways in this coun-
try. Beer is poisoned. Whisky is not
like it used to be. It gives a fellow the
shakes.”

“Will you ever fight again?”

“No, never. Iam too old. A man
should never strike a blow after forty, I
am fifty-two.

title: The Shooting of Frank Rush at Allen’s Saloon
text:
STILL A MYSTERY.

The Shooting of Frank Rush at

Alien’s Saloon.
oe

A Theory That the Stranger Fired the Shot
in Revenge for Previous Rough Handling
—Rush Not soc Dangerously Injured as Was
First Supposed.

—

The police of Central District have another mys-
terious shooting case on hand. At 1 o'clock this
morning Frank Rush was shot in front of Tom
Allen’s saloon at 621 Market street by an unknown
man, who made his escape after a very deter-
mined attempt to murder his man. The statements

of the various parties failed to agree in important

details, which are not matters of hurried im-

pression but questions of fact concerning which

there is no reason for irreconcilable stories.

Free and easy concerts are given — at Allen's

piace. Each persen in attendance is called upon to

add to the entertainment, which is filled out py
regulars when the time tags. Among_ those
attaches of the place 1s Frank Rush, a coal miner,
who lodges over the saloon. Recently, according
to the proprietor’s statement, Rush has been labor-
ing about the city, spending his evenings atthe
saloon. Last night the crowd had dwindled down,
; When a stranger, who is described as5 feet 10
inches high, dark complexion, slim built, smooth
| face, wearing a long, dirty grey overcoat,
low uarter shoes and about 25 years old,
entered the place. The statements of the subse-
quent oceurrence, which may possibly result in a
murder, are as follows: Tum Allen, the proprie-
tor, said: “I was playing cards in the concert-
room when this fellow came in. He said he was
here from Chicago on a spree and asked for a wom-
an on Highth street. He was so drunk he couldn't
light his cigar and Rush hit him a tip. He staggered
out after falling against the Erg
tition and then he fell ainst the window.

Christ Hoff, the bartender, told Rush to go out and

Seethat the fellow didn’t tumble in through the

window. It wasn’t haif a minute before we neard

the shots as fast as a man could fire a gun, When
we got outside the man was gone.

Rush's first statement was as follows: “I gave
him a light and he staggered out against
the door. iwent out after him to brace him up.
He feil against the window. I grabbed him by the
shoulder and said: ‘Loox out, old man, you'll break
the window.’ He said: ‘Let go, d—n you,’ and
puiled out a revolver and began shooting. I said:
‘Don’t shoot, I won’t hurt you,’ and he said: ‘I

} guess you won't.’

Those who saw the man run dway say he was not
drunk but ran rapidly. At the saloon even all
| parties admit that possibly the man thought he was
| being robbed, a theory sneraliy shared by the
| officers. Rush had one ll extracted from his
| shoulder. The seconu is lodged in the chest. Two

of tue shots evideatly missed the mark.

Frank Rush, the wounded man, is now resting
easy at his room over Allen's saioon. He denies
that he knew the man, but on reconsidering the
shooting, he said that

IT SEEMED LESS MYSTERIOUS

than it did last night, as he did not believe the man

was really as drunk as he appeared to be.

A crowd including Tom Allen, a young

fellow named Spelker and the bartender assembled

around Rush’s bed this morning and on an inter-
change of opinion they came to the conclusion that
the shooting was premeditated. On entering the
saloon last night the man said he was from Chicago
and had come to this city to en-
joy a spree. He was then. apparentiy
drunk, but a few minutes later sharpened a lead
pencil, putting a fine point on without once break-
ing it. This was overlooked at the time, but, in the
light of the new tueory, it istaken as a strong evi-
dence that the man was dissembling. He then walked
back to the rear of the concert rgom, in which Alien
and a young man were playing “‘seven up.” On
his return he bought a cigar, which he put in his
pocket, relighting a stump which he had in his
mouth. He staggered against Rush and apparently
ouly gained the door by chance. All are ag

that a very short time elapsed between the exit of

Rush, who went to see that the window was not

broken, and the shots. The manner in which he

made his escape confirms the theory that he was
not as drunk as he appeared to be

The statement made by one of the habitues of the
Champion's Rest was that the stranger resembled a
man who was roughly handied and ejected
from the place some time ago.

THE BARTENDER
was of the impression that he had seen the man be-
fore in this city. The story of the previous trouble
could not be traced, but seemsa very reasonabie
explanation of the shooting. Rush admits that he
took hold of the man, anda it is possible
that the revengeful stranger also belie ved
that he was being assaulted and robbed.

Rush’s wound in the chest 1s not as serious as was

supposed. Dr. Nidelet, who madea casual exam-

ination at noon to-day, said he a think any of
the vitals had been struck by the bafl.

Joe Goss’ American Career.

Joe Goss had considerable history in England,
but to readers on this side of the creek his Amer-
ican experience is of chief interest. He had a
world-wide redutation asa fighter when he came
here, arriving at Boston, Mass., in company with
Mace, April 15, 1576. One of the objects of Goss in
coming to America was to make another match
with Tom Allen, who had gained fame and made
money during his sojourn in the States, and was
generally regarded as the rightful possessor of the
championship title. Joe issued a challenge to Tom
to contend for the honors of the position and a
stake of $2.500 a side, and, as Allen was perfectly
willing toagain face him, he promptly accepted
and a match was speedily made. They fought
September 7, 1876, on Kentucky soil, the ring being
first pitched in Kenton County, and subsequentiy,
owing to magisterial interference, it was erected in
Boone County. They fought twenty-one rounds in

all. in forty-eignt minutes, when a decision was
given in Goss’ favor. on account of a foul. Ailen
wasin much the better coadition of the two, Joe
being trained too fine and going = some-
what stale; but he was as plucky
as ever, and took h:s punishment like one of the
zood old stock. Indictments were fonnd by the
Grand Jury of Kenton County against the princi-
pals. seconds and other prominent persons, bui Joe
was the only victim, Allen jumping his bail, $3,090,
and cros“ing into Canada, whence he proceeded by
steamerto England. Goss was arrested in New
York City, March 7, 1877, upon a requisition
from the Governor of Kentucky, charging
him with violating the State law. He was
taken to Burlington, Ky., tried, convicted,
and, on March 168, was sentenced to sx
months’ imprisonment® and to pay a. fine
of $250. He was committed to jail,
from which he was released July 27 upon paying a
portion of the fine imposed, the payment of the re-
mainder being guaranteed by friends. Shortly
after his release he came to ew York, where he
for some years resided. After Johnny Dwyer re-
tired from the P. R., leaving the championship
open, Paddy Ryan issued achallenge to fight any
one for the title, which was accepted by Goss, and
a match was made for $1,000 asideand the cham-
pionship. After one postponement and two altera-
tions in the place of fighting they met at Collier
Station, W. Va., June 1, 1850. when Goss proved
himself the more scientific po = sil by far, but he
had grown slow, and ne was ultimately compelled
to succumb to & younger man by inanv years.
eichty—seven rounds Leing fought in lh. 28m. This
closed his career as a principal in ring events. it
Was at his benefil in Boston, previously to the fizht,
that he first met John L. Sullivan, aad it was from
the showing tbe iatter made against Joe that his
name first came to be talked about outside of
Boston. Sullivan and Goss were always fast
friends, the veteran’s admiration for the
young phenomenon being unbounded. He was
one of Sully’s seconds against Ryan at Mississippi
City. and was behind hiimin several of his impor-
tant giove contests. Forsome years prior to his
demise Goss was wvroprietor of the sporting house
where he died. and he dida prosperous business,
but Was too open-banded apd sociably inclined to
accuimulate money.

title: What becomes of pugilists who have passed their prime
text:
STALWART, BUT STALE.

(acne eset in i iS eS sh ses st eS NS TS SL ST SS

What Becomes of Pugilists ‘Who Have
Passed Their Prime.

Saloon-Keeping a Business They
Naturally Fall Into—Local Resorts
Presided Over by Ex-Champions—An
English Free-and Easy—Fun in the
Twelve-Foot Ring.

In the life of all athletes, whether of the ring, the
cinder-path, the oaror other department of sport,
there comes a time when the limit of exertion and
endurance has been passed, and the necessity of
earning a living insome new way becomes a matter
of necessity. Looking at a pugilist, in those days
when he really used to fight, as he came up smiling
in the thirtieth round, after an hour or two of hard
fighting, and ready for an indefinite continuance of
the supplying and receiving of punishment, one
would almost think that so little and powerfula
piece of physical machinery could never wear out;
but the taps of time, day after day, tell upon prize—
fighters as well as the less generously endowed
individual, and an invincible tendency to embon-
point, a dullness of the vision and a stiffness of the
joints are the warnings which nature supplies him

to abandon asphere of usefulness for which he is
no ionger fitted. Of course these warnings are
generally disregarded. It is as difficult to persuade
& pugilist that he has become “stale” as it is to
convince a veteran prima donna that her voice is
losing its charm, and it is not generally until he
has been made a spectacle of by soms coming
champion that he resigns himself to fate and retires
to spend his days as the presiding genius
ofa piace of public entertainment. The public
*ouse, or, as it is generally abbreviated, the pub’, is
the inevitable final refuze of the English pug, and
itis not surprising thatim this country the expo-
nents of the manly art should follow their exampie
and become saloonkeepers. In St. Louis there are
two such establishments run by mea who in their
younger days were admirable examples of the race
who fought one another with bare knuckles and to
the finish, and to whom the kid glove and abbrevi-
ated exhibitions of modern days are subjects of
more or less openly expressed contempt. One of
these is presided over by Tom Allen, a representa-
tive of the English school of pugilism,who came over
here years ago, fought his way to pre-eminent
Cis-Atiantic fame, and finally settled down in St.
Louis as the proprietor of a ‘“‘free and easy.” pat-
terned after those in voguein England, To this
piace the Post-DispatcH speciai artist paid a visit
yesterday evening. Passing through the busy bar
he found himself in a hall where at a dozen circular
tables sat a gathering of the place’s patrons,
among whom,alon= thesaw-dusted floor, passed the
waiters, very actively engaged. At the eastern
end of the hall was a platform containing a piano,
and immediately bvelow was a table at
whose head sat a large man, of middle age,
whose big, good-natured face beamed with jollity
as he answered the questions which were fired at
him by surrounding admirers. There were about
a dozen in number, and they ranged from beardless
youth to venerable grandsire. The large man evi-
dentiy found it warm work, for he was in his short
sleeves and his ponderous right hand manipulated
afan with energy. His voice was loud and deep,
and his careless disregard of the letter H revealed
the fact that he was an Englishman. Presently he
ealied a haltin the conversation, rapped on the
table with a gavel, and announced asong, thereby
revealing the fact that he was the proprietor.

THR REDOUBTABLE TOM ALLEN.

During the singing, which was by no means as
bad as might be expected, perfect silence prevailed
throughout the company, but directly it was over,
conversation broke loose. and the ex-pugilist was
once more made the target of a severe examina-
tion. His most persistent questioner was a very
old man, whose appearance was rendered quite
distinguished by a somewhat bloody handkerchief
tied round his head, giving the impression that he
had recently made a plucky but unfortunate vent-
urein the pugilistic line, on his own account. He
had been drinking and had entered upon the gar-
rulous stage of intoxication and was, consequently,
a trifie tiresome. Unlike the rest of tke company,
who discussed different heroes of the past in turn,
he was determined to convert the proprietor
and the others to his belief that, present company
excepted, there kad never been a prize-fighter like
Tom Paddock, At last the more modern Tom gave
him a conversational righthander which ‘sent him
to sleep” for the rest of the evening.

“Shay, Tom, ole fler,” he asked for the twen—
tieth time, “now, shay, wash ever a man could
Gown Tom Paddock?”

“Yes, sir, and there’s a man can down John Sulli-
van, or you or any of them.”

“Where’sh the man, Tom? Whash his name?” the
old man asked eagerly.

“There he isin your tumbler, and his name’s John
Barleycorn,”’ was the reply, which was greeted with
such a roar of laughter that the venerable individ-
ual tossed off his whisky to conceal his confusion
and lapsed into a condition of listening silence.

The strange feature of the gatherings at Tom
Allen's is their remarkable decorum. Presided over
by a pugilist and surrounded by admirers of the
fistic art, their proceedings are marked Dy a quiet
which would do credit to a much more respectable
meeting. There is a flavor of sentimentality in the
musical part of the entertainment, too, which is
surprising.

QUITE AT HOME.

The place presided over by Tom Kelly is of a
different type from the one previously visited. Ic
is more American in its features, the principal one
of which is a bar, which, Saturday night was pre-
sided over by the veteran himself, a man of about
45 years of age, upon whose vigorous frame the
hand of time has laid but light touch as yet, though
still serious enough to prevent him from entering
the ranks with the new race of gladiators. While
the artist was gazing upon the stirring scene, the
crowd beganto repair to an adjoining room and,
following, he found himseif in the place where
votaries of the art of slugging can indulge their
appetite within the restrictions placed by
thelaw. Inthe middie of the room was a space
twelve feet square, one of its sides being the wll
separating the apartment from the bar-room, while
the other three were enclosed with stakes and
Pha 0 after the manner in voguein regular prize-
fights. Uponthe wall were a set of well-worn
boxing gloves which a couple of stout fellows who
had entered the enclosure proceeded to put on,
while the crowd ranged themselves upon the rising
platforms on either side.

TOM KELLY.

although still im sunny middle age,is a grand-
father. His sons have inherited the paternal skill
of offense and defense, and, though they lack the
weight of body necessary to carry them tothe
front of the profession, it is comforting to know
that the third generation, thus far, has developed
remarkable gifts of bone and muscle which, it is
hoped, may before many years transfer the cham-
pionship from East to West.

Tom Allen is an_ ineorrigivle bachelor.
There have been, from time to. time,
hints that he was going to enter
the matrimonial ranks and transfer his pith
and pluck through a race of American prize fight-
ers, but the event has failed of accomplishment.
Tom remains invincible in love asin war, and will
so remain unless thereis some truth in the story
that a certain pretty widow—but, a halt had better
be called, as although past his ring glories. the pug-
ilist is still an ugly customer, and, weighing some-
where in the neighborhood of fifteen stone, is by no
means the person with whomto conduct an ani-
mated personal controversy.

title: Kelly’s Courage
text:
| KELLY’S COURAGE.

/| HE STOOD UP FOUR ROUNDS AGAINST
| JACK BURKE,

But Got Knocked Down Nineteen Times and
Fell Twice—“The Irish Lad” Fails to Get in
His Great Right-Hander and Ed Gets His
8100—A Decision Withdrawn—Much Blood
and More Words—Particulars of the Contest
at the Casino Last Night.

The much talked of contest between Jack
Burke, the champion of England, and Ed
' Kelly of local fame, took place last night at the
, Casino Theater in the presence of one of the
' largest audiences the house ever held. Every
, local sport, prominent and obscure, was on
| hand and the even was distinguished by the
| presence of one or two city officials and a city
Councilman. The regular programme of the

evening was gone through, and
at 9:45 the stage was prepared for
| the pugilists. After some discussion

| Mr. Dick Roche was fixed uponas referee.

| Mr. Al. Spink was chosen time-kceper. Pat
| Kien and Oscar Floto seconded Burke, and
! Tom Kelly and Tom Allen acted as seconds for
i Keliy. The final upshot of the affair was the
| decision by Mr. Roche that Burke had failed to
| knock out Kelly in four rounds, such being the
| proposition, and consequently, that he must
| forfeit the $100 he had staked on his ability to
| doit. Burke will pay the money to-day.
It was past 10 o’clock when the principals
| stepped upon the stage and shook hands be-
fore starting in to work on the _ first
round. They were greeted enthusiastically.
The men then went at each other, sparred tor
afew moments and Burke finding an opening
lanted a terrible blow on Kelly's neck which
anded him on his back. He wasup again but
was downed a second time by Burke's left, the
round finishing with a fall-down on the part of
Kelly. The second round saw the St, Louis
boy hammered about generally, the English
Champion downing him three times in rapid
succession.In the third round Kelly came to the
scratch still plucky, but a littlefrayed at the
edges. In_this round Burke brought the
blood from Kelly’s nose and mouth with some
heavy right-handers, laying him atevery blow.
He was knocken down twice and fell once
without being touched.

BURKE CLAIMED A FOUL
and the referee warned Kelly that if this oc-
curred the second time he would declare for
Burke. In the fourth round Kelly was still in
the ring though ready to fail from the mere
wind of Burke’s fist. In this round Burke
hugged him to preyenthim falling. Kelly was
badly battered and fell from the slightest blow
from Burke and took whatever advantuge he
could of the ten seconds allowed him to re-

inain on the ground when he fell. These tac-
tics rattled Burke considerably and when time
was up he stepped to the front and said:

‘*Gentlemen, how can I knock aman out when
he is on the ground all the time? Our agree-
ment was to fight with two-ounce gloves, while
the fight has been with four-ounce gloves. I
can’t knock a man out with pillows.’’

At this juncture Mr. Roche approached the
footlights and declared the tight a draw.
Some hot words were had all
around and the curtain dropped,
while the crowd dispersed with
expressions of disgust atthe evening’s work.
After the curtain had fallen Mr. Roche’s atten-
tion was called to the fact that his decision
was erroneous, as a draw could not be decided
in the premises. Burke had either failed to
Enock out Kelly or he had not; therefore,
there could have been no draw. On this ex-
planation Mr. Roche withdrew his former de-
cision and merely announced, privately, the
fact that Burke had failed to knock out Kelly
in four rounds.

‘*That whole business last night was ‘Tug’
Wilson and Sullivan over again,’’ said Oscar
Floto, Burke’s manager, this morning,
to a PostT-DISPATCH reporter at the
Laclede Hotel. **T could stay with
Burke four rounds myself like maak did.
The first time he went down and stayed his ten
seconds out, I knew the whole thing was fixed
andI said to myself that if Jack didn't get
his right hand in then on Kelly's
neck, the thing could go on all
night. That's what we wanted, and
if Jack ever got that right-hander of his in,
Kelly would have been knocked cold. How
could he do it though when Kelly kept run-
ning around as though he was ina walking
match instead of a fist match. Burke’s opinion
ofthe thing was expressed in a telegram he
sent to Davies last night, in which he merel
said: ‘it was Tug Wilson and Sullivan.
Pshaw; Kelly ought to be able to stand up
nineteen rounds hke he did last night without
phasing him.’’

KELLY’S FRIENDS
feel generally jubilant over what they claima
victory. Tom took his son home and fixed
him up in good condition. Beyond a scratch
on his arm, which he received in a fall against
the flies, and a little blood from his nose, Ed is
all right.

‘*There was nofnecessity fora decision’‘at all’’
said Tom to-day. ‘‘lt wasn’t a fight at all.
The understanding was that Ed was to stand
up four rounds, and he did it; that settled it.’’

The contest was according to Marquis of
Queensberry rules. During the four rounds
which were fought Kelly was knocked down
nineteen distinct times and fell down twice.
Calculating on the ten seconds given to re-
main down, and he stayed it out every time,
this would give him 210 seconds rest
on the floor, or a little over one
full round. The on the whole was
a hae 4 funny affair. Young Kelly
was backed up by his father and Tom Allen,
who did everything to encourage him and push
him to the front, and the yells of ‘‘Kellv!"’
**Kelly!’’” ‘‘Give it to him, Ed!’’
and a score of such mmarks of
approbation from the audience man-
aged to hold Ed up considerably. After the
contest was over, Burke claimed that the
agreement was to fight with two-ounce gloves,
The fact of the matter was, that there was a
split on the gloves, Burke insisting on usin
two-ounce and Kell on tour an
three-quarter-ounce gloves. A compro-
mise was then effected on four-ounce
weapons, it being clearly understood that soft
and not hard gloves were to be used. Many in
the audience held rather strong opinions as to
the affair, one gentleman, won versed in ring
rules, holding that the decision should have
been rendered in Burke’s favor because of the
foul in Kelly’s falling without being touched,
the Queensberry rule on this point y Bae nee that
a foul loses the fight. 1t wast ought, further,
that Mr. Roche erredin ‘*warning’’ Mr. Kelly
as the simple fact that he had fouled gave the
fight to his opponent.

- soe JACK BURKE
as no particular regret that youn Kell
stayed with him the four rounds, beyond what
little irritation he might naturally feel. The
fact will not derogate, in the slightest, from
his reputation asa pugilist as it was altogether
a negative contest. Had Kelly stood up to the
scratch and endeavored to lave used his ag-
gressive and defensive tactics at the same
time, which reaily constitutes the art of
poeee. Burke would have Paralyzed him as
ne did Cleary in Chicago. One good thing,
at all , events, will come out of it and that to
Kelly’s benefit. He learned a lesson last
night which he will never forget and which
taught him more than he ever knew before.
Athis next encounter he will have more con-
fidence and pluck.

title: Mike McCoole
text:
MIKE M’COOLE.

INTERESTING REMINISCENCES OF THE RE-
CENTLY DECEASED PRIZE-FIGHTER.

The Brutal Scene Which Followed His Defeat
by Joe Coburn—Red Leary as His Friend—
Mike’s Later Opinion of Thumpers—Sport-
ing Gossip—Macen’s Melange.

Special Correspondence of the Post-DISPATCH. |
PHILADELPHIA, October 22.—The death of
Mike McCool caused hardly a ripple of sur--
prise in sporting circles, though there was a
time when it would have been an event of
considerable note. He had been so long in re-
tirement from the ring and lived so humble
and obscure a life that many thought nim dead
for years. The younger generation of fight-
ers and sporting men only knew of himina
Vague sort of way as a big, strong slugger
who had once been a sort of somebody
in the fistic ranks. I knew him
well, and saw him fight Bill Blake,
the Western ‘‘Dublin Tricks,’’ Joe Coburn,
Aaron Jones and Tom Allen. He was aslug-
zer, pure and simple, and his knowledge of
the manly art was but rudimentary. He was
as game asa pebbie, though he had a way of
flinching when he was hit hard that would lead
one to think otherwise. Dublin Tricks would
have whipped him with ease but for the crowd
present. It was largely composed of the deck
hands and roustabouts, friends of McCool,
and they made no bones oftheir intent to kill
Blake ifhe won. Small wonder that he lost,

as he did, purposely.
x*6 .

That Mike was a brave and thoroughly cour-
ageous man those who knew him best were
the quickest to attest. Uncle Dave Bidwell of
New Orleans toid methat the morning he wis
to fight Tom Jennings he had some difficulty
with his backers, and they refused to get him
a boatto carry him to the fighting ground,
which was on the west side oftheriver. This
was afier Jennings and his party had left the
city. Nothing daunted Mike set out solitary
and alone, with his fighting togs tied ina
handkerchief and slung over his shoulders and
walked up the levee to a point oppo-

site where the ring was pitched. His calls at-
tracted the attention of the crowd. Jennings’
boxt went over and ferried him across the
rive ‘*T haven't airiend with me,’’ said he,
**Lucif anyone will second me I’m ready to
fight.’’ Two men volunteered to handle him.
He went into the ring and he had no diflicuity
in whipping Jennings, who was a much over-
rated man. Jenniags had taiked freely about
fighting Heenan, but when the Benecia Boy
reached New Orleans he wouid not putup
either to fight him or Ned Price, who was then
in his retinue. There was talk of matching
him against Charley Perkins of Rochester, but
it came to naught.

a > .*

Mike’s fight with Joe Coburn showed how
superior skill and pluck were, when backed
with a fair degree of strengtb, to mere pluck
and strength alone. Yrom first tolast McCoole
never had the ghost*of a chance against his
wily opponent, Who gave him a terrible
whipping. Afverthe fignt some of the gang
wanted to abuse the poor beaten man, but
**Red’’ Leary took his part and would not per-
mitthem to touch him. Mike lay groaning
and moaning with pain and refused to
be dressed. ‘*Get up,’’ said Australian
Kelly, his second, trying to frighten him into
activity; ‘‘the police are coming.’’ ‘‘I don’t
care,’’ was Mike’s piteous reply, ‘‘I can
neither sit, stand nor walk. Let me lie here
and die.’’ He didn’t die, but got well, and
was afterwards so sure that he could whip his
conqueror that he madea fresh match to fight
him. This came to nothing, owing to Coburn
having been amicably arrested by a United
States Treasury detective.

*
* *

Previous to this Mike had met and defeated
old Aaron Jones. The great opponent of Tom
Sayers was but a ghost of his former self when
he met McCoole, and only once inthe battle

r did he fight with anything like his old time
“erra. That was about the middle of the con-
‘test when he fet go suddenly with his left and
landed on McCoole’s right eyebrow, cutting it
as though it was done with a razor and !etting
the eyelid drop down like Ben Butler’s. The
blcod flowed so freely that Mike could hardly
epg out of the eye. iad Aaron put

@ the other shutter in the same
snanner the fight would haye been
his beyond a peradventure. He did
notand McCoole beat him so terribly that he
never perfectiy recovered, as he often after-
ward said. The finishing blow was a fearful
one. It wasaright-hander onthe forehead
and it floored Jones like ashot. It did not
knock him insensible, however, but he flop-
ki around on the ground like a chicken with

taneck wrung. That afternoon Jimmy El-

liot, who had arrived in Cincinnati too late to
see the battle,met McCoole in the then famous
St. Lawrence saloon, and said to him: ‘*You
call yourself the champion of America. Why,
you haven't whipped me yet.’’ ‘‘No, and I'll
not fight with you, either,’’ answered Mike.
**T’ll not fight with a thief.’’

*
> =

Tom Allen made a chopping block of MeCoole
on two occasions. The first time the enemies
of Ailen broke into the ring and robbed him of
the ight. The next time Mike was beaten so

title: Allen coaching a fight
text:
LATEST EDIMION

M’MANUS WINS.

He Knocks Out Artie Flint
To-Day in Seventeen
Rounds.

The Much-Talked-Of Mill
Fought This Morning
at St. Clair.

Flint Has the Fight Well‘in Hand, Appar
ently, in the Last Round, When He Is
Suddenly Knocked Senseless by McManus
—A Desperate Battle, in Which Science
Was Forgotten] and Slugging Ruled the
Day—Both Men Terribly Punished—The
Fight in Detail—Scenes at the Ground
and on the Train—A. Disgusting - Exhibi-
tion,

By Telegraph to the Post-Dispaton.

ST. Crain, Mo., April 16.—The prize fight
between Arthur Flint of 8t. Louls and Hugh
McManus of Kansas City took place in a elear

ing in the woods about five miles
from this station to-day, about sixty
miles from &t. Louis. The train

bearing the principals and the crowd
was delayed at the ’Frisco Depot at Grand
avenue in St. Louis, from which place the ex-
cursion left, It waa the intention to leave on
the train, which was chartered specially for
the purpose at 4:30 this morning, but Mo-
Manus forgot his valise and a delay of
an hour was theresult. The party arrived on
the fighting grounds at 7:20 a. m. and after a
long delay there the ring was pitched. The
affair had been nolsed abroad yesterday and a
lotof uninvited and disagreeabie people met
the train at Grand avenue, St. Louis, and
climbed Into the cars through the windows.
There were fully 150 men present, among them
being some well-known attorneys and a big
gathering of saloon-keepers and quasi sporta.
Whisky was used freely on the train
and many of the spectators were beastly
drunk when thetrain halted at tnis place.

Among those present were Tom Alien,
Tom Kelly, Charley Woods, Dan
and Charley Daly, Dutchy Neale and
Rusty Evans, both of whom rode

out om the cow-~-catcher of the engine and
-anumber of other more or less reputable
|people of the city. The fight was for $1,000 in
stakes and a purse of $1,000 made
up of the sale of tickets which
were disposed of at $i2each. The men were
to weigh less than 152 pounds. McManus was
a trifle overtrained, and scaled at a trifle less
than 150, Flint welghing about one pound
less. There was little betting, and that
wasdone at even terms. The men fought
in a 24-foot ring, Queensbury rules, with kid
gioves.
Jack Brohn his trainer, and McManus by Tom
Kelly and Jim Evans. About $600 was bet
even mouey on the fight.

IN THE RING.
Shortly after 10 a. m.the men entered the
ring. Afteralong wrangle P.J. Tucker was
chosen referee. McManus won the choice of
corners and took the corner looking to the
sun. Time was called at 10:18 a. m.

THE FIGHT.

First Rovysp—Light sparring, several inef-
fective exchanges on face and neck. This was
followed by severe in-fighting. Flint hit his
opponent a heavy blowon the jaw with his
left, felling himto the ground. Heavy ex-
changes followed, both men bleeding from
mouth and nose,but no blood claimed on either
side.

Secoxsp Rovuyp—Terrific and unscientific
slugging, clinches without number and nu-
merous exchanges on body and head were the

rule. Flintatthe close was bleeding at the
ear and staggering. This was McManus’
round.

THIrp Rovunp—Poth men came up pretty
fresh. Forty seconds were spent In sparring
for wind and lighter sparring at long range
and easy body exchanges right and left.
There was one good count for Flint on the
jaw, but nothing more was done.

FovurtH Rounp—This was more sparring for
wind, followed by pretty cross-counters in
the face. Flint led for the face several
times, but failed to follow up. Then Me-
Manus ran Flint around the ring, slugging him
desperately right and left in the face and
stomach, but Flint took the medicine well.
The round closed with light sparring.

FiretH Rouxnp—Toweards the end of this round

the men got atclose quarters, and did some )p

heavy and indiscriminate work. McManus
fellin his corner and Flint’s spike struck his
‘arm, hurting it severely. This was Flint’s
round.

SixtH Rocyp—McManus ran Fiint around
the ring, hitting him in the jaw and breaking
it. Flint returned by knocking his man down
with a fiat-hand blow, and he rose weax,
This was Flint’s round, too.

REVENTH RovxypD—McManus used bis right
with good effect on Flint’s left jaw. He then
clinched, and destructive right and left work
on Flint’s face and mouth followed. Flint
was now bleeding freely at the mouth. All
the fighting was done in the Kansas City man’s
cor:er. At this time it was any one’s fight,
altLc gh McManus had done 4 trifle more
damage than his antagonist.

EIGHTH Rounp— Flint feints and stops
Mac’s lead for the face. Mac followed him
up, using his right with great advantage on
the mouth and again on the stomach. A sud-
den stomach blow downed McManus again,
this being the last blow struck.

NISTH EOUND.—Flint came up with a hen’s
egg under hislefteye. Pretty cross-counter-
ing was begun, followed by a heavy right-
hander on Flint’s mouth. Still again did
Flint make his foe bite the turf py one of his
flerce body-biows.

TestH Rounp—There was intense excite-
mentin this round among the sprectators.
Flint twice felled McManus in his own corner,
and Kansas City claimed @ foul, which was not
allowed. Mac’s ieft eyo was badly discol-
ored.

ELEvesta Rovyp—Still the fight went on tn
MeManus’ corner. It opened with two hard
ones right and left on Mso’s face. Flint re-
the same ‘fol«

Flint was seconded by Tom Allenand |

lowed by cleverexchanges on the face and
jaw, blow for biow. Flint, when time was
called, had the better of the round.

TWELFTa Rounp—The fighting still went on
all in Mac’s corner, opening with a hard one
from Flint’s left In Mac’s stomach. Fiint
came at his opponent now with a series of ter-
rible right and left blowsin the chin and
under it, which caused the biood to
spurt In streams from MeManus’ mouth.
Maoc’s lower lip was cut In two. The round
ended with McManus very sick, weak and un-
fit.

THIRTEENTH ROUND.—In this round the fight,
which had all along Deen in Flint’s favor now

_turned its fayor toward McManus, who, al-

though felled three timesto the ground, In-
filcted terrible punishment on his man, leav-
ing him as weak as water at the end, Much
blood was let on both sides, but Flint seemed
to have weakened terribly.

FOURTEENTH ROUND. Flint’s left eye was now
entirely closed. The work was even on both
sides in this round, but the men were growing
weak. Fint seemed to be badly winded and
nearly gone,

FIFTEENTH ROUND.—Nothing was done in
this roand except sparring for wind.

SIXTEENTH ROUND.—Flint struck twice on
Maoc’s jaw and Mac returned the compliment.
Flint played for the stomach and
McManus got back heavily upon
the body and face. Fiint’seye was now the
size ofa goose egg. Tom Allen sucked the
blood out of the wound.

SEVENTEENTH AND LAST ROwuND: Flint was
the fresher of the two, and pounded McManus
all around the ring, beating him unmercifal-
iv with both hands ane confining his
blows mainly to the face. Blood came freely
from McManus’ mouth, nose, andears. He
suddenly recovered, however, and by two
sharply dealt blows, one on the left jaw with
the right and one onthe right side of the
neck, with the left knocked his man prostrate
onthe ground. Flint lay there like a log and
did not respond. The referee decided the
fight Iu MacManus favor.

A QUEER FIGHT ENDS QUEERLY.

This last round was probably one of the
most peculiar that was ever seen ina prize
Tring. Up to this time the fight was any-
body’s victory, and in the first three
quarters of this round Fiint had everything
hisown way. It was pitiful to see him beat
the bleeding face of his opponent, and the
really marvelous gameness whieh he dis-
played. Flint was fighting with one eye.
The other was swollen and i. bruised
and cut and bleeding fromthe sharp incision
made by his second’s lance. No less marvel-
ous was McManus’ rally. He seemed to
awake from his stupor with the quickness of
a lightning flash and wheeling around on
hisman dealt him the two deadly blowa that
finished him. Flint turned around twice likea
man who was shotand then fell on the flat of
his back with his legs spread out two feet
apart. Ten seconds passed, and then Tom
Kelly rushed over to the corner of the ring
where Flint lay and flourished his right hand
over his body like a Roman gladiator, shout-
ing at the same time.

A TERRICLD SIGuT.

What he said was utterly lost and swallowed
up Inthe unearthly tumult that took posses-
sion ofthe men around the ring, who, drunk
with a!cohol and frerzied by excitement, acted
more Ike wild beasts than rationel beings.
It was faliy 12 minutes before Flint
recovered his consciousness and 15 before he
could stand erect upon his feet. McManus had
to be helped up the hill to the station by his
brotber and Flint was led between Tom Allen
and Dan Daly. It required both their efforts
tocarry him. He was laid on the floor of the
baggage car and cried continually: *‘Oh, my
head! Oh! My head.’’

Great interest was manifested In the fight by
the country people, of whom about twenty-
five were present atthe battle. Flint’s defeat
is a terrible disappointment to his friends, who
confidently expected himto win. The time of
the fight was one hour and filteen minutes.

The Men and Their Records.

Hugh McManus is about 25 years of age, and
was little known In St. Louis before he arrived
here three months ago to make this fight with

Flint. He is a middle-weight, a
coal miner originally, who has followed
fighting and fisticuffs for a living.

He came here about the time Flint was chal-
lenging Dan Daly to meet him, end as Dan and
Flint had some trouble in coming to terms |
McManus took Daly’s piace and the match |
was made. McManus’ only fight of note, and
about that there is some doubt, is one
with Jim Fell, who has since made
some stir in the East. They tought |
ie “hg rounds, and the fight |
was then given to McManus onafoul. Sic-
Manus trained for his fight In St. Louls, and
made many friends ainong sporting men here
while preparing for the battle.

Artie Flint’s record as a fighter is as brief as
that of McManus. He wasa cab-driver, hung
around Allen and Keliy’s places and took to
fighting naturallv. He is about the same age

as McManus. His 7 other fight of —T
importance was with Dan Daiy_ at
Central Turner Hall itn April, 1886. |

The fight wasabitterand desperate one with
skin gloves. Daly knocked Flint out in the
twenty-seventh round. Both were weil
thumped, but neither suffered much perma-
nent injury. Beforethis fight the men had a
zo at a local theater, but it amouuted
to littie, Daly havin the best of it.
Flint has been aching to have a go at Daly ever |
since the Turner Hail fizht, but the men have
never come together. Flint, like McManus, is |
a middie- weight, and Is in business in St.Louis
as a saloon-keeper.

WALKING TO ST. LOTIS.

Old-Time Leg Champions Pointing for St.
Louis.
By Telegraph to the Post-DIspaTcu.

Wuitk HALL, Ill., April 16.—J. 8. Harriman
of Haverhill, Boston,the man who walked 6,000
miles in 104 days, six years ago, andjOwen
Briscoe of Spain, champion long dis-
tance walker of that country, arrived
here last evening, sixty-seven miles shead of
Dan O'Leary and Henry Vaughbs. The four
are walking over the ‘‘O’’ track from Omeha,
Neb., to St. Louis to complete
1,000 miles In a@ hall in that city for
a purse of $2,000. Harriman and Briscoe wili
remain here to-day until O’Le and Vaughn
arrive, when the whole party will start for st.
Louls, where they will arrive to-morrow.

Mr. Chas. E. Barney’s daughters, Mrs. Dr.

hai, China, March 10, and from Yokohama,

their way to St. Louis on Saturday. Al h
there is no sickness on the vessel, it has
been quarantined for fourteen days.

title: The Daly-allen fight
text:
THE DALY-ALLEN FIGHT.

Judge Cady Hears Both Sides and Distributes
the Fines Evenly.

The impromptu mill which took place early
Sunday morning between the Allen and Daly
prize-fighters was aired before Judge Cady
this morning, Tom Alien, Charley Daly and
Jobn Ryan being up on counter charges of
disturbing the peace. Not much light was
thrown on the affair, both sides testifying

diametrically opposed. The Daly faction had
the preponderance of testimony,and their wit-
nesses told a more connected story and
corroborated each other better than did
Ailen’s witnesses, who were woefully defect-
ivein their statements as to how the trouble
origninated. The Daly story was to the effect
that three man ran down Seventh street, pur-
sued by Tom Allen, John Ryan, ‘‘Dutchy’’
Neal and Steve Hearne. Allen came up and
abused Dan Daly, who was sitting on the steps
infrontof his place. He called Daly vile
names and pronounced him and his —— gang
of Irish prize fighters no good. Dan remon-
strated with him and Charley came out to
pacify the ex-champion ofthe world. When
he did Allen remarked, ‘‘Hi ‘ave two
Dutchmen ‘ere hand heither one
hov "em can lick you.’’ Charley
replied that he could lick them both, where-
upon Allen struck him. ‘Then Charley told
Dan totake care ofthe ex-champion of the
world and hewould attend to the other two.
Charley testified that he started for Ailen’s
two ‘‘Dutchmen,’’ Neal and Hearne, but
had torun them two blocks to get a punch at
them. When he came back Dan had
knocked down Allen and the latter had cried
enough. Charley got Dan to let Allen up.
Harry Allen, anemploye of the Dalys, testi-
fied that when Charley told Dan to attend to
Alien the latter said: ‘‘He’d ‘ave a bloody
puddin’ in you.’’ Dan sailed in and knocked
Allen off his pins, while in the language of
Harry Allen, Charley made the other two
sneak, running one as far as Tom Kelly’s,
while the other ran into Allen’s place.

John Ryan, a young Englishman who was
with Allen, gave his testimony in avery funny
manner, He showed a disposition to wrestle
with words which were too large for him and
threw him. Ina most graphic manner he de-
scrii -d how he and Allen fought a whole army
of Daly pugilists, while Hearne and ‘‘Dutchy’’

OF INSANITY,

Has Hematoma—Boxers Who Work
Hard Always Have It—In Their Cases It

g. fighting gentlemen.
Perhaps thatis put-

they hired them to

their ears for acon-

PRIZE- FIGHTERS’ EARS.

Dr. Field is the first physician who has ever

fighters’) ears in the in-
terestsof science. For
generations physicians

pictures to insanity.
Prize-fighters so rarely
come under physicians’
care that their aural
peculiarities seem
never to have attracted
attention. Little Joe
Fowler used to be
featherwetght cham-
pion of England, and
= : “ he has been in many

Tom Auen’$ Beauly. hard-fought battles. A
hard, right-handed swinging blow landed on

his left ear while he was trying to pound a

fellow-citizen in a ring, about eleven

years azo, and caused it to swell
and tura outward like the han-
dle on a jug. Five years later his right
ear was caught In the same manner witn a hot
left-handed swing, and it, too, puffed out.
. epeated blows since then have added to the
=eauty of the swelled ears until now Joey can
congratulate himself on having the prettiest
pair in this country. While Dr. Field was
reading his paper the fighters felt of their

mouths widely, as who should say, ‘‘Ilam
badly rattled.’’ The doctor said that Dr.
Frederick Bird of the Insane Asylum at Sie-

curicus condition of the insane (othe-
meatoma), in 1883. Since then many pbhy-
siclans had reported cases of permanentiy

among the sane. For some time the
occurence of thess strange growths was not
ascribed fo violence. Dr. ield read: ‘*It

reuce of this disease among the insane is due

Brown-Sequard and Claude Bernarde are cited
as having a bearing upon these cases. A few
observers have held
; that though there
might have been a pre-

stibility existing, yet
the most prominent
cause was external
violence. The larger
pumbsr of Gases re-
ported seem to have
occurred on the left

been urged by the be-
lievers in traumatic
origin of the trouble to
be due to the fact that
a blow received from a vim Menuga's.
right-handed individual would be wost likely
to fall for mechanical reasons upon the left
side of his antagonist, while those holding
the opposite view have accounted for this on
the ground that the left carotid artery is
n@rer the heart and comes directly from the
aorta, and therefore there is amore powerful

circulation on the left side of the head than
on the right.

**Statictics seem to Indicate that it oceurs
more frequently among males than among fe-
males. Hun, who reports twenty-four cases
from the records of the State Asylum at Utica,
found twenty-threg males and but one fe-

writes me that he has nineteen cases now in
the asylum, sixteen unilaterals and three
Dilaterals; this out ofatotal number of 1,672
female patients. He belives that hematoma
occur more frequently among females than
males, and places the ratio as five te three.
Hematoma tas generally been looked upon
as a4 grave complication when occurring
among the insane. Hun remarks that it ac-
companies those forms of insanity which are
essentially chronic or incurable, and conse-
quently its presence indicates a very unfavor-
able prognosis.’’

THE EARS OF A STATUE.

Having quoted the above ‘and many
other well-known authorities who believe
the swelled esr to be an accom pani-

ment of insanity, Dr.
Field spoke of a re-
rently discovered
statue of ancient Gre-
cian make, represent-
ng &@ boxer wearing the
cestus, who sits resting
between the rounds.
His ears are swollen,
and bear a close re-
semblance to those
whose pictures adorn
bis column. Men who
ought with the cestua
were fond of using the
swinging or round-arm

Tommy Barnes’ te. Diow, and  doubtiess
the heavy cuffs they bestowed on the sides of
one another’s beads brought on hsmatoma
as boxers, and sometimes foot-ball players,

among sane men, and in nearly every in-
stance violence was the cause.

THE STAKES IN THE DALY-M’MANUS FIGHT
TAKEN DOWN.

Daly Is Determined to Drop the Affair and

Decisive Mill—Sporting News and Notes

“OTHING short of a
miracie can now be
done to bring off the

There is now no
doubt that the
money will beturned

by the stakeholder,

ty be done to-mor-
row. Dan Daly is

» 72, ‘ é
EE —SSye, iiving at his house

friend and trainer, has given up the train-
ing quarters at Tower Grove, and has
agauintakenup his abode in thecity. Daly

the course which he outlined in the SUNDAY

and said there that hewould so arrange it

hardly possible. Daly is disgusted and so are

said this morning: ‘‘After I fought with
Eddie Kelly | swore 1 would never fight again,
and Imeantit. McManus knew this and took
advantage of it by biuffing and challenging
meinthetheaters. He splayed his bluff and

of itthe best way they could. Of coursc, Mc-
Manus says he’s willing to fight, but he

knows there’s no danger of a fight now and he
can go ahead and blow. I will pay no more
attention to him. I’m done fighting now for-
ever.*’

**If McManus agreed to fight and started out
to the battie gruound,’”’ said Woods, ‘the
would be arrested on the road tothetrain. It
would be the easiest thing‘in the world to step
the fight, and there's no use bothering with it
any longer.’’

A very well-known man in the business is
Said to have stated that Allen put up the first
$250 foifeit, and that other parties were to put

second deposit the parties were not forth-
coming, and in order to save the $250 already
up Allen made the second deposit.
When the time arrived for the
third deposit the parties were still absent and
then Alien put that up also, and so on until
the entire $1,000 was deposed, and Mr. Allen
was face to face with the situation defined by
the words ‘‘fight or forfeit.’’ If he fought he
would lose, or was convinced that he would

; lose, and _if he forfeited he would be

considerations ,which, it is said, the

| wellknown man in the business stated, in-
duced the fat and festive Thomas to stick on

The man who regrets most that the fight is

chink,’’ as he calls it, which he would have
got if Dan won.

The training expenses of the Daly party
amounted to about $350, but Daly says the
work has done him that much good. He was
at it five weeks.

TOM KELLY,

,®xpress an opinion of how this mill wiil re-

Was no man to fight Sullivan. Ihave no way

aman as Smith. That would indicate that

Ido not think he was. Iregard Sullivan asa

It’s likely to provea hard fight. That is the

DAN DALY SAID:

**Sullivan will win sure and wineasily. I

dition for this fight. I will certainly~ put up

think he will win. I shall certainly put my

_ money on Kilrain. It is doubtful whether the

fight will ever be finisned, |however. They are
very apt to break it upatthering. Now you
mark what I say.’’

TOM ALLEN.
**Kilrain will win, sure,’* remarked Tom
Allen. ‘‘The people generally greatly over-

estimate Sullivan. He made reputation by
going around’ the country sparring and

nocking people out with gloves, but has

der London prize ring rules. My money shall

**‘Tam ps co the fight with Tom Allen and

he will win because he knows much more
about the London prize ring rules than Sulli-
van and isa better fighter under them. In
Chieago, from which place Ihave just re-
turned, I found everybody Sullivan, but that
does not change my opinion one whit. Sulli-
van is asparrer, and nota fighter.’’

HUGH M’MANUS.

*“‘Tthink Kilrain will win and have placed
some money on him,’’ remarkea Hugh Mc-
Manus, the middile-weight. ‘‘The odds here
are about5to4in Sullivan’s favor, but the

ple, in my opinion, are mistaken in their
udgment of the men. Sullivan is not the
man he used to be, and it is questionable
whetner he ever was the man Kilrainis. Cer-
tain is that the big fellow has injured himseif
a t deal by his dissipation and I do not
think he will prove Kilrain’s equal. The lat-
ter is a great fighter, as his meeting with Smith
clearly shows.’’

HANK WIDER.

**It will bea walk-over for Kilrain,’’ said
Hank Wider. ‘‘At one time Sullivan could
whip any of them easily, but he can’t do it
now. Dissipation has broken him down, and

igmo tonger fit forafight. No man can

nk and carouse as Sullivan has done and

‘n his strength and condition. It is against

‘les of nature, and any man who does it

\bly falls.’’

COLE ULLMAN REMAKKED:

Sullivan when he whipped Paddy

title: Personal items stolen from customer at Allen’s saloon
text:
THEY AKE UNDER ARREST

And Charged With Robping a Sleeping
Stranger in Market Street Saloon.

Thomas Barrett and George Ohls are under
arrest at the Central District Police Station
charged with petit larceny.

James St. John is a young man whose home
is at Sulphur Springs, Mo. He fell asleep in
Tom Allen’s saloon, 619 Market street, yester-
day. When he awoke about 10 o’clock last
night he found that his watch and chain,

which he had purchased but a few hours be-
fore had been stolenefrom his pocket.
He at once notified Allen of his loss and the
latter called in Sergt. Shoemaker and
Officer Carr, to whom he gave a description
of two men who had been seen hanging about
the place that night. Barrettand Ohls were
found on an adjacent corner and placed under
arrest.

W hile Officer Carr went across the street to
call the patrol wagon Sergt. Shoemaker re-
mained in charge of the men. He noticed
Barrett acting in a suspicious manner. Fin-
ally Barrett drew something from his pocket
and threw it in the ailey. The Sergeant picked
it up and recognized the missing watch, St.
John identified his property this morning and
a warrant charging Barrett with petit larceny
was sworn out.

Both of the prisoners are badly crippled.
Ohls is minus his left arm, which he said he
had crushed between the bumpers of two
freight cars while switching in Kansas City.
Barrett had his right leg broken some ten
weeks azgoin asaioon on Market street. He
was released from the City Hospital on last
Wednesday.

Assaulted Tom Allen.

John Craig, an Irishman, was hauled be-
fore Judge Morris in the First District Police
Court this morning to answer to the charge

of disturbing thie peace of Tom Alien,
the retired prize-fighter, who Keeps a saloon
on Market, near Seventh street. Craig was
what is commonly called ‘‘a sight.’* His
features were dislocated; his eyes were biack-
ened and swollen, his forehead cut, his nose
torn, his cheeks swollen and scratched
and he displayed great ingenuity in
keeping his tattered shirt an ts on
his bruised person. He looked as though he
had passed through a college cane rush or
hard fought foot-ball game. When asked if
he was guilty of disturbing Tom Alien’s
peace, he said:

‘*“Mebbe I did, yer honor.’”’

‘*Did you assault him?’*’

‘*‘Well, now, that would be hard to say.
There wuz so many fists pluggin’ me th’ face
to wunst an’ a soré-eyed dog at me pants an’
me a hittin’ back that Oi don’t Know as O!
hit Mr. AJen orno. Oj} guess Ol’m guilty.’”’

Judge Morris could not see how a man could
disturb Mr. Allen’s peace and still wear a
bloody face like Craig’s, so he discharged

him.

Yesterday was Tom Allen’s birthday and
the veteran ex-champion of America and his
friends celebrated the event inroyal style at
Tom ’s headquarters on Market street. When
seen by a POST-DISPATCH reporter Tom was
ensconced at a table surrounded Dy a large
number of his admirers, who were intently
listening to the veteran’s story of
his career in the prize _ ring. **Yes,’”’

said he, **this is a great day.
it’s my birthday and Billie Shakespeare was
aiso born and died on the 22d of April. Inthe
old country itis known also as St. George’s
Day and Itell youthey celebrate it in royal
style. When i was over there in 18821 had
the pleasure of participating, andit was one
of the happiest periods of my life.’* Tom
and his two daughters are alithat is left of

the oid country andthe other endeavors to
make my last days comfortable at home,’’
and the champion leaned backin his chair
and gave the interviewer a kKEnowing
wink. ‘‘However,’’ said he, *‘il expect to
celebrate a good many birthdays yet.’’ It
was the ex-champion’s intention to give his
friendsa banquet yesterday morning, but he
was up so late Friday evening receiving con-
sratulations that he decided to abandon the
scheme. ‘‘Iwill doit next year, though,’’
said he, *‘‘whether they keep me up late or

title: Downtown buildings being knocked down for future changes including a row of fighters bars on Market
text:
OLD ST. LOUIS.

QUEER BUILDINGS HERE AND THERE
WHICH HAVE STOOD FOR YEAR}.

Written for the SUNDAY POST-DISPATCH. :
**Bits of Old St. Louts’* would have been a
very prolific subject five years ago, when
everything was old in this city, but to-day it
is quite different, as the homes which looked
old then have either assumed new phases, or
they have nearly all of them been wiped out
of existence within the last half of a decade.
The sites they occupied only a short time
since are adorned by grand and costly com-
mercial buildings. Indeed columns could
easily be written about the rookeries and
the fabulous rents they produced on
inside lots and at commanding corners
where now stand the best buildings in the
city, every one of them bullt within the past
five years. Many other old landmarks have
been torn away during the past year, and the
places where they stood are now the scene

under the cornice of a six-story
structure at the northwest corner of Locust
street, there is a little, old, two-story brick,
lately burnished with acoatof green paint.
It was built more than filty years ago by D:
L. Patterson when J. R. Shepley occupied a
residence at the corner of Locust and Seventh
Next to that on Locust, in
days, was St. George’s Church, then

Dr. Oliphant’s residence, all of them

opposite Henry Shaw’s old that
has been taken down stone by stone, carted
awayand rebuilt inthe Botanical Garden,
in accordance with provisions of Mr, Shaw’s
will, No. 413 North Seventh street never did
produce a heavy rental, and the florid repu-
tation of the premises would not bean in-
ducement for moral people to occupy it. An
old resident says he remembers this Mttie
house when he wasa lad, wading, with his
pants rolled up, through a pond of water that
used toextend along Seventh street across
Washington avenue. Considering its his-
tory, there will probably be no regrets when
the little 2242x150 foot dive is torn away,as it
will be soon, for the property has been leased
for ninety-nine years at ¢ per cent per annum
ona valuation of $25,000,to a party who is
now making preparations to improve the site
with an elght-story commercial building,

The Mascot, Fourth and Lucas Avenue.

of active building operations for the con-
struction of eight to fourteen-story palattal
business blocks, the erection of which will
cost all the way from $390,000 to $1,000,000
each. The city is improving at a very rapid
pace. The demand for more business apart-
ments is constantly increasing. Large com-
mercial buildings have proven most profita-
able investments in St. Louls, and with the
growing demand for other improvements of
this character, the rookeries are fast dis-
appearing. -

Space in the business center has become so
valuable itis now no uncommon thing to see
apparently substantial structures of two to
four stories in height torn down to make
room for new and more imposing improve-
ments. Five years ago work of this nature
in St. Louis was viewed very reproachfully
and with a feeling that such destruction bor-

dered close on vandalism, Expres-
sions of this kind were frequently
heard when the Jaccard Batiding, a

very fine stone-front, of quite pretentious
architecture, too, was torn down to make
a place forthe National Bank of Commerce
building, eight stories in height, at the north-
east corner of Br oadway and Olive street. A
four-story structure at the northwest corner
of Seventhand Oliveis being cleared away
fora fourteen-story building, but no regrets
are heard about that. for now it is plain that
aspirit of progress has taken possession of
St. Louis people, who no longer look with re-
gret on these old vanishing land-marks. Oc-
casionally, as they disappear, some
sentimentality is indulged in by a
few silvery-haired veterans whose youth-
ful days were associated with these mile-
stones that markedthe progress of a great
city, but the inevitable is readily if not
cheerfully accepted by the majority of the
patriarchs, who no doubt feel melancholy at
times,just as Col. David Armstrong did when
his home for so many years, the old Pianters’
House, was doomed to destruction. The
foundations are now about all that is left of
the old hostelry, but the site bids fair to be
more renowned in the future than in the past,
for it is to be the location of a new $1,000,000
Planters’ House, Where the Rialto Bullding,
of such grand proportions and design, is now

being reared, at Fourth and Olive
streets, there was an old land-mark
which has entirely disappeared since
last January, and one of the

most unsightly rookeries was on the site of
the Security building, now nearing comple-
tion, at the southwest corner of Fourth and
Locust streets; another one that used to be
nearly as bad isnow being substituted by a
large building at the southwest corner of
Third and Locust streets. The Wainwright
building, nearing completion,has supplanted
aquarter of a block of tumble-down tene-
ments at the corner of Seventh and Chestnut
streets. Just north of this elegant structure

—————$—

ipa.”

The only frame structure left in the busi-
ness section is on Market street at the north-
west corner of the alley Detween Sixth and
Seventh streets. It Is a two-story building
sway-backed by the snow of more than fifty
winters and warped by as many summer
suns. Old as it is, this house harmonizes very
well with its present surroundings, for the
block it fronts on is, taken as a whole, the
most wretched looking square in all the city.
It occupies ground which has enhanced in
value from comparatively nothing to up-

generally rejuvenated to conform with the
requireraents of a street selected for an en-
trance way tothe city. Up to the present
time less changes have been made in the
style of Market street shops than in the ap-
pearance of buildings on any other of the
business streets for more than thirty years

The most pretentious specimen of old time
architecture in the business center is to be
seen at the northwest corner of Pine and

th streets, where Oliver Hart put up a
bufiding three stories high that was the talk
of the town halfacentury ago. The front of
it is recessed, and from the second story up
there are fluted columns, with decorated
caps which, even at this day, command the
attention of passers-by. In the days of its
pristine freshness Dr. J. J. Clark made the
place his home and later it tecame the res!i-

Gence of Nathaniel Paschal. On the
same side of the biock, nearer
the alley on Pine street, there

is another house precisely the same style.This |

was occupied inthe early days by Prof. De
France, an eminent artist of his time, who
owned the place. These houses are land-
marks indeed. Their architectural outlines
more than entitlethem to this distinction,
but that will not save them long from wreck
and utter ruin, as better buildings are
wanted on Pine street, and they will be sup-
plied before a great while.

On Broadway between Market street and
Franklin avenue there is only one house that
may be properly classed among the old bits
of St. Louls, and that stands at the southeast
corner of Lucas avenue, diagonally opposite
the Union Market. Back to the days in
which that house was bulltthe memory of
man runneth not. The agent, one of the
oldest house-renters inthe city, says he has
collected rents from it since 1860, and at that
early date, thirty-two years ago, it was con-

sidered one of the oldest houses in
St. Louis. Ever since he knew the
place it has been a_e saloon, and

as one of its barkeepers remarked yesterday,
**It has been a mascot for every man who
Started here.’’ A dozen or more saloon-
keepers have retired from the place with
fortunes. It has been renting for $176 a
month for fifteen years past and could be
forced toa higher figure. The place is only
about 30x60 feet, and its two-story walls have
been in a crumbling condition for many
years, and they are likely to stand there till
they fall,as the owner, Mrs. G. M. Speir of
New York, is thoroughly satisfied that she
could not erect another building on the site
that would pay as well.

On the northeast corner of Sixth and Chest-
nut there isan old rookery that will rank for
age with any that have been mentioned, but
it is already doomed, and will soon be
numbered with things of the past. Thisis a
valuable corner, grown so within the past
few years. It has been leased for a long
term of years and the site will be improved
before long withan elegant building of the
cloud piercing order.

GREEK PIRATES.

Two Murderers Arrested for a Crime Com-
mitted Six Years Ago.

New Haven, Conn., July 23.—An assault by
two Greeks upon two fellow countrymen at
Lake Whitney, near this city, a few days

ago, hasled tothearrest of a man wanted
for murder and robbery committed six years
ago near Constantinople. He is now in
the custody of the New Haven police, and arf-
ter answering for the crime of assault, he
will be turned over to the Greek Government
should a demand be made for his extradition.
His name is Lagonedy Vourgares, and for five
years he has made his home at No. 130 Wal-
cott street in this city.

In March 1886 Vourgares and others engaged
as sallors on a ship owned by a Greek onthe
Island of Andres and from that place set sail.

On the day before the vessel reached
Constantinople these men drew
the rest of the sailors into

the forecastle and locked them in. Then they
wenttothe captain’s cabin and demanded
his money. He began to parley with them in
the hopes of gaining time but they would not
listen. They stabbed him to death, took
2,000 Napoleons (about §8,000), sailed the ship
into port and made their escape, but
only one of them got very far. The mur-
derers had overlooked thecabin boy when
they locked the other sallorsup. He secreted
himself over the stern of the ship among the
anchor ropes and when the vessel reached
port he slipped down the side and
told the authorities about the murder.
Vourgares’ companions were caught, tried
and within three months executed. Vour-
res escaped on a sailing vesselto Asia and

CHICAGO, Sept. 2.—On Sept. 7, those lovers

reproduction of the slugging match right
here in Chicago. Harry Sommers, Manager
of McVicker’s Theater, concelveda scheme

figured on receiving a handsome profit. Mr.
Sommers has secured Battery D., where a

out, and the Delsartean poses of the con-
testants will beso reproduced that only an
expert could tell them from the genuine
article. They will fight per instructions and
the instructions will be from New Orleans by
our own special courler.’’

Itis proposed to havea wire direct from

large, Well-poised and classic, Corbett’s

head is set on a neck like that of a Thessailan
bull—thick and powerful and sinewy. The
face is strong and full of character.

Over Corbett’s bony face rises his stiff pom-
padour mop, standing up like bristles upon
the fretful hairbrush, Itis rather long just
now, but Jim will have it taken off before he
tackles Sullivan. Critics have said that Cor-
bett is too narrow across the chest. Yet it is
this narrowness that gives him his tremen-
dous reach. Were he broader chested he
would be shorter armed. His wind and
stamina are something wonderful. He can
hit hard enough, too. Those who saw him
punch the bag in Madison Square Garden
came away convinced of that fact. Then,
egain, all the talk about his lack of hitting
powers comes from men who judge him by
the past.

Corbett as he stands to-day js a ihird better
man than ever before. The peculiar training
he has undergone has developed his striking
muscles wonderfully; so much so in fact that
in a recent visit Dr. Pancost picked them out
as the best developed muscies of his body.
The Corbett that fought Jackson weighed 176
pounds, ye og ad trained. The Corbett
that willfight Sullivan on Wednesday next
will weigh between 187 and 190 pounds,
after three months of hard training. The
difference is that between what may be
termed callow manhood and the brawn
strength ofa full-fledged man. His stomac
is fullof hard ridges that have all the ap-
pearance of wire cables, and his legs look
like those of a thoroughbred. They seem
compact cords of muscle from the size of a
fiddle-string up to a two-inch hempen rope.

The difference between Corbett and Sulll-
van, although not so marked as that between
those ancient gladiators, David and Goliath,
has still many points of resembianee. Sulli-
van has a torso like that of a behemoth. His
strength 1s terrific, and whenever he hits a
man under the earthe unfortunate individual
temporarily forgets mother, home and
friends. But can he land on Corbett? The
build of the latter is that of a thoroughbred
horse. He is as quick as a flash, as aglie asa

title: Local Pugilists
