LOCAL PUGILISTS.

Knights of the Fives Who Have Lived
in This City.

ST. LOUIS WAS AT ONE TiME THE
HOME OF CHAMPIONS.

Reminiscences of the Days When Cham-
Pionship Batties Were Fought Near
This City—Letters and Records of Mc-
Coole, Allen, Kelly, Farrell, Daly and
Clark —Local Boxing Celebrities.

St. Louis has at various times harbored
within her hospitable gates many shining
lights of the pugilistic fraternity. Before
San Francisco and New Orleans came into
prominence and overshadowed all the rest of
the Union the Maqund City could almost be
said to vie with New York and Boston asa
pugilistic Mecca. She has at various times
had the honor to reckon among her
citizens the holders of championship honors
and though none of them have shed such ef-
fulgence on their native townas the man
from Boston, there wasa time when the
eyes ofevery Knight ofthe Fives was turned
to this city, which was at that time the home
of champions.That was in the days when Mc-
Coole, Allen, Kelly, Chambers and Madden
had set up their household gods
in the Future Great, and were pur-
suing the even tenor of their
ways with much public support and little in-
terference from bluecoats.

All this was away back in the 70s, and old-
timers can remember weilthe frequent trips
by boat to Bloody Island to witness a scrap
between local buffers, and the journeys up
and down the riverto the great champion-
ship fights that took place near the city. in
those daysthe principals did not travel to
the appointed spot in luxurious
equipages, but were picked up
from the river bank along the
route like ordinary mortals. But delegations
from other cities were not infrequent and
every big mill on the banks of the Mississippi
was attended by sporting men from Chicago,
Cincinnatiand New York. The most noted
starsinthe pugilistic firmament that have
made St. Louis their home are Tom Allen, |
who at the time of his retirement was heavy-
weightchampion of the world; Tom Kelly, —
the middle-weight champion; Mike McCoole, |
atone time champion of America; Charles
Daly, ex-light-weight champion of America.
The SunDAY PostT- DISPATCH to-day presents
its readers with pictures of these men anda
sketch of their lives and principal battles.

TOM KELLY.

Tom Kelly was born near the town of Cas-
tlerea in the County of Roscommon, Ireland,
Nov. 10, 1838. In 1851, young Kelly, with his
mother, three brothers and a sister crossed
the channel and settled at Dewsbury in York-
shire, where he went to work ina woolen
factory. The boys about the place were fond
of using the gloves and Tom’s cleverness
soon made him ‘‘cock of the mill.”” When 19
years of age, 5 feet 914 inches in height,
the cotton lads clubbed together
and made up a purse to match Tom
against a local champion named Johnny
Moran. They met near Dewsbury and fought
seventy-seven rounds inih. 55m. Kelly had
the worst of the fight for the first hour, but
he kept gamely on until the arrival or the
police put anend tothe fighting. When he
met Moran two years after he came out with
fiying colors aftera brief contest. Tem then
adopted the custom of that time, traveling
about and boxing at the various races and

fairs. Tom married about this time
@nd was bent on quitting the ring,

Tom Kelly.

but his friends wouid not have _ it
that way and put up £25 for a match be-
tween him and Jim Connor of Leeds. They
met at Dewsbury Oct. 1, 1860. Tom whipped
his men in fifty-eight minutes. After this
Kelly joined a boxing company run by Mickey
Bent and was carded to fight any novice in
Engiand at 146 pounds. Fifteen months
elapsed before his next battle. On Dec. 24,
1861, the day before Christmas, Known in
England as boxing day, he fought Dan Lomas
at Staleybridge. Afterseventy-seven minutes
fighting, with Kelly’ the favorite ali through,
Lomas adopted the dropping game and
lost the fignt through going down
without being hit. <A fresh match was made
for Feb. 4, 1863. Aftereluding the police all
day the men met late in the afternoon and
Lomas lost the fight through the identical
offense which lost him the first match, after
forty -s1x rounds had been fought. On Sept.
22, 1863, he met Bill Brown, Lamas’ old

Aldershot, Jem Mace seconding Kelly. The

hammer-and-tongs and punched him out in

belabored him with it. Keily was awarded

Kelly, to show that he had no knowledge

Rooke thesame week for £200 a side, but
Rooke declined. They meta second time on
April 25, 1865, and Tom was put out in the
thirteenth round, He then took a breath-
ing spell of seventeen months before he was
pitted against Harry Alien, a brother of
Tom’s, for £50a side. They met at Flouch
Sept. 78, 1866. The fight mes # terrific one,

closed. Hestood up to his antaxonist for
thirty-six rounds before he was put out. on

The referee ordered the fight on for the next |
day, but Richard had enough. Aiter this”
fight Kelly sold out his goods and
chattels and salled for America, land-

ing in New York Jan. ill, 1868. He

challenged unsuccessfully any 150-pound man

in the country. After traveling on a
sparring exhibition tour Tom settled fn this |
city. Here he was backed againsta local
favorite, Fred Bussey, who had defeated Andy
Duffy and ‘‘Soap’’ McAlpine. Tom Allen sec-
onded Bussey. ‘lhe fight lasted twenty-seven

rounds, and thougi Kelly was almost.
whipped at the start his gameness won him

the fight. This was his first and last fight in |
his adopted country, for though he
challenged any middle-weight In the world
he met with no response. He then retired |
from the ring. but has acted as second in |
mapy fights, the most notable of which was |
the tullivan-Ryan battle, when Tom was in >
the Irojan’s corner.

BOB FARRELL,
Bob Farrell, who is recognized as one ofthe

PROF. BILE CLARK.

Prof. William Clark, who in his younger
days was christened the ‘‘Belfast Chicken’’

The fault with most authors who try to
write stories about city life is that they have
caught only a glimpse of their subject, and
think it is the whole. People who write avout
the slums are especially prone toerr in this
way. The low lifeof acity cannot be de-
scribed by one who has visited the abodes of
squalor oncs or twice. The description may
be exact, the language true to the tongue
of the subject, though that is
harder, but the story will lack
the essence of the life that the author {!s try-
ing to describe.

Here ig avery well printed little book by
Allnie Bronson King, published by
D. D. Merrill of New York.
It is called ‘*The Children of the
Slums,’’ and it contains a number of sketches
of life in St. Louis. None of themare realis-
tic, in spite of the author’s evident labor to
make them so,

*‘Saturday night, and 9 o’clock at
Tom Allen’s*’ one of the sketches
begins. A poor woman from the Salvation

Army comies in, brings with her a little |

child and then rough men help her. The
place described is not Tom Allen’s, and the
woman does not behave like the women of the
Salvation Army. The sketch is pathetic, but
no more like a scene from real life than one
of T. 8. Arthur’s descriptions in ‘‘Ten Nights
in a Bar Room. ’’ 3

Yet the sketches are well done, the descrip-
tion is sharp and clear and the interest of the
reader iscaught and held. The author has
much more to learn aboutlife than about
writing. ;

Was indicted in Kentucky for his battie

_ @ffort to extradite him from this State, but

CRIPPLE CREEK, Colo,, Dec, 29.—
At a meeting of representative citizens
held this evening a committee headed
by Mayor Perkins was appointed to
Becuw” the Corbett-Mitchell fight for

come off in Florida. " Mayor Perkins
sent a telegram to the pugiliats to-night
guaranteeing a purse of $25,000 if the

JACKSONVILLE DISCONSOLATE.
JACKSONVILLE, Dec. 29.—The fact
that the passagé of an ordinance reg-
ulating licensing authorizing glove con-
tests in Jacksonville did not have the
effect of quieting the governor's oppo-
sition to the Miichell-Corbett mill was
a disappointment to the patrons of the
event, and the later declaration of Gov-
ernor Mitchell that he will pay no at-
tention to a decision of any circuit
judge who may affirm the validity of
the Jacksonville ordinance has had a
still more depressing effect upon the
Projectors of the enterprise. Cool-
headed people do not agree with the
enthusiasts who profess to believe that
the fight will come off whether or no
e—eoCC—_——C_____—__—- =—_—_—

CORBETT’S CHEST

and at all hazards. Governor Mite ‘3}l
is as stubborn as a mule. He has
Started out to |wevent Mitchell and
Corbett from having a public meeting
in Florida, and those who know him
best say he will do it, even if he has
to take charge of affairs in person.
His declaration that he knows as much
about the law as any cireuit judge in
the state is borne out by the facts,
as he is a lawyer of eminence, and
his assertion that nothing short of the
decision of the supreme court will pre-
vent him from taking measures to pre-
vent the fight, is regarded by many as
tantamount to a declaration that he
believes it te be within his power to
effectively interfere and that he will
do so.

PUGILISTS ON THE GROUND.

The two pugilists now at Jacksonvile
are surrounded by hundreds of admir-
ers. The physical proportions of the
champions are the subjects of contin-
ued comment, and the points of differ-
ence and of advantage are counted
over and over and form the theme of
endless disy .ssion.

Admirers of Corbett mention his
bouts with great prize fighters when
he was yet an amateur. They tell
how, when a mere boy, he bested Jack
Burke in eight rounds; how he gave
Joe Choynski three drubbings; how he

feated Dominick McCaffrey, and to cap
the climax, whipped Sullivan at New
Orleans.

Few venture to predict that Mitch-
ell wil! outfight Corbett, yet a good
many decline to admit that he will
lose. By Mitchell's admirers it is
pointed out that when Sullivan was re-
garded as invincible and before the
great Boston man had suffered the ef-
facts of inebriety and fast living, which,
they say, had rendered him unfit for
the ring long before he met Corbett
at New Orleans, Mitchell fought him to
a standstill at Chantilly. They be-
Heve he is a better man now than he
was then, and that Corbett is about
to find it out to his cost.

PHISIQUE OF "THE MEN.

As for the physical development of
the men there is room for disagreement
as to which shows to the best advant-
age. Corbett recently said that he re-
garded an inch advantage in height
as equal to ten pound advantage in
welght. Corbett attributes great im-
portance to advantage in reach, and
evidently relies strongly on the fact
that he possesses this advantage over
the Englishman. In his fight with
Sullivan he jabbed the champion in the
face, bread-basket and shprt ribs at
his pleasure, and got away without
receiving a hurtful blow. He expects
to serve Mitchell the same way, and
his admirers contend that he will have
no difficulty in doing se.

ing into a sprinting match, as they
}say he did in his battle with Jackson,
he will be compelled to fight af close
range. They point out the fact that
\|}while he struck Sullivan repeatedly,
he did not inflict the slightest injury
upon him, and they insist that he mere-
ly pounded Sullivan until the Boston
man swooned trom exhaustion, They
}say that this kind of fighting will sult
|| Mitchell, and as the latter is equally
as active and a harder hitter, Tom
Allen will be there,

Tom Allen of St. Louts says that Cor-
bett jabbed his way to the champion-
ship; that in his fight with Sullivan he
never struck a blow that by any means
could be decisive of a battle, Others
say that Corbett is incapable of deliver-

MITCHELL'S BACK,

ing a knockout blow unless against a
very inferior man or by accident, Mitch-
ell’s friends claim Mitchell with not jab
Corbett, but will hit him and hit him
hard, and that if he get# in on the cham-
pion with a crack or two it will bring
Corbett to a standstill, and that in this
way Mitchell may get the best of the
meeting

Tom Allen will go to Jacksonville to
assist in preparing Mitchell for the
fight. Tom is 2 cook of rare accom-
plishments and a good deal of a doctor,
He has had much experience in prize
ring affairs and especially in the train-
ing of pugilists, He will have charge
of the preparation of Mitchell's food
and may be one of his seconds in the
ring.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla., Dec. 29.—
Governor Mitchell today hurled anoth-
er bomb at the Duval Atnletic club,
the promoter of the proposed mill be-
tween Corbett and Mitchell. The story
gees that the governor is exceedingly
wrathy at the course of the Duval
county judicial authorities in arrest-
ing Corbett and Mitchell. It is said
that the governor has been keeping
the wires hot all day roasting Sclicitor
Christie of Duval county, in the mat-
ter, charging that Christie and all the
other judicial officers of this county
are in collusion with the Duval Ath-
letic club and are abetting the club's
efforts to pull off the maich and that
the arrests and proposed test of the
law are not in geod faith.

The governor goes further, it is said,
and reiterates that the proposed fight

CORBETT'S RIGHT.

is in violation of the laws of that state
and asserts that it shall not come off
unless the supreme court decides that
such contests are legal. The judicial
authorities of this country, who, it is
said, the governor has attacked, re-
fuse to either deny or affirm the cur-
rent reports. They admit that they
have received telegrams from the gov-
ernor in regard to the arrest and the
proposed test of the law, but the nature
of the dispatches they refuse to divulge.
From other sources, however, it is
learned that the tenor of the telegrams
was such as has been deseribed and
that Governor Mitchell is highly indig-
nant at what he terms the “collusion”
of the Duval county authorities with
the promoters of the fight.

At any rate this has been a rather
“blue day" for the sports and there js
a rather “shaky” feeling in regard to
the pulling off of the fight.

The situation is about as follows:
Gov. Mitchell and Attorney General
Lamar, the highest law officers of the
state, assert that the contest will violate
the laws of the state; Bowden of the
Athletic club and his lawyers say it
would not.

Governor Mitchell was once on the
supreme bench, and it is believed that
he knows as much about the laws of the
state as the attorneys of the club. It is
also believed that the opinion of Attor-
ney General Lamar, that the proposed
fight would be illegal, was prepared af-
ter a consultation with the governor
and members of the supreme court as
to the law in the case.

It is significant in this connection
that Governor Mitchell says no decis-
ion save that of the supreme court

MITCHELL'S RIGHT.

will deter him from every effort to
stop the fight. Those close to the gov-
ernor believe that this declaration
means that the governor knows that
the supreme court will not decide in
favor of the legality of the contest.
Several things have conspired to
make the governor very bitter in his
opposition to the fight. One “special
| dispatch” sent out from Jacksonville
has, it is said, cut him to the quick
and hardened him in his determination

that no slugging match shall occur in
Florida, The “special” referred to sta-
ted that while the governor was at
Tampa during the holidays certain par-
ties who favored the fight pro; to
get him off on a camp hunt and “mel-
low him and jolly him” into allowing
the fight to come off,

A dispatch just received from Tampa
saysi that the governor stated this
evening in the most positive terms
that “the fight will not come off in
Florida.” He says that he has his
plans for preventing the fight consum-
mated and that at the proper moment)
he will act.

‘The “proper moment” is supposed to
be, in the governor's opinion, when
Mitchell and Corbett are about ready
to face one another. The governor is
further quoted as saying, “Il regard
this proposed fight as an offense
against the peace and dignity of the
State and my determination to prevent
it is fixed.”

Meantime Corbett and Mitchell are
engaged in slinging billingsgate at one
another to the great disguat of the pub-
lic. Corbett yesterday in an interview
called Mitchell “a convict and a sneak"
and Mitchell replies today, applytag
similar choice epithets to Corbett. If
the promoters of the fight should, by
any chance, succeed in pulling off tie
contest despite the governor, and Cor-
bett and Mitchell fight half as well with
their fists as they do with their tongues
the spectators will be sure to receive a
good run for their money,

title: Gov Mitchell and Bowden will fight to a finish
text:
Chances of the Great Battle Occurring
in Florida.

GHARLEY,MITCHELL TRIES HIS HAND AT
ROASTING THE CORBETT CROWD.

The Britisher Replies tothe Stories They
- Have Been Circulating About Him—A
Rabbit-Foot Voodoo Sent Him—Fior-
ida’s Governor Somsthing of a Sport,

The Club’s Check to the Stakeholder.

JACKSONVILLE, Fila., Jan. 14.—Everybody
here considers that Bowden and his merry
men played the trump card, which will win
the trick, when they sent the check for the
$20,000 purse to John Kelly, and if sports in
other parts of the country arrive at the same
conciusion within the next few days the di-
rectory of the Duval Athietie Oiub will be
immensely pleased. They now say that the
limit as to receipts for admission, upon
which the possibilities of a fight hinged until
yesterday, has been removed, and that
the men will have it out if only
two persons pay for tickets. This
is a strong statement to be sure since it is
not entirely in accordance with all prece-
dent in human nature for men to throw
away calmly $25,000 or $30,000, whena few
words would, in a measure, save the money.
It is not to encourage'the sport that the club
has taken this stand altogether. It has come
to a fight for supremacy between Bowden
and his friends and Gov, Mitchell, who 1s
practically single-handed, unless the State
troops show more of a disposition to help
Bim out than has yet been manifested.

Bowden Is a rather bright person at times,
but for stubbornness he could give the
champion mule *‘thirty yards in a hundred,’’
asthe saying goes. He is a fighter who, un-
like many other kinds of fighters, doesn’t
know when he’s whipped,

IT IS BOWDEN VS. MITCHELL.

Now, if the Governor did not happen to be
the same sort of a man, the struggle would
have been over longago. When he says a
thing he means it, and his friends here say
nothing will stop him. So it’s Bowden
against Mitchell to a finish, but in
this contest the sports do not say, ‘*‘May
the best man win.’’ They want Bowden
to win, and hope that it will not come toa
draw of revolvers.

The mention of Mitchell’s name to Bowden
stirs him up as much asthe casual sugges-
tion that malaria may be contracted in Flor-
ida rilesanative. Any person who has ever
spoken of quinine in Jacksonville will at once
understand how Bowden acts when discuss-
ing the Governor’s personality. He handles
the Chief Executive without gloves at least
once every twenty minutes.

If the Governor is not between his satanic
majesty and the deep blue sea just now, as
he appears to be, he may make known
to-day, just how he proposes to knock out
Bowden etal. What the ace is which he
may lead at the last moment nobody knows,
and Bowden, for one, doesn’t carea rap. The
strongest part of the whole business is
that the Governor himself ts just a trifie in-
clined to be asportina modest way. This is
no state secret, for just after the Sullivan-
Corbett battie his friends hata good chance
to jacket him for baa judgment. The story
that he lost $200 on the result is said
to be absolutely true, therefore, he is

not opposed to the fight for the reasons at-
tributed to him by many. Not one orf tts
projectors opposed him politically. The
thousands of letters from reform leagues and
private citizens which he has received, offer-
ing financial ald (butin every case failure to
contain anything that might be turned into
money) may have had something to do with
it, but the consensus of opinion is that Gov.
Mitchell said that the fight should not take
piace here from the start,and couldn’t afford
afterward to take water.
CHANCE TO GET EVEN.
i: Mitchell is trying to get even
on us for the money he _—ilost
on Sullivan,’’ said one of the directors,
**Harry Mason will bet him $5,000 that the
fight takes place in Flori@&, which will make

talk this,but the talk Inthe clubis at times
decidedly stronger. There has been no bet-
ting to speak of here. Most of the wagers
have been at evens that Cor*ett ns in

text:
ALLEN AND THE PORPOISE.

Tom Allen, while taking his constitutional
on the beach this morning, saw a large fish
struggling violently in the shallow water.
**God stroke me bilind,’’ ejaculated the vet-

eran as he sought safety on the shell walk.

**Hi, there,’’ yelled Allen, ‘‘Look hout a

**It’s a porpoise come ashore to die,’” said

forland. .This fellow isdying now.’’ ‘The

**You’re 6n,°’ said Robbins, and the por-

‘*That brings the bloomin purse down to
$19,900. °’

title: Tom Allen Now thinks Corbett can whip any Pugilist
text:
CHANGED HIS MIND.

Tom Allen Now Thirks Corbett Can
Whip Any Pugilist.

Tom Allen, the famous retired champion of
America, who was one of Charley Mitchell's
seconds, returned to the city from Florida
yesterday. The veteran enjoyed his trip to
the land where oranges grow, but says
the great fight wasa ‘‘bloody’’ farce.

‘*Mitchell was outclassed in every respect,
and Corbett would have chopped him into
ribbons in a few more rounds,’’ said Tom to
a Post-DISPATCH representative last night.
‘*‘The Californian has improved fully a thou-
sand per cent since he defeated Sullivan,
while Charley is not anywhere near the
man he wasa:few years ago. Of course I
must confess that I fancied Mitchel], but
after seeing and comparing the pair before
the fightI concluded not to bet a centon
him. While he never said so, I am confident
Charley Knew all along that he was up
againsta hard game. Although game asa
pebble, Idon’tthink he would have made
much of a row if his namesake, Gov. Mitch-
ell, had succeeded in preventing the fight.

*“‘I was given to understand that Corbett
trained for the affair as he pleased. It was
said his punches lacked steam and amounted
to but little. Well, this might be true, but
excuse me from coming in contact with
any of them. If his appearance
after the fight can be taken fora criterion, I
don’t think Mitchell wants to stop any more
of them.

CAN WHIP JACKSON.

**Yes sir, Iam thoroughly convinced this
Californian can whip them all, including
Peter Jackson and Ed Smith. The latter
told meafter the fight that he was really
anxious to meet Corbett, but my advice to
himis stay away. The champion has more
confidence in himself now than heever had
before, and I expect to see him polish off
Jackson next June handily. Mitchell’s
cunning did not count. Corbett simply made
a hurricane fight and Charley was unable to
keep out of his way. Whether Jackson
will be able to do s0 remains to
be seen. My idea ig that he
won't, and the Californian will

soon have the refree counting the ten-second
limit when they come together. Bat Mat-
terson was greatly disappointed over the
result and informed mehe was ashamed to
return hometo Denver,’’ continued Allen.
‘*Bat declared right along that Corbett was
acur, but I have an !dea he has changed his

mind since Thursday. The Cor-
bett-Sullivan and Corbett- Mitchell
fights can hardly be compared.

sullivan cut out the work at New Orleans
and Corbett took his time finishing, and I
thought it was rather,in fact altogether, too
long. Thursday, however, he set sail] for
Mitchellin the second round and, blamed
me, bur whut a bloomin’ monkey he did
make him look like! If he had fought the
same way at New Orleans, Sullivan would
never have lasted anywhere near as long as
he did.’”’
ALLEN’S OX-TAIL JELLY.

Allen says his famous ox-tail jelly hardened
up Mitchell’s stomach all right, but Corbett
insisted upon pun@hing him in the face and

the true merit of the jelly was not in this
fight developed.

text:

Joe Goddard, the big Australlan, who was

Jake Kilrain aiso runs a saloon in Balti-
more, and Frank Slavin operates an innor

Bob Fitzsimmons, the middleweight cham-

weight champion, Jack McAuliffe, is very

McAuliffe is a well-Known character on thle

JacK Dempsey was the middleweight cham-

his own home near Boston, |

title: Robber found at Tom Allen’s saloon
text:
FOLEY IDENTIFIED.

Said to Be One of the Carroll Masked
Robbers.

John Carroll of 1626 North Broadway called
| at the Fourth ‘District Police Station, at
Tenth and North Market streets, this morn-
ing anc positively identified a suspect,
who calls himself John Foley, as one
of the three men who entered
his saloon last nightand robbed him and his
friends of $192and two gold watches in true
Western style. To Michael McGill, allas
**Midget.’” a young man who witnessed the
bold hoid-up and whocalled atthe station
this moraing with Oarroli, is due Foley’s
capture,

McGill was sitting behind the stove in Car-
| roll & Harrington’s saloon, on the southeast

andsohad a good opportunity to see them

rested him and took him back to the station,
but he stonutly denied his guilt. He claimed

that he did = not have a cent of
| money about him, but on be-
ing searched the police found
a $10 bill and a $5 bill in his inside pocket.
This made the m suspect they hadthe right

| Early this morningCapt. Kiely set special

this morning wore an expression
ofsupreme disgust. When seen he suriily

THE ROBBERY.

The robbery occurred at 9:20 o’clock last
evening and was a most audacious hold-up.
Dennis Spillane, Jerry McMahon and

the son of a neighboring shoemaker,
were playing cards ata tableinthe rear of
the saloon with Jonbn Carroll, one of the pro-
prietors, who was on watch. James Minogue
sat near the table reading the Post-
DISPATCH and Pete Mc Govern and

He yelled again, ‘Throw up your hands!’

a sack coat held Spillane and

after Carroll. He was a powerful, big man,
but Carroll tussied with him. The man with
the gupb, and who had a mustache
and wore an overcoat and a
cap, angrily said, “Get out of the
way tilil shoot; he’sthe fellow I'm after,’
referring to Carroll bya vile name. The bi
man threw Carroll over against the back
door and the saloon-keeper threw up his
hands. He with Spillane and Mc: ahon, who
had thrown uptheir hands, weretheld at bay
by the man with the gun while the lit-
tie fellow went through his two men
and gotu watch fromeachand the Dig fel-
low gotinto Carroll’s pocket and got $175.
Then he went behind the counter and robbed
the till of some $17, but failed to seea watch
which was lying on the shelf. Having se-
curedali the booty they were after, they
fied through the front door, the
man with the weapon keeping
his pistol leveled all the timeatthe card
players. As he went out the door he re-
marked, ‘If you—you I mean—pointing to
Carroll—foliow me out of here, Ill blow your
brains out.” With this the two disappeared.
We were too frightened to attempe to catch
them and so they got away safely.’’

the leader of the trio and to have known that

title: Allen writes letter to the editor
text:
TOM ALLEN.
| To the Editor of the Post-Dispatch:

Andy Bowen's seconds are to be cen-
sured for their failure to throw up
the sponge three rounds before their
man was sent down and out forever by
| George Lavigne. To my mind Bowen was
clearly whipped then. e might not have
showed outward evidence of the terrific
|} punishment administered him, but his
vitality was exhausted. In these glove con-
tests a man may be all but out, and still
it show little evidence of the fact, except to
an experienced eve. When a pugilist reaches
this stage, there is no use of prolonging the
battle and his seconds should surrender
for him. Had Bowen been fortunate
enough to have a man behind him who
understood his business, I believe he wouid
be still in the land of the living. When
Bowen went down, he was no doubt com-
pietely exhausted. Fresh air might have
relieved him, but it could not be gotten in
one of those inclosed fighting arenas. Thou-
sands of sjectators are packed inside,
smoking and chewing, and the atmos-
phere on 2 warm night is polluted like
sewer water. Inhaling such poison in
his lungs is anything but beneficial to an
unconscious man, especially after he has
received a drubbing like Bowen got from
Lavigne. 1 am a firm beHever in figchiting in
the open air, and if Bowen’s death puts 2
quietus on tegalized glove contests, the old-
time methods will come into vogue once
more. Bowen's death may affect the sport
for the ttme being, but if it. does it will be
only a temporary set-back. This talk about
pugilism being dead because the Louis-
iana authorities are expected to legislate
against it is all rot. Fighting flourished be-
fore the New Orleans’ clubs were ever
heard of, and it will continue to do so after
they have gene out of existence.

| THOMAS ALLEN,
Retired Champion of the World.

. Wrestling Match.

THE RETIRED CHAMPION TO FURNISH
HIS SIDE STAKE OF $250,

The Match to Be at the Lightweight
Limit, Any Style and the Winner to
Take All—Purse Offered in London for
Craig and Choynski or Creedon—
Sporting News and Gossip.

Tom Allen, the retired champion, an-
nounces his willingness to back Al. J. Neist
against Mike Mooney, in a wrestling match
any style, at the light-weight limit, for $250
a side. Neist is a boxer and wrestler, and
he is anxious to meet Moorey at either
game,

“There is no chance to pull off a fight
in any kind of shape around St. Louis now-
adays, however,” said Allen, “and for that
reason, I advised Neist to try and get
Mooney to wrestle him, I have great con-
fidence in Neist, and with proper handling
he will be a hard man to beat at his weight.
We have $250 ready to put up, any time
Mooney feels like making a match, and the

winner can take all, including the te re-
ceipts. Neist doesn’t want a cent if he can’t
win, and if Mooney wants a match, now is
his chance. He can have either style—
Graeco-Roman or catch-as-catch-can. All
we shall stipulate is that he get down to
the light-weight limit, and as he claims to
be in that class, both as a boxer and
wrestier, we expect no kick from him on
this point. Mooney, by the way, has done
more challenging and less boxing and wrest-
ling than any man in St. Louis, a the
ast year. If he is as anxious to do busi-
sess as he would have the public believe,
‘e should not hesitate any in accepting
Neist’s challenge. We are ready to post
our stake at any time.,and Neist will wrestle
within four weeks of signing articles.”

title: Pranks gone wrong at Allen’s bar
text:
HE THOUGHT IT FUN.

Matthew Groves Pulls Chairs From Un-
der the Wrong Men at the Wrong Place.

Mathew Groves, aged 40, who claims to
live at 115 North Second street, but who is
said to be a “hanger-on’’ at Tom Allen's
saloon on Market street, near Seventh,
walked into the Four Courts Friday morn-

ing at an early hour with a badly swollen
jaw. He said he had been asaulted without
provocation in Allen’s saloon. Inquiry by
the police revealed the fact that Groves
went into the saloon among a iot of the
“chair-warmers” and bégan to amuse him-
self by pulling chairs from under them.
Andrew Flynn, the bartender, first re-
quested Groves to stop, and when this had
no effect he went up to Groves and lan
his ht on the latter’s jaw, fracturing it
slightly. No arrest was made. Groves
was sent to the City Hospital.

title: Allen Roasts Modern Boxers
text:
MODERN BOXERS.

The.Retired Champion Says
They Are Not Fighters.

ONLY BUM PUGS AND POOR ACTORS.

Tom Alien, the retired champion pugilist
of the world, has decfded views on modern
pugilism, and the new school of fighters.
The veteran frequently refers to them as
bad actors. and bum pugs. The following
letter is characteristic:

THE ONLY CHAMPION’S REST.
To the Editor of the Post-Dispatch.
®I regard it as a duty to enlighten the
young and likewise mind the old about
the prize ring. There are a g _many of
the younger generation who do Not know
what a prize fighter is. They have never
seen anything but glove fighters in these
days. A prize-fighter is a fighter who bat-
ties with bare knuckles in the open air and
on the turf, regardless of hail, rain, sun-
shine or snow. A boxing champion, or
glove-fighter, is one who has feather pil-

TOM ALLEN.
lows on his hands when he enters the ring,
which must be in a warm, comfortable
room. In my time we had prize fights; now
there are boxing matches with top-heavy
purses hung up.

It has been said that I am not the retired
champion pugilist. After my fight with Joe
Goss in 1876 «6d went to Chicago
to box a week at one of the theaters, Mike
McDonald told me that Jem Mace, who was
also in Chicago, was going to answer my
challenge. I told Mike I would fight Mace
for $10 or as much more as Jem could raise.
I knew Mace was broke, and I did not
want to bluff him by naming a figure he
could not get. I wanted to have another
go at him. The upshot of it was that Mace
and I traveled together all over the coun-
try. I was billed and acknowledged as the
champion of the world, and Mace is the
ex-champion. I am the only pugilist who
ever left this country, open to fight any
man living. On my arrival in England I
beat all the best men of that country and
retired. I was then 39 years of age, and had
been in the ring nineteen years. I have
fought more battles than Jem Mace, Joe
Coburn, John C. Heenan and John Morris-
sey all put together.

The dirtiest deal I ever got, and I have
had some prétty hard ones, was in my
fight with Joe Goss. After I had been
robbed out of the fight and I got back
to Cincinnati, Johnny Dyer, one of Goss’
seconds, said he would fight me for $1,000.
He was just what I wanted, as he had
done me a great lot of dirt when I was
fighting Goss. We put up a $250 forfeit to
fight in four weeks, but he forfeited. That
was the last I heard of him until I was
across the water. Then I saw he was chal-
lenging any man in America. I was, mind
you, in England. Dave Kendal, Eph. Hol-
land, the referee, Black Edwards, a Cin-
cinnati newspaper man, and Red Leary, got
about $10,000 out of my fight with Goss,which
I was swindled out of on a claim of foul.
That was the first fight this man ‘“‘Macon,”’
as J. B. McCormack calls himself, ever saw.
He was on the Enauirer then. The reason
I mention his name is that he is giying his
opinions in the ‘papers about the prize ring
of thirty years ago, and comparing the
fighters of that time with the bum boxers of
to-day. There is John L. Sullivan, ‘Ma-
con’s’’ idol, and the greatest man he ever
saw fight. Let’s see what his opinion and
John L. Sullivan amount to. Billy Madden,
an old beer-slinger of mine, took Jack Sul-
livan to New York, and matched him
against a big dock-walloper named Flood.
They boxed on a barge, and Sullivan won.
He next beat Jimmy Elliott, a blind man,
that Charley Gallagher beat in two rounds
in 1868, when all the crooks from New York
broke into the ring. Jim Corbett, of Phila-
delphia, the partner of Dan Noble, who is
now doing twenty years in England, was
referee. 4

SO-CALLED CHAMPIONS.

Paddy Ryan called himself champion of
America by beating Joe Goss, who. was
never champion of anywhere, because
Johnny Dyer forfeited $250 to me at Cincin-
nati three days after my fight with Goss.
Dyer and Elliott fought for the champion-
ship of America. So I don’t see any man
that Sullivan ever met that was a cham-
pion. Charles Mitchell was never, cham-
pion ef England and never fought for that
title, but he had so much to say that you
would think he was champion of Jupiter
and this earth was too small to think about.

Then there was Tug Wilson, a man old
enough to be Sullivan’s father, and a 140-
pound man, The next man is Af Green-
field. He boxed Sullivan four rounds in
Boston. The papers said he could have
knocked Sullivan out, but he was afraid to
do so. This man Greenfield was working on
a canal near Birmingham, England, when 1
took him in hand. I showed him how to box,
but I could not learn him how to fight. J
got Greenfield to fight at Lord Lonsdale’s
estate. Tug Wilson was the other fellow.
The Prince of Wales and the gentlemen who
saw them fight with the bare knuckles were
disgusted. reenfield and Wilson are both
in Sullivan’s terrible record. Everybody
from St. Paul to San Francisco has beat
the Maori and Patsey Cardiff.

Then comes the biggest farce I ever saw
in my thirty-four years’ experience in the
prize ring. Sullivan and Kilrain pulled and
tugged at each other for over seventy
rounds. Sullivan stood in the middle of
the ring in the fiftieth round vomiting and
not able to move a foot. Kilrain asked him
to make a draw and would not go at him.
No man could call that fighting. Then Kil-
rain fell down, and this “‘greatest of pugi-
lists” deliberately jumped on him, not only
once, but twice. It was foul, but Sullivan
could not have lost if he had kicked Kil-
rain’s head off. Prof. Mike Donovan can
prove this. “‘Macon” calls this record a
world-beater. Then John turned actor and
went to Australia. Joe Goddard followed
him and challenged him in every town he
showed in. He got back to this country on
the bum and borrowed money to bring him
and his actors back. After three years of
acting he agreed to box Corbett. As he

DAN’S DEPARTURE,

Creedon and Party En Route to Galves-

Dan .Creedon, who is matched to fight
Herman Bernau at Galveston next Sat-
urday night, left last night at 11:30 for

don’s corner when the latter was defeated
by Fitzsimmons at New Orleans, will assist
Tom Tracey in handling him at Gaiveston,
Bat Masterson will be in his corner.

title: Two old fighters see Jim Corbett
text:
TWO OLD FIGHTERS.
SEE JIM CORBETT.

Tom Allen and Tom Kelly Discuss the Champion
Pugilist’s Physical Condition.

Two wise old prize fighters, who learned all that they know about fighters and
fighting righ: in the ring, have looked Jim Corbett over carefully, and declare him fit
to step into the ring to-morrow and fight for the championship of the world against all
comers. The decision was not arrived at offhand, nor was it givem at the request or
solicitation of Jim Corbett.

The two fighters whose verdict was obtained are Tom Allen, who was for years the
heavyweight champion of the world, and Tom Kelly, whose fame a8 a middleweight
was almost es great as that of Tom Allen. They are both old men now, hale and
hearty, but long past active work in the ring. They both are running prosperous saloons
on Market street, between Sixth and Seventh streets, Allen having in addition a concert
hall, over which he himself presides every night.

At the request of the Post-Dispatch the old champions consented to inspect Cor-
bett and give their candid, unbiased opinions of him. They had seen him at other times
—on the stage, in the ring and at private exhibitions. Allen had seen him whip Kilrain,
Mitchell and finally Sullivan. Kelly was master of ceremonies at a private exhibi-
tion Corbett gave two or three years ago at the Exposition Music Hall. They, there-

fore, know the man well, and are able to make a fair comparison between his condition

young champion was making a most favorable impression on the two old ones.

When he first stepped on the stage’ Kelly said to Allen:

“Tom, doesn’t he look a bit Jight?’’

“Hit’s the bloomin’ military jacket he has as does it,”’ said Allen, and they became
silent again, watching the show with renewed interest.

any defects if there were any existing. Every blow he struck McVey was watched
as if something important depended upon it.

Both men were convinced that Corbett is a better man to-day than he ever was,
and that all stories about his being out of condition were unfounded. They both fur-

Exciting amateur contests are expected

In the athletic events the smallest field

rider in St. Louis, and Miss Tottie Shaw,
her most dangerous rival. The other three
ladies do not expect to be able to finish in
front of them.

A special feature will be a foot race be-
tween teams of six each from the schools
of St. Bridget, St. Malachy and St. Law-
rence O'Toole. The six best sprinters from
each school will compete in a 220-yards
| dash for gold medals. Some of the eracks
who will compete in the runs are J. Lewis
Holland, Walsh, Withers, Bland and Gib-
bons of the Christian Brothers’ College
and Dillon, the champlon of Washington
University, who took off the honors at the
recent Washington University field day.
He is a former St. Louis University and
| Georgetown College man, and is in the
Washington Law School.

The entries closed last Saturday, and at

WILL FIGHT ANY MAN.

——e aes

‘Denver Ed” Smith Ambitious to Mix
With the Top-Notchers.

“T never was much of a hand at fighting
in the newspapers, but I will fight any man

in the world, bar none.”
This is the declaration made by ‘“‘Denver

Fd” Smith, one of the top-notchers among
pugilists, whom Tom Allen and many people
believe can eat up and spit out Sharkey
or Maher or whip either Corbett or Fitz-
simmons, Goddard or any of the other upper
lights of the heavyweight class. Smith is
a big, stout fellow, with all his front teeth

missing as a memento of one of his fights.
He doesn’t look much out of condition, and
would probably find it easy to get down to
fighting trim.

Whatever his ring tactics may be he isa
pugilist of the Tom Allen, John L. and old-
time school when it comes to his conversa-
tion, and he doesn’t use the impid English
of “Gentleman Jim.” |

He refers to other prize fighters as ‘‘guys,”’
“stiffs,"’ ‘“‘blokes’’ and ‘‘dead uns,”’ and his
sentences would have to be quarantined
and disinfected before they would pass in
public society. Smith came from Pittsburg,
and in a week he will go to California via)
Hot Springs, accompanied by his brother, |
Pattie, a lightweight pugilist, who also
aims high.

“I am matched to fight Jeffreys, who
trained Corbett for his Fitzsimmons fight.
It will take place in _Octuber before the
Olympic Club of San Francisco for a purse
of $3,000. I’ll fight any man in the world
for all of the purse, and my brother Pattie
will fight any lightweight in the world bar
Kid Lavigne. He has good backing and
will* be staked for any amount by Bill
Stekle of Chicago and Dominick O’ Malley
ot New Orleans. He has been sick, but he
is better now than he ever was.

“Il have had two big iights lately and did
not lose either time on merits.

“In California I fought Choynski and
ought to have won easy. The referee gave
us the same instructions that Corbett and
Fitzsimmons had—that we could hit in
clinches and break-aways with ene hand
free. I did it and rapped Choynski two or
three times in breaks, and the crowd hol-
lered ‘“tholy murder,’ and, I believe, would
have broke into the ropes at me. Then
Choynski used his head and butted me
twice. Then I went to fighting in his fashion
and put my nut into his wind. You never
heard such a squeal as went up from the
crowd. They yelled foul so Many t-mes and
so loud that the referee gave the decision
against me. I should have won.

“My defeat by Goddard was also unex-
pected. 1 whipped him in New Orleans in
eighteen rounds, before the Olympic Club,
when Tom Allen handled me, and I thought
him so easy that I took a Jong trip to South
Africa to get on a match with him. If Allen
had been handling me I would have won. As
it was, I was careless in training, somewhat
reckless, and just before the fight go: a
touch of the weakening African fever. [ lost
the fight to him in four rounds. He is a tre-
mendous big fellow, stands 6 feet 2 inches in
the ring and weighs, as he walks around,
260 pounds. !

“Tl am after a fight with Sharkey and we
might be able to get a good purse in the
West. After his recent break with Maher)
he would have trguble in getting a purse in.
the East. I am not out after Maher, for we
belong to what might be called the same
Stable. Fitz is a better man than Corbett.
I don’t think Fitz will ever fight again, un-
less he meets Goddard for the worla’s cham-
pionship. The fighters are ail glad that Cor-
bett was put out. That stiff was a hog and
would never give another man a chance. He
was after the almighty dollar all the time,
and made it easier than any other pugilist
ever did. By whipping Sullivan, when any
other man could have done it, he got up. He
stayed up by whipping Mitchell, who wag
then the worst kind of a has-been. When he
first met a real good man he got whipped.

“In all my fights I have never found any
soft spots and have always had to fight up
hill. George La Blanche. the Marine, was the
lightest man I ever met in the ring, and he
was six pounds heavier than I.

“IT have backing and am ready to meet
any man in the world."

title: John Sullivan is running for Mayor of Boston with Allen’s support
text:
JOHN L. FOR MAYOR,

SULLIVAN WILL SURELY RUN
FOR THAT OFFICE IN BOSTON
THIS FALL.

PRIZE FIGHTERS IN POLITICS.

The Big Fellow Not the First Grad-
uate From the Ring to
the Rostrum.

Special to the Post-Dispatch.

BOSTON, Aug. %.—John L. Sullivan will
run as an independent candidate for Mayor
of Boston this fall with the added intention,
if not himself elected, of defeating Mayor
Josiah Quincy, who will be the regular
Democratio candidate for re-election.

When Mayor Quincy refused to shake
hands with John L. Sullivan, a native of
Boston, at Oarsman Ten Byck’s reception
in Feneull Hall, he comnmitted what may
prove to be a fatal political mistake. Sul-
livan was dumfounded. According to one
of the Mayor’s official organs, the big

fighter was easily the idol of the occasion,
The crowd chased and cheered him. Ten
kyck was almost ignored at times,

Sullivan's amazement at the slight Rog
wpon him by Mayor Quincy gradually
changed to anger, and this anger has be-
come vindictiveness.

At first, after thinking the matter over,
be was inclined to content himself with
supporting an anti-octopus nominee like
Mr. Wardner or Judge Sianker. Now he
has crossed the Rubicon and put hie foot
through the bridge timbers.

John L. Suliivan will now ask the sup-
port of his fellow citizens at the polls. At
one t.me he could have gone to Congress,
but he declined. Then his professional du-
ties were in the way. Now he feels that
he can spare the time to serve his towns-
gen.

There is nothing unprecedented about Sul-
livan announcing himself a candidate for
Mayor of even so staid and steady a town
a@s boston

The prize ring has brought better men
than Sullivan io the front in politics.

The Sullivan-Kilrain fight—which took

lace at Richburg, Miss., eight years ago—

rought to the front the best Mayor, New
Orleans has ever had.

Who that was there will ever forget that
fearful day in July?

The trip to the battle ground was an all-
night one, and St. Louis was weil repre-
sented in the big crowd which made the
journey.

Tom Allen and Tom Kelly were there, and
f0 were Fred Watkins and Jake Esher, who
are now fighting their battles in another
land. Abe Slupsky was there, too, with
Dan, Charley and John Daly. So, too, was
Bob Farrell. Those of the St. Louis arose
who are still in the land of the living wil
recall the one startling incident before the
fight. Its managers had charged $10 for
tickets to Richburg and when the crowd
reached there it was announced that an-
other charge of $5 would be made for seats
around the ring.

“Don't pay it,"’ shouted a brawny, broad-
ehouldered man, as the crowd from the
train surrounded the ring only to be con-
fronted with the deenand for the extra $%.
“Don't pay it. Be men. Stand out against
this highway robbery. They have already
charged $10 for a ride in a cattle car. Now
they propose to hold us up for another $%.
Follow me men. Let us take charge here.”

All that crowd needed was a leader.

The strange man led and the mob fol-
lowed. There were none there so bold as
to dare to bar the way of that army.
When it was seated and quiet and order
restored there were cries for a referee, but
no one dared accept the place.

The men suggested for the position by
Sullivan's friends were noi to the Kilrain
men’s liking. It looked as though there
would be no fight owing to the absence of
a referee, when Tom Kelly of St. Louis
shouted: ‘There's a man there that would
make a good referee. What's the matter
with him?”

All hands looked at the individual whom
Kelly had singied out of the motley gather-
ing. They recognized him as the brawny
fellow of the few moments before who had
led them into the ring and helped them hold
possession of it. Like Kelly, too, they
recognized him as the man for the place,
and from one end of the ring to the other
the welkin rang with cries of ‘‘Yes, yes,
he’s the man; he'll do.”

The brawny fellow was cornered. He
etood his ground for a. moment, begged in
@ manly way to be excused, and then, as
the mob thundered its demand, he capitu-
lated and took up his plece in the roped
arena.

The fight was for the championship of all
the world. A king’s ransom depended on
the issue. But here to decide the great
points of the contest was chosen @ man
unknown to those who had the great battle
in charge and unknown to the vast army
of sports who had come from all corners of
the world to see it.

But the unknown proved the best in all
the wide world for the place. Only once
Was one of his decisions questioned. That
was when Pony Moore, one of Kilrain’s
backers, said: ‘tHe has money on the
fight.”’

Then there was a pause in the proceed-
nes. The referee stopped the fight just
ong enough to look Moore in the face and
to say, “Take that back!"

Moore took it back, and so quickly that
the crowd around the ring side scarcely no-
ticed the interruption.

The man who refereed that fight by his
@ingle bold act leaped from obscurity into

|
|

Mational notoriety. He gained for himself
in a single hour the reputation of being a
man of nerve and good judgment and that
in the south means everything.
That notoriety made John Fitzpatrick the
best known man in New Orleans and a
ear after the Suillivan-Kilrain fight had
aken place this same John Fitzpatrick was
elected Mayor of the Crescent City.
It has often been said since that he was
the best Mayor, New Orleans has ever had.
But Fitzpatrick is not the only man who
ba See ihe from the prize ring into politi-
Jo! Morrissey of Troy, N. , (
who beat Heenan and who aut ines
Sullivan that historic battle in the long ago
had a seat tn Congress once and held it
down henorably and well. The old English
champion, John Gully, was a member of
the Eritish Parliament
of his life, and there are others beside he
and Morrissey and Fitzpatrick who were
@raduated from the prize ring into the
political arena Why with sueh precedent
therefore, hasn't the only Sully, the man |
whom James Boyle O’Relliy, the Boston |
poet, immortalized as the apotheosis of the
prize ring, the right to aspire to the highest
office within the gift of the people of -Bos-
ton. And if not, why not? /

Tom Allen was born in Birmingham, Eng-
land, in 1810. fle °s 5 fett S inches tall and
when he was in the ring his fighting weight
was 17% pounds. Allen began his pugilistic
career in the old country in 1861. He fought
several stiff battles, including a draw with
Joe Ge in March, 1867. He came to this
country in the following July, and,in the
very first ring event in which he partici-
pated a revolver and threats to kill played
star parts.

Allen had been selected to second Témmy
Kelly of Baltimore in a finish fight with
Billy Parkinson of Pottsville, Pa. The mill
took place at Acquia Creek, Vermont. The
fight was for a $2.62 purse. Parkinson was
feared by the hackers of Kelly, and a large
crowd of thugs and bullies accompanied
Kelly from Baltimore and Philadelphia. It
Was arranged between them to start a row
if the referee didn’t give the fight to their
man. Willfam E. Harding, then sporting
editor of a New York daily, and afterward
prominent through h‘'s connection with a
sporting weekly published on pink paper,
was the referee.

From the first round Parkinson began to
hand it up to Kelly so cleverly that Tom
Allen went wild. Before the signal to start
the wrangle he putled forth a long navy

| pistol and announced that he would kiil

Harding !f Kelly ddn’t get the decision on
alleged fouls. Kelly’s friends crowded
around the referee and for a moment it
looked as though Harding would be kitled.
Alien, who led the crowd, was desperate
to the point of doing murder. But Harding
would not be intimidated. and Allen, fol-
lowed by this rufifianly mob, cut the ropes
and carried Kelly out of the ring. Park:n-
son was, of course, declared the winner.

Allen’s first battle in America was with
Bill Davis. The fight was pulled off on
Chouteau Island, near St. Louis, Jan, 12,
1869. Allen wonin 43 rounds. He next tried
on Charle Gallagher of Cleveland, the fight
taking place on Carroll Island, near /St.
Louis, the following Feb. 24. Allen was
lacd low after a terrific three minutes of
fighting.

Mike McCoole of St. Louis and Allen
fought on Foster's Island, July 15, for a
$10) purse and all of the excursion money.
A great crowd of St. Louisans went to see
the mill, and they saw Allen give his ad-
versary a mighty whaling. They also saw
a bloody free-for-all riot started by the
MecCoole crowd. Clubs were wielded, while
the referee was besieged by angry brutes
armed with murdgrous weapons, who sav-
agely demanded a decision in favor of the
helpless, shapeless bleeding mass of hu-
manity who had been a chopping block for
Allen. These rows were characteristic of
almost every fight Allen ever had.

Allen afterwards took on Charley Galla-
gher a second time, defeating him on Fos-
ter’s Island, Aug. 17, 1869. The crowd in-
terfered as ustial and Gallagher was de-
elared the winner, though fairly whippel.

Allen's best known fight was with Jem
Mace at Kinnerville, near New Orieans,
La., May 10, 1870. Sporting men from all
over the country congregated to witness
the fight. It was a short and bloody
battle. Mace was too much for Allea and
won the $5000 prize in ten rounds.

Joe Coburn declined to fight Allen and
Mike MecCoole was accommodated with a
second contest. They fought on Chouteau
Isiand, Sept. 23. 1873. Allen made quick
work of McCoole, punishing him so brutal-
ly thac the spectators begged McCoole’s
seconds te take him out of the ring,

Alien’s last fight was with the famous
Joe Goss for the championship of America
and $2000. The fight took place in Boone
County, Ky., in 1876. After 21 rounds Goss
was declared winner on a foul. After the
fight Allen was arrested and jailed in that
State on a charge of prize fighting. He
was released on bond, jumped his bond and
went to England. After a year on the other
side, which he put in on the race tracks,
he returned to this country and he then
created something of a sensation in New
York by offering to fight John L. Sullivan,
After issuing that challenge, which never
bore fruit, Allen returned to St. Lou's and
opened his saloon on Market st.

Soon after his return his Kentucky bonds-
men appeared here with requisition papers
for his arrest as a fugative from justice.
Allen’s lawyers secured his release by writ
of habeas corpus which was argued before
Judge Claiborne in the Court of Criminal
Correction. On hearing the testimony the
court ordered Allen’s release and his Ken-
tucky bdndsmen returned home without
their man. Allen’s last appearance in any
ring as a ‘boxer was on July 4, 1884, at
Union Baseball Park when he and Tom
Kelly boxed four friendly rounds.

TRUE BILLS CHARGE MURDER.

Tom Allen, Former Champion Pugilist,
and Ex-Detective Jack Williams
Among the Accused.

Ex-Detective Jack Williams and ex-Cham-
pion. Pugilist Tom Allen were indicted for
murder Wednesday afternoon by the grand
jury.

Williams is charged with killing Edward
Kassebaum and ‘‘Bud”’ Pearce at Natural
Bridge road and Grand avenue before a poll-
ing place during the Republican primary.
A warrant charging murder in the second
degree was issued against him and his pre-
liminary hearing is still pending in the
Court of Criminal Correction. He was re-
leased en a $000 bond. «

Allen shot Tim Confoy to death in h's
Saloon recently during a quarrel. He was
arrested and given a preliminary hearing
in the Court of Criminal Correction, after
which he was discharged, his plea being
self-defense.

The final report of the grand jury was
brief. Concealed weapons are held respon-
Sible for the majority of crimes and a
rigid enforcement of the law against carry-
ing them is recommended. Disreputable sa-
loons and the winerooms are arraigned and
branded as the most dangerous institutions
operated under the protection of the law.
The Excise Commissioner is requested to
revoke the license of every saloon that is
not operated in a strictly legal manner. and
effective measures for suppressing the wine-
rooms are Suggested.

STRANGER’S SKULL FRACTURED

Fell Downstairs at Tom Allen’s
Saloon—Musician Arrested.

Edward Hodo of Granite City. Ill... re-
ceived serious injury early yesterday morn-
ing at Tom Allen's saloon, at No. 619 Mar-
ket street. He is now at the City Hospital
suffering from a fracture of the skull.

Officer Schleifstein of the Central Police
District saw Hodo fall down a flicht of
Stairs at the saloon at 1:40 o'clock yester-
day morning. Hodo alighted upon his
head and was rendered unconscious. A
moment after Hodo had fallen, Jesse Gar-
raher, a musician employed in the saloon,
cume down the stairs. The poiiceman
placed him under arrest pending investiga-
tion of the case.

Hodo was tuken to the hospital. but for
a long time could not talk. When he recov-
ered consclousness he stated that he had
come to St. Louis Saturday evening, and
had been drinking before he entered Tom
Allen's place. He would not say how he
happened to be upstairs at the Allen sa-
loon, and in response to queries whether
he had been fighting with anybody or had
been shoved down the stairs, he replied
that he “could not remember.”

Carraher said that a man named “Red”
had told him that there was a drunken
man in a room above the salocn. He avers
that he went up to investigate, but that, he
had no sooner reached the room when the
drunken man reeled out and fell down the

stairs.

VETERAN TOM ALLEN
CONFINED TO HIS BED

Noted Pugilist of Former Days At-
tacked by Severe and Per-
sistent Colds.

WAS CHAMPIONSHIP CANDIDATE

Met the Celebrated Jem Mace for
Heavy-Weight Title—Santora
Gives Much Promise as
a Boxer.

Tom Allen, the veteran pugilist who won
the first battle in England ever fought un-
der Queensberry rules, and who was for
years considered the strongest candidate
for the heavyweight championship of the
world, is lying sick at his home on Mar-
ket street between Sixth and Seventh, and
is believed to be seriously ill.

Peristent coids, which have cling to him,
for the last two or three weeks, and which
have confined him to his bed, are respon-
sible for his condition. Although he has
improved in the laet day or two and hopes
to be about again shorily, his sickness has
reduced him considerably and has caused
him considerable pain.

The veteran hag been complaining of
pains in the regions where his opponents’
punches landed in years gone by, and states
that his arms, ribs and stomach region have
been throbbing where they sustamed pun-
ishment in his battles of the past.

Ailem Was a representative fighter of the
old school and of the bygone bare-knuckle
days. Ile started his ring career when 71
years oid, in 1868, and for eighte>n j}ears
he was a prominent factor among the fore-
most men in his class. Born in 1539, he
took up the ring rather later than do most
of the pugilists nowadays, and he continued
at the game until his celeorated battle for
the championship of England, when ke
Knocked out Charlie Davis in five rounds.

This was the first champlonship battle
fought in England under Queensberry rules.
As a reward he received a purse of f19
and a massive silver cup, emblematic of the
title, which now hangs over his bar.

In 1867 he fought the then celebrated Joe
Goss for the heavy-weight championship,
the bout ending in a rict and Allen’s sec-
onds being mobbed. In 1870 he fought Jem
Mace in Louisiana for the heavy-weight
championship and a purse of $5,000, Allen's
seconds throwing up the sponge at the end
of ten rotnds, after Tom had injured his
arm. The bout lasted fifty minutes.

Allen's re tay around this city are well
remembered, especially his battles with
Mike McCool on Bloody Island He beat
McCoo] there in seven rounds,

Don Murphy, manager of Allen's p
stated that he believed the veteran woul
be out again soon, but that the effects of
his illness had told on him considerably.

Nick Santora, who defeated Sport Sulll-
van in the chor pattie’ | at the est Hind
Club last Thursday, will be one of the at-
tractions in the preliminaries next week,
when Jeffries and Fitzsimmons appear
here. Santora displayed great cleverness in
his battle. and the boy seems to be about
as promising a youngster as there 1s in
the ring at his weight.

Dominick has none of the clumsiness
usually apparent in boys of the 105-pound
division and thereabouts, but handles both
his feet and hands well. He has footwork
down to a finer point than Sullivan, and
undoubtedly is one of the hardest men eat
his weight ever here.

He is now not quite 17 years old, and
has been fighting little more than a year.
He has lost bul one battle and forfeited
one on a foul. All his bouts, save that of
last Thursday, have been fought in Chi-
cago. His record to date is: Knocked out
ony Sorensen in four rounds; knocked
out Young Slasher in four rounds; knocked
out Neil Simons, four rounds; drew with
Carl Walters, six rounds; lost on foul to
George Quinn, five rounds; drew with Geo.
Quinn, six rounds; knocked out Danny Gil-
len, one round; drew with Frank Lucas,
six rounds; knocked out Neil Simons, two
rounds; lost to Cooney Kelly, six rounds;
won .from Frank ucas, six rounds;
knocked out Buddy Glover, three rounds;
won from Sport Sullivan, eight rounds.

Hugo Kelly, who won from Mike Schreck
Thursday, will depart to-night for Chi-
cago, thence heading for West Baden. Jake
Chain, who represented him here. has a
bantam named Johnny Kelly in his care
and has issued a challenge to Harry
Forbes for a bout at that welght. Ac-
cording to Chain, Hertz has promised to
let Forbes meet Kelly before the Tokell
bout and to make Harry weigh in at 115
pounds.

(hain is also representing-Tommy Love,
one of the 118-pounders of the East, who is
now in Chicago.

The open-air battles, even when fought in

The loss of this edge of speed removes

“What do you want?" he demanded in

, Zen was the only man in the history

' of the ring during the time when no gloves

He was defeated by Jem Mece in a ten-

Tom Allen. while he had been one of the

had a wife living in Birmingham, Eng-

’s place on Market street, which |
ago was given thé name of “The
pion’s Rest” and the headquarters of

the most notorious resorts in the city, not
that it is in any way dangerous, but that
it is the resting place of a large number of
the city’s unfortunates who have no means
with which to secure a place to rest.

For years “Old Tom,” as his patrons were
wont to style him, personally conducted the
affairs of the “Champion's Rest.” His char-
acteristic was to preside over the
plano and direct the concert which took
place nightly.

Six weeks ago, when Allen took to his

When his condition became serious he was
removed to the Baptist Hospital From
the time he was taken there until his death

\ Tom Allen was born at Birmingham, |

fight was fifty rounds with Bob Smith, June
2, 1864. when he was defeated.

Allen fought eleven important fights tn |
Wngland. He came to America as the
champion of England in 1869. On May 1.
187, Ee was beaten by Jem Mace for the
championship of the world in a ten-round
contest, but regained the title on Septem-
ber 2, 1873, when he defeated Mike McCvol

Allen fought several battles in which he
was robbed either of the money or the
decision. On two occastons the friends of
his adversaries broke into the ring and
forced the champion to give in, the threat
being made th revolvers and other

weapons.
‘adorning the back bar of the “Rest”, is
a silver cup which was presented to Allen
in England. It is known as the “Champion
Boxing Cup of England.” ‘Tne champion
led the cup as the greatest treasure

jen returned to England in 1877, where
he defeated Charlie Davis for the cham-
of England in five rounds. His

fight was on March 1, 1879, when he

Ho then came to America and locating |

in St. Louls opened a saloon. which he

| TOM KELLY TALKS ABOUT

Tom Kelly, who rins a saloon on Market

er of Allen. Keily was here when Afien

WAS GAME FIGHTER.

“I saw the first and the last battle that

_The last fight Allen e sed in in the].
United States was with Joe Goss. whom ||
he had previous'y defeated in England.

| Goss's friends outnumbered those of Allen,
| and the referee, it is claimed, favored Al-

The fight was tor $2500 a siCe—the largest | |
amount that had ever been wagered on a | '
prize fight up to that time. The fight took | |

rounds. In this round Allen landed a blow |

immeciately rushed into the ring and
Claimed a foul.

According to the Allen version of the
story the referee. being a friend of Goss. <l-

thorities admitted that Al'en had fairly won

The most noteworthy battle that Allen

to kill hizn.

Alen foucht his last battle with Jim
Stewart in 187. in England. Allen was vic-
ltor. The stakes were £0 a side. The fight |

| lasted fifty-five minutes.

Allen, of late years, was a great pugilistic
rrognomicator. Before a championship bat-
tle many followers of the ring would go to
) him to seek his opinion as to the winner.

PICKED SULLIVAN TO WIN.

In 1839. when Sullivan apd Kilrain were
matched to fight for the world’s cham-
vionship Allen was arked for an opinion
/@s to the outcome. The veteran pugilist
mnade a reply that was quoted all over the
Tnited States. He said: “‘Kilrain couldn't
whip Sullivan with a baseball bat.”

Tom Alien, the Pagilist, Dies.

St. Louis, April 6,—Tom Allen, re-
tired heavyweight pugilist of the
world, whe for the past 25 years has
conducted a small saloon here, died
yesterday from general debility. He
was born in Birmingham, Eng., April
23, 1839. Allen won his laurels in the
days of bare fist fighting and hore
the title of being the only pugiliet
who lost the world’s championship,
regained it and retired with it.

title: Passing of ‘Champions Rest’ the dingy place of late Tom Allen
text:
PASSING OF “CHAMPION'S REST; THE
DINGY PLACE OF LATE“70M’ ALLEN

‘TOM” ALLEN AS HE WAS THE LAST YEARS OF HIS LIFE—A NIGHT SCENE IN “CHAMPION’S RESI.”|

waa
Me MAL Ain

Tene ERE
“Champion's Rest” will soon be no more.
The dingy, wretched, forbidding looking

shop at 615 Market etreet,/ where former

Champion Pugilist Tom Allen held iron

sway for 21 years, known to followers of

the fighting game in two continents as the
heme of an oracle on ths sport, and to

many thousand drifting ‘“hoboes” as a

hcuse to cha’k with a credit mark, will

shortiy follow its presiding genius into ob-
livion, sc far as tha general public is
concerned.

Its name will be retained, but announce-
ments made by those into whose hands the
dead fPugilist's assets will fall are to the
effect that the place will be altered, im-
Froved and brought up to date. Gilt and
tinsei will be introduced where once every-
thing was as plain as the leg of a kitchen
table—made so to suit the whim of the
proprietor. Alterations will only mean the
tocal effacement of one of the ‘city's land-
marks.

Certainly if the deaa champion, out in
Bellefontaine Cemetery, could have a voice
in the matter, not a chair would be moved,
not a chromo on the dingy wall changed,
not an improvement made, except, perhaps,

to renew the datly distributign of clean

sand on the floor.

Nor, if those were consulted who followed
the hearse to the cemetery Wednesday
hard-faced, deep- ;

, ep-chested rgen of the stripe
of Allen himsel?, would there be any vote
for a change. The establishment bore the
Stamp of Allen himself and for this it was
known and in its way appreciated.

Loudest in the protest against change will

be the flotsam of humanity that Allen was
wont to harbor on cold nights, and that he
undemonstratively benefited for 20 years.
_ For these it was not merely a place where
amusement could be purchased cheaply, but
a haven when the winter winds pierced bit-
ingly through threadbare garments and
diligent search of pockets revealed a melan-
choly emptiness of wherewithal. Grimy, al-
most as themselves, the Champion's Rest
invited them then. “Improved” it will be
no place for them.

The Memories
Will Remain. ‘
Though its identity as representative of

the man Allen will be lost with th
to-date’ improvements contemplat
memory of “Champion's Rest,” as it Is
today, will be difficult to efface.

For nearly a quarter century it has stood,
one Vg the unique places of its kind In the

ago, and indeed today,
to Allen’s place paused
before enteri .

pe oe
ree

-unshaven workmen, and even men whom
the pelice might have been glad to get a
second sight of.

But then, as now, Allen’s place was
much worse looking than it was in reality.
In all the score or more years of its ex-
istenca the place his never figured much
in police annals. ;

It has never been considered a dangerous
place for anyone toenterand Allen always
thought himself in honor bound to protect
his guests from possible troub‘e. Thieves
he could not tolerate and drove them from}
his establishment &@s soon as their eenae 4

was made known.

Once the prospective visitor had made
up his mind to enter the place and cross |
the threshold, he found himself in the
“tap room," as Allen was wont to refer to
it. On the right was the dingy walnut
counter with a mirror in back, in front of
which was PDP we 4 the cup emblematic of
AHlen’s Engli ampionship victory. On
the left was a row of stalls.

Beyond was the concert hall, still main-
tained as such. In the northwest corner
was the prize ring in which bouts of some
sort, many of them desperate, were held
nightly. On the opposite side of the hall
was a raised platform on which was
‘placed the piano.

He Was Master
of Ceremonies.

| Near this was a table at which the cham-
jon himself sat with a small gavel in

hand and a black skull cap on his head,
directing the evening's entertainment.

He was referee of all fights, director of

the musical entertainment and arbitrator
ef all diffictilties that might arise. In the
early days of the establishment these were
not a few.
_ Whenever two guests thought it neces-
sary to throw a few hot words and get
violent, Tom promptly rapped his gavel.
At once the waiters dropped their tasks
and flocked to thie scene of action, where
the comPatants were separated, gloves
tied on their hands, and they were told to
climb into the ring and have their argu-
‘ment out there

This had a triple advantage; it offset
police interference, ended the difficulty to
the satisfaction of the ieved parties
and afforded infinite entertainment to the
spectators.

AS soon as one or the other of the com-
batants signified that his honor was
ave dor that he had had about all he
could stand at one taking, the ring was
cleared and the concert permitted to pro-
ceed

;
|
|

Sometimes the encounters were desperate
and savage, however. A few vears after
‘Allen had opened his place, Tom Kelly
onened a similar groggcery in the same
block, while Danny Daly, father of sév-
eral pugilistic celebrities. opened a place
around the corner on Sixth street.

The rivalry for patronage between these
three places was intense, and each had its
coteric of followers, most of whom were
pugtiists, ready to ret at the batti of
an evelld, and at all times ready to uphold
the claims of thelr respective ostabiieh-

ments.

The bitterness thus engendered resulted
in ee brawls, saloon fights and ring
combats.

f= ce Be 744

1 scrap. That

=—/ | SF
out after a vicior
Was later, in i892.

Even old Tom himself. though he was
long out of the game, occasionally took a
hand in the fray. Once or twice the enemy,
primed with raw spirits dared to invade
the old lion in his lair and proceeded to
heap abuse on him. Then Allen proceeded
to show his championship form and put
the enemy out bodily.

Once the tables were turned on him, and,
in an attempted invasion of Dan Daly's
| ‘joint, a fight occurred in which he and
Daly had it hammer and tongs clear out
into the street. Daly whipped Allen—
about the tmly cecasion in which the
|champion ever finished second after leaving |
| the ring. i

With constant brawling and scrapping to!
enliven it this feud, growing more bitter
each year, lasted until the death of Daly
in 18%. It {s natural to suppose that, under
the circumstances, AlJen would have been
glad rather thgn otherwise that his ancient
enemy had been finally disposed of. Such
Was not the case, however. It was char-
acteristic of the man that he was one of
the first to go to Daly's relatives, follow-
ing the news of the death. and offer his
services and substantial aid in money.

With Daly ,the feud died. and the wane
of the prize fighting feature of the “Cham-
pion's Rest’ began. There were fewer occa-
sions for fights, and, who knows, perhaps
even the old champion himself wearled of
continual turmoil, broil and unrest.

Fighting was far from being the sole
feature of the establishment, however, in
the earlier days. Allen was a lover of mu-
sic. In a way it was a sort of PR: radox of
nature, for, in the ring as a fighter, he is
said to have beer one of the most savage
and vicious men who ever fought under
London prize ring rules. He had to be
killed to be beaten, and it was his bulldog
tenacity of purpose that pulled him
through on top of many engagements.

Ballads Were
His Delight.

His appreciation of, tender ballads, rol-

licking songs and even classical music was
of the keenest and in his later days he
would rather listen to a song than sce
a prize fight. Almost the first thing he
purchased when he fitted up his place was
the piano—the same one that now wheezes
out popular and mournful airs under the
fingers of the gray-haired veteran who
for 15 years has rformed the service of
“musical director” under Allen's guidance.
In appearance the ‘Rest’ presents
practically the same features. accord-
ing to the testimony of the “Belfast Chick-
en,” Tom Kelley and others in a_ position
to speak authoritatively, as It cid when
first opened, nearly a quarter of a cen-
tury ago. The same furniture, a -—
less highly polished, supports the Pr;
tables have taken the place of stalls in the
front room, and the my ring. once a fea-
ture of the concert hall, removed. few
more fly specks serve to half-obliterate the
pictures of fights and fighters on the wails,
the piano fs a trifle more cracked in voice,
but the general aspect of the place is the
same as Of yore.

re of the establishmen
chuawed qrondertally, soem pee
Gayot tues Geter at ty
it was the home of fish

laid t

Sites. es

he foundations of that proletarian ad-
miration which made him an idol with the
mmoner classes.

“Sie made for his establishment and h's
entertainments an ironclad code. If broken
he employed physical means to call atten-
tion to it. though he avoided fisticuffs when-
lever he could. His conduct of his concerts
was with an assumption of dignity that
would have been laughable had it net been
{n deadly earnest, as many found who
| came to scoff.

'Concert Was

a Ceremony.

Gradually he impressed the idea upon the
regulars of the establishment that a con-
cert was a ceremony and not a performanc:.
Its unvarying routine bore out this ea.
As often as one went to the place the code
never changed, save for incidental inter-
ruptions foreign to the program, such
as the suppression of an obstreperous on.,
or the substitution of a new musical num-
ber for a wornout one.

‘Allen had a good idea of economy and he
practiced it in his place. The parties
who rendered concert numbers, when not
occupled in trying to drown the rattie of
the plano, were engaged in the role of
waiters. Most of them were broken-down
Englishman, some from the stage or con-
cert halls. others from various walks of
life and all of whom had been brought low
Toke pianist, whose real name perhaps was
known to Allen alone, but whose playing
and voice has been heard by thousands in
the fifteen years he remained in Allen's
employ, rose above the dignity of waiter,
and he looked the part. His especial forte
was singing ‘Annie Laurie” in a deep bass
yoice, with a tender quality to it that
wrung an unconscious sigh from more tha n
one homeless, tattered wanderer. with
heaven knows what histories hidden be-
neath the outer grime, who was profiting by
the privilege of getting warm near the big
cannon stove in the corner,

Alien was accustomed to announce this
number with peculiar unction: Mr. Me-

The fight was attended with many excft-

Jem.Mace brought Goes to the country

trained in this city. Goes prepared himeecif

joy the fresh country alr. Alien, it is said,

his time chatting with friends who came
from Cincinnati to see him “work” and in-|

The day of battle arrived.

It was early on the morn of September 7

move about. In the resorts around town

Eph Holland was the busiest man in

train which was to be run to the battle

and giving instructions. The sports were
told to be at the Little Miami Depot, at

When Holland and the backers of the men

adjoining County of Boone, and there on a
level piece of farming land the fight waz

pulled off without further interference.

There was one woman spectator present.
She said her name was Gorman, and the
sports made a place for her at fhe ringside.
She had read of the fight match and seemed
much interested.

The fight was started. Goss showed much
cleverness, but it was plainly apparent
that Allen had the strength of the pair.
Eph Holland was referee, and what.a time
he had. Every few seconds some one would
call him a vile name or set up the claim of
fovl. The friends of Goss seemed to out-
number the men on Allen's side, and it was
not long befpre it became noised about that
if Alien did win. his life would pay the pen-
alty. Allen had Goss groggy. but every
time Allen knocked him down the Goss par-
ne would hoot old Tom so as to rattie

™.

In the twenty-first round Allen rushed!

Goss and planted a hard blow in the wind.
Goss groaned and sat down. It was then

threats against Allen, and the iatter be-

in danger. Suddenly, with a determined
look in his eye, he walked over and smashed
Goes, while he was attempting to rise. There

Goss was given the decision, while Allen

evident that Alen could have whipped Goss
to a certainty, but he was afraid to punch
him on account of the surroundings. Both
men were arrested, but Alien. after getting
cut on ball, fled to England. Goss died years
ago in the city of Boston, while Allen. after
returning to this country, took up his abode
in St. Louls, where he conducted a saloon
known as the “Champion Rest,”’ up until a
few weeks of his death.
