title: Uneasy Spirit at Champion’s Rest
text:
UNEASY SPIRIT AT
~ CHAMPIONS REST

It Rebelled When New Man-
ager Undertook to Change
Things.

IT RANG THE BELL
AND SMASHED GLASSES

Linoleum Man Was Sent Away and
Sawdust and the Old Fixtures
Will Remain Out of Re-
spect to the Departed.

Denizens of Market street, whose habitat
is the saloons between Sixth and Tenth
streets, have a mystery. They are trying

.to account for the ringing of Tom Al-
len’s bell.

When Tom named the place “Cham-
Fion’s Rest,” he thought only of the rest
for his old age, which it was to be.

Tom Allen, retired champion pugilist and
proprietor of Champion's Rest, in dying,
left much litigation.

His housekeeper, Tillie Hartgrove, took
possession under a document purporting

to be the will of Tom Allen, while Al-
len’'s daughter was left out in the cold,
so far as a share in the inheritance went.

Proceedings to dispossess the house-
keeper were brought by the daugh-
ter before the father was fairly buried,

but the court probated the will and a
manager was put in to run the place.

This manager had been a bariender under
Allen, dnd he knew the ways of Allen well

enough to keep the old trade and run the
place as Allen had done. But he did not
see it that way, and the “Weary Willies”
that used to bunk under the piano were
unceremoniously iired out whenever the
midnight trade fell off enough to war-
rant closing the doors that in Allen's time
aad never been locked

The rize ring simplicity that had
characterized the place in the champion's
regime was to give — to the tinsel and
glitter af the modern bar. Sawdust was

| no longer to cover the floor, and gq measur-
er Irom a carpet house was called in to
make estimetes for a linoleum outfit.

Uutside the door the old patrons of the
place often stopped and many a head -was
shaken with the remark;

“Poor, old Tom. Wouldn’t he turn over
in his grave at such goings on.”

The man from the carpet house was figur-
ing at a table in the concert hall, a table
whee Allen used to sit and drink his ice
water. With him sat the manager and
two tall glasses adorned the table.

A sound of warring voices rose above the
noise of traffic on the street, and the two
men went to the door.

Suddenly the bell behind the bar rang.
There was only one push button connect-
ed with it and no one had ever pressed it
except Allen when he wanted a drink or a
bouncer to quell a réot.

“What are you doing to that bel], you
rascal?’ shouted the manager at the negro
porter.

“I nevar tetched ft, sah,’ returned the
porter.

Again it sounded, more insistently than
before.

The porter retreated to the end of the
bar nearest the door and again the bell
rang out followed by a crash of glasses.

The manager was game, and he waiked
back into the concert hall.

There on the table where the carpet
salesman had been figuring was a pool of
what had been ‘“forty-road” whisky high-
balls. Both glasses were broken and the
estimate ofr the salesman, which had been
written with an indelible pencil, blotted
and blurred beyond the power of man to
decipher.

“What was it,’’ said the carpet man, “a
cat?”

“Cats don't ring bells,”” said the manager,
“and we haven't a cat aibout the place.”

“Well, what do you think it was?” insist-
ei the carpet man as he started to make
out a new estimate on the Hnoleum ques-
tion.

“I don't think anything about it; but
say, we might as well call this deal off.
Tom Allen don’t want no linoleum on his
floor and I guess sawdust will be the car-
pet of this place wisile I run it.

The new plate glass mirrors were taken
out the same day and the old wrinkled one
put back behind the bar. The place !s
again just as Tom Allen left it and the old
trade is coming back to be well received.

This mystery has not been brought to
the notice of the Society for Psychical Re
search as yet. but the Market street world
grows more confident each day that it was
nothing else than the spirit of Tom Allen
come back to this world to make known to
the new regime that the old ways and sur-
roundings had been good enough for htm
—_ to protest against the planned innova-
ions.

Over the push button will be placed a
box, that no strange hand may press it
unawares. As for the habitues, they give
that table a wide berth, not. as they say,
that they are afraid, but. “Tom might not
like it, you know,” {is the reason assigned.

None of the many visitors of the past few
days has failed to be impressed with the
Story except an advance agent of a weil-
known actress, who was run out of the
place ™ a hurry because he winked at the
manager during the telling of the story.

Nowadays bis place is filled by Gillespie.
The Market street summer garden is op-
@rated like all summer gardens. ‘

No admission is charged at the door, put

‘majority of that crowd come of
‘Many of ‘them are the eons of farmers.
Some, éven, have fathers who ere even

better established in the business world. _

Talk with the members of the Allen audi-
ence and you will find, not occasionally, but
frequently, men whose fathers are bankers,
brokers or well-to-do merchants In cities.
eee did they get in their present condi-

on

There is almost the same reason for every
man,

He left home when a mere boy. Tried to
get work and failed. Took to drink and

Became a tramp. Concluded after
awhile that he wasn’t good for anything
else. Then he became a professional hobo.

Occasionally he finds work-

He makes a few dollara and as sdon as
he is paid off he spends them.

The only real pleasure he gets out of life
is in having a few dollars and in spending
them.

And the place he spends them is just such
& resort as this one formerly operated’ by
&-.pugilist and now in the hands of the
Klondike fortune-seeker.

Allen used to regale his patrons with
Stories of his famous encounters.

Gillespie tells them weird tales of the
frozen North. 5

The king is dead and the new morarch
is giving satisfaction. ;

No one utters a word of protest. )

The same men. frequent the Champion's
Rest and the schooners and the prices are
the sgme as in the days of old. |

On the fioor of the Champion’s Rest
there is sawdust. = |

It would not be the Champion's Rest if
there was not sawdust on the floor.

Dim lights flicker In wow aghaee and eg
rete! apartment. Ww Gillespie
dubbed the “parquet.” ;

There is an alr about the place that
breathes a welcome to the downtrodden
hobo, and when he is there he knows that
he ts at home.

The profzramme begins about 8 o'clock.

It generally requires fifteen minutes of
patient work ‘to get the picture machine
in operation, for Gillespie bought it second-
hand and at times {t has to be coaxed.

Very often the pictures are dim, for the
film has been used many, many times, but
the entertainment is free and the hobo js
eatisfied, even if everything is not conduct-
ed in good style. :
MOVING PICTURES AMUSE
PATRONS OF THIS “GARDEN.”

As a matter of fact, there are only six
rounds to the McCoy-Maher fight, but some-
how Gillespie manages to pull off a long
fight, and, although his patrons never seem
to realize it, the first. second, third, fourth
and fifth rounds are repeated at every per-
formance.

The sixth round, in which the knockont fs
ecored, ix held back pending purchases, and
the unsuspecting patron of the Market street
summer garden believes that he is withess-
ing a long fight, when in reality he only
wees six rounds of actual battle.

But what matters it to the hobo?

He is being entertained. That. to him, fs
sufficient.

Gillespie operates the pictures.

Tt Is he that turns the little crank upon
which the changes depend.

It is he that talks jokingly to the crowd.

Not always jokingly, either, for at times
@cme careless patron will get within the
focus of the kinetoscope and obscure the
@cene. :

Then, in. @ commanding tone,. Gillespie
erdere the unmannerly patron to be seated,
and if he falls to sit down immediately there
is w strong-armed gentleman in the rear of
the room. whose touch is far more forceful
than words. ~~ ;

The patron either sits down or leaves the
There is but one alternative.

After three rounds have been shown, dur-
{ng which the audience is thrown into a
wild state of enthusiasm, the picture ma-
chine stops suddenly and a young man
about 20 years old furnishes diversion by
singing a song through a megaphone,

| Just why this megaphone is used will
trade ae puzzle the visitor until he gets @ |

trade secret from Gillesple,

The megaphone makes a loud sound, one
that can be heard in the street.

Nothing appeals so strongly to the hobo
as sentimentai music. :

_ Hearing the notes from within, the man
on the street enters the. saloon, then the
Pparquette. and the chances are that, once
seated, he will remain and in the course of
time will buy something.

Additional interest attaches to the songs
because they are illustrated.

Gillespie manages the slidea, too. and
when the finn! chorus is rendered the
words are thrown upon the canvas and the
audience joins in the finale, thereby as-
sisting the singer.

This makes more noise, even, than the
megaphone effect, and as a consequence
a greater number are induced to enter.
PERFORMANCD OF CONTORTIONIST
IS ANOTHER DIVERSION.

After the song the fight pictures are re-
newed.

Gillespie repeats the rounds that were
shown and after the exhilarating effect of
the song the hobos enjoy the fight even
More than they did formerly.

A second diversion is the performance of
the contortionist. ,The contortionist is a
hobo, . He was engaged that morning.

He arrived in town without money.

He needed some and negotiations between
him and the proprietor of the Champion's
‘Rest were quickly brought to a close. F

Although the hobo realizes that a theater

Or a park job would be better, atill he is
levoted to his art and he likes applause.

Like all actors of high and low degree, he
Hi a “hand.”

he knock-out round finally shown
about 11 o'clock. -

Ere that time has arrived the hoboes have
spent as much as their means will allow
and enthusiasm in the Champion's Rest
Tuns high.

By midnight things have‘ quieted ‘a bit
and by 1 o'clock many have departed, while
others remain in their chairs,

A hobo is always welcome to a chair in
the Champion’s Rest.

He may not have room rent. and if he
has not he always knows that a chair in
the parquet is at his disposal, even if-he
has no money.

IMPOVERISHED PATRONS
APPRECIATE PROPRIETOR’S FAVORS,

The wise proprietcr knows that the hobo
may have money on the morrew, and if he
has he willspend it with the man who has
befriended him.

This is a characteristic of the tramp ele-
ment.

On some nights trade in the Champion's
Rest is good until 2 o'clock, but as a rule
most of the hoboes are asleep at this hour,
and during the remaining hours of the
vidi the night porter keeps a silent
v

Protection ts afforded all patrons, and the
man who sleeps in a chair feels reasonably
assured that no one will steal his hat while
he slumbera, although there are frequenters

suns will do it 1£ the opportunity presents !t-
self.

There are hoboes, too, who will rob their
fellow-hobo.

If the sleeping hobo has a dime in his.
pocket he may wake up without it if the
ttt porter has proved derelict in his
auty.

Should the porter fall asleep the unfortu-
ngte hobo would quickly seize upon the val-
uables of his more fortunate brother, and
he would show no hesitancy, for there have
been times in his life, no doubt, when he
himself was “touched” for his all;

It is the aim, however, of Gillespie, to
eliminate crime from the Champlon’s Rest,
and any man “caught in the act” is warn-
ed never to show his face in that place
again.

At four e’clock in the morning all is quiet
in the Champion's Rest.

Every one is asleep,and so silent is it that
ane can almost-hear a pin drop in the saw-

just.

Shades of old Tom Allen are said to arise,
and the {ill-fated hobo may have dreams of
the day that is gone.

In his dream he may see old Tom at the
plano, singing the love songs of a genera-
tion ago. :

The pictures on the wall give evidence of
the victorious days of old Tom, and while
the hobo slumbers he sees many a cham-
plonship battle fought again.

The dusty om cup, pbs shed ger

Waterloo, which hangs over the bar, lead,
nae en d and

But the hobo must awake, and the night,
dorter is there to urge him, if necessary.

PARQUETTE MUST BE a3
VACATED AT 6 O'CLOCK. io

Five o'clock is the hour when the “pare’
quette” must be vacated, and the gentle’
prod of @ broom notifies the sleeper 4
the time has arrived. | n “i

In ‘this case the man who finds
“broke” in the morning fs always

days, but when the checks are handed o

CHAPTER AIL.
HERE has been so much talk and
MP diversity of opinion as to whether
I was ever the real champion of
the world that I feel it incumbent upon
me to produce facts and figures to show
that I really earned that title. Fre-
quently I see this question asked in the
newspapers and in many cases I see
that the sporting editors answer that I
never was champion.
To e¢tart with, Dr. Dudley A. Sargent
,in his “Life and Reminiscences of a
| Nineteenth Century Gladiator,” calls
me the champion of the world. Enz-
land is a part of the word ergo, wc-
cording to Dr. Sargent, who is an
, authority, I was champion of England.
Let us begin at the start. Tom Fig
was considered the first champion of
| Hngland. He bloomed in 1719. The next
| champion of note was Tom Cribb, who
\ received a champfonship belt that was
‘mot transferable in 1819. The next cham-
| pion was Tom Spring, who was cock of
the walk in 1820. Then comes Jim Ward,
| who appeared five years later. In 1841
, Gaunt defeated Nick Ward for a belt
| that was subscribed for. Four years
| later Bendigo beat Caunt and got the
| belt. In 1850 Perry, the Tipton Slasher,
| after his draw with Paddock, claimed
‘the championship but never defeated
| the then champion, Bendigo. In 1853
| Perry again claimed office because
| Harry Broome forfeited a match with
| him. Four years later, Tom Sayers beat

| Perry for a new belt and $200 a side.
When Heenan and Sayers were in the
ring an American put the heel of an
old shoe into Heenan’s hand, saying,
“This is the heel of Yankee Sullivan's
‘shoe, Jack; he swore he never lost a
‘fight while it was in the ring. Leaye it

there and go in and lick Engiand!’

\ Open for Competition.
A LTHOUGH the heel did not prove

strong enough to get for Heenan
the English championship belt, it
must have discouraged Sayers, for he
left the belt open for competition. This
was the time when Jem Mace won it,
conquering the giant, Sam Hurst, known
as the “Staleybridge Infant.” Tom Say-
ers and Heenan fought their memorable
battle in 186. Chamber’s Encyclopedia
under the head of boxing or pugilism,
has this to say of the Henan-Sayer’s
fight: “The year 1860, however, wit-
“hessed a strange revival of the pugilistic
sport on occasion of a fight between
Tom Sayers, the champion prizefighter
of England, and John Heenan, the Ben-
‘ieea Boy, an American, for £200 a side,
and the belt, a badge of honor won by
ihe champion. The battle, which was
_ elevated to the dignity of a great in-
ternational contest by sporting papers,
took at Farnsborough, April 17,
1860. It lasted for more than two hours,
« in which time the American was beaten
, almost blind and the Englishman dread-
fully bruised. The continuance of the
battle was prevented by the breaking in
of the ring, caused by the interference
| of the police.”

Honor for Champton.
f ibis A FTER the battle the English
champion was ranked by
many newspapers, not sport-
| ing ones, with the heroes of the Crimea
, and of Lucknow” Hundreds, if indeed
not thousands, of pounds were sub-
| scribed for. him fn admiration of his
' bravery by persons of all conditions
of life and residing in all parts of the
country, and he wag feted by merchants
en the London and Liverpool *changes.
| His opponent received equally flattering
and substantial testimonials from Amer-
|ieans. The fight formed the subject
_ of discussion in the House of Commons,
in which the Home Secretary announced
that not only the principals but all pres-
ent at the spectacle were amenabl: to
| the law. Though no steps were taken
| to bring the offenders to Justice, it was
| intimated to those chiefly concerned
that if a renewal of the fight were at-
| tempted the law should be put in force
against those aiding*»and abetting It.”
Here is one American account of the
Night: |“April 17, 1860, John Heenan
fought Tom Sayers in England. Battle
was for £200 and the championship of
England and America. Friends of Say-
ers, seeing the condition of their cham-
pion and fearing he would lose, cut the
ropes and the battle ended in a wran-
gie. The stakes were drawn and each
pugilist was presented with a champion-
ship belt. The belt given to Heenan had
not been paid for, and he was obliged to
return it.’
Mace te the Top.
N 1861 Jem Mace beat Hurst. In 1863
| Tom King beat Mace and claimed
the belt, which he Subsequently gave
up, declining again to meet the gypsy.
Mace again claimed the belt. In 1866
Jem Mace and Joe Goss fought a draw
for $1000 w side and the belt. In 1869 Mc-
Coole beat Tom Allen in this country
for the championship of the world, Ln
Init Jem Mace drew with
here for the championship of the
Tn 1870 Jem Mace and Tom
for the title and $5000 at
Orleans, Mace won.
Tom Allen beat McCoole on Sept. 23,
1873, at Chouteau Island. near St. Louis,
and on Noy. 18, same year, Ben Hogan
fought Tom Allen for $2000 and the
championship of the Pacific coast. Allen
Was Wihning when a Wrangie broke

world.

Keanville, New

up
the fight. On Sept. 7, 1976, Joe Goss
fought Allen for $2900 and the champion-
ship of "the world in Kentudky. Goss

/ Was declared winner.
brought+over from Bn,
Mave. On May 30, 1886, Joe Goss fought
Paddy Ryan tok gio and the cham-
Pionship, at Collier Station, W. Va. and
after one hour and twenty-seven minutes
of hard fighting Ryan won.

In commenting on the fight the Kan-

The latter was
giand by Jem

Joe Goss out in four and _ one-half
minutes on Feb. 7, 1880, while it took
Ryan one hour and 27 minutes to do the

Police Save Mitchell.
Y victory over Slade of Austra-
MI lia (the Maori) brought here by
Jem Mace, is a matter of his-
tory, as is the slaughter of Chariey
Mitchell in Madison Square Garden,
when I begged Capt. Thorn to let me
get one more crack at him. This was
when Charley’s seconds had propped
him pp against the ropes after the po-
lice interfered during the third round.
Turning to Mitchell, Capt. Thorn said:
“Go to your dressing room. I stepped
in to save Sullivan from killing you.”
Alf Greenfield was brought from En-
gland in 1884 to defeat me. He was sent
over as Albion’s champion. On Novy. 1i,
that year, in Madison Square Garden,

sas City Times said: “Sullivan :

I had Alf in a semi-conscious state on
the ropes and all hands (principals and
seconds) were arrested. Charley John-
son awarded the decision to me.

Greenfield again met me. This time
in New England Institute, Boston. M.
Keyes of San Francisco refereed. This
was on Jan. 12, 188. When Greenfield
came back to life after the fourth round
and he was asked if I could hit hard,
he turned to Jack Burke and Said:
“Sullivan could beat you, Mitchell and
myself, in the same ring.”’

I guess that came pretty near mak-
ing me the champion of the world.

As a further proof I would like to
reproduce the challenge that I issued
after I had arrived in Boston imme-
diately following my defeating Paddy
Ryan for the championship:

“There has been so much newspaper
talk from parties who claim that they

Joe Coburn

are desirous of meeting me in the ring |!

that I am disgusted. Nevertheless, |
am willing to fight any man in this
country in four weeks from signing
articles for $5000 a side, or any man
in the old country for the same amount
at two month’ from signing articles,
I to use gloves, and he, if he pleases, to
fight with bare knuckles, as I do not
wish to put myself fn a position amena-
ble to the law. My money is always
ready, so I want these fellows to put
up or shut up.
“JOHN L. SULLIVAN.

where the air is so foul as to stifle

TEE LEEINEGABUBLRs.

Few Sc. Louisans do not member

the 9rganization of a series if saloons
Im Wwious parts of the city by a man

This man, by his strange prsonality.
always had a following ofidle men
to Whom he gave and sold Wid whisky

sheds and basements. were of the
vilest kind and the army of “Heine-
gabublers” drank, ate and slept on the
floors and tables

The “Heinegabubler” saloons were
equipped with trapdoors, sliding stair-
ways, chairs with legs broken and all

stalled for the amusement of the B
guests of the resort and to be used

It was known that the “Hieneza-

It was proven that more than one

surance policy. the beneficiary of

Heinegabublers held their carousals #

Tom Allen’s saloon at Seventh and
Market streets, where the American §

open all night and the men siept in

saloon consisted of one big barroom
in a tumble-down frame building over

which the proprietor lived. The walls
were decorated with signs of both a
sacrilegious and immoral character.
On the front window was posted this
significant sign, ‘““‘We are lower than
the lowest.”

In the dingy room of Tom Allen’s
joint as many as 200 men slept on
cold nights. These men ranged from |
18 to 65 years of age. Some of them §
were men who had falien into the

The story of a man by the name
of Knight illustrates this. Knight
was arrested for a minor offense by
the St. Louis police in the hey-day of
Tom Allen's activities. He told a
story that sent a chill of horror over

‘the city. People did not know such

things existed outside of fiction.

Knight said that he staggered into
a certain dive and asked for a drink.
He was about 50 years old at this
time, had been a drinking “man for

“I think I'll take a chance on you.

Knight acceded and after sobering }!
up, he was insured for $1,@00..He

z

hundreds of these men who do not

Evidence has shown that for the
most part the dive keepers who sell

“I have been told, upon good au-

LOOKS LIKE WHISKY.

From all outward appearances, this
bad whisky looks like the real thing.
Carome! coloring is used to give it the

ask why the United States Govern-
ment does not go after these moon-
shiners, but the Revenue Department
has nothing to do with the retailer so

their particular rules. The Revenue
Department closely watches the dis-

whisky concerns whose reputation is
undoubted rectify whisky, but they
must comply with the laws. A gauger

“from the revenue office is on hand

when this rectifying is being done and
his stamp must be upon the keg or
barrel to show the same. He sees that

THE FIGHT BETWEEN
TOM ALLEN AND JEM
MACE FOR $10,000

PART L.

BY BILLY MURPHY.

“Tom Allen, who for years was a)
resident of St. Louis, was one of nn
greatest fighters the world has ever!
known,” reminisced Prof. Bill Clark. |
yesterday, while we were discussing
famous fights.

“Allen's battle for $10.000 and the
championship of the world with Jem)
| teroct Engiand’s great fighter, was @

ferocious one.
“The men signed to mix, January |
17, 1870. They met the May 10, fol-
lowing, within ten miles of the city!
of New Orleans. Of course this bat-
tle was fought under the London
Prize Ring Rules on the turf, which
| permitted hugging and wrestling, the
bare knuckles being used.
SPORTSMEN ASSEMBLE. c
“On the afternoon of May 9, 1870,
j the St. Charles Hotel in the Crescent
| Cit. was crowded with sportsmen
nil all parts of America,, who had
come to see the great battle. Betting
| was fast and furious till Allen’s back-
\ers stood out for such long odds that
the other side refused to give. Both
| heroes were present, and each was
the center of an admiring crowd.
| Mace was accompanied by his cousin,
a Pooley Mace, and his trainer, Jem
Cusick, who had trained and seconded
John C. Heenan, the “Benecia Boy.
for his great fight with Tom Sayers,
the English champion, years before.
“Jem had commenced his training
at Mobile Bay, but, to escape the at-
tentions of the sheriff, he had moved
|to Magnolia, in Alabama, and had
lfnally taken his breathings on the
|old Metairie race track, on the out-
skirts of New Orleans, the scene of
the great contest between those two
mighty heroes of the turf, Lexington
and Lecompte, whose rivalry was as
famous as that between Hermis and

;
| Colonial Girl, World’s Fair year. It;
was at that old track that Lexington
performed his memorable feat of cov-
ering four miles in 7 minutes and 19
seconds.

PRAISE FOR MACE.

“Everyone was full of praise of
Jem’s condition,” rambled on grand
old Bill. “At the St. Charles Hotel
beautiful Creole girls and handsome
white women pressed forward, eager
|to be introduced to the good-looking
| Englishman, and they kept poor Jem’s
heart in a flutter, as he told me after-
| Wards. Jem never in his life had
such an enthusiastic receptier, and
|he commented on the warmth 5* sym-_
pathy and geniality of the Southern- |
ers. ;

“Tom Allen, attracted comparative- |
ly little attention. It was Mace, the}
|Most scientifiC boxer im the world: ;
| Mace, the hero of a score of fights:
| Mace, the champion of Great Britain,
| that men and women were eager to
|see and to shake hands with. Allen,
|who had trained right here in St.
| Louis, under Jack Goulding and Joe
|Coburn, had of course plenty of at-
|tention from his backers, and the la-
| dies condescended just to cast one
'eurious glance at him to hundreds for
| the champion.

“Tt was a case of early to bed that
night for all of us, for the start for
the — ground was to take place
from the Jackson Railway depot at
4 o'clock the next morning; and, as a
matter of fact, many prominent citi-
| zens, merchants, lawyers, physicians,
ex-officers of both the Federal and
Confederate armies, from the grade of
general down to lieutenant, were at
the rendezvous by 3:36 a. m., thougn
it Was 5 o’clock before the specially-
chartered train moved out of the sta-
tion.

san nection patctiiaepnni sent HensiiNA titi mea

POLICE PRECAUTIONS :

“The municipal authorities would
not alow the fight to take place any-
where within their immediate juris-
diction, but they dispatched seventy
| policemen to see the special safe out
; of the station. The train was halted
about © quarter of a mile from the
| depot, and then boarded by the police,
| who ejected every person who was
unable to produce a ticket, and thus}
; the rowdy element was effectually ex-
cluded. The combatants and their
seconds were not in the special itself,
| but followed behind in what was then
‘called a “dummy’’—that is a loco-
; Motive and passenger car combined
|in one, the former being fitted 7

meet ssesenes hiner NRARttl ester tenestponitnuse nomena Hu
SS

| condensing engines to avoid the noise
of escaping steam.
About eight miles from New Or-
leans, at a place called Kennerville,
the train disgorged its freight. The
twenty-four foot ring was quickly set
up, and the spectators, some 1,000 or
1,500 in number, quietly ranged them-
| selves round it. A more orderly
crowd never assembled to witness a
prize-fight, which was no doubt due
to the fact that quite three-fourths
| of those present were what the Cres-
cent City papers called “‘men of ‘
.

ture.”” The Chicago Baseball Club
| had come en masse to see the sport
| and there were few sporting societies
in America and even Canada which
were not represented.

ALL KINDS OF MEN.

“The Louisiana Jockey Club, which
had its headquarters in New Orleans,
had turned out in full strength to do |
honor to the occasion, and not since!
the great fight between Heenan and |
Sayers. had such an assembly graced
the ringside. The men were of ail
nationalities there; Creole dandies, |
glossy-coated and patent-leather boot-|
ed; broad-shouldered planters, in suits
of white nankeen; smartly-togged
sports from New York; backwoods-
men in homespun—any variety of cos-
tumes in fact.

“Loud cheers greeted both men as |
they stepped on the smooth green-|
sward, attended by their seconds, Jem
Cusick and Pooley Mace for the Eng-
lishman; Joe Coburn, whom I boxed
at the Natatorium tvrenty years ago,
and Thurston for Tom Allen. There
had been a good deal of shaking of
the head among us old-timers, who
believed in the old adage, “Youth will
be served,’ at Mace’'s rashness in tak-
ing on @ man so much younger than
himself. For Allen was but 27. ana
thirteen years is a lot to give away. |

“But they forgot that Jem Mace
had been notoriously careful of him-
self. Indeed, I don’t know of any
pugilist with maybe the exception of
Jem Ward, who took better care of
himself than Jem Mace, and, like
Ward, he, in consequence, preserved
his health end vigor in a surprising
manner. Jem’s condition that day
was perfect.

IN PERFECT SHAPE.

“He was as hard as nails, though
he scaled 168 pounds, which was ten
pounds more than his fighting weight
in England. You may think that was
light for a heavyweight, but I have
always maintained that a 165-pound
man is not handicapped against the
heaviest fighter in the world, if the

|

165-pounder has courage, skill and
streneth. We have instances thet
support my theory in Mace, Mitchell.
Fitzsimmons and McCoy. Any of

these men would have beaten tr
death the man Jack Johnson won
from at Reno, July 4, 19106. ?
“Tom Allen, that no*’able May day
weighed 175 pounds. He appeared
ruddy and well, but there was too
much flesh about his face. My recol-
lection of Tom is that he was rather
light and thin about the shoulders
jand back that day, but with good
| loins and first-rate pedestals. He was
‘ like as muscular or weli-
pee ge tao the bust as the English
ichampion, but he had the advantage
of an inch in height. Mace, tl

hough
Was much the oider man, but he
moved with all the suppleness as
panther, and was clear! the more
agile of the two.

HOW AN IRISHMAN
WON A RING TITLE
FOR UNITED STATES

PR te LIEW MY

BY BILLY MURPHY.

The writer was a guest of Professor Bill Clark, the Beifast Chicken,
Sunday afternoon. It had occurred to me, that it would prove interesting
reading St. Patrick's Day, if I could present to the readers of The New Star
an authentic story of how the world’s ring championship came to America.
I had never seen such an article and knew that the beloved “Belfast Chicken” |
could tell me. In fact, I believe he is the only man in the world today, who!
is acquainted with the true story of the retrogression of the Britisn fighters |
and the rise of Americans.

Here is old Bill's story, which I report as accurately as it is possible for :
metodo. “The Chicken” talked in this manner: : |

“That grand old institution, the prize ring, which has an ineradicable |
charm for all men, attained the height of its popularity in the year 1860, when
that gallant little champion, Tom Sayers, after a struggle with John Camel |
Heenan, the American champion, which may be truly described as stupendous, |
retired from active work, and left the old Champion Belt open for compe- |
tition. The troubles of the prize ring then commenced. In turn the trophy |
was won by Sam Hurst, the giant from Stalybridge, Jem Mace, Tom King,
Joe Wormald, Mace again, and finally, after a number of scenes not of a |
very creditable nature, the police made matters so hot that a number of |
prominent pugilists determined to try their luck in America. Just prior to!
their departure, however, Joe Goss, the English champion, and Tom Alien!
signed articles to fight for the premier honor.

“That intended battle really put an end to the sport in England, for both |
men were arrested on the eve of the fight upon bench warrants, and from |
the activity and earnestness shown in the matter the pugilists realized that
jit was all over with their vocation for a time.

OFF TO AMERICA.

“Among the foremost arrivals in the land of the Stars and Stripes were |
Joe Wormald, O’Baldwin, Bob Prettie, Bill Ryall, Jem Mace, Joe Goss, and |
Yom Allen. Only the doings of the two last-named, however, need claim our |
present attention. At that time (1867) Tom Allen was at his very best, and
was a splendid specimen of an athlete, fully 5 feet 10 inches, and about 164
pounds. He could hold his own in any company, and soon after his arrival in
America he made a match with Mike McCoole, a man almost big enough to
eat him, and he was fast making mince meat of Michael when the latter’s
friends opened on him with ball cartridge, and stopped proceedings. At that}
time ring fights were conducted on very free and easy lines in America, pistols!
and knives playing a very prominent and lively part in the proceedings, while |
in some of the encounters the men themselves fought on the “all in” prin-;
¢ciple, and half the battle was frequently fought with both men on the ground. |
BARKERS AND BOWTES. |

“With the introduction of the British brigade, however, things mended |
somewhat, and when, after the departure of Mace and Co., Goss and Tom
Allen were once more matched for the championship—not of England, bear
in mind, but for that of the world this time—a fairly decent display was
given. The men, of course, fought under the recognized London Prize Ring |
Rules, and all would have gone weil but for a gang of ruffians who had
backed Goss somewhat heavily, and when the latter was seen to be getting,
the worst of it they presented a few barkersand bowies to the notice of the |
referee, and that worthy was induced to give his decision in favor of the man
who would in all probability have lost if the fight had been allowed to proceed.
PADDY RYAN.

“While the British brigade were reaping a golden harvest by fighting
among themselves and giving exhibitions of the noble art, there arose a young
Trish-American from the city of Troy, who laid claim to the title of champion. |
He fought and defeated a number of local men, and challenged Joe Goss to.
fight for the championship. There was a tremendous amount of enthusiasm |
over the event; in fact. so much was. made of it that the Attorney-General
of Ontario, where the fight was advertised to take place, ordered out three
companies of the Third Battalion of Infantry to arrest the disturbers of the
peace. As a consequence the meeting between the men had to be postponed,
and finally, after being hunted about from place to place, the men fought on
the border line between West Virginia and Pennsylvania, where a terrific
encounter was put up. However, Ryan, the younger and stronger man,
eventually compelled his antagonist to give in, after fighting nearly an hour
and a half.

THE GENESIS OF GLOVE FIGHTING.

“After the Goss and Ryan battle, the authorities bestirred themselves,
and issued a warrant for the arrest of both men, but they managed to é€s-
cape to Canada, where they had to hide until the matter was settled. Tue
legal business was rather a lengthy job, and by the time it was finished and
Ryan had returned to New York he found that a new star had come to the
front. This was a young Bostonian, John Lawrence Sullivan by name, who
had been creating quite a sensation by the marvelous manner in which he
put his opponents to sleep with the gloves. Sullivan chailenged Ryan to
fight with these weapons, but the latter replied that as he had won the cham- |
plonship from Goss by a fight with nature’s weapons the Boston sglove-slinger |
would have to meet him under like conditions, A tremendous amount of time | _

Compliments of John L.

FEW days after the Jack

Dempsey-Bob Fitzsimmons

fight which was itn New Or-
leans on January 14, 1891, I went
to Chicago. The morning after my
arrival I sent a messenger boy
to the West Side Theater with $15
and a written request for a box
seat. John L. Sullivan was. ap-
pearing at that playhouse in “Hon-
est Hearts and Willing Hands,” and
I was anxiotis to look at the great
giadiator once again.

The boy came back a short time
later with my $15, six tickets call-
ing for an entire box and a note
from Jim Wakely, who was asso-
ciated with John L. at that time
in his theatrical tours. The note
read: ¥

“Your money is no good at
this showhouse, Jim Corbett.
Please accept these tickets with
the compliments of John L. and
the rest of us.”

That night I went to see the
show, but hardly had I been seated

when Wakely came to my box
greeted me, and then sald:

“The big fellow would like to see
you, Jim. Come around to the

stage entrance.”

And so, with Wakely leading the
way, I walked to John L. Sullivan's
dressing room. As I entered it the
idol of my early voyhood and the
“champion of champions” stepped
forward, pushed out his huge
hand, smiled and said:

“And so you're Jim Corbett, eh?
Glad to meet you. Sit down.”

After more than seven years my
yearning to shake the hand of the
mighty John I. was realized.

Chat "With Champion.

D WILLIAMSON,then the fa-
mous Chicago shortstop, was
in John L.'s dressing room at

the tfme. John L. introduced me
to Williamson with:

“Ed, this is the kid that whipped
Jake Kilrain down in New Or-
leans."

“Yes,” answered Williamson, “I
read about it."

John I. looked me square in the
eye and then his glance traveled
up and down my frame in an ap-
praising way. ;

.“And you're the kid that’s going
towfight Peter Jackson, eh?”

“Yes.”

“Well, young fellow, I don't like
the idea of you fighting a negro.
I have drawn the color lHne.”’

“Somebody’s got to fight him,”
I answered.

John IL., silent for a while,
asked:

“Do you think you can whip
him, young fellow?”

“Yes, I really think I can.”

“Well, I hope so; I certainly
wish you luck.”

From then on until near the
end of the play, John L., William-
son and I engaged in general con-
versation that had more to do with
baseball and theatricals than with
pugilism. Williamson's presence
in the dressing room balked me in
my plans to deliver my message
to John L. there. So I decided to
wait until another day.

Near the end of the play, I got
up and said to John I:

“I think I'll be going along
now.”

John L., in the dominating way
that was his, exclaimed:

“You aren't going to do anything
of the sort. You'’r@ going to stay
with me for a while and we'll sée
the town. Wait for me until I get
washed up.”

Hitting High Spots.
WAITED Immediately after
I the show John L. and I

jumped into a hack and John
lL. proceeded to show me the
town. Together we visited a half
dozen hote! bars and in each and
every place the entry of the cham-
pion was greeted with joy by the
other patrons. In most of the
places those who were there at-
tempted to buy wine for John J.,
but the champion pushed everyone
aside and said

“Only my money ts good in this
place.”’

And then he proceeded to “set

up the house.”

We went from one barroom to
another and as our trip continued
I became more and more amazed
at the drinking ability of the
on. Iie was consuming un-
countable glasses of champagne
But his imbibing that night, great
as it seemed to me, was only
tri fliy

champic

ig in comparison with the ca-
pacity of his earlier years. The
1% " - ~o ¢ Tanhr io k the

liquor tha John L drank that

night in Chicago would have put
:
€

an ordinary man “under the ta-
ble" in an hour or less. But John
I.. showed no signs of unsteadi-
ness The only effect the liquor
seemed to have on him was to
flush his face, to make his eyes
brighter and to make him more

talkative than ever

John Ls Big Heart.

/ T last we entered the place of
Matt Hogan, famous in

Chicago in that era as a
r high-class sports. <A
met John L there and the
hampion took me along with him
to one of the rooms where he held

big-hearted way that was his, in-
troduced me to everyone as:
Bors, this is Jim Corbett, the

“alifornia Kid, who whipped Jake
Kilrain a while ago and is now
going out to whip Peter Jackson
And boys,” declared John IL as
though the fact was a great bit
of news, “this kid doesn’t drink

anything but seltzer water.”

CORBETT TELLS OF |

TOM ALLEN DEBUT
IN AMERICAN RING

In First Appearance St. Louisan |.

ALLEN’S FIGHTS FOR TITLE ||

Battled Famous Joe Goss to a/'
Draw in First Match for

BY JAMES J. CORBETT.

The name of Tom Allen figures):
conspicuously in ring history of a:
long gone era. Allen, after a num-
ber of years of activity in English
rings, came to St. Louis, and for near-
ly ten years afterward he was some-
thing of an “on-again-off-again” king
ef American heavies.

Birmingham, Engiand, was Allen's
birthplace. Born in 1840, hé@ battied
for the first time in a prize ring
against a man named Wagener, in
1861, in Birmingham. The pout was
for a side bet of $25 and Alien
emérged a victor. That triumph en-
couraged him to make a match with
a fellow named Goud for a stake of
$2060—and once again Ailen won.

Those achievements determined
him upon a career as a professional
ringman. He sought a bout with
Posh Price—and was whipped in fif-
ty-five minutes. That was in 1862.
| Undiscouraged, Allen fought Bingley |
Rose. in Nottingham, Engiand, for
$250, and pounded his way to vic-
tory in twenty-nine minutes. in
June, 1864, he waged his next night
against Bob Smith, a Liverpool negro
Pow Allen got the surprise of his

2

The Birmingham youngster expect-
ed an easy victory. The most he
could get Smith to fight for was $50
‘a side. Figuring that Smith was
“easy money,’ Alien bet heavily on
himself, with the ringside crowd giv-
ing big odds. And Smith whipped
| Allen in two hours and fifteen min-
| utes of furious fighting. .
} Jack Parkinson fell a victim to Al-
jinn’ prowess after twenty minutes

in their bout early in 1865. Soon
afterward Allen coaxed Price, his
iearly conqueror, into giving him a
return bout for a side bet of $125.
Allen, spurred on by an intense ha-
tred for Price, fought one of the most
merciless fights of his lifetime, final-
ly forcing Price to quit in the fourth
round, after two hours and five min-
| utes of warfare. |.

On June 12, 1866, Allen whipped
George Illes, which put him_in line
for a battle with Joe Goss.. The two
met for the championship of England

: March 5, 1867, for a side bet of

$500. After thirty-five rounds—one

hour and fifty-two minutes of des-

perate fighting—the contest was halt-

ed and calied a draw by thé referee. |
Allen as 2 Second.

Allen then made matches with Bill
Thorne, Mike Cocklin and Peter Mil-
‘lard in turn. But thesthree “ran |
out,” electing to forfeit their postings
of $250 earch rather than fight the
|wertier from Birmingham. After
several ineffectual cfforts to get an-
other chance at Goss, and unable to
get any of the second raters in En-
giand to try conclusions with him,

For that reason seating possi-

fight location. In that case it
would be up to St. Louis to meet
the demands of other centers.

Just at this writing, it appears
that there are not many states
able to comply with Jacob’s de-
mand for a 15-round bout. This
is true of the communities which
have ready to hand stadia such as
Chicago and Philadelphia. Cleve-
land is best equipped to handle
the show. New Jersey, accord-
ing to a New York dispatch, is
the only State now being consid-
ered. An arena would have to
be built there.

If an arena must be built, St.
Louis could afford to do it quite
as well as another city.
event, which would lend prestige
to the city and bring a lot of
spending money from the South
and West, seems well worth

reaching for.

Long Time Between Fights.

F the championship fight

should come to St. Louis it
would not be the (first world
title event decided in this dis-
trict. The last heavyweight,
championship fought in this dis-
trict was the Mike McCoole-Tom
Allen battle of 1873, held on an
island in the Mississippi, a short
distance above St. Louis. The
island has since merged with tHe

mainland and is now part of
East St. Louis.
There Allen and McCoole

fought a bare-knuckle match—a
bloody battle of seven rounds in
which Allen, weighing about 170
pounds, made a chopping: block
of McCoole and regained the
crown that McCoole had taken
from him four years before un-
der questionable circumstances.

That was the last heavyweight
championship fight held here, as
Allen, when he finally lost his
crown to Joe Goss, fought his

losing battle near Louisville, Ky.

title: Wrav’s Column
text:
He’s an “Able Seaman.”’

UR habit of selling Great
Britain “short,” in all matters
pertaining to fighters, will
get us into difficulties, if not
curbed. Only the fact that there
is practically no monéy left to

risk on fights either in England
or America, saved the East from
a financial loss in the case of
“Seaman” Watson, England’s
featherweight champion, who beat
Fidel La Barba last Friday at
odds of 5 to 1 against him.

There were no facts available to
justify such odds against the
Briton. On the contrary, he came
over well recommendeéd. He was
hailed abroad as the best man
England had produced since Fred-
die Welsh and Jimmy Wilde.
London critics staked their repu-
tations on his ability, Yet, when
he came to this country to do his
stuff, he received the frosty face.
He was forced to show his wares
in a private trial before the com-
mission in New York consented
to let Khim appear for an impor-
tant match.

Thought Watson a Joke.

|
|
|
|
|

;

Our skeptical critics typed such
paragraphs as this: “The end of
Seaman Watson, recent British
importation, may occur Friday
night when he meets Fidel La
Barba in what Madison Square
people are pleased to call a warm-
up for a bout with Kid Choco-
late. The tip is out that the Sea-
man, who conducts a ‘pub’ back
home, is one of the worst of a
mediocre crop of Britons that has
come to our shores since the war,
and that he will be cold instead

| of hot, after the warm-up.”

Watson beat La Barba decisive-

ly and is now being sought for a
| title bout with Chocolate.

Imag-
ine what would have happened to
our betting public if it had had
the money to back La Barba lay-
ing $5 to win $1.

Watson is coming back to this
country again and when he does
he will not be worse than 7 to 5

| against, if he faces Kid Choco-

late.
aa = >

Just a Bartender.

ATSON is on his way home

:o England because he can-
not remain away from his job
any longer. Instead of being the
proprietor of a public house, as
stated, he is just a bartender at
“fi’-pun’ a week.” This, as ex-
change goes today, would be
about $17 weekly. His employer
gave him a limited leave of ab-
sence and he’s due back to don

the apron once more.
= & -

/Two Champions Ran Saloons

Here.

If the American public learned
that one of its prominent fight-
ers was a bartender it would
promptly call off all bets and
look for another hero. A _ bar-
tender is supposed to have no
place in the fight world, probably
because of the difficulty of main-
taining strict training under such
temptations.

However, in other days, when
saloons were going big in this
country, and when fighting was a
much more serious matter than
it is today, many of the famous
fighters owned and _ operated
public houses, while still active
in the ring.

+ a

T. LOUIS had examples of

this, and two world champlion-
ship battles were fought by St.
Louis residents who owned and
operated public houses. Mike
McCoole and Tom Allen, each of
whom held the heavyweight title
while residing in this city, were
in this class. Later on the Allens,
Dalys and Kellys all owned
saloons and fought many famous
battles.

Not only did their saloon duties
not interfere with their condi-
tion, but it may be counted a fact
that in many cases these men
performed heroic feats of train-
ing, their conditioning work last-
ing over many weeks.

In England the fight game is
still to some extent centered
around “public houses.” But don’t
make the mistake of thinking
that fighters developed under
such auspieces are necessarily
out of condition.

Time to Loosen Up.

NNSYLVANIA now is the
only State in the major-league
baseball circuit with an anti-Sun-
ay baseball! law. Both major
leA€gues are affected by this an-
cient statute, the National League
in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia
and the American in Philadel-
delphia.

Washington and Boston have
shaken.off the shackles and now
permit Sunday games. But the
ancient Quaker sentiment has
thus far kept Pennsylvania safe
from the encroachments of mod-
ernism. On Sunday, Philadel-
phia is stil] the “Unconscious

ee

ext month there may be a
change. The anti-blue law fa--
tion is going to advance on
the Penn Legislature, headed by
none other than Bill Roper, for-
mer head coach at Princeton and
now a lawyer. He will sponsor
a law repealing the old Sunday
law, so that baseball may flour-
ish on Sunday in the State’s big
cities.

Roper ought to score a touch-
down. Legislatures are in the
mood to favor proposals which
will cause mioney to circulate and
which will contribute to putting
more men to work. It’s about
time that state legislatures un-
derstand that recreation and
healthful enjoyment no _ longer
are classed as Sabbath desecra-
tion.

7 oe *

Due for a Change.

HILE the National League

players and managers are
talking hopefully both as regards
a close race and expected attend-
ance, the Ameérican League is
having little to say and less to do
about its really important prob-
lem.

There is no doubt that Presi-
dent William Harridge and the
club owners, too, even the inde-
pendent Jacob Ruppert, are alive
to the fact that another run-
away race by the Yankees is im-

pending, with all the drawbacks
and losses that this seems to im-
ply.

Once more the East seems Cer-
tain to produce a pennant win-
ner; and when one remembers
that the West has not had a look-
in since Cleveland beat Brooklyn
for the world championship in
1920, it may become apparent
that the West will be just another
total loss, especially if the Yan-
kees again get away to another
galloping start.

Unlucky Thirt-:en.

OR 12 vears, with a good

prospect that it will be 13, the
American Leaguers have been
dominated by the East, with the
Yanks figuring in seven pennant
victories, Philadelphia three and
Washington two. Another vic-
tory for the East would make it
No. 13—and we don't have to call
on superstition to prove that it
would be a very unlucky number.

It appéars at this writing that
nothing can be done about it. As
they line up today the Yankees
are standouts, even over the Ath-
letics and Washington. Nothing
in the West figures to have a
chance. The only alleviation
could come if the Yankees delib-
erately weakened themselves hy
trading some stars-—and perhaps
baseball fans would not look
kindly on that, either.

x» = 8

But something will HAVE to be
done about it, soon. Even men of
wealth like Phil Ball, a game guy
if ever there was one, cannot
afford to pay out $100,009 in losses
years after year. It is no exag-
gerated guess to figure that Ball's
baseball allegiance has cost him
this amount annually for the past
five years—although he doesn’t
emit any yelps about it.

With business what it is, in-
comes what they are and taxes
what they are going to be, all the
sport connected with being a
baseball magnate has been knock-
ed into the ash can.

“Pie” Traynor says that no good
can come of magnates making a
small mouth about the baseball
outlook. Maybe he’s right. But
“Pie” belongs on a club with a
pennant chance and is in a league
which will have a tight race.
“Pie” himself might be using a
loud speaker, if he sat in with

Bob Quinn, Sidney Weil or Phil
Ball.

Long before the manly art of self-

|Gentleman Jim class, the west had >

He wasn’t a popular hero in the
sense that Corbett and Fitzsimmons,
John Lawrence Sullivan and Demp-

but he was the heavyweight cham-
pion and he held the title for seven
years, with a chip on his shoulder
every minute.

Students of St. Louis history of |

the more serious sort react to the

name of Tom Allen as that of the)
Iron |

man who engineered the
Mountain Railroad and built the

Southern Hotel, but there was an-|

other Tom Allen, and al! he built

with bare fists.
There may be left in an older

clined in their youth, who remem-
ber a gnarled old Englishman who
operated a saloon about where the
American Hotel now stands.

Cafe, refreshment parlor, buffet and
Similar ladv-like terms were not in
Tom Allen's vocabulary. He was
frankly a saloon keeper and prize

|fighter, not a boxer, who fled sher-

iffs and once left the country with
John Law on his heels. Yet his
name is in that dignified compen-
dium of persons and events known

‘|as the Encyclopedia Britannica!

“Prize fightin’ ‘as got to be a
lydylike sport,” he grumbled. “W'y,
the blokes axchully wear gloves, they
do”

When a fight was decided on, a

side bets, were the stake.

Cockney accent, his tale ran

; “In one of the first fights, umder
j the patronage, as I recall, of the
| Earl of Yarmouth, one of the fight-
fers wore his hair unusually long.

{ter a good many rounds, his op-
ponent reached out with his left
hand, took a strong hold on the
|head of hair, and, with his right.
/put his man out. There was an
|; awful protest from the other side
| while the defeated man lay on the
'grourmi, but the referee held against
a foul. That was before the Mar-
quis of Queensberry made his cele-

“I got that in my fight with

HE entire sports worid extends greetings and felicitations to

Maxie Adelbert Baer. He is the new heavyweight boxing cham-

pion. Administering a swishing, crushing, two-fisted attack on
Primo Carnera, Maxie battered the “Man-Mountain” of Italy into
submission in New York last night.

Carnera, whom many boxing critics insisted would never lose his
crown, believing the European giant would carry on as king unti!
age caught up with him-and forced his retirement, wilted under the
power of Baer’s fists and chucked it up in the eleventh round.

Carnera, regarded as a bogus champion by unbiased fistic observ-
ers, did not go down fighting with his boots on, so to speak. Reeling
and staggering around from the effects of Baer’s blows, Primo made
@ wWéak effort to retain his crown. He allowed Referee Art Donovan
to stop the battle. Fighting champions have always gone down offer-
ing the last ounce of strength in their bodies. But then, I have
always contended that Da Beeg Preem was not a fighting champion.
He did not fool me when he retired to the field of ex-champions last
night.

Was on the verge of a nation-wide close-up. In the first place

Baer is a son of America. He was born at Omaha, Neb., and
received many jolts and knocks in his bovhood davs. He was a
butcher boy, then a kid out of the loose who went sightseeing through
life.

When Baer entered the boxing profession he donned a dinner
jacket. He felt that a boxer could be a gentleman and a showman.
He made friends with everyone. He joined the movie colony in Cali-
fornia, spent his money at night clubs in New York, and lollied around
the beaches of Florida. It was his desire to sit in the front row at all
times, mainly because he was going to become the world champion;
he wanted to be the idol of the people.

Baer was not going to limit his friends and acquaintenances to
members of the cauliflower industry that hang around gymnasiums.
He was going to meet the folks—say howdy to them and elevate the
profession that for the past several years had fallen into bad repute.

When I received the final flash last night—“Baer wins!"”’ I wanted
to grasp Maxie’s right hand and say: “Great stuff, Maxie—you're
the type we need in the sports world—especially in boxing!”

And did I join the throng that cheered Baer’s victory? I hopped
aboard the “I-Told-You” band wagon for in yesterday's forecast I
said: “Baer is my choice to win—on a knockout or the decision.”

Reign of Bogus Champions Is at An End.
HEN Baer won from Carnera he closed the reign of bogus
W heavyweight champions that has existed since Gene Tunney
went into retirement. When the ex-mariner stepped out of
competition the title became vacant. Through an elimination series
of bouts, Max Schmeling emerged on top. The German was awarded
the crown on a foul in his bout with Jack Sharkey.

Then Sharkey came up with the honors by gaining the decision
over Maxie in fifteen rounds, but his conquest was tainted by Joe
Jacobs’ famous outburst—“We've been robbed!” There were many
who agreed with Schmeling’s manager that Maxie had received a

raw deal when the decision went to Sharkey.
ce) 2 ®

things over in America’s pugilistic harvest. Primo weighed
270 pounds, measured six feet, six and one-half inches in height and
wore No. 17 shoes.

America, the sucker country for shrewd promoters, fell for Primo’s
bulk. He was paraded into rings and ballyhooed as the “man killer.”
He knocked over a flock of fistic bums and the build-up to lead him
to the championship was on.

Carnera made the grade officially—by knocking out Sharkey in
June “of last year. Despite his victory over Sharkey, Carnera re-
mained unimpressive in the judgment of many boxing followers.

“Carnera has pasted a bunch of palookas, but what'll he
do if he ever meets a boy who is inspired to charge into the big guy
and who has no secret strings attached to his fists?” was the ques-
tion that was heard frequently around the rialto.

The answer was delivered last night—Maxie Baer, unencumbered,
laughed and joked with Primo, even yawned at the Italian’s clumsy
antics in the ring and brought the heavyweight title back to Amer-
ica where it belongs.

Good by Primo, when does the next boat sail for Italy!

Boxing Official Describes Early
Prize Fighting in St. Louis

Fighters of the bare fist and small glove days, when the
present 15-round limit was unknown, are shown here. Jake
Kilrain, left, fought a 75-round battle with John L, Sullivan,
July 8, 1889, in Marion County, Mississippi. Kilrain, now 75
years old, is employed as a night watchman in a shipyard at
Quincy, Mass. Center is Harry Sharpe of St. Louis, as he ap-
peared when lightweight champion of Missouri. Sharpe, who
went 77 rounds to win the longest match ever fought under
Marquis of Queensberry rules, is shown, upper right, as he
appears today. In the lower picture Tom Allen, heavyweight
champion in the 80’s,who died in St. Louis April 5, 1904, is
driving. Seated with Allen is “Denver” Ed Smith, heavy-
weight fighter of Denver, Colo., who was training in St. Louis
for his fight with Joe Goddard of Australia. He knocked out
Goddard in 18 rounds at New Orleans March 3, 1893.

Bare Fists Flew in Late 80's’
and Early 90's When Most
Bouts Were Fought to a
Finish — Skin-Tight Gloves

Came Later.

The following is the first of a
series of articles by Har: y Sharpe
veteran St. Louis boxing official
which will review the sport in St.
Louis from bare-fist days to the
present.

BY HARRY SHARPE.

Prize-fighting in and about St
Louis in the late 80's and the early
80's was popula: with the sporting
fraternity, but it was neither promi-
ment nor profitable except In rare
instances. Matches of any im-
portance were slow in the making
and. because they were all fights to
a finish, there were long periods ot |
training. In addition, the fighters |
had either to tack themselves or
find someone who was willing to
risk fortune upon their chances
This was not always easy to do, and
when e@ “backer” was found he in- |
variably insisted that his fighter get
in the best possible condition before
he would let him fight.

There was generally considerable
wrangling before signing the “arti-
cles of agreement,” it being an ad-
age of the ring that “a match well |
made is half won.” Most of the ar-
gument concerned where the men
would fight. when, and for how
reuch. It was taken tor granted
that the fight would be to a finish
and there was no trouble coming
to an understanding that the fight
would be with small gloves, skin-
tight gloves, or bare knuckles. These
tights were nearly all governed by
the Marquis of Queensberry rules
there being only a few fights in the
vicinity of St. Louis under the Lon-
don Prize Ring rules following the
defeat of Mike McCoole by Tom
Allen in 1873.

Prize-Fighting a Felony.

The fight betw2en Allen and Mc-
Coole had taken place on Chouteau
Island (nicknamed “Bloody” Island
by fight followers). in the river a
short distance above St. Louis. This
fight so outraged the citizens of St.
Louis that in the following Janu-
ary the Missouri Legislature passed
a statute making prize-fighting a
felony and even declared giving an
exhibition of boxing in public a mis-
« emeanor

This probably accounts for the
fact that there was little prize-
fighting or boxing in St, Louis from
that time until about the middle
80's. It seems to have started again
about the time of Tom Allen’s re-
turn to St. Louis, after having failed
to secure a match with John L. Sul-
livan for the championship of the
world.

Allen had returned & #£London
England, following his victory over
McCoole and in the meantime Sul-
livan came into prominence. Rich-
ard K. Fox, publisher of the Police
Gazette, a publication given over to
sporting and theatrical events. con-
ceived a violent dislike for Sullivan
and vowed he would find a man io
beat him

Fox sent for Allen and arranged
an exhibition with Joe Goss, whom
Allen had previously defeated. This
exhibition took place in Madison
Square Garden in New York City
and Allen made such a_ miserable
snowing that Fox dismissed the idea
of his fighting Sullivan

What Has Happened?

AKE KILRAIN, bare knuckle

fighter of bygone days and
opponent of John L. Sullivan in
their 75-roune finish fight in
1889, celebrated his seventy-sev-
enth birthday recently.

Although he came up in London
prize ring days when fighting
was supposed to be exceedingly
rough and tough, Kilrain ap-
parently is none the worse for his
ring career.

This may seem = surprising,
when it is considered that the
limited-round fighting of today
leaves sO Many physical wrecks
and haif-goofy or blind relics in
its trail. |

If we look through ring his-
tory of the bare knuckle and
finish fight period, we find un-
mistakable evidence that it was
not as productive of broken-
down bodies as the fighting of
today.

Jem Mace, one of the really

clever men of his day, was in his
eighties when he died.

The previous generation will re-
member Tom Allen, former
champion of the world who, when
he quit the ring, opened the
“Champion’s Rest,” a public house
on Market street here. Old Tom
died at the age of 65, and he didn’t
do any dieting to help prolong
his life.

Many will also recall the “Bel-
fast Chicken,” Bill Clark, so long
a ring character in this city. The
“Chicken” came up in the ring
the hard way. He was featured
in a boxing show connected with
a British carnival show meeting
all comers. He fought his way to
the top in bareknuckle and fin-
ish fight days and he lived well
into in the eighties,

Old John. L. himself was around
60 when he died, and if his
constitution was impaired, it was
not due to his long, hard fights,
but to his persistent foe, John
Barleycorn, whom he finally
knocked out late in life.

Harry Sharpe, whose 77-round
fight ending in a knockout in one
of the ring’s classics, is hale and

hearty, although in his middle
sixties.

HERE were heard  expres-

not seem so to this writer, for
Louis was reeling in a daze at

Louis was punished much the

There was no doubt of his abil-

Will Max Regain Title?

HE Braddock-Schmeling fight

of next September is interest-
ing the writers and fight officials.
Already speculation is heard as to
the probable outcome and whether
Schmeling will be the first man
of modern fight days to regain a
heavyweight championship he had
lost.

One world champion in past his-
tory accomplished that feat, in the
heavy division. He was Tom Al-
len, an English fighter then mak-
ing his home in St. Louis. That
was in 1873.

Four years previously, through
rough-house ringside stuff and in-

timidation, Mike McCoole had got
an undeserved verdict over Allen.

The fight took place on an
island in the Mississippi and there
was so much bulldozing that the
referee declined to render a ver-
dict at the time. He was still
scared, later on, when he rendered
a decision from the stage of a
downtown theater.

In the return match Allen took
care that he would be protected
and he won back his title. He was
then widely tecognized. A defeat
by Joe Goss later sent Allen to
the discard.

Schmeling, who won his title
on a foul and then lost it back
to the man from whom he had
won it, Jack Sharkey, now has
an opportunity to become the Tom
Allen of modern times.

Whether he has the goods re-
mains to be seen. Not many of
the professional seers and clair-
voyants are practicing their pro-
fession this morning. Some of
their professional morale was
knocked out by the battle of
Yankee Stadium. That goes for

us, too.

New Credit for German.

EW credit is bound to be
given Schmeling for his fine
display and it seems likely that he
may be a favorite when he meets
Braddock. This affair will be
something very different, however.
Two canny old vets will be meet-
ing and both are careful fighters.
Neither has anything on the other
in youth or age, but Schmeling
has traveled farther and risen
higher than his prospective rival.
It is written that only three
fight experts in the country picked
Max to win.
However, we know of one who
had the right hunch, That was

Harry Sharpe of St. Louis. In an

interview with this writer, Sharpe
predicted that the experts would
be out of line on Schmeling and
conceded the possibility that the
German would put up a great
fight.

He favored Louis in case the
bout went the limit, but the result
was evidently no surprise to him.

He is alone in his class among
other fighters who, almost unani-
mously, figured that Max had no
chance whatever.

The result takes its place with
the big surprises of the fight
world, on a par with the downfall
of the mighty Jehn fT. Sullivan,
the overthrow of Jeffries by John-
son and the defeat of Baer by
Braddock.

McCoole Given

It Happened Before.
Fy Max Schmeling should defeat Jimmy Braddock in a title
bout, would he be the first heavyweight champion to regain
a title after having lost it?’’ asked a ring fan, during a re-

—s

cent ficht fanfest.

‘Tne almost unanimous answer
of those present was “yes.”
And, as far as modern fights zo,
that is to be the case. Actually
one might credit first honors of
the sort to the late Tom Allen,
proprietor of the old saw-dust
floored tavern on Market street
near Seventh, known as “Cham-
pion’s Rest,” famous throughout
the West 40 years ago.

Allen operated that resort up
to his death in 1904. It derived
its name from the fact that Al-
len, who was widely recognized as
world’s champion after he came
from England and settled here in
here in the early sixties, opened
and operated the place after his

retirement from the ring.
> °

IKE McCOOLE, another St.
Louis tavern keeper and him-
self a nationally known fighter
of the “bruiser” type, challenged
Allen for the title and they fought
on Chouteau Island in the Mis-
siseippi. Allen was winning, but
the referee, intimidated by
reughs, gave the verdict to Me-
Coole, who claimed the title for
four years.

Then he and Allen met again
in 1873, and Allen cut him to rib-

Biased Verdict.

bons and made him quit in seven
rounds, regaining his title rights.
- * *

Champion by Decree.

7 has been contended that Al-
len, who learned boxing in En-
gland where he fought leading
opponents, was not universally
recognized as champion. On the

In all the years since the Allens
and the Daleys first put fighting
over big, in this city, more than
70 years ago, no Xi.
boxer, whether of the  bare-
knuckle or glove variety, has ever
risen high enough to establish a
valid claim to a world title.

In the present century several
capable fighters developed here—
men like Harry tTrendall, Leo
Kelley, Harry Kabakoff, Kid
Bandy, Benny McGovern, George
Kirkwood, Ollie Kirk and several
others; but although several of
these were on occasions matched
with titleholders, none ever came
through.

= - =

The only St. Louis fighter mak-
ing his home here to claim the
title and gain at least partial
recognition as a world champion
was not native-born. He was the
late Tom Allen, whom many still
remember as the proprietor of a
saloon on Market street east of
Seventh.

“The Champion’s Rest.”’

LLEN, English born, settled in

St. Louis in the sixties and
brought with him a pretty good
fighting reputation. He claimed
the title before a championship
match in 1869 with Mike Mc-
Coole, another publican.

Although Allen won the fight,
the referee, intimidated by Mc-
Coole’s backers and a mob of
toughs, gave the decision to Mc-
Coole, who then claimed the
championship.

They fought four years later on
an island in the Mississippi and
this time Allen cut McCoole to
ribbons in seven rounds and re-
gained the crown. He held it until
beaten by Joe Goss. Afterward Al-
len retired and changed the old
name of his saloon to the one it
carried for many years—"“Cham-
pion’s Rest.”

Allen’s influence had much to
do with the development of St.
Louis as a boxing center. His
Place, besides the saloon in front,
included a large back room with
a ring pitched in one corner. In
another corner was a platform
for a piano.

Did He Maintain Order!
LD TOM, skull cap on his bald
head and gavel in hand, sat
near the doorway between the
two rooms and acted as master
of ceremonies or, if need be,
bouncer. Tom had icy blue eyes,
a handlebar mustache and a
heavy hand. This was reinforced
with a gavel which he beat on a
table to enforce order.

If disputants became too noisy
and belligerent they were thrown
into the ring, hands gloved and
told to fight it out.

On other occasions regular box-
ing bouts were arranged and the
spectators tossed coins to the con-
tenders in proportion to the in-
terest their bout excited.

Tom died in 1904 and the
“Champion's Rest” passed out of
existence soon after, to make
room for modern buildings.

But since Allen’s time this city
has not claimed a titleholder
either home-bred or one who es-
tablished a permanent residence
here, with the exception perhaps
of Abe Attell and Harry Forbes,
who dwelt here for a year or so
in the days when MHardluck
Charley Haughton operated.

It was here that Attell defeat-
ed Forbes for the featherweight
title, knocking him out in the
fifth round.

Brooklyn Tommy Sullivan, who
still resides here, has been given
credit for winning the feather-
weight crown when he knocked
out Attell at a local arena. That
fight aroused plenty o grapevine
comment, however. <A foul was
claimed by Attell but not al-
lowed.

As a matter of fact, the fight
was n at the featherweight limit
and no title was involved. Sul-
livan weighed 124 pounds, where-
as the maximum in those days
for this division was 122 pounds,
ringside. A short time after-
wards Attell knocked out Sullivan

in San Francisco in four rounds.

It Doesn’t Make Sense.

IM ISN

a}
/

OMEWHERE in South America a certain heavyweight leather-
G pusener is sounding off loudly. And if he is a bit incandescent
about matters relating to justice, fairness and that sort of thing

you can’t blame him.

The party is one Arturo Godoy
and he’s from Iqueque, Chile.
Very properly Godoy wants to
know how it comes that a vener-
able third rater named Jack
Roper and a beer-guzzling bar-
tender named Tony Galento rate
championship matches with Joe
Louis.

Roper is to fight the Brown
Bomber at Wrigley Field, Los
Angeles, April 28, and there will
be a lot of money in the park.

Galento gets the mid-summer
plum, which in advance has been
estimated to gross three-fourths
of a million dollars.

Godoy gets—well, Arturo gets
the run-around, notwithstanding
in 1937 he knocked out Roper in
eight rounds and, in the same
year, twice defeated Galento.

Both of his victims are past the
age when improvement is likely
to set in.

If records mean anything,
therefore, Godoy rates a title
bout ahead of both the men now
awarded championship events.
Ignoring him in favor of the
other two men really does not
make sense,

o * =

It’s a Rum Go.

APPARENTLY ALL the cum
laude graduates from the college
of hard knocks, alias the boxing
game, wind up in the saloon busi-
ness first—and later in the bank-
ruptcy court.

The white light that beats
upon Two-ton Tony’s New Jersey
wet goods emporium shines also
on the thirst palaces of Jack
Dempsey in New .York and
Florida, of Tom Heeney and
Johnny Risko in Miami, of
Mickey Walker in Manhattan, of
Jack Sharkey in Boston, and on
numerous other establishments
of the same type, in various sec-
tors.

Nearly all of these, if history
repeats itself, will wind up in
the discard although Jack Demp-
sey and Sharkey have hung on
for a number of years. Jim Brad-
dock and Mickey Walker already
have lost out, although the neon
lights bearing Walker's moniker
still shone over his establishment
a short time ago.

It’s an old, old custom among
pugilists of note—going into the
saloon business. It originated in
England and got a start long ago
in this country here in St. Louis
when the British fighter Tom Al-
len settled here in the sixties.

Allen was rated world cham-
pion until late in his career Joe
Goss defeated him. That was in
the seventies and Alien retired
soon afterwards and opened a
saloon on Market street near
Seventh, which, very appropri-
ately, he named “Champion's

Rest.” There Tom flourished un-
til his death early this century.
+ > *

It Was No “Boat Race.”

DON’T LET THE NAME fool
you. A Kayak may be an Es-
quimo canoe but Kayak II's vic-
tory in the Santa Anita Handi-
cap certainly was no “boat race,”
to revert to turf vernacular.

The South American racer real-
ly did something to establish his
class. That time of 2:01 2-5 sel-
dom has been equaled and only
once or twice has it been beaten.
It was a full second faster than
Bull Lea’s time for the same dis-
tance over the Hialeah track
which itself is a pretty fast rac-
ing strip.

The light impost of 110 may
have helped Kayak II, but he still
appears to rate near equality with
the great handicap horses of the
year — War Admiral, Stagehand,
Bull Lea and even his stablemate
Seabiscuit.

However, Seabiscuit will not be
shipped East to face another test
with War Admiral and the oth-
ers, but will remain in Califor-
nia to recover from his lameness
and prepare for the $50,000 Hol-
lywood Stakes. Victory in this
event would put him over the top
as the winner of more money
than even the mighty Sun Beau,
which now has a total slightly
above $376,000. Seabiscuit is with-
in about $30,400 of this mark

now.
* > .

Overlooked a Good One.

THE RACE TRACK CROWD
let its judgment get away with
it in thgt Widener handicap, at
Hialeah. It backed Stagehand to
win the race at 1 to 3, with a far
better investment showing on the
“tote” board—Buli Lea at better
than even money to finish sec-
ond,

Bull Lea ran Stagehand to a
head in a previous race and had
a three pound advantage in the
weights over that effort. He
really figured to be right there at
the finish, Stagehand made his
move too slowly and could not
get up in time—perhaps he never
could have caught the son of Bull-
dog that day.

a + *

Hialeah’s mutuel handle fell off
some during the 46-day meet just
ended. Still the machines aver-
aged $472,980 daily of which the
track kept seven per cent and
“breakage,” or about 8% per cent.
The State got three per cent.

What with admission ticket
sales and other sources of rev-
enue, receipts must have aver-
aged around $45,000 daily. No
wonder the track could afford
bonuses of from $1000 to $10,000
to officials.

title: The Expected Mill
text:
THE EXPECTED MILL.

Chicanery cf Rooke and His New
York Backers.

A Row Raised About the Final Stake-
Holder.

Rooke Not to Appear in the Ring
To-Day.

He Sends a New Proposition to Allen.

[Special to the St. Louis Repnblican.]

NEw York, June 16.—For the past two
weeks sporting men have been eageriy look-
ing forward to the fight between Tom Allen
and George Rooke of New York for the honor
of the title champion of America and $3,000.
Preliminaries for this contest were arranged
in sucha business-like manner that those who
had looked upon the match with suspicion and
distrust changed their minds and believed the
pugilists would fight. On Jane 1 the final |
stake-holder was selected, Mr. Jno. Chamber-
lain. He accepted. A few days later he was
informed that Joe Coburn had organized a
gang of rutiians to go on ito Pittsburg
and win the fight for Rooke if he
Was not able to do so himself. This plan was
to be carried out strictly to the letter, as fol-
lows: If the Rooke party could not secure a
referee in their favor they determined to win
the fighton an alleged feul. If they were
| balked in the referee business the gang from
| New York were to crowd im Allen’s corner
|and when Rooke forced the fighting a cry of
foul was to be raised in Allen’s corner by
Rooke’s friends. Then the latter were to
break down the ropes in Allen’s corner and |
itooke’s seconds were to claim the fight
ou the ground that Allen’s friends
broke into thering. The referee would then
| be cbliged to give his decision in favor of!
Rocke, according to the rules. Backers of
Rocke would then receive the stakes, and if
Allien sued he could not recover. Chamber-
lain, however, at the eleventh hour, declined
haying avything to do with the affair becanse
twe of nis friends had money in Rooke’s
$1,590, and they understanding they were to
be cheated out of it, claimed the money they j
had put in the stakes, and he refused
to haye anything to do with the affair.
No blame can be attached to Allen. He
thought he had oniy to fight an@win. Rooke
Was also anxious to fight, knowing that if he
could not win the Coburn gang would win
for him.

}

|
Prize-fighting has fallen into decay, not only
among the once reputable sporting men, but

among the rougher element who have patron-
ized pugilists. The wretched bruisers who
have formed the central figures of the brutal
gatherings found that getting a shocking drub-
bing with the usual mutilations put money
only into the purses of their backers. A prize
tight for $3,000 meant that certain well-to-do
brutes stood a chance of winning as much
more as they could extra from the savage
curiosity of the motley crowd by excursion
money. Because there was no possibility of
an excursion from Pittsburg is one of the prin-
cipal reasons why Rooke’s backers would not
agree to Harry Hillof New York for stake-
holder. The victorin one of the latter-day
fights found himself a beggar around the fishy
haunts of his patrons, while the vanquished,
with a face like a piece of claret jelly, thrown
aguinst the wall, was despised and left help-
less on the scene of the contest. So
the pugilists wisely deserted what
was miscalled ‘‘the manly art,’’ to the swind-
ling tactics of their backers. Fights were ar-
ranged, excursions got up at five dollars
each; no fights took place, except occasional
**scrimmages’’ during thetrip when some cit
izen objected to being robbed by gamblers -and
thieves, whe were passed on board free in or-
der that theymight break up the fight if wanted.
The principals in the meantime are purposely
arrested or take the wrong train, or if they do
get inte the ring, they failto agree upon a ref-
eree.

To-day the backers of the men met to
decide upon a final stakeholder, when it was
discovered that Shaughnessy, one of Rooke’s
backers, had put an attachment on the stakes
now held by Harry Hill. Mr. Muldoon, an-
other of Rooke’s backers, authorized Billy
Edwards, Allea’s representative, to notify
Allen that when Shaughnessy withdrew his
share of the money ne would make up the de-
ficit to one thousand, and if Allen would agree
to fight Rooke for that amount, within ten
days, 50 miles from Pittsburg, he would post
that amount with Harry Hill. Rooke is here
waiting Allen’s reply. He would have left for
Pittsburg but his backers would not give him

money to go.
