title: Allen and Rooke
text:
a

ALLEN AND ROOKE.

Arrangements Again Made for the
Fight.

The following special telegram to the RE-
PUBLICAN was received last night:

**NeEw YorK, June 28.—Sporting men here
are again rejoicing over a fresh match being
arranged between Allen of St. Louis and
Rooke of this city. The latter, with Billy
Borst M. Shaughennessy and many gporting men
were at Harry Hill’s, this afternoOM, when ar
rangements were made by them to tight within
fifty miles of Detroit, on the 15th of July. The
men are to fight forfun, and the champion-
ship of America, and on them backers are to
wager $1,000 aside, or more at thering,
which Harry Hill is to hold and give
to the winner. Rooke is allowed
to select the battle-ground, and _ will
have to notify Allen five days before the day
elected for the battle. Rooke has continued
training since the fizzle. Upon the above
terms there is every prospect ofa fight. Har-
ry Hillrepresented Allen, but Rooke trans-
acted his own business. The $3,000 stakes
at the first match between Allen and Rooke
Was returned to the parties who posted them
to-day. Harry Hill retains $1,000 of Allen’s
money to post on the coming contest.’”

INTERVIEW WITH ALLEN.

On receipt of the above intelligence, one of
the intellectual emissaries attached to the lo-
cal department of the REPUBLICAN was dis-
patched to seek an interview with the muscu-
lar celebrity whose residence among us has
made our city the headquarters of one of the
cherished institutions of the country. Deep
within the classic shades of ‘*‘Tom Allen’s
Free and Easy’’ the champion himself was
fonnd, in the centre of a collection of choice
spirits. The reporter announced to him
the intelligence received trom New
York concerning the new arrange-
ments for a fight between himself and George
Rooke, and asked if this were thus. Allen re-
plied that the information was new to him;
that ’Arry ’Ill was duly authorized to act for
him, but had not as yet sent him word of the
consummation of the new arrangements. The
REPUBLICAN could ascertain definitely by tele-
graphing to ’Arry. Having ample contidence
in its New York correspondent Mr. Hill was
not consulted by the REPUBLICAN for confirma-
tion or denial of his statement; and it may be
expected that unless some contingency at
present unforseen should arise Allen and
Rooke will meetand punch one another’s heads
at the time and place hereinbefore stated.

title: Tom Allen Dead
text:
TOM ALLEN IS DEAD.
Once Famous Pugilist Died Sunday at
the Baptist Hospital.

St. Louis: Tom Allen, retired
champion pugilist of the world, died at
the Baptist Hospital, Garrison and
Franklin avenues, at 7:35 o'clock Sun-
day morning. The end was expected,
as Allen had been very low for several
days.

Tom Allen was an Englishman, born
at Birmingham, England, April 23,
1889. He figured in 14 prize ring
matches in England and ten in Amer-
ica, his last fight, according to his
own Official record, being with Jim
Stewart on March 10, 1879, in Eng:
land. This match was for 50 pounds
a side. It lasted 55 minutes, was 16
rounds in duration and was won by
Allen.

Allen opened a saloon near the pres:
ent home of the Boatmen's bank, at
Fourth street and Washington avenue,
in 1868, and ever since had been a
tenant of the same real estate firm, in
different parts of the city.

title: Bare Knuckle Boxing: Only the Strong Survived
text:
Bare knuckle ~
boxing: Only.
strong survived

By ROBERT L. BURNES
Executive Sports Editor

It will be 100 years to the day next May 22 that Tom Al-
len, almost the last of the bare knuckle boxing champions,,
enjoyed the greatest moment of his life.

He was no longer the champion, having lost the title to
Joe Goss on an island near Covington, Ky., on Sept. 7, 1876.
Allen was disqualified for committing a foul in the 2Ist
round and it must have been a flagrant violation because in
those days gouging, kneeing, heeling, kicking and tripping
were established niceties of the sport.

Two years later he returned to his native England and on
May 22, 1878, appropriate ceremonies to honor him took
place. :

He was presented a huge silver cup on which were in-
scribed the words ‘‘Presented To Tom Allen, Champion
Boxer of England, by his buddies and admirers as a token of
their admiration of his skill and science, May 22, 1878, at the
Cambridge Hall, Newman St., and Oxford St., London,
Engiand.”

That cup today holds a place of honor in the home
of his great grandson, Thomas Allen Taylor, chairman of
the board of Seven Up Bottling Co.

“My father retrieved this cup from a pawn shop on Mar-
ket Street in 1938,” Tom Taylor said, ‘““but I have no idea.

where it was from the time Tom Allen died just past the

turn of the gentury until my dad found it.”’ :
The cup is the sole remaining tangible reward of the

career of Tom Allen, St. Louis saloon keeper. If some of the...
episodes have a ring familiar to what you read about boxing” °

today, it is ample evidence that the game hasn’t changed
much except to put gloves on the combatants.

Allen’s saloon was called Sportsmen’s Rest and was lo-
cated on Market Street, between 6th and 7th, where the old
American Theater once stood. The site today is a parking lot

' just west of Kiener Plaza.

By Tom Allen’s frank admission, Sportsmen’s Rest was a
saloon, nothing more, a rugged drinking place for fur trad- '
ers, for river men and for anyone else who wandered in.

Whenever an argument broke out up front and could not
settled.with words, the principals retired to the back room,
accompanied by anybody who happened to be in the place
and settled the difference with their bare hands. It was a
dangerous procedure because boxing or fighting was strictly
against the law. If someone in the place ran out on to Mar-
ket Street yelling “fight,” the police would move in, arrest
the principals and haul them off to the constabulary where
heavy fines were assessed. ;

Because St. Louis is hard by the Mississippi,

the area was the hub of bare knuckle fighting in the ’60s and
70s. If the fighters really meant business, they and friends

would hire a boat and everybody would go out to one of the

many islands in the Mississippi.

When they arrived, the spectators would form a ring.

around the fighters (which is why the squared fight area of »

today is still called a ring), some planks would be laid on the .

ground. The fighters, their seconds and the spectators would
then put up the money for which the combatants would con-
test on a winner-take-all basis.

There was one further bit of formal ceremony. Each
fighter would stand in the crowd until the challenger took off
his cap or hat and tossed it into the ring. That expression
“throwing his hat in the ring,”’ still exists.

Most of the onlookers would crowd around the fighters
*but a few had a special assignment. They would clamber

into trees, not only because they could have a.better view of

the proceedings but they could also keep a wary eye out for
police who might have been alerted and were en route
across the water to break up the brawl.

This particular bare knuckle era started in
1865. John Heenan had been the champion, had been inac-
tive for several years. Assuming that Heenan had retired,
Joe Coburn fought Bill McCoole in Cumberland, Md. in 1863
and Coburn won on a knockout in the 63rd round.

Two years later Coburn announced his retirement and
McCoole ciaimed the title. In 1869, Allen reinforced his
claim to No. 1 challenger by finishing off Bill Davis in 43
rounds on Chouteau Island and issued a challenge to
McCoole.

McCoole, a huge Irishman who outweighed Tom by-as
many as 45 pounds, and Allen did not like each other. It was
more than a challenge for boxing supremacy. They had vio-
lent arguments whenever they met. On some occasions they
came to blows with nd{hing at stake. Alllen accused
McCoole of ducking him. —

Finally McCoole agreed to put his claim to the title on the .

line and he and Allen met on Carpenter’s Island on June 15,
1869. News stories said Allen was winning fair and squareg |

when the bout was Stopped. The next night, on the stage of a
theater, the referee announced that McCoolg had retained
his title, that Allen had been disqualified for a foul.

Later the referee was to amend his story, say that he had
been intimidated into declaring McCoole the winner. Appar-
ently more than the normal amount of money was bet on the
fight, estimates going as high as $25,000. Professional gam-
blers were betting on McCoole. When they saw things going

“badly for their fighter, they swarmed the ring, assaulted the
_ referee and brought the fight to an end in a bloody brawl.

The whole thing was not a total loss for Allen. He
had the liquor concession.
“Whenever we arranged a fight on one of the islands,’’ he
Bid, “Td take care of the whiskey. For that first fight with
-McCoole; we must have had 1,400 or 1,500 men assembled
and they all came to drink and watch the fight.”
_ Four years intervened before Allen got another shot at
_McCoole.
: A year later, the famed Jem Mace came into the picture,
took on Allen at Kennersville, La., won on a 10th-round
knockout. (Rounds ended in those days when one fighter

was knocked down...if he could not continue the bout was «

over.) Mace claimed the heavyweight title. One of those to

contest his claim was an aging Joe Coburn who came out of

retirement.
Mace and Coburn fought twice in 1871 without conclusive

a}
a!

“result. The first was stopped by police. On the second occa-. -
sion, they fought 12 rounds...then suddenly quit and walked»

out of the ring without explanation. -(It was later said that —

their seconds told them that the gambler holding the side
bets had absconded with the money. Since there was no
point in continuing, they quit.)

Mace and Coburn ceased their ring activities with that
unsatisfactory performance and that left the field once more
to those old rivals, Allen and McCoole.

After many threats and challenges, they agreed on
a rematch on Sept. 23, 1871, on Chouteau’s Island. Allen beat
McCoole into a bloody pulp in three or four rounds, at the
end of which time McCoole’s seconds wanted to cail it off.
He refused and took a savage pounding from Allen until he
collapsed into a heap in the eleventh round and that ended
it,

Allen’s claim to the title was without dispute then until he
lost on the foul to Joe Goss. After that Allen took leave of his
saloon briefly to return to his native England where in 1878
he received the coveted cup.

He returféd to Sportsmen’s Rest which he continued to
operate until he died on April 6, 1903.

He was living evidence of why the rules had to be amend-
ed. He had paid a terrible physical price. His face was lined
with scars. He had another terrible scar on his right hand.
In a fight with one Charley Gallagher, someone fired a shot
and the ball struck Allen’s hand. A dcotor examined it, pried
the bullet loose, swabbed the hand and ordered the fight to
go on. “It didn’t hit the nuscle,”’ Allen said, ‘“‘so I just kept
on fighting and won.’

The most obvious —- and gruesome —- evidence of the toll
the fights took were Allen’s hands. Pictures of him in later
years showed his hands to be shapeless hunks, the knuckles

gone, eroded by the constant pounding they not only inflict-
ed but absorbed. x

We would like to finish a story which
began on the special sports page in the
weekend edition of The Globe-Democrat.
Because of space problems, the finishing
touches to the life of Tom Allen, one of
the last of the bare-knuckle heavyweight
champions of the world, were left un-
told.

He had been a saloon keeper in St.
Louis, had operated the Sportsmen’s
Rest at Sixth and Market, had defeated
Bill McCoole for the championship on

’ Chouteau Island in the Mississippi in
September of 1871. He defended against
all comers until 1876 when he lost the
title on a foul to Joe Goss. Two years
later he returned -to his native England
for a visit, was presented with a huge
silver cup by his friends and admirers.
That happened exactly 100 years ago on
next May 22.

Allen lost interest in boxing when the
Marquis of Queensberry, appalled by
the bloody carnage he had witnessed in
the bare knuckle brawls, refined the
rules of the game. Fighters wore skin-
tight gloves, gouging and kneeing and
tripping were barred — and Allen re-
tired.

“‘They’ve made it a sissy sport,”’ he
said. ‘‘I want no part of it.”

His daughter Mary, who also was
called Polly, returned to the United
States with him and she subsequently ~
married Edward Taylor of St. Louis.
They are the grandparents of Thomas
Allen Taylor, chairman of the Board of
the Seven Up Company, who has the
famed cup in his possession and who in
his spare time has tried to find out more
about his great grandfather without too
much success.

Just memories left

“‘All I know is what I’ve read in old
newspaper accounts,’’ says Tom Taylor,
‘“‘plus some family memories.”

When Allen died in 1903, it was as-
sumed he left some money. After all, his
saloon had been prosperous, he had
made a fair amount of money selling
whiskey to the spectators who gathered
for the fights on the islands. In addition,
the side bets on several of the fights

. were substantial, amounting in at least
one instance to $25,000.

His will left everything to his daugh-
ter, Polly Allen Taylor, and to a friend,
Tillie Hartgrove.

When the will was submitted to pro-
bate, however, it was discovered that he

‘had gone the way of fighters up to this
day. The will amounted to $278.35.

“T have learned,’’ said Tom Taylor,
“that the silver cup went to Miss Har-
tgrove - but where it was from 1903
when Tom Allen died until my father
retrieved it from a Market Street pawn
shop in 1938, I have no idea.”’

There has been a story in the family,
too, that Tom Allen came into possession
of a diamond belt, emblematic of the
world championship. ‘‘Various of my
relatives have talked about it,’’ Taylor
said, ‘but no one can verify that it ever
existed or where it is today.”

He plans to offer the silver cup, the
lone remaining memento of his great
grandfather’s reign as champion, to the
Missouri Historical Society.

World of its own

As the foregoing suggests and as the
following substantiates, boxing always
has lived in a world all its own. There is
nothing like it really. To those on the
outside, it is inexplicable and perhaps
repugnant. To those who have been a
part of it, the sports borders on a reli-
gion.

Henry Armstrong, the greatest fight-
er of them all, recently received a book
written by an old friend, Everett Law-
rence Sanders, close to boxing from the
days of Jim Jeffries, long time officer of
the California State Boxing Commission.
The book has the longest and most un-
usual title we ever have seen. In its en-
tirety (are you ready?) it is ““Who’s Who
in the World Friendship Tempie of
Fame, An Echo and a Beacon into a
Mirror of Greatness, compiled by Eve-
rett Lawrence Sanders and Enshrined in
the Golden Treasury of Perpetual Re

membrance.” :
The first two words suffice to tell that

is is an informal recollection of all of the
great boxers who did most of their fistic
work in California, plus rememberances
by sports. It is as big as a metropolitan
phone book, embellished with Sanders’
recollections.

This is his tribute to Armstrong, lean-
ing on the words of sportswriter Eddie
Muller....‘records made by boxing’s
immortal, Henry Armstrong, will stand
forever. As long as there is the sport of
boxing the man they called Perpetual
Motion will stand alone. :

The first reaction is to be amused at
the book but after reading it, you realize
how much it all meant to the man who
wrote it and it winds up being beautiful.

“WITH AN AIR OF GENTLE DIGNITY.”

A LITTLE SALVATIONIST.

SaturpDayY night, and nine o’clock at “Tom Al-
len’s.” The stained glass doors are continually
swinging to and fro; a ceaseless throng of young
men and old men passing in and out.

A woman stands in the doorway. She is about
twenty-two; she has a quiet face, and an air of
gentle dignity. She wears a dark-blue dress, and
a black bonnet with a searlet ribbon bound about
the crown; a silver badge at her throat confines
a collar on which are two broad red stripes.

She leads a little girl by the hand. The child
wears a little blue gown; a broad scarlet ribbon
about her waist is stamped, “Given to the Lord.”

“A Salvationist,” says some one with a sneer,
“selling her papers.”

She enters the door and asks the first man whom
she meets to buy The War Cry.

“Clear out,” he answers roughly; “I want my

nickel for whiskey.”
35

36 OUR CHILDREN OF THE SLUMS.

She looks at him quietly, saying, “God bless -
you, sir,” and passes on.

Some young fellows stand near, and one of them
cries out:

“We'll buy your papers if you'll sing for us.”

The woman hesitates; she has visited saloons
before — indeed, that is one of her regular Saturday
night duties in the selling of her papers,— but she
has never been asked to sing.

The soldier sees the opportunity, however, and
answers quietly :

“Tl sing a hymn if you like, sir.”

“ Sing, ‘ Nearer, my God, to Thee,’” calls out some
one.

And clear and sweet above the clink of glasses,
the click of dice, the soft thud of rapidly dealt
eards and the whirr of talk, the hymn rises:

‘“‘Nearer, my God, to Thee,
Nearer to Thee,

Fen though it be a eross
That raiseth me,

Still all my song shall be,

Nearer, my God, to Thee,
Nearer to Thee.”

“Sing us another,” calls out the first voice.
This time it is one of the Salvation Army songs,
and this its chorus:

A LITTLE SALVATIONIST. 37

“You are drifting, drifting to your doom,
But there’s mercy still for you, but there’s mercy still for you.”

The little girl, frightened at first, begins to sing
with her mother.

“Tell you what, boys,” calls out one of the young
fellows, “we'll all sing with her, if she’ll sing ‘ Hold
the Fort,’” and they do.

And then they crowd around, and each takes a
War Cry.

“T don’t call any man a gentleman who looks out
for any change,” says one man.

One of the barkeepers hands the child a sand-
wich. She is very hungry and sets her little
white teeth quickly upon it, when she remembers
something.

“Thank God for a good dinner,” she says, look-
ing down. Her mother turns to go out; just then
a man speaks to her:

“T should think you'd be afraid to come here
with your child, aren’t you?”

“Oh no,” she answers simply as she goes by
him.

She does not speak to any one except a young
boy who stands by the door. He sang with such
a beautiful voice and he is so young, she cannot
pass him by.

88 OUR CHILDREN OF THE SLUMS.

“T wish, sir,” she says, “that voice was singing
in God’s service.”

He does not answer and they go out into the
bitter night, a long walk before them to the cheer-
less barracks; part of the way she will carry the
little girl.

“Good heavens, Jack!” says one of the young
fellows, “what gives that woman courage enough
to come here? She was as pale as death; I know
she was frightened.”

“T don’t know, old fellow. She’s a good woman,
sure. What do you say to going home?”

TOM ALLEN.

ENGLAND.

OM ALLEN was born in Birmingham, England, in April, 184o. He stands five feet,
nine and one-half inches in height, and weighs at the present time in the neighborhood
of 200 pounds, In fighting condition he tipped the beam at 175 pounds. His first
battle was with Waggoner, of Birmingham, $25 (45) a side, in the autumn of 1861,
which Waggoner won. Six months later he met Young Gould for g1oo (£20) a side,
and the latter won, Posh Price whipped Allen in fifty-five minutes in July, 1862.
Allen’s next engagement was with Bingley Rose, of Nottingham, England, for $125
(425) a side, whom he conquered in ten rounds, lasting twenty-nine minutes, January, 1864.

Some six months later, Bob Smith, the “ Liverpool Black,” whipped Allen in two hours and
fifteen minutes, He then fought Jack Parkinson, whom he “cut into ribbons” in twenty minutes,
for $125 (£25) a side. Meeting Posh Price a second time, for $125 (£25) a side, the two men fought
forty-one rounds, lasting two hours and five minutes, in November, 1865. Allen had decidedly the
best of the fight, and as Price gave a tip to the police and had himself arrested, the stakes were
given to Allen.

On June 12, 1866, Allen defeated George Iles, and on March 5, 1867, fought a draw with
Joe Goss for $500 (£100) a side. The fight took place in Monmouthshire, and lasted one hour and
fifty-two minutes, in which time thirty-five rounds were fought. Allen afterwards received two
forfeits of $250 (£50) each from Bill Thorpe, Peter Millard and Mike Cocklin.

Allen came to this country in July, 1867, and his first fight was with Bill Davis, at Chateau
Island, St. Louis, January 12, 1869, when he won in forty-three rounds. On February 23, 1869,
he fought Charley Gallagher at Carroll Island, near St. Louis, and was knocked out by the latter

in the second round, after fighting but three minutes. On July 15, 1869, he fought Mike McCoole
.

on Foster’s Island, in the Mississippi river, for $1,000 (£200) a side, and’ the excursion money.
Nine rounds were fought, and Allen made a chopping-block of his opponent. A crowd broke into
the ring, and the referee gave the decision to McCoole. He again met Charley Gallagher, at
Foster’s Island, near St. Louis, August 17, 1869, and although he had Gallagher whipped in the
eleveuth round, after twenty-five minutes of sharp fighting, the referee decided in favor of the
latter. On May 10, 1870, he fought Jem Mace at Kennerville, near New Orleans, for $5,000
(£1,000) and the championship of the world. Mace won in ten rounds, lasting forty minutes.

On September 23, 1873, he fought Mike McCoole again, for $2,000 (£400) at Chateau Island,
St. Louis, Allen being declared the winner after twenty-nine rounds, lasting twenty minutes, had

been fought. He afterwards fought a draw with Ben Hogan, the reformed preacher-pugilist, near

Council Bluffs. His last fight was with Joe Goss for the championship of America and $5,000

(£1,000), in Kentucky, in 1876. The men fought in two rings, the first being erected in Kent,
and the second in Boone county. ‘Twenty-one rounds were fought in fifty-three minutes, when Goss
was declared the winner by a foul. Allen was arrested and put under bonds. He afterwards

settled down in St. Louis, where he still lives.

stand a chance of getting one of the
best thumpings ever given aboye the

belt.
HIS OPINION OF HOGAN.

-Tom seems to estimate Hogan’s
chances of winning the coming fight
as rather slim. “Hogan,” he_ says,
“never_intended to fight me. He has
never been in the ring to my knowledge,
and when he challenged me to this fig) t
he knew just what he had to expect.
$ By he do you think he challenged
you

_“Oh! just to get a'little cheap noto-
riety. He is now playing his cards. for
a draw.”

“How so?”

Why, only yesterday he made propo-
sitions to J: Looney to forfeit his
share of the movey, which is $1,000, if
we would draw off and make it a draw
and not fight.” f

“What does he mean by that 7”

“Oh! just this. He don’t want to
meet me. He never intended to meet
me. Why, he refused to fight Jack
Madden, my trainer, and then had the
impudence to challenge me. Any d—d
fool can challenge me, but coming into
the ring is another thing.”

“What does Hogan gain by this back
down ?”

“It is as I told you before. He wants
notoriety. He thought it would be a
big thing for him to get up all this
noise,and then after getting Jack Loone:
to declare it a draw fight, go East an
show himself as the man who had made
a draw fight with Tom*Allen.”

Then you think Hogan will not fight

you?

“I did not say that. But I do think
he never intended to put up his fins be-
fore me, and I now am sure he wants to
back down from the fight.”
= ei this fight comes off, where will it

e

“At or near Omaha. Excursion tickets
are being sold from St. Louis and return
for $20, and we expect to see a pretty
large mob there.” ¥

“will Hogsn come to Kansas City ?”

“I think he will. The whole mob of
St.Louis sports will be here on Wednes-
day night.” t
| ino will the fight take place, if at
al
“On the 18th of this month, or two
weeks from to-morrow.”

“Is it your opinion that there wasa
‘put up job’ about that capture of the
steamer Continental last week 1” :

“I do. I don’t think Hogan or his
friends had anything to do with it, but I
think the officers of the boat put up the
entire job.”

“Wiil you and Looney take Hogan’s
$1,000 and consent to call it a draw ?”

“No; I will not, nor neither will Jack
Looney. You will see by the St.
Louis’ papers of to-day just what
Looney as to say about it.
He explains the whole busiaess.
‘As to Hogan’s money, he has no money
put up; it is the people’s money by right
and justice. They paid to see the fight
and are entitled to the worth of their
money, and if Hogan had met me and
put up his “fins” to me, they would have
seen what they paid to see. The truth
of-the whole matter, Mr. Editor, is just
this: Hogan don’t want to meet me.
But if I can get_bim before me once, we
will decide just what is in him.”

“Why don’t you “fight at Kansas

City?”

(Laughing) “Oh, you see we are bound
so by bonds that Missouri soil ain’t good
to dance on just now. Besides, they say
they are after me with a requisition
from Illinois for my fight with Mike
McCoole. But I don’t think they want
me very bad.” 2

The gay and festive young boxer con-
tinued. the conversation at some length,
relating some of his former experi-
ences in the ring,and assured the TrtEs
that while he did not particlarly “ban-
ker” after the business, he was always
open to proposals, and would be happy
to amuse any ambitious young gentle-
man in Kansas City for a few rounds at
any time. He will give an exhibition
here this week with Arthur Chambers,
Jack Madden and others, when we shall
see and know more about him.

title: Pugilist Worth a Fortune
text:
HOME TS OF TE BOERS

40M SHARKEY PREPARING AN
ELEGANT HOME FOR HIS AGED
FATHER AND MOTHER

PUGILIST WORTH A FORTUNE

Tom Allen's Patient, Faithful and
Devoted Daughter—Prof. Clark’s
Venerable Mother—Demp-

sey's Loyal Wife.

The public sees onty the flerce side of
the nature of the boxer or pugilist, but
there is another side that is human, and
it is pleasing to be able to say that it ap-
plies to many of the famous ring glad-
fators who have been noted for their fe-
rocity. Tom Hyer was ashamed to go
home after a battle in which he received
a black eye, for the reason that it might
distress his relatives. Nat Langham lov-
ed a lass who was opposed to his call-
dug, and after his successful fight with
Tom Sayer he agreed to never again cn-
ter a ring. Had Andy Bowen followed
the impulse once expressed tg the writer,
in his New Orleans home, he might not
have lost his life at the hands of George
Lavigne. Mrs. Bowen was a sweet-faced
little woman, who dreaded the hours dur-
ing which her husband was engaged in
battle. She had a foreboding that he
would be killed, as he finally was. Bowea
worshiped her, and his home was bright,
and hap He had prov d h’s
wife and himself that so soon as he had
gained sufficient worldly goods to embark
in some other business he would fight n>
ore. But that day never came. Death
in the ring intervened.

SHARKEY’'S FILIAL AFFECTION.

‘Tom Sharkey, the sturdy man-of-wu''s-
man, who has fought many a desperate
battle in the ring, has amassed a fortun>,
and is today said to be worth near $193,-

000. He has just purchased a big estate
at Sheepshead Bay, N. Y., and h er-
manently located there. Of his inten-

tions Sharkey sa

“My motive in I ing this property was
ovide my dear parents a home of th:

i order. I mean to stop at nothing in
the way of expense, but will go right
ahead and furnish every room with t

be

cost.

of everything required, regard] ss of

T am determined to fulfill my in-
tention of showing gratitude and love for
my dear father and mother.”

Sharkey mone; as well as
ma . His habits are of the best. He
is not what the boxing world would des-
fgnate “good fellow." That was the
title worn by John L. Sullivan, and it
meant#to him the expenditure of more
money than any other man in the rinz
has been able to earn. And yet Shark y
is really a good fellow, as is shown in his
solicitude for the happiness and com-
fort of his aged parents,

THAT GIRL OF ALLEN'’S.

In the tumble-down, ramshackle bulld-
ing in the “Tenderloin” of St. Louis, on
Market street, in which Tom Allen, “re-
Ured champion,” nightly directs a con-
cert fer the entertainment of his patrons,
resides a woman who is known to but
few of the people of that city. She ts the
daughter of the once probably best
known heavy-weight prize fighter in the
World. She is the jewel of the home of
the retired warrior of the ring, and she
has devoted her life to her father, ‘There is
an unwritten romance which coupled her
name with that of the late Col, Fred
Waikins, the Iffe long friend and backer
of the ring gladiator, in which it is re-
lated that for her father's sake she de-
cided to remain in charge of her home.
It is also said that in all the years that
Tom Allen has conducted a concert hall
in St. Louis M Allen has never crossed
its threshhold. She shines above, in the
tion of the building in which tho
Allen's reside, but knows no more than
does one who has never been in the
pl of what the concert hall jooks like
Allen is rough and surly, as a rule, with
all he meets, but is as kind and gentle
with the daughter as though she were
yet a winsome maid in short skirts.

PROF. CLARK’S OLD MOTHER,

Three years stnce, Mrs. Clark, mother
of the veteran boxer now conducting the
Natatorium, in St. Louls, died of old age.
The professor now approaching the
ei ear mark, so it will be seen th.
Mr: ark lived to quite an old age. |
“Willie” had been her support from his
boyhood. After the father died, “Willie,”
now ‘‘prefessor," entered the boxing
booths at English fairs, and met ail com.
ers for a mere pittance, which went to
sustain mother and the eight little |
brothers and sisters at home. Many a
hard knock “Wille” has received at the.
hands of the horny-fisted miners and
ether ambitious athletes of all weights,
in order that the weekly stipend might
be turned over to mother for the rent ot
the humble cottage and the grocer and
butcher. When Prof. Clark came to
America the mother came with him, an@
his tender solicitude for. her comfort
compensated for all the reputation he
had earned in the ring as a ferocious
fighter. Even to this day ‘Willie’’ pays
regular visits to the green spot in the
cemetery where his mother rests, and
speaks of her as reverently as son eyer
spoke of the woman who gave him life

DEMPSEY’S LOYAL WIFR,

When Jack Demp wedded, it was
with a promise to his sweetheart that he
would fight no more. Had he kept that
promise he might haye been alive today.
But the temptation Was too great.
the day when the gallant “Nonparei
earned his title of middle-weight cham-
pion of the world, fortunes were not co
ing to prizefighters in a night. Twelve

is a aver

|

thousand dollars was the bait that caused
Dempsey to do what he had promised
to not do, and the match with Bob Fitz-
simmons, which resulted so disastreusly
for Dempsey, was made. It was prac-
tically his last fight. He never recov-
ered from the humiliation of the affatr,
and took to that which wrecks while tt
cheers. Womanlike, the patient and de-
voted wife was loyal to her husband in
defeat. That fateful night, after Demp-
sey had been sorely beaten by the
Cornishman, without a chance for him to
win, she sat at his bedside and com.
forted him in his sorrow. She. told him
that defeat must come to all at some
ume, and reminded him that his fame
would not die because he had been once
vanquished. She did not taunt him with
reminders of his broken promise, but |
painted word pictures of all that was in
store for them now that he was done
with fighting.

CHARLEY MITCHELL'S HOME.

Charley Mitchell, the English boxer,
who has the glory of a draw with the
enly John L. Sullivan on his ring record,
wedded the pretty daughter of “Pony”
Moore, England's famous minstrel. Be-
cause of her influence Mitchell is today
a wealthy man, and hes a most Interesi-
ing family of which he is proud. Mrs.
Mitchell is pictured as a rarely beautiful
woman, refined and domestic. Charley.
Mitchell is far from the rough that his
calling would indicate. In his home lit
he is more than many man whose sur-
roundings should better him, No word of
censure has ever been heard against
Mitchell in his treatment of his family.
On the contrary, it is a matter often com-
mented upon among those who know him
best that he is a model husband and
father. Not one of his boys will follow
the profession of the father, They have
received the benefits of an education that
will fit them for the battle of lifé out-
side of the squared circle. His daughters
are lovely girls, and the Mitcheil family
is highly respected in its home circle.

FiITZ’S BRAW BABES

Rob Fitzsimmons is at the mercy of his
eldest when at home. Bob would rather
face Sharkey than that bey of his, when
the youngster is in playful mood, for, in
the case of Sharkey, Fitz could repay
blow for blow, while young Fitzsimmons
is lord of the Fitzsimmons manor, allel
and abetted by his good mother, who Bob
worships as the heathen dces his god.
Rose Julian was weil known In the the-
atrical profession when she wedded the
pugillst whose name is known through-
out the world. No word has ever beea
uttered against her. In referring to the
marriage, Col. John Hopkins, the well-
known veteran theatrical manager, said:

“Ll cannot understand how a sweet girl
a womanly woman, with all the rejine-
ment and gentleness possessed by Rase
Julian, could fall in love with that bear
Fitzsimmons. She is as lovely a girl as
ever faced the footlights, and I am afraid
a prize fighter will not make for hor a
suitable husband.”

But Col. Hopkins was in error. Rose
Julian made of Fitzsimmons a better man
than he otherwise would have heen. She
has yet to find cause to regret the day
that she became his wife. Witzsimmons
lavishes affection and comforts, as well as
luxuries, upon his family. A day in hts
home would be a revelation to those who
naturally regard the prize fighter as a
fierce, uncontrollable animal. Mrs. Fi
simmons is queen, and the young Fitzsine-
mons are lords of the manor in that
home. Fitz is as meek as the proverbial
lamb. <

MANY SIMILAR INCIDENTS.

John L. Sullivan did much for his pa-
rents during his phenomenal career in the
ring. His father was small of stature.
but it is related that John obeyed orde
delivered by Sullivan pere as meekly as
though he were a pigmy ruled by a giant.
Out of his earnings he lavishly provided
for his parents. That and the charitable
contributions made by Sullivan were t
redeeming features of his career. Jacx
Wilkes, of St. Louis, provided for his wid-
owed mother and sisters, with her two
boys, and appeared in the ring as “Jack |
Wilkes” in order that their friends misht |
not know that it was Robert Walker wh

was a pugilist.. Dick Moore, of St. Paul,
has a soft place in his heart for h's home
people. Terry McGovern’s wife and boy |
are his first thought after a battle. They |
are ever near, and Terry enjoys nothing |
better than a romp with that young glad-
iator. Joe Choynski married a gente gil,
unused to anything connected with such
rough doings as her husband is famillar
with in his ring encounters, and she finds |
no room for complaint of trea‘tnent by |
her prize fighter husband. A man is what
he is, despite his calling.

—Willie Green.

title: The Last Triumph of Jem Mace
text:
Sr ae oS se a Oe ES Saar ae
HE LAST TRIUMPH OF “JEM”’ MAC

4

PECTACULAR Fighter Who Dominated the Ring for Ten Years Came Back
for the Third Time “When Near the Age of Forty and Revived Clean Sport

“Jem” Mace in Fighting Costume.

FTER John Morrissey withdrew the best
DX ciaimast to the American title was ‘‘Joe”
s Coburn, who defeated “‘Mike” McCool in
1863. “In the following year Cobitn was to
have fought with “Jem” Mace, then holder of

. the world’s title for the second time, in Ireland.
The unsportsmanlike conduct of Coburn, or his ~
backers, broke up the match, and left Mace with
the honors, Mace’s position. was further
strengthened when “Joe” Wormald forfeited a
belt to him, which he had won from Andrew
Marsden, and when he beat “Joe” Goss in 1866,
Mace retired.

"The scene of the big fights then shifted defi-
nitely to America, where for several years inde-
cisive battles and counter claims confused the
{issue of the championship. Several so-called
championship fights were mere wrangles; others
‘were little more than conflicts between rowdy
partisans armed with knives and pistols.

Fair examples of the two varieties were “Ned”
O”Baldwin’s “victory” over “Joe” Wormald in
1868, and “Mike” McCool’s “triumph” over
“Tom” Allen in 1869. Fivially, in 1870, “Jem”
Mace came out of his retirement and obtained
a match with “Tom” Allen, the best available
boxer in the American ring. , 2

‘Copyright. 1910. by the New York Herald Co All rights reserved.)

T was an enthusiastic gathering that filled the

special train out of New Orleans on May 10, 1870,

bound for the spot where the championship of the

world was to be decided once more. Not since the

great international contest between Heenan and
ayers bad the pugilistic world looked so bopefully
toward a promised test of skill or given proof so
notably of its faith In the possibility of lifting the
game from reproach, “Jem” Mace, Iatter day ex-
ponent of the manly science developed by its masters
Mendoza and Belcher, had come to America and had
been matched with “Tom” Allen for $2,500 and the
World's title,

Mace was in every way the veteran of the profes-
sion. He was thirty-nine years old. As a youth he
had been an itinerant Instructor in boxing. Before
bis two meetings with “Tom” King, In 1962, he had
been prominent {n the ring for seven years. He had
fought thrice as many pitched battles as any other |
man who then flew colors within the “squared circle.”
His circuit had included England, Ireland, Australia
and America. And now, well past the boxer’s prime, |
with an established and “honorable record, be volun-
teered to restore the ancient traditions of the sport
after a period of confusion and disorder by. one more
honest test of manhood.

Allen was the fittest opponent to dispute the great
fighter. Born in Birmingham in 1841, he had the ad-
vantage of Mace by ten years. His career in the ring |
bad been busy and successful, including n dozen fights
before his departure from England and four tn this
corny. A meeting with “Mike” McCool near St.
Louis the preceding year had been broken'up by a
mob and he had lost the decision after leading all the
way; but subsequent negotiations for another trial
with McCool had ended with the withdrawal of the
nominal champion and Allen was now in actual pos
seasion of the title.

The special, after an early start, proceeded to a
stretch of open ground some three miles above Ken- |
nérville, La. where the ring was pitehed near the |
tiyer. The crowd of one thousand, which included
many well known fight followers from all parts of
the country and from abroad, army officers and the |
members of the Chicago Baseball Club, ranged tn
orderly manner about the ropes. Mace and Allen,
who bad followed the train on a.dummy engine, were |
called forward by Rufus Hunt. the referee, and en-
tered the ring with their attendants for_a general
handshaking. Mace: was seconfed by “Jim” Cusick |
and “Jerry” Donovan; and: Allen by “Joe” Coburn and

At the Ateipping Doth! men.showed in magnificent |
condition. proof of long and faithfal training: ‘The
spectat dwelt curiously and admiringly upon the
wonderful physique of Mace, his trim muscle knobbed
figure, his brisk, lithe tnovements, The old champion,
full of the pride of body, had never allowed bimself
to get out of hand’and revealed none of the softened
Mines and'flabby rolis which might have been pardoned,
ip Founding ils score of fighting years, His eye
stoath thes his ‘skin as fresh and firm upon, the

‘ridges, bis pose as erect and easy as when

first the championship. And with tt ail
was the calm, youthful, confident smile that had over-
looked so many btricken flelds. pstigs tear aly a
at 165 pounds, just seven pounds over his weight in bis

with his back to the sun, though, as proved in the
Pevent, the advantage was of little importance to s0
shifty and nimble a boxer. At the cali of time the
men moved forward slowly to the centre of the twen-
ty-four foot ring and thelr hands met for an instant
in the final handclasp from which they whipped in-
stantly on guard. Mace fell away with springy tread,
studying his adversary, alert to every line of his att!
tude, every slightest indication of strength or weak-
ness, Then, advancing a cautious step, he slid easily
into the tapping spar and whirl of fists with which
be was wont to test his man.

Allen met him speedily and well, though it was not |
in him to show the grace and deftness of the veteran.
He was one trained to a rough handed school of
pugilism that had put aside many of the fine, scien-
tific tactics of the art In favor of hard blows and tough
bodies. In this “Tom” presented an Ideal contrast to
(Mace, survivor of the third great period of fisttc his-
tory, which produced, besides himself. such strategists
jas Sayers and King. Allen stood sturdily on his own
ground, playing only enough to cover himself and
watchful of the chance to hammer through with his
heavy fists, Mace was here, there and around, circling,
weight poised for advance or retreat, handling himself
Iike the fast, compact, adjustable fighting machine he
was.

Arms and bodies flashed swiftly, silentiy, as the
gindiators feinted and parried in their preliminary
‘clash, constant applause’ from the eager spectators
testifying to the keen interest aroused by the skilful
exhibition. Then, with characteristic suddenness,
Mace moved in with a quick shuffle and swept over «
tinging left to the right eye, stopped Allen’s quick
drive with sure judgment and repeated the blow to
the nose before springing’ back. Allen’s retallatory
swing passed him harmlessly and he was once more
at his chosen distance, balanced, tense for any move,
The slower Allen now: showed a disposition to even

scores and broke inja rush. driving right and left.
“Jem” warded both blows aggressively; met the charge
, with a side step, smashed’ a straight left to the ribs
“that stopped Allen dead in mid career and got away
\ with his customary grin.

“Tom,” it was evident, had no preconceived plan of
campaign, and having been checked fell back upon
the sparring once more, hopeful of ‘drawing Mace
within range. “Jem”, met Hitm in some rapid. light ex-
jchanges, pressing craftily on. Allen was awake to his
chance, and lashed out sharply ‘with’ right and left,
tapping .the veteran. Mace ducked the volley, worked
in and shot his famous one two to the left eye and
chin, Uke a compound fiash of lightning. Those
among the’ watchers who. bad-seen-bim in former
days knew that It was indeed the spectacular “Jem”
Mace of old as he. went, through this manoeuvre. If

BREAK IN THE BIDDLE STREET
SEWER.
Stampede at the Theater Comique—
Tom Altten’s Benefit Postponed.

A dense crowd of bummers, loafers, shoulder-
strikers, lunch-grabbers, and curiosity mongers as-
sembied on Saturday night ai the Theater Comique (old
Mozart Hall) to attend the pugilistic display for the
benefit of Tom Allen, the renowned prize-fighter. It
had been anreunced that the magnificent $1000 cham-
pion belt would be presented to Allen, and that Joe Co-
burn, Mike McCoole, Tom Allen, and other pugilists
wonld put on the gloves and display their muscular
skill in friendly passages at arms. The house was lit-
erally jammed, andthe fun was about to commence}
when a dull, heayy crash was heard in front of the
building, and the alarm was given that the Biddle street
sewer had caved in, The break occurred directly in
front of the building, and carried away a portion of the
sidewalk, and the striped pole at the barber-shop next
door. The crowd made s rush for the door, and
in a few minutes the hall was deserted. Two sections
of waterpipe were cracked, and a jet of water forty feet
high shotup into theair witha hissing noise, while
another stream was poured with great force against the
north side of the pit that had been opened, threatening
to undermine the building. The gas pipe also broke,
and the smell emitted was anything but pleasant to the
olfactories. The lights in the hall went out, and dark-
nese reigned supreme. .Not even a tallow dip was there
to make the darkness visible, Of course the performance
could not go on. It was announced that the benefit
was postponed until Wednesday night, and the disap-
pointed crowd scattered,

The break in the sewer is about twenty feet deep, and
extends half way across the street. A few days ago the
sewer cayed in at the same spot, and had just been re-
paired. The patch work must have been poorly done.
The water was turned off ina few minutes, and the
police placed a barrier around the dangerous hole,

summary: The St. Louis Globe-Democrat reported that a pugilistic benefit for Tom Allen at Theater Comique was postponed when a sewer collapsed in front of the building during the event.

On November 16, 1863, Goss defeated Posh

Then came the pugilist’s ‘first defeat. |
He was matched to fight Jem Mace,
each to weigh 150 peeeets Maco stak-—

Goss’ last battle with Tom Allen took place

owing to the interference of the police, They |

The referee, seeing that both men were ex-
hausted and unable to continue, declared the

The match between Goss and Tom Allen for

days. Of course, that bar-room rowdy 3

title: Heenan and Mace Assault at Arms Exhibition at Varieties Theater
text:

THE MANLY ART.

HEENAN AND MACE AT THE VARIETIES

:

Outpeuring of the Fancy.

’ ”

An “Assault at Arms’’ Between the
Pugilists.

A Delighted Audience.

Few cities of the Union can boast of a larger number
of admirers of the manly art of self-defence than St.
Lou. Not only haye we hundreds of amateur boxers,
but a fair proportion of professional pugilists, and
those of no mean pretensions. The herculean Mike
McCoole, who was at one time regarded as the best man
in America, is a prominent resident in thecity. Tom
Allen, who now wears the colors of champion, is alsoa
denizem here. Charley Gallagher, who won a match
with Alien, kept a saloon here for several months. Bill
Davis sometimes makes this his home. Jim Coyne
liyed here for a short time, and Wm. Ryall died here.
Besides these heavy weights, we havea number of
light weights of acknowledged skill, and several retired

With such an array of buffers in our midst, it is not
strange that a growing fondness for the bloody en-
couniers of the roped arenashould be observable among
our people. This partiality for the prize ring is not
confined to the eamsgcet | classes and saloon-keepers, but
extends to the more refined walks of life; and the oc—
currence of a prize fight between tried pugilists, within
a reasonable distance of the city is sure to cail to the
a! a goodly crowd of gentlemen of respectable social

OD.

peThe announcement, therefore, that those famous
wee John C, Heenan and James Mace, would ap-
pear last night in an assault atarms on the boards of
the Varieties Theater, was hailed with satisfaction by
many quiet and sober sheers, as wellas by the ciass
known as ‘‘the fancy.” The fact that the moral town
of Chieago had prohibited these pugilists from showing
their ekill with the gloves, only added to the desire to
see them, and tickets of admission sold freely at a dol-
ar.

Heenan and Mace arrived here at a late hour on
Monday night, and put up at the Plauters’ House.
Yesterday hes showed themselves in the streets, visit-
ing Billy Carroll’s, on Market street, Mike MeOovole’s,
on Fifth street, Jack Looney’s ‘*Pearl” on Pine street,
ind Tom Allen's ¢oncert room on Washington avenue.
rhey were followed in their perambulations by an ad-
miring crowd, andseemed to enjoy the honor of be-
ing stared at. Both men were dressed in new suits of
fine cloth, and bad the exterior appearance of gentle-
men of wealth. Heenan isreallya fine looking man;
possessing a splendid form and a countenance marked
by great intelligence. He is agreeable in his manners,
conversing freely and intelligently upon various topics,
sud exhibiting considerable politeness to those with
whom he conversed.

Mace was not so communicative, but freely answered
11 questions propounded. He las « square English
face, witb abheavy jawand bull neck; is slightly stoop-
shouldered in walking, and has broad and powerful
shoulders, amnscular arm andfnll ard firm chest. His
walk is not so graceful as that of Heenan, and he takes
pretty long sfrides. His accent betrays the English
sountryman—Yorkshire or some other sbire—and his
anguage is not always constructed upon the principles
9f Lindley Murray. Mace’s weight is about 180 pounds,
nd he general y figit.at about 160. When reminded
hat in fighting ‘om Aen he was departing from the
zereral rule inthis country in making a match with a
:ountr; man, he said, ‘‘Well, it’s not my fault, LItried
Oo avcid it, but it was forced on me.”

THE VARIETIES LAST NIGHT.

The Varieties has seldom been more densely crowded
shan it was last night. Every seat in the pit, and first
and second circles was taken, and the colored gallery
was nearly filled. The women werefew and far be-
ween, A private bor, away up under the ceiling,
showed four or five painted faces peering ont from the
jarkness, but the usual array of frailty was lacking in
he circle usually sppropriated to females. The pit was
xecupied by a mixed crowd of gentlemen, loafers, pick-
nockets, etc., who exhibited their breeding by taking
off their hats, while the occupants of the circles re
mained covered—ihis, however, may bea rule of the
house.

Patiently did the multitude wait through the medley
of Irish and African songs and dences, the piroucttes
of numerous dancing girls, and the drolleries of the
burnt corkonians. Before such an audience, the ac—
tors did their best. and some of them were rewarded
with applause, while others were coldly received.

At length the curtain fell, and the stage was sprinkled
md swept for the ‘‘crib-scene” in Tom and Jerry.
Then the curtain was rolled up, and the Benicia Boy
ané the English champion stepped to the center of the
stage, preparatory to entering upon their

PASSAGE AT ARMS.

The pugilists were dressed in white drawers snd
‘hirts, and had ontheir boxing gloves, They showed
their points admirably. Mace had his sleeves rolled
up, exhibiting apair of stout muscular arms. Heenan
showed to great advantage in his boxing costumes, his
all, well proportioned form contrasting favorably with
‘he more clumsily built Engliahman, The heroes of
-he hour -were formally introduced to the audience in
whe following style:

**Gentlemen, I have the honor to introduce to you
James Mace, champion of Engisand, [bow from Jem.
Applause], and also Mr. Jehn C, Heenan,” [applause.
Bow from Heenan. }

Without losing any time, the boxers faced each other,
putting themselves in fighting attitude, with -their
gloved fists in front of their breasts. Mace at once shot
opt his right, which was caught by Heensn on the left
arm, and Jem gotin one or two light taps on John's
face. The Benicia Boy countered on she Englishman’s
fiy-trap, and there was a mutual exchange of compli-_
ments, the blows all being oy and falling s) rapidly
that it was impossible for eye to see where they
struck, The round lasted about half a minute, andthe
mem stepped back. Heenan smiling and Mace looking
grave. [Loud applause, |

On coming to the scratch for the second round, there
was some preliminary sparring, Heenan putting his
“left duke” forward, and Mace using both mauleys
slike. Mace led off, and tapped the Californian on the
snob, and Heenan put in three or four in Jem’s face,
making the Englishman wink and turn aside his head.
Phere was not much advantage on either side, and the -
round was quite short,

The third round was rore lively, both giving and

aking freely. Mace reached up to fecl of Heenan’s
‘tontis piece, and the Boy making a feint, Mace ducked
nis head, and the left duke landed on his crown.
feenan laughed, and the crowd lIanghed, snd the
jloves were plied at a rapid rate, both feeling the
oressure of the buckskin on their cheeks and fore-
neads.
. In the fourth and lest round, Mace made a feint and
Heenan struck out his left, and took one on his breast.
He countered on Mace’s head and as Jem bent forward
he Boy reached over and gave him s reminder on the
peck of the-neck which straightened him up, and he
pat in several cn tke cheeks*and at the same time took
s full share in the face. This was a rattling round.
fiecenan smiled to show it was allin fun, and both men
xhibited the perfection of pugilistic skill.

The great, gaping aulience roared with delicht and
slepped tte r bands and stamped their feet in sttesta-
ion of the bliss they experieaced.

The curtain fell. but the crowd were not satisfied,
put yelled and clamored for more. Up wert the
screen, and the boxers came forward and had another
round, which was similar to the others. Mace began
the fun and took the ‘‘duke” on the breast, and then
they patted each other on the face and head, and wheel-
ing, walked away.

Comparing the two men aa scientific boxers, wa
should have no hesitation in bestowing the crown upon
Heenan. Hestands erect, and seldom backs or dodges,
sat gives his blows with a wonderful rapidity of mo-
iom, ard takes what comes without flinching. Mace, on
he contrary, depends a good deal upon his pins to take
1im away from danger, and some of the motions of his
1ead reminded us of Tom Allen He is evidently s
ough customer. andcan standa terrible quantity of
sard blows. Heenan asa fancy borer cannot be ex-
‘elled. He is quick as lightning and as graceful asa
jancing master. The voice of th sndience was with
sim wh, the best sparrer, and he was rewarded witha
30T qe!

Mace and Heenan will repeat the exhibition to night.
from here they go to Cincinnati, and thence to New
Yrlean#, where Mace will go into training for his great
sattle with Tom Allen on the 10th of May.

————e

THE COMING PRIZE FIGUT,

The national “mill” for the pugilistic champion-

Allen, of California, to come off on the 12th of Jan-

eurious world which revolves around the prize ring.

very sad indeed, but such things do exist, and will
be to the end of the chapter, so far as present ap-

illustration:

Allen on the day and at the time appointed. The
trick wasasmall one, and as disgraceful to those
who originated it as to the rowdies who attempted
to carry out the idea practically.

title: Coming Prize Fight Between Allen and Gallagher Generates Interest
text:
THE COMING PRizE FiGut.—Among the sporting
fraternity the chief item for discussion and wager
is the approaching prize fight between Tom Allen
and Charlie Gallagher, both of Cleveland, to come
off on the 23d of this month.

Last evening McCocle’s new house, opposite the
Court-Honse,was absolutely thronged with the fancy
and those who take an interest in the “manly art of
self-defence” to hear the reading of the articles of
agreement and to witness the fina! deposit of $300 a
side made into the hands of the stake-holder, Wil-
liam Murray. Among the noted sports were Mike
McCoole and Charlie Gallagher, fightists; Dublin
Tricks, John Looney ard Tom Riley, backers; P.
H.Connallm and Tom Kehoe. Enthusiasm was
manifested on both sides, but the betting ran rather
slowly in favor of Allen. The greatest conviviality
was maintained, and the “flowing bow!” was drained
“frequently and oft,” while amid a continual din
rang the standing toast of “May the best man
win!” Allen looks in excellent condition, but Gal-
lagher appears as it he was somewhat over-tralned.
summary: The St. Louis Republic reported that the sporting fraternity was discussing the approaching prize fight between Tom Allen and Charlie Gallagher of Cleveland, with final deposit of three hundred dollars a side made to stake-holder William Murray.

‘When the Uncle of the Nephew drove into Paris

were unmistakable children of Old England, who

title: Tom Allen Fights McCoole

| A Piece of Advice to Tom Allen.
-We observe that certzin parties are busily eu-
geged in striving to bring about a renewal
of the fight between Allen and McCoole, and
are certainly laboring with a zeal worthy of
3 nobler cause. These efforts are not for
the sake of “seeing fair play” or settling the question
asto “who isthe best man,” but simply to secure
another battle with all its sensational accompani-
ments and disgragefal surroundings. We hope the
movers in this miserable business will fail, and that
the fight will be indefinitely postpened. The public
have had enongh and more than enowgh of it al-
ready, and the two gladiators wil! earn the gratitude
of the decent portion of the community if they will
amicably divide the stakes and drop the subject.
Which view of the case leads us to give Tom Allen
a piece of advice gratis. His conduct in this affair
has been as manly and honorable as anything con-
nected with prize-fighting can be. He has shown
himeelf the better man of the two in more ways
than one, and thereby earned the gooi will of per-
sons whose good will is worth having. Allen ought
to be satistied from his recent expezience that fight-
ing for money dees not pay, and that the ring has
sunk so low that no amount of courage and pluck ©
can elevate it into decency. Therefore letjhim turn |
his back upon it, and wash his hands of the profes-_
sion forever. Let him dispose of his saloon, and rid
himself, so far as possible, of the associations which
have heretofore surrounded him. His acknowledged
skill as a scientific master of “the manly art of selt-
defence” will insure him more pupils than he can
attend to if he will opena genteel sparring school,
with or without a gymnasium attached. He will be
liberally patronized, make money, and, what is much
better—make character. If Tom Allen wiil take this
hint kindly and act upon it, be may have reason
hereafter to consider us much better friends to him |
than those who are now endeavoring te drive him
back to his old ways.

ns

The much talked of prize fight between Tom Allen, —
the famous English pugilist, and Charley Gallagher, the
Irish Canadian, took place, as announced, at Foster
Island, about 30 miles below this city.

The steamboat Louisville, with s large crowd of rags-
muffins, shoulder-hitters, loafers, lunch-grabbers, pea-
nut-eaters, short-haired, bull-necked bruisers, and a fair
sprinkling of respectable citizens of pugilistic propensi- |

ties, left the foot of Elm street about ten o’clock in the
morning for the seene of the conflict, |

No impediment was offered by tho authorities to tho
departure of the motley crowd of excursionists, and
hundreds of people gathered on the bank of the river to
see them embark,

As public taste demands full accounts of these brutal
prize fighte, a deputation from the reportorial corps of
the Democrat was sent on the voyage, with instructions

to send back early and faithful reports, |

Some account of the combatants may not be out of
place, and we commence with a sketch of

TOM ALLEN, |

Allen came over from England in company with Bill
Goes, champion of England, to a draw in long battle:,
and their reputation naturally preceeded them, more

particularty as it was ¢iven out that both were anxious
for engagements with the best m:ttle of America. After
giving sparring exhibitions in company in all the large
cities of the country, both Allen and Ryall tarried long
in St. Louis, wliere they made hosts of friends. Ryall
- fimally located in s hostelrio on Wasbington avenue, be-
tween Fourth and Fifth, where he opened s beer house
| somewhat on the European plan, giving free and easy
concerts every Saturday night, Allen
journeyed farther, to Clevoland, where he
| Spenet-e-aslon, which was liberally patronized. Both
/ men came to St. Louis whilst “MoCoole was in training
| for his fight with Coburn. Ryalland MoCoole became
‘bosom friends at once, but MoCoole and Allen did not
iin, and in the comree of s fortnight the remarks of
either were trumpeted by their partisans, until the telk
resulted in a challenge from McCoole to Alien fora fight
within the time mentioned for the battle with Coburn.
It was wrongly asserted that the challenge resulted from
a set-to between Allen and McCoole, in which the latter
was roughly handled; but at any rate the friends and
backers of McCoole prevented the match with Allen, and
Alles! wended his way to Cleveland,

Whilst Allen was in the latter city, quictly vend-
ing his beer and tanglefoot Bill Davis came to
St. Louis, eager for a match. He had been beaten by
MocOoole, had threshed s talltwo hundred pounder in
New Orleans, and knocked Chariey Gallagher out of
“time, and was desirous of a bout with Ryall. Ryall had
grown fat, was getting old, and wanted to attend scrupu-
lously to his beer house; so he turned over the little job
to Allen, who was telegraphed to at Cleveland, and re-
paired to St. Louis in time to fix his ring {shoes, pickle
his hand, walk a few miles, and whip the ,Californian in
forty rounds, which lasted forty minutes.

In that fight, at Chouteau Island, midway between
here and Alton, Ryall acted as Allen’s second, assisted by
Tom Kelly. Gallagher was atthe ring side, having been
measurably in training, anticipating s second fight with
Elliott, who had trounced him near Cleveland. The ground
wav bik: "ised, © ap apertaed ty: the. Lenton rules, but |
was sandy, and very porous at that, so that each pugil-
iy wcubononod raat, mnt Gor to oot
‘his leg. Gallagher treated the exhibition a a ludicrous
one, and during the battle remarked in inclegant terms |
| that ‘‘he could lick any Englishman in Allen's corner.”
Tom Kelly informed him that he could be accommodated
after the fight, but Allen wanted to fight Gallagher in
the same ring, after having tramped around in the sand |
for forty minutes. His friends prevented this, but on
the boat, whilst returning to the city, s match was made
between Allen and Gallagher to fight within three
months for $1000 a side. ;

_ After Allen lost in this battle by a chance blow, he
challenged Gallagher again, but after much blow
and ee of agreement were drawn
up between and McCoole to fight on the 15th of
June for $1000 a sidv. The result of this last battle is
yet fresh in the minds of our reeders,

Allen's record in the old country is a hard fighting,
and very Successful one, He was twenty-nine years of
age im April last, and yet he has fought thirteen hard
battles. He -commerced in 1861 with ‘*Wagner,” alias
Morris Conner, whom he defcated in twelve rounds,
lacting but twenty minutes, for twenty pounds a side.

In the same year lie beat ‘*White” in eight rounds and
fifteen minutes, for five pounds a side,

In 1962 he best Gould in thirty-one rounds, fifty-five
minutes for fifteen pounds a side.

And in the same year met one of the gamest men and
hardest fighters oh English turf—‘‘Posh Price”—for
twenty pounds 6 side. They fought desperately for
fifty-five minutes, in which forty rounds were contested,
resulting in Allen’s defeat. But in 1866, four years
thereafter, ‘Tom agair met Price in the ring, and whip-
ped in a long battle of fifty-cight rounds, lasting two
hours and five minutes, the stakes being fifty pounds a
side, — 5

In 3864 he beat ‘‘Bingy Rose” in ten rounds, in fif-
teen minutes, fifty pounds a side.

Same year, was beaten by ‘‘Bob Smith,” the black;
threes hours and twenty minutes, five pounds a side.

1865,. beat Jack Parkinson in fifteen rounds, twenty-
two minutes for fifty pounds a side.

_ Bam year, beat George Iles, the Giant, in eighteen

rounds, fifty-five minutes, for one hundred pounds a

side.

In March, 1867, his fight with Joe Goss took place for
four hundred pounds # side and the championship. Af-
. ter fighting one hour and fifty-seven minutes the battle

3 CHABLEY GALLAGHER,

Next to Ned-O’Baldwin, Gallagher is the tallest pugil-
ist-in this country, his hight being six feet one and a
half inches. His complexion is pale and his face emaci-
ated, as though from pulmonary disease, His eye is
clear and sparkling, however, and his movements are
elastic and sprightly. He was born on the 10th of May,
1845, in Canada, two years after his parents emigrated
from Ireland. He fights under the national colors of
Ireland, and considera himself a full-blooded -son of
‘Erin. His weight is about 170,

Gallagher’s first fight was with Richard Lowe, at Har
per's Ferry, at the time when he was a soldier inthe Hi-
bernian Guards (3th Ohio), under the command of Gen.
Hancock. ‘Thise fight was for $100 a side, and was
very. severe. one, lasting two hours anda quarter, in
Which there were eighty-seven rounds, Gallagher won
the fight, but waa severely punished. He was in thirty- |
seven battles of a different kind, and fought in sll the |
engagements of the army of the Potomac, f26m the first
Bull Run to Petersburg. 7

His second mill was with Charley MoCarthy, at Horse
Soe Bend,. nearCleveland. His opponent, a 220-pound-
er, was knocked out of time on the second round, by a
blow on the jaw.
he paid a forfeit of $160,

‘The fourth fight was with Bill Davis, at Fighting Is-_
1:57, amd Gallagher was knocked out of time and lost
the wager, although he had knocked Davis out of time
three times. i

The fifth mill wes with Jim. Elliott, at Peach Island,
seven miles from Detroit. This fight, after 21 rounds
had been fought in 1;1%, was broken up by the crowd,
end Gallagher was cut in the side with « knife, struck
with bottles and sticks, and had to fies for his life. His
second had abandoned him, andhe fought the last ten
rounds without s second. Tom Allen and Blacksmith
Dan were the seconds of Elliott, who had three ribs bro-
kee .

His last fight before this one was with Tom Allen on
the 234 of February, éf{Carroll’s Island, near this city.
Im the second round he struck Allen a light blow on the
left side of the neck, a little behind the ear, paralyzing
him completely anf knocking him out of time. The re-
gult astonished the spectators, as Alien was in fine con-
dition and confident of victory, while Gallagher was un-
well and did not appear to have muchconfidence in him-
self.

Gallagher is a man of some education, and is a good
penman. He has been in the city but a short time.
Formerly he lived in Cleveland, Ohio, and most of his
fights were on the shorea.of the great lakes. He keeps
a saloon on Broadway, and has beem doing a good busi-
ness, his place being the resort of a large number of the
patrons of the prize ring. In his manners he is affable
god, of a peaceable and kindly disposition.

Gallagher has long cherished an old grudge against
Allen, om account of the conduct of Tom at Charley's
mill with Elliott, The Englishman has also, on several
public occasions, allowed his tongue to wag rather free-

ly to the detriment of the Canadian, and it is said that,
-gome time ago, in a rough and tumble at Cleveland, |
_ Charley gare Tom a severe pounding. |

Gallagher intends now to beck his trainer, Ben. Ho-
= against Jim Coyne, for any sum the latter may

mame. Coyne is ready for a mill with almost anybody,
and is anxious to wins reputation. Hogan isa good
match for bim in sige and appearance, snd both are
good men,
THE TRIP DOWN.

The Louisville left the wharf foot of Elm street at

balf-past nine o’clock. ‘The crowd was rather a motley

one, and the boat was crowded. Over $1530 was taken
in a6 passage money.

Af Carondelet docks a landing was made, and Galla-

gher, who had proceeded to the river bank in a carriage,

was taken on, Further down, at lower Carondelet sta-
tion, Allen came.on, attended by hia seconds, Butt Bi-
ley and Jim Coyne,

‘The behavior on board the boat was at times disorder-
ly in the extreme. There were four fist fights, in which
countrymen were victimized in bloody noses and missing
pocketbooks, One old gentleman was robbed of $153,
and was left without money tg buy a sandwich,

There were three games of chuck-#-luck, including
‘high ball,” ‘‘Eagie Bird,” and the like, which were
lit&rally petronized.

Sandwiches eoid at 25 cents for an inferior article,
whisky for 25 and beer for 19 penta the drimk,

title: Tom Allen fights Gallagher on Foster's Island
text:
sng LATE “MILL.”
- f)

—__»

Present Status of the Prize Ring.
—

It cannot be denied, even by its*most devoted admir-
ers, that the ancient and honorable code of the prize ring
has of late, and especially in this vicinity, fallen into
much and deserved contempt.

In the accounts given in all the city papers on Wednes-

_ day morning of the fight en the previous day, between
Allen and Gallagher, on Foster’s Island, below the city,
it is stated, and the facts are corroborated in every par-
ticular by respectable citizens who were present and wit-
nessed the combat, that Allen was the winner in 26 min-
utes, after eleven severely contested rounds, and
that on call of time for the twelfth round, Tom Kelley,
one of Gallagher's seconds, threw up the sponge in token
of defeat, which was seen by Allen and his party, one of
whom, Jim Coyne, asked Kelley if he gave up the fight,
the latter replying in the affirmative. It is further stated,
a fact to which particular attention is directed, that

**Alien walked quickly over to Gallagher’s corner to
shake hands with his adversary, when the latter sfruck
at him spitefully, but without hitting him.” After the
parties were out of the ring, however, and the contest
was closed, not to be reopened without mutual agree-
macnt, then the referee strangely declares the fight a
draw, for the reason that he did not see who threw up the
sponge; asif there were not more ways than seeing, to
decide from which corner it came, thus culpably neglect—
ing to determine on the spot, before leaving the
scene, when it would afterwards be too late.

And thus through unaccountable neglect the referes
puts it out of his power subsequently to decide on ac-
count of the matter being lost in the inextri¢able con-
fusion that always follows on the return-trip, and the
honest victor must lose the fruits of his hard-carned
success, and instead of the battle-money, boat-money,
colors and the green laurel wreath of victory and right
relations and good feelings being established between
him and his adversary, he finds himse]f destitute of all
these, and the necessity of bringing a lawsuit on his
hands, which will prolong the dispute indefinitely, and
engender permanently between the parties much bad
feeling and bad blood, the very thing which the prize
ring was established to prevent. ‘

One writer, in giving a history of the origin of the
code of the prize ring, says that, ‘‘it leads to a general

_ sense of fair play and honor; that it discourages and
renders infamous the use of the knife and of deadly
weapons, and lastly, that as quarrels must arise between
man and man which cannot be decided by law, and
which it would not be desirable so to settle if they could,
the best way of settling them is to fight them out fairly,
see who is the better man, then shake handsand be bet-
ter friends than ever.” Gouging, pulling hair, striking
below the belt, Lickin - and biting ware fcrm>rly prohib-
ited by the rules of the ring.. But it is related that at
the fight between Jim Elliott and Gallagher
at Peach Island, near Detroit, after Gallagher had
knocked his competitor out of time thrice the fight was_
broken up by the crowd, Gallagher was cut in the side
with a knife, struck with bottles and sticks, and had to
flee for his life, Tom Allen being one of Elliott’s seconds
at this battle; and it iswaid Gallagher long cherished an
old grudge against him on account of Tom's conduct on
this occasion, which he partly vented in giving Tom a
severe pounding in a rough and tumble at Cléveland,
and desired finally to settle after the unsatisfac-
tory contest between the two at Carroll"s Is—
land, last spring, in a conclusive combat, which
was agreed upon and took place accordingly on
Iset Tuesday. But the denouement of that
fight by Gallagher ‘‘spitefully” striking at the proffered
hand offriendship and good will of his competitor and
_ victor, showed that the controversy between them was
' in no wise healed, and the bad feelings in no manner
- dissipated, thus showing that the first object in the es-
tablishment of the code of the ring was defeated. Who
can say that any better feeling exists between McCoole
and Allen, by reason of their contest within the ropes,
which resulted in no honest decision at all, but a miser-
able farce, by reason -of one of the parties claiming a
fictitious foul, which the other would not agree to—the |
whole matter winding up in a wretched wrangle in the

courts?

A long and sanguimary prize-fight is described, in the
fifth book of the Hineid, in one hundred and twenty-five
lines by Virgil, between Dares, s youthful Trogan boast-
er, and Entellus, an old hero and Sicilian, on the Island
of Sicily, in the presence of Mineas and his party and
King Acestes, his host, and his party, during the cele-
bration of games instituted by Zineas in honor of the
anniversary of the death of his father, Anchises,

But, although they did not have the benefit of the
rulesof the London Prize Ring, and had no seconds,
umpires, bottle-holders, or referee, yet the victor was
allowed to win, and, though s Sicilian and an old
man, was crowned with the green laurel ; nor is it related
that any crowd of Trojan roughs and bruisers—and they
were a hardy set of soldiers and sailors, tried in long
wars and hardships—broke up the fight ina row when
they saw that Entellus was pounding the head of their
favorite Dares to jelly, with his lead-bound boxing
gloves, or exstus; nor ie it stated that they threw
stones and sticks, or drew their swords to prevent the
fight. But the contest came to an end, was definitely
settled, and the victor was allowed to wear his honors in
place. And so it was among the ancient Greeks, their
prototypes. But notso with the fighting fraternity in
Bt. Louis. we find thatthe art of boxing, arising in
England in the midds ages, and continuing in that
country down to the present time, has done
much to establish a manly independence of character,
among the English as indviduals, and added to their
reputation for coursge asa nation; has settled among
Jpumerous individuals many purely personal disputes
and cther controversies, for the settlement of which they
would have had to resort to the courts, to be spun out
in tedious, vexatious law suits; and has done much to
sbolish the murderous practice of dueling.

But we do think that the morals of prize fighting in
this country, apparently copied from the usages of the
London Prize Ring, are sadly perverted and have be-
come very degraded. Thera should be new rules of
the American prize ring, or, better; no prize ring at ell,
For evidently the custom has outlived the period of its
usefulness, and should be discountenanced by all honest
and fair-minded men, as it is now made a profession not
for the purpose of deciding who is the better man, set-
tling dispute and developing manliness of character, but
ia made a cloak for obtaining money by false pretenses in
boat excursions, swindling and all manner of unfair-
ness. Thoee that are in it are counseled to betake
themselves to some more honest employment for s means
of livelihood.
summary: The St. Louis Globe-Democrat reported Tom Allen won his fight against Gallagher in 26 minutes after eleven rounds on Foster's Island below the city. The victory was disputed when the referee declared it a draw despite witnesses seeing Gallagher's second throw up the sponge.

There bas been another pugilistic contest in the St.
Louis circuit, particulars of which may be found in an-
other part of this issue of the Clipper. The combatants
were Tom Allen and Charley Gallagher. « Allenis the man
who recently defeated McCoole, but who -vas declared to
have lost the stakes through an imaginary foul. That
.Allen proved himeelf to be the better man no one denied,
for he had placed the Western giant hors du combat in
less than a quarterofan hour. The twoare matched for

| obliging disposition, consented to give Charles Gallagher,

1869, En nt, we may be permitted to remark that
Charles Tien a lack of courtesy in asking a meeting
at the hands of Sir Thomas at a time when that gentle-
man was already under engagement to the McCoole;
while, on the other hand, Sir Thomas exhibited his po-
liteness in a marked degree by acceding to the request of
Charles, in according him a meeting on the 17th, as
already stated. While awarding to Sir Thomas Allen all
praise for the courage, science and shrewduess he has
evinced in his fistic encountersin ‘‘the land of the free -
and the home of the brave,” we are forced to admit that
he lacks in one very imaporkat essential to success in the
arena of the Western continent, caused, not so much by
his own actions, but by an oversight on the part of his
parents before Thomas was born, and with which, most
certainly, he Ley a hay had nothing whatever todo. |

Sir Thomas, unfortunately for his career in America, _
was born in England! Had Thomas meant te have re-—
mained ‘‘on Albion’s sea-girt shore,” this would not
have been a pea Spee 4 to him; but when he resolved
to stem the billows of old ocean and visit this beautiful
land of freedom, he put his foot in it by being an Eng-
lishman! Had his paternal and ‘maternal ancestors
been aware of the deleterious infiucncé this little mat-
ter of birth was destined to exert in his pilgrimage to
the western world, it is but fair to infer that they would
have cone to Dublin, or Cork, or Paris, or Switzerland,
or they might have been induced to visit New York, ,
and there given the light of day to the young warrior, |
and thus obviated the necessity of his being an Eng-
lishman; but, unfortunately for Thomas, his parents
were not gnfficiently far-secing, and in an evil moment,
for the subject of our discourse, the infantile
pugnacious Allen was begat and lawhched into life on
the soil of England, and from this lamentable indiscre-
tion on the part of his derelect parents, dates all the
misery attending Sir Thomas’ fistir career in Ametica. |
His meeting with MeCoole settled the question as to his

| meritsas an out-and-out prize fighter, but ‘‘kill the

| Englishman” was one of the unpleasant remarks that

| greetcd him during the progress of the dreadful fray,

ster at short nctice, and at avery small outlay of money;

feeling of sympathy for his man, for which he is de-
serving of a medal from the ‘‘Scciety for the preven-

ing to wound the feelings of Charles, gently and quictly

further collision with Thomas. Everybody, probably,
who saw the contest, took it for granted that Allen was
the winucr, and would getthe money; but everybody

pointment, on the 20th inst., and then declared that he

conreqnently cond, not see that Allen was entitled to
the stakes: in the kindest manner, however, and no
doubt much to the gratification of the op proc the
referee decided the match a draw, and the stakes and
excursion money were thereupon divided between ‘‘the
two gcnticmen who gave the party.” And here we
should say, that a great point has been gained, because,
¥hen Allen beat jaa McCoole was awarded the
Tcney; whereas, when len defeated Gallagher, the
