Fights at Wash Home and Trouble at
the Mansion House.
A DISGRACEFUL AFFAIR

The fancy held high carnival yesterday at the Wash
Home, a sporting rendezvous about four miles west of
the Court House, and near the St, Charles rock road.
Tom Allen is now training ‘at the Home for his
coming fight with Mace, and his presence,
with the addition of sparring, foot races,
and other sperts announced to take place, were attrac-
tions sufficient to draw a large crowd of gamblers,
shoulder-hitters, sports and fast men tothe locality.
The large quantities of poor whisky consumed by the
crowd soon began to assert itself, and numerous fights
took place, in one of which | George Bowman,
the man who wrote the letter to Spahr which caused the
slaying of Baldwin, in the Southern Stables, @ short
time since, received a severe cut in the back of the
bead. The original cause of this fight, it was said, was
the fart of Dick Roche, (a well-known sporting
man) reproaching Bowman with having been the cause
of Baldwin's death. A free fight, at any rate, took
place, in which Bowman received a cut in the head and
Roche was stabbea witha knife, but was not danger-
onsly hurt. Bowman succeeded in getting away from
the crowd, and, entering his carriage, drove to the
Mansion House, where he was followed by Roche
and quite a number of others. The trouble here re—
commenced and Bowman was obliged to jump from a
window and fiee for his life. When doing so he was
fired at by some one in the bar-room, but was not hit.

Aman named Gouper, who at that time was ina
room over the bar-room, and who had alzo mixed in
the affray at first, was set upon and beaten almost toa
jelly by some bruiser, with whom, it appears, n> one
attempted to interfere.

While this was going on at the Mansion House, seve-
ral fights took place at or near Wash Home, in which
another man was dreadfully battered. The rows at
both places are said to have been of the most disgrace-
ful character. and it is to be regretted if some meas-
ures cannot be taken to prevent a recurrence of such a
&cene upon the Sabbath.

Sparring Exhibition at Mozart Hall.

There was a large turnout at Mozart Hall last
night, some 800 being present on the occasion ofa
sparring exhibition for the benefit of Joe Coburn:
All the noted sports in the city were present, in-
cluding Coburn, Allen, McCoole, Sherman Thurs-
ton, Billy Carrol, Jack Looney, and any number o

The entertainment was varied by a violin solo;
the carpet antics of an Indian boy—and a succession
of sparring bouts between Punch Morris and young
Gallagher; Charley Collins, the ‘‘cast tron man,”
and Gallagher, together with such heavy weights as

The episode afforded amusement, however. A

The announcement, as was expected, last night drew

The hall is a large, grimy, ill-lighted and rather

title: Allen Whips Gallagher Easily in Sixteen Rounds
text:
| THE PRIZE FIGHT.

- Allen Whips Gallagher Easily.
Sixteen Eounds Fonght—A Quiet But

_ Bileedy Aair—Police Of the Track.

The fight between the pugilists Tom. Allen and J.
C. Gallagher, came off early yesterday morning on a
small island near the arsenal. After the recent fias29
steps were taken by the friends of the parties to ar-
range a contest which might take place without dan-
ger of interference, and it was agreed ostensibly to
fight within fifty miles of Kansas city, on Tue«iay
next, and this false report was industrieusly clreula-
ted, and found its way into print. On Friday even-
ing it was determined that the fight should come off
on the following morning, and secret pre-
parations were made for it. Reports
contrary to this were industriowsly circulated, an),
by dint of bard lying, were believed by some, and the
police were kept ignorant of the proposed action.
Only a small number of persons were infirmed of the
affair, and the profoundest secresy was enjoined upon
them. As aconsequence, instead of the fight being
witnessed by 500 or 604 persons, it was only witnessed
by 40 or 50, and the scandal was in this way some-
what diminished. Then, too, there was no prize-
fight excursion with its demoralizfng scenes, and the
buffers lost their $1,000 or $1500.

The men fought only for the stakes—$1,500;
$1,000 of which was placel by Allen against
Gallagher's $500. At half-past three yesterday morn-
ing, Looney and several others drove down to the
boat Bertha, at the foot of Barton street, where
Alen and Gallagher afterwards met them. The pu-
giliats and their friends were conveyed to the island
in two boats, and the ring was formed. Allen had
for seconds, Barney Aaron ald Geo. Collins, and was
in excellent fighting copdition. Gallagher’s seconds
were Mike McCoole and Tom Kelly. A. Boyd and D.
Ryan were selected as referees.

Everything was in readiness at twenty minntes
past seven and the fight commenced at half-past.

In the first round Gallagher won the first knock-
down and Allen had the firet Mood. There was some
lively sparring In the next few rounds. Allen aimed
to close his opponen’’s eyes and soon inflicted a gash
beneath the left optic. Gallagher's inexperience was
apparent to every spectator, while the the agility and
ekill of Allen were equally evident. The
pugilists clenched and fell several times.
Allen had a great advantage over
bis antagonist and bis blows were given with crusb-
ingeffect. The spectators were vociferous in their
cheers for Allen, but sympathy was openly mani-
fested for Gallagher, who was being badly punished.
Gallagher was very plucky and stood the peunding
with great fortitude; his face was mashed and swol-
Ten, and he was almost blinded. He was covered
with blood, and bis excitement hastened his defeat.
Allen on the other hand was perfect-
ly cool through the fight. Sixteen
rounds were fought. Before these were finished, it
was seen that Gallagher could win the fight by noth-
ing but the sheerest accident, and demanis to arrest
the brutal display were meade. The seventeenth
round was called, and Allen with scarcely a mark on
him, came promptly to the scratch. Bat the sponge
was thrown up for Gallagher, and Allen was declared»
the winner. The fight occupied 26+; minutes. |

A subscription was taken up for Gallagher and
$100 collected, $50 of which was given by Allen. |

The pugilists with their friends returned to their
headquarters at 9 o'clock.

‘The men in the fight may have fought pluckily, but
the whole affair was a small one, and in the records _
of prize fighting hardly deserves a place. The action
of the police destroyed the spirit and eclat of the
meeting.

title: Accidental Shooting: Nelson Adams Killed in Allen's Saloon
text:
ACCIDENTAL SHOOTING.
Man Killed im Tom Allen’s Saloon by the
Proprietor.

A young man named Nelson Adams came to his
death yesterday morving by the accidental dis-
charge of a pistol, in the house of Tom Allen, the
pugilist.

| The tragedy occurred at the latter's saloon, on

Washington avenue, near Fifth street, about
eve o'clock. Allen and Adams were talking together
about fire-arms, the former maintaining that the
English patiern waa the best, and in order to ex-
plain the matter, according to Ailen's statement, the
the latter pniled out his pistol, and Adams, being
rather full at the time, made a grab at the Weapon,
and as Allen pulled back it went off, the ball pene-
trating the abdomen. Tae unfortanate man feil
ever on the counter where heleaned. When the
terrible result was fully reatized, Allen it appears |
ran for a physician and also called in the police. Tae
young man lived but an bour and fire minutes.
He spoke only one werd between the time the fatal
stot struck him and his disolution. When told by
acompanion, “ Reddy you are shot,” he answered
“Yes.” The inquest was;eeld attne Third district
station. The biood oozed from the wound oa
the lower right side of the abdomen,
The pistol was a_ silver-mounted Derringer ef
Evglish pattern. Tom Allen entered the room, tol-
lowed by a group of trrends, and appeared amch af-
tected as he gazed at the dead maa, the victim of
bis own band, q

The toltowing is the testimony of two of the most
important witnesses:

TESTIMONY OF THB PIANIST.

Charles R. Dockstader: I was present before the
shooturg ; 1 knew the deceased; I live at 913 Frank-
fim avenue; I am a musician: I know

deceased, bis bame is Adam Nol-
sop; he is a single man, an uphol-
_sterer ot about 26 years ot age; I was awekened
this morping about 7:30 bya man who said Reddy
was shot by Tom Allen this morning; I saw lay
ceased last night drimking at Allea’s saloon ; I jett
| there aboui eleven o'clock ; Reddy was there thes,
enly three or feur others there ; last I saw of bin be
fell over a chair, wiere one of the men watters
pushed him ; 1 was playing on the piano at she
saloon ; Reddy talked principally with Mr. Allen
Snring the evening; I saw no difficulty between
them ; they were always on the best of terms: Ne’-
son looked to him as a brother.
Neleon gave Allen some money Satarday
to keep tor him to buy him some clothes,
and told Tom not to give it back to him under any
consideration, when be wanted it; “Reddy” feil
asleep occasionally there at the saloon; Mr. Allen
was sober when he left; “Reddy” gave Mr. Allen
#5; Mr. Allen had advised him to straighten up;
along in the evening he came and wanted 2 back;
“Ready” said he wanted it tor a friend; Mr. Allen
then gave him the money; there was no difficulty
or quarrel about the money; heis very quiet; wit-
ness did not see the pistol when be was there.
TESTIMONY OF THR BAR-KKEPER.
Jewes Garvin sworn: 1 am a bar-keeper for Mr.
| Allen ; I know Nelson; tbe first time I noticed Nelson,
was after the concert about 11:40 P.M. He then
came out in the bar-room, and then commenced
talking about relative 1ze of states and cities, thea
about gups ; about five minutes atter, I asked him
to go bome ; be said be would, but asked for a glass
of ale first; Tom Allen stood there and said you
are not going to drink alone, are you! no, said
“Reddy,” come cu; Tom took a drink of gin; as
they stood there, he had his revolver im his
band ee its spring; the barrel was then
turned off; a5 he was explaining, Reddy wadea
grab for it, avd Tom said, “No: co away ;” as he said
this the pistol went off, and Reddy fell over on to the
counter where be leaned: Tom was seared at this;
he said, “have I shot him!" He dropped his pistol
ob the counter, and rar to Dr. Hill's office. and then
called for the police. I ran around to Reddy, and
asked if be was burt; hesaid, “Iamsbot.’ I
then canght him, as he was talling, and
just then twopolicemen came in, and we laid bim
down. The conversation at the connter was aboat
tke pumber of square miles in Pennsylvania and
New York. They made a bet as to which was the
largest state of thetwo. Nelson lust. Got to talk-
ing about cities, too. A man by tbe name of Marpby
was first engaged in the talk. Reddy argned any
ove smart enutgh to get a charter could get ap
a city. The witness testified to trying to get
Nelson to go bome ; the time of the sheotiag was
about ope o'clock ; the way tbe pistol became in-
troduced into the conversauen was this: “Reddy”
spoke of his native place, Birmingham, which he
said was a town, notacity ; a great hardware town
where a great many guns are made; Tom spoke
then of bis being a lock smith, and speaking of locks
and sprisgs, ke pulled eut his pistol to explain mat-
ters.
VERDICT OF THR CORONER'S JURY.

The verdict was as follows: Taat Adam Nelson
came to bis death from the effects of a pistol shot
wound in the right side of the aodomen, about one

inch to the right of the median line, aud about four
inches below the umbilicus, on the morning ot May
20, 1872, at 417 Washingion avenue. And the jury
further find that the pisto! shot wound was the resn't

ot Thomas Allen, at his saloon, 417 Washington

oes anything about sporting matters. He was
a professional gambler, and had been for many
Years; but his attention was not always en-
grossed merely by the gaming-house or houses
in which ‘he happened to be inter-
ested. He was a ‘‘sporting man” in
every sense of the expression—on the race
track, in the Spares oe and atthe prizering. He
was aman of striking appearance, of nedium
height, erect, compact 1®ime, straight and
square. His hair and whiskers were tinged with
gray. His features were reguiar, and his face
was one that would attract a second glance from
themost careless observer. His eyes, in par-
ticular, challenged attention—small, flashing,
hazel-gray ae that penctrated whatever they
were turned upon, and would light up suddenly
into a tierce blaze when an angry thought passed
through the brain back of thei.

To this man Cincinnati, Si. Louis and New
Orleans were indebted—however questionable
the character of the business—for the occurrence
ofinany prize fights and attempts at ‘‘mills.”
It was Franklin who started the Jones-McCoole
match, and the MeCoole-Coburn affair at this
point. He was responsible tor several fights
near St. Lonis, one of which resulted in the
magnificent drubbing of the giant MecCoole at
the hands of the game man, Tom Allen. And,
tinally, he brought Allen and Coburn together
at New Orleans.

Until 1860, Franklin's career was one of wild,
and sometimes desperate, adventure. He was
born in Albany, N. Y.,on or about 1826. His name
was John Murray, and when a mere lad, he was
known, on account of his trim, compact form, as
**Taut’” Murray. When yet a child, he displayed
that aggressive disposition that ever after char-
acterized him. From that time forward he was
always known as aready and quick fighter, who
always wentinto win, whatever means had to
be used. Early in life he adopted his step-fath-
er’s name, Franklin, and was always known as
Jobnny Franklin.

Betore he arrived at age he became a profes-
sional gambler and adventurer. We have no
positive datu us to his career for many years—
only a few _— that serve to show the wild
career that he must have led. In Butfalo when
he was some ¢cightecn years of age, he had a
tight with a notorious negro named Brickhouse
Juck, whose skull he fractured. Forced to leave
Buttalo, on accouut of this atfuir, he went South,
through Central America and upto California.
He was one of the party that started out thence
ou a filibustering expedition in the schooner
Gamecock. This party bad Honoluln in their
mind, but they were routed as soon as they
landed. Those who were cot taken had a hard
time of it in escapiug. Frankiin managed to
reach Anstralia a5 a passenger on a whaler.
Ue then shipped before the mast, his money bavy-
ing given out, and reacbed Callao, Peru. His
next siep, after many privations, was to start a
drinking and gambling seloon on oné of the
Chineia islands. In the course of his cureer in
Callao, Litaa and other cities of Peru, in 1856 and
1557, Franklin was frequently involved in quar-
rels, some of which resulicd in desperate work.
In oue of them he had a hele knocked in his

whenever he thought the emergency required it.

it was in one of his fights imone of the Pern-
viun cities that Franklin killed an attache of the

prison twenty-six months, until at last released
through the efforts of Lewis Cass, then secretary

Leaving South America, Franklin proceeded to
Cuba, and thence, after 2 short residence there,
to New Orleans. When he came here, in 1862,
aud entered upon a prosperous fambliug career
in Cmeinnati, he was suffering greatly with
affected lungs. From that time until his death,
which occurred recently in New Gricans, he fed
the flickering game of his existence with excite-
ment. He was nota heavy drinker, but he was
always on his feet in the midst of whatever ex-
citement he could find. If it wasn’t to be
tound he would create it. As he lingered on, year
after yeur, fighting the disease that was surely
eucrouching upon the system with all that won-
derful nerve that characterized him, he becaine
wa subject of curiosity and wonder to all who
knew him. When the news of his death in New
Orleans, three yeurs azo, reached thle city it was
generally supposed tobe trac, and in some of
the pupers note was made of it. But in the
course of a# month orso who should turn up in
Cincinnati but Johnny Franklin. He was pale
and emaciated, to be sure, anda cough racked

ever, and ready for any excitement to which he
could drag himself. For about two years pre-
vious to his death he had kept a cambling house
or two, a drinking saloon anda grocery store in
New Orleans. To the lust heclimg tenaciously
to life and its excitemments. In July last he was

ever, and died shortly alter his return to New

| The appetite of the REPUPLICAN’s sporting re-
porter for his breakfast yesterday morning was
feeble, Mis mind was ina perturbed state and
| the intimate fmeudcship which bas always sub-
sisted between his brain and his epigastrium
| caused a sympathetic action resulting in the
| wforesaid loss of appetite. The imeutal
disquietude and the cousequent epigastric de-
| tangement were caused by the presence. in the
columns of asomewhat obscure morning paper,
| of a card which suggested disturbance and bore
atits base, 50 to speak, the ominous signature
| of Tom Alien. Thejsperting reporter's pusgilistic
| experience having been in the mein contined to
| the chronicling of other men's fights aud the
compromising of His own, and, moreover. being
the possessor of an admirable facial contour
which could not possibly receive any embellisi_
ment from an unpleasentness with Mr. Thomas
| Alien, he did not bunger nor thirst
| for the opportunity which seemed to
be faintly suggested by the champion’s cerd.
| The more he pondered upon this distressing sit-
uation the more, the 8. R. became convinced
| thatit was best to take the bull by the horns,
| which, being interpreted, means that it was
| epnsidered best to visit the champion at his
headquarters and have the matter definitely aa-
| jusied at onee. The matter which had aroused
| the tiger iu the customarily placid bosom of Mr.
- Allen was the publication of an interview of the
sporting reporter with a notorious New York
bruiser, in which the iutter had expressed opin-
ions uncomplimentary to Mr. Allen, in a discus-
sion of his capacity to confront Mr. Joseph Co-
burn in the istic ring. The method Mr. Allen
touk of signifying his displeasure was by the
before-mentioned card in the aforesaid obscure
morning paper. j
AT HOME.

Accordingly, having made up his mind to face
the music, the sporting reporter persuaded a
militury geutieniau of his acquaintance to ac-
company him to the naunts of the ceivbrated
pugilist. One reason for this selection of an as-
sociaite was because the latter was a man of
blood; but the principal reason was because he
Was the possessor of a horse and buggy, witch
would be the means of saving $5 livery hire. At
about 2 Pp. M. the 8. R. and his milltary friend
set out on their expeditior. A de
tour was made to take in Wash
Home, ana pay a fiying visit to Mr.
Hegan, but that bird had ilown, and the home
looked drear and lonely im cousequence. An
aifadlc and Milesian individual imparted the in-
teliigence that Mr. Hogan had gon? to town to
prepare for his benefit at Deagle’s theatre.
Thercupon the horse’s head was turned in tie
direction of the

EIGHUT-MILE HOUSE,
Which was reached about 4 P. M.

**Was Mr. Allen at home?”

*‘No, thank you, he had just gone ont, accom-
panied by his trainer and Arthur Chambers, for
his regular afternoon prémensde.”

**When would he be likely to return?”

“Well, he generally walked abont eight miles,
and it took bim an hour anda halt.”

This information was elicited from a small boy
who seemed to have a conception of the require-
ments of pusgilistin far beyond his years. The
S. R. and his military friend then set out on foot |
down the roac, which was indicated as the one
on which they would be most likely to meet Mr. —
Allen returping from bis salubrious pilgrimage. —
After a juunt of half a mile orso three deures
were descried in the distance, which closer in-
spection revealed to be Messrs. Allen, Madden
and Chambers. At the point of concurrence
there was@ mutualhalt and a passing of the
compliments of the season, when Mr. Allen in-
quired, with some evidences of acrimony in
his tone and inanner, ‘‘Who’s the bloody re-
porier -that put that talk in the RervusBLican
about Coburu and me 2?”

The sporting reporter modestly advised Mr,
Alfen that the sanguinary journalist alluded to

was in his immediate presence.

“*‘Well, well,” quoth the champion in a tone
which at once restored the app-=tite of the sport-
ing reporter. ‘*I didn’t think you’d give me
Such @ game as that. I didn’t Know of any rea-
sou you lad for hard feelin’s and I was surprisea
to see the REPUBIACAN goin’ back on a St. Louis
man and takin’ up fora bloody New York auffer.
The ReruBLicaN has always reported my fights
square up and up, end—”

@ilecre the loquacious champion wasinterrupted
by the military gentleman before alluded to,
with the explanation that the publication of a
man’s opinions in tie shape of an iuterview did
not by any means stamp the saine with the sanc-
tion of the paper. This cxplanation was sup-
plemented by the remark of the sporting report-
er that the REPUBLICAN would give equal promi-
nence to whatever Mr. Allen mignt desire to say
about Mr. Coburn. This struck the champion as
being the dead square thing, and his face hghted
up with that good-natured and genial grin which
nature gave him in lieu of asmile. ‘*Let’s wait
till we cet up to the house,” pnrsued the cham-
pion, amiably, ‘‘and then we'll have a chat.”

IS SHAPE.

Tom isin good condition—hetter, if anything,
than he was when he shied his eastor preliminary
to the recent demolition of McCoole. He weighs,
stripped, 172 pounds, his face looks fresh and
ives ali the evidences of perfect health, and he
seems 28 hard and kesarty asa three-pronged
buck. Now that his ire had vanished he was in
the most bubbling of cood spirits and Lumor and
chatted us gaily as a Yorkshice yokel on his way
toamarkelt fair. Arrived at the house a requi-
gsition was made upon the commissary
department for a supply of medi-
cul stores—this metaphor is employed
out of deference to the nulitary gentisoman, who
set’emup, as it were—and 1t was noticeable
that the champion’s training did not seem severe
cnough to proscribe brandy, of which he in-
duigediu a moderate hora. Seating himself at
a table, he drew a chair at iis side and another
in his front, the former of whichhe tilled with
the chubbed proportions of Arthur Chambera,
his second, and the light-weight champion of the
world, while he gracefully waved the sporting
reporter to aseat in the latter. The military
gentleman 'depolyed upon the opposite side of
the table and stationed hLimselfin a position to
cover the base of supplies.

“Now I'll tell you about that card,” said
Thomas. ‘*When [ saw that interview ia the
REPUBLICAN I was hurt. [ wasn’t mad, sec, but I
didn’t know what to make of it. I thought it was
how as some reporter might have something
agin’ mo, and was tryin’ to stir up sentiment
against me.”

The sporting reporter assured Thomas that no
attache of the REPUBLICAN ‘‘had anything agin’
lim,” and added that, if they had, it would
vot be vented in the columas of the paper.

*‘Listen,”’ said Thomas, carnestly, *‘I’ve livea
in St. Louis a number of years, and ’erept as I’ve
broke the pence, as they call it, by fightin’,
I’ve nevtr done anything out of the way. I defy
any man to say that Lever wronged him in any
way or gave him any game. I’ve always paid
my debts and had a civil word for everybody.
I never made any rows or fusses with unybody.
Atter my fight with Mace I wanted to leave the
ring. L didn’s’ want to fight apy more. I
wanted to live the balance of my life in quiet.
Thad made a littl money and had a way to
geta living without fightmme and [ retired from
the ring. But 1 am an Englishman and the
lvish-Americans, a3 a nationality, hate me.
There are some exceptions, of course, and [ have

-agood many friends uwmong them, But asa
class they hate ms. They couldn’t rest con-
tented without baviug me whipped. So they
| began to get up this talk about McCoole.
Tdidu’t pay any attention to it for a long time;
| bat finally ane night some of my friends
| came to me and said that they were talking o,
MecCoole’s whipping me on tie street if I did not
| ight himinthe ring. That made me a little
mad, and Isays: ‘Here, now, I'll fight So-and-
) 50, and we'll have an end of this chatter.’ So

the fight wasmadeup. Well, you know what
| come of its I knew Mike would have the major-
1ty of the crowd with him, and all that; but

that didn’t make any difference. I went tnere
| to whip him, and never had any idea of getting
| whipped.”

The sporting reporter observed that
this was not what one would
calla conversation about Mr. Joseph Coburn.

**But I’m comin’ to that,” persisted the cham-

| pien. ‘**Yousce, after [had whipped MeCoole
| these men were crazier than ever. Then the ery
was, ‘Joe Coburn’s the boy that'll cook the
goose for the d——d Englishman!’ So they tele-
graphed to him and he made some ta!k in the
Dapers. When I seen that f got to business. I
wrote a letter to the New York Herald, offering
| to fight Coburn anywhere for any moncy be-
tween $500 and $5,000, and proposed to plank a
forfeit right down. ThenI seen a dispatch in
the papers that Coburn said he would fight me;
but I didn’t hear anything about any money,
norTain’t heard about any yet. And what's
more, I don’t expect to hear about any.”
TOM THROWS DOWN THES GAUNTLET.

**Now then, you'll do me a favor,” resumed
the champion, ‘‘if you'll print this: [’ve retired
once from the ring, this nationality of Trish-
Americens has hounded me back intoit agatn,
ani I’m goin’ to stay now till they are satisfied.
I've got some money and some property. And
I’li make a standing bet of any part, or all of it,
that they can’t bring any man, Joe Coburn, or
whoever else they can get, that can win a cent of
itfrom meinany rmg. ll put it shorter and
bhinter. ri fight any man of
that nationality anywhere, for any
money, so it’s enough to cover expenses of
trainiog and the like.”

**That’s » broad proposition,” observed the
sporting reporter.

‘““My shoulders are broad enough to back it,’’
replied the champion, quietly.

**Do you know Coburn ?” asked Thomas. .

The S. R. admitted that he had a casual ac-
quaintance with that worthy.

_ “Well, then,’’said Tom, ‘‘If you know him

you know what sort of man heis. » Nobody can
beat him in a newspaper tight. That’s his best
holt. But he is a rufian, Joe is. He 1s swell,
flash, bad. He isacrimmal. He is a brute;
the meanest kind of a brute. He whips his
wife, and I can whip any man that’s got
enough of the curin him to strike a woman.
Now (m notarnifian. I defy any man to say
thatI ever didan unmanuerly thing to him.
I’m notacriminal, beyond prize-fighting, and
that’s only a misdemeanor. I’m not capable of
striking @ woman; and i'm not a brute, though
the Globe saysIam. But sce: I only blacken
peoples’ eyes sometimes, The Globe blackens
their characters! Which is the brutalest? I
leave it to you.”

The reporter promised to ponder the subject,
thinking he would display due deliberation—like
the old Mohawk Dutchman who was elected
county judge. When his first case cante up for
decision he rose and said:

*“*Shentlemenus: Ishall take four tays in fwich
to tecite this case, but shall effentually find
shugement for der biaintiff.”

We shall tako tour days in which to deciae
the case of Allen vs. the Globe, but shall event-
ually declare it a draw.

THE MILITARY.

‘*Tom,” said the reporter, ‘‘have you heard
that Gov. Beveridge will have a boat-load of
militia on hand to follow the excursion and ar-
rest all the parties the moment they touch the
Lilinois shore ?’’

‘Blast the militia,” responded the champion;
‘*where will he get them?”

*‘Chicago,”’ suggested the reporter. ‘

“Oh,” said Tom with a broad grin; ‘‘then
we've got a soft thing. We'll take along our
Nacional guards. Pll back them against all the
blokes you can find iv Chicago. Here’s the
lettenani,” pursved the champion turning to
the military gentleman, ‘‘we'll turn out in
force, eh?’

“Who will command the expedition?”

**T will,” said Tom, ‘‘I used to bé a soldier. I
served under Sir Henry Havelock all throuch
the Sepoy mutiny. Had a good dealof rough
work too.”

The balance of the interview consisted of
Tom’s reminiscences ot the Sepoy
rebellion, which, though perhaps
as interesting—if not more so—as
the matter in tand, more properly belongs in a
separate article.

Finally the champion accompanied his guests
to their buggy, remarking as we were about
starting for home, ‘‘ I’m a going to have a

BENEFIT AT DFAGLE’S
On the evening of the sight, whenI will give a
sparring exhibition.”

**Don’t you make any allowance for accidents,
Tom %”

**Never mind the accidents,’ rejoined Thomas,
and again that broad, good-humored Lan¢éashire
grin lighted up the western horizon, and thus
we left the champion in his glory. Thatis to
say, We caine to town and he tackled his supper.

OBSERVATIONS.

After all, there was something almost pathetic
in tae way Tom talked of his enemies ‘“ hound-
ing him back into the ring again.” That sturdy
Saxon blood of his is all up, and as he under-
stands the meaning of earnestness, he is thor-
oughly in earnest. Lard, rude and bluff as he
is, ‘‘ne wasn’t capable of striking a woman,”
and feltin his inmost bosom that he ‘*could
whip any man who wascur enough to do that
thing.” There are worse men in the world than
Tom Allen, but the majority of them are in bet-
ter business than prize-fighting.

Ren’s Benefit. -

Deagle’s theatre was crowded and packed last
night from pit to dome with the admirers of the
handsome Pittsburger who may not be as hand-
some next Tuesday night as be is now. Aiter
returning from his ‘interview with Alien, the
8. R. proceeded to Desgie’s. That gentleman

*Coujd the sporting reporter go behind the

At this moment Mr. Hogan came to the res-

to the young ladies of the bailiet. Nice girls

The scene was animated. It leoked like a
fancy dress, cr rather fancy undress ball in an
oid junk-shop. Much like a convocation of
seraphim in a horse-barn. Moving around
here and there the reporter recognized many
gentiemen whom he kuew. Several elegant
young gentlemen of fashion were there. Also
several elegant gentlemen of faro. Out of
regard for the feclings—of the  ballet-

of affection. And sq on.

one of the young ladics, who Was attired in a

upon the reporter. This young lady’s name is

Presently thero was a buzz and a flutter,
te BEN HOGAN AND JERRY DONOVAN,
dressed asif they were about to retire, came
upon the stage and were greeted with a storm
otapplause. They put some pillows on their
hands and then proceded to business. Ben Ho-
gan is asplendid sparrer. He is quick as a cat,

in the same place in leas time than any

summary: The St Louis Republic published Ben Hogan's response to Tom Allen's challenge, stating that Allen offers to fight within six weeks. Hogan noted that he was recovering from severe illness before their recent fight and did not have adequate training.

title: Proposed Fight Between Allen and George Rooke
text:
—

It seems that, despite Tom's oft-arowed re-
tirement from the ring, and in the face of his
recent denial of the report that he was about
to make a match with George Rooke, he has
gone East to arrange the preliminaries for that
encounter, anid that a deposit of $500 a side,
being one-sixth of the agreed stake, is now
in the hands of Harry Hill.
The fight is arrangefl to take place withiu
fifty miles of Pittsburg, on the 17th of June.
The chanees are about five to two that the
fight will not occur, but as it will probably
attract a good deal of attention from the sport-
ing world a brief review of the careers of the
combatants and of their respective pugilistic
abilities will not be uninteresting.

Tom Allen is too well known to require any
detailed description and the sporting public
is already familiar with his history. He is in
prime health now, fat asa bear and will have
to do some of the hardest training of his life to
get down from his present 210 pound
of adipose tothe 172 pounds of bone and
muscle requisite to fit him for the roped arena.
Moreover Tom is getting

A TRIFLE STALB. |
Not that his age—36—has begun to tell on)
him, but he has trained down and then fat-
tened up again so many times that his sys-—
tem docs uot take to the flesh-reducing
process as kindly as itused to. indeed it is
seriously questioned by sporting men whether
Tom is not a better man at 200 0r 210 than at
172. It is trne that, in his present flesh he
might be a trifle slow, and his wind might give
putin a protracted struggle, while his face
would present a cushion for his antagonist’s
knuckles, and could be cut and carved like
2 tenderloin of beef. Butto offset these dis-
padvautuges it ie held that he loses streugth in
training so much that the increased activity of
his trained condition is not of suflicient advan -
age to counterbalance the loss of brute force.
Moreover ,it appears that all the fights Tom has
won of late years huve been gained by

QUICK WORK, ;
Aud even his friends adiniit that he can’t stand
whe heavy joltingofalong and evenly con-
tested battle. Infact, he has never fought
but three dragging tichts in his life and those
were ull fought in Englaud several Sears ago.
The longest time he has stood up in’the ring in
this country was 44 minutes with Mace, and
pf this about 30 minutes was a sparring
match, not more than 14 winutes
having been devoted to business. From these
facts if would seein that Allen’ main reliance
is in his science and sirength, ind that his ena-
pacity to endure cuts but a smali figure among
bis fighting endowments.

iis prospective antagonist, George
Rooke, is about two years his junivr,
and is his exact opposite in build,
temperament and appearance. Rooke is an
Irishman, but hus lived nearly all his life in
England and America. He is about five feet
ten and a half inches.in beight. The New
York Sun puts bim at six feet, but if that be
true he must have grown an inch anda half |
since the sporting reporter saw him fight
Rockey Movre eight years ago next fall,
ut Isle of Shoals, New Hampshire. He is
broad shouldered, fat-chested, angular, bony, )
big-jointed and just a trifle bandy-legged; his |
complexion is dark, his face

VICIOUS AND FORBIDDING

And his head shaped like a cube; his forehead
is low and broad, his brows projecting and
lowering, his nose somewhat twisted
‘*out of true’’ . from the ef-
fects of Rockey Moore’s fearful left-hand
hitting, and his eyes are small an/fl black like a
weusel’s. In short, he is as repulsive a speci-
meu of the genus rouch as could be imagined.
But he is a game fighter, either in the ring or
in the rough and tumble, and is what is known |
in pugilistic parlance as a thorough glut-
ton—that is to say, #2 man who can
stand up aud be mauled all day. His swarthy |
skin is like leatherand his spare desh is like
gristle, sothatno hitting shortof the bone-
smashing variety can ‘‘fuze’’ him to speak of.
He is not, however, a very scientific boxer,
bis low grade of intellect rendering science in
anything impossible to him. His ring-experience
is nut brilliant. He beat Hussey, a third-rate,
receiving hurdly a scratch, in 1565. Then he
fought a draw with Collins, whain the presi-
dent’s son-in-law, Sarioris, recently culled
about to suit himself. Finally he was

AWFUCULLY WHIPPED |
By Rockey Moore, aperfect novice, who fought
him out of a pure freak of boyish cussedness,
and whom nobody expected to stand before
him five ininutes. Since that time Rooke has
been keeping saloon in Newark and has made
two matcbes which were never fought—one
with Joe Coburn and the other with Jem
Coyne.

Wis Oght with Moore was a most peculiar af-
fair. Moore was a young fellow belonging to
one of the best families in Brooklyn,
and his roystering preclivities led
him into many asécrape, and his family
into much sorrow. His older brother,
Hon. Hugh Moore, now state senator from the
Eighth district of New York, was something of
a sporting man in a high-toned way and when
Rockey got embroiled in a dificulty with Rooke
which led to achallenge by the latter, Hugh
encouraged his younger brother to take
te up, and, we believed, backed
him for the $2,000 which was the stake of the
combat. The difficulty which led to this tight
was the result of a lark, and cousisted of an
impromptu knock down between Rooke and
yapve Moore, in which the swarthy pugilist
of Newark was badly worsted by the gay and
festive

SOCIETY YOUNG MAN ,
Of Brooklyn. Arrangements for a regular ficht
according to the ruies of the P. R. followed,
andtbe battle took place at Isle of shoals,
New Bampshire, in October, 1867.

When the two men shook hands in the ring a
greater contrasi than they presented could not
be imagined. We have already described the
personal appearance of Rooke, and need
not repeat the§§ description. Rockey
Moore, then about 23 years
of age, was as handsome a specimen of phisi-
cal young manhood ascould be found. He
stood about 5 feet 8‘ and weighed about 155
pounds. He was built like the Apollo Belvi-
dere, his skin was almost white as snow, his
cheeks were rosy a8 a girl’s, his eye was
bright and full of frolicsome humor, aod his
chestnut bair, which he had not cropped
as prize-fighters usually do, curled gracefully
about his temples and over his

VINE, INTELLIGENT-LOOKING FOREHEAD.

Nearly everybody thought ita pity that so
fine a face should be mashed up by the big fists
of u brute like Rooke, and nobody imagined
that Moore's fate would be in doubt
for more than ten minutes at the
outside. Betting was all one way among the
sports; but there were a few of Rockey
Moore’s friends and associates present who
still backed their favorite by taking the great
odds that were offered. Time was called and
the fightcommenced. It was one of the most
Sanguivary and savage fights in the history of
the ring, and lasted an hour and
sour minutes, Rooke. being fairly hammered

‘and mauled to exhaustion and imsenszibility,
while Rockey received much punishment about
the ribs and chest, his face escaping with only
a few bruises and «4 couple of trifling cuts.
Moore’s tactics were to save his
face from distigurement aud to blind
Rooke’s eyes, the latter a most difficult task,
because it seemed almost impossible to make
the fellow’s fiesh swell with any amount of
bruising. At the beginning of the fight Rooke
went in with all the assurance of a man who
is confident of an easy victory and is inclined
© take bis case about winning it. He was
SUDDENLY AWAKENED
From this pleasant dream by a slashing left-
bander from Moore, square con the bridge of
his nose, which laid him sprawling and drew
first ¢laret, amid the plaudits of the astounded
bystanders. Then Kooke lost his self-control,
gotmad and fought wildly. Thenceforwurd
the fight became a = struggle between
the brute force,” pluck and buill-
dog endurance of Rooke on the one hand, and
the sagacity, intelligence and ¢ourage of
Moore on theother, Rooke’s evident raze
naturally excited the wrath of his antagonist,
and every blow was sent in with all the tierce
Vigor that resentment can give. But the brutal
Pluck and stolid endurance of Rooke availed
Bothing against the science and intelligent
Strategy of Moore. And besides it seon up-
peared that Moore, tenderly and luxuriously
vFaised as he had been, did not lack endurance,
while his plnck showed al} the stubbornness
’
Shes distinguished the gwarthy Books's. Be.
fore the fight was half over it be-
came evident that Rooke’s defeat
was only a question of time. His face was
one blotch of bloody jelly, several of his teeth
were knocked out and bis eyes were nearly
blinded, while Moore’s hands had been lacer
ated
BY THE BONES OF ROOKE'S FACE
Worse than his face had been punished by
Rooke’s fists. At Ilast, at the  begin-
ning of the thirty-eighth round, Rooke’s
brute endurance gave out and he fell down
Uvice from exhaustion as his seconds tried to
bring bim up toe the scratch. Finding that
liooke was exhausted from loss of blood, while
Moore was fresh 25 a race-horse and ferocious
as a leopard, the seconds of the former
‘threw up the sponge and Rockey
‘Moore, the novice, was declared middie,
weight champion of America. At that mo-
| ment the scene was sickening. Rooke was
splashed,spattered and soaked with blood from
| head to foot. The dried grass in the ring, the
garments and bodies of his seconds, the chair
in which he sat between rounds and the ropes
in many places where he had fallen
against them were also stuined with
gore. The victor had lost but very little blood
from his face, but his knuckles were bleeding,
and his hands, face, breast and arms were
spattered with Rooke’s blood, which latterly
in the fight
FLEW LIKE WATER
Whenever Moore hit his mangled face. Rooke
wis assisted out of the ring and taken away.
Moore dressed himself and went home
to New York that night with
his frienda. He never fought another battle,
but went back to his people and behaved him-
self. Heis now a politician of considerable
note in New York. Those who saw this fight
rate Moore as the natural equal of Tom Sayers,
and say that he showed qualities never sur-
pussed by any middle-weight fighter in prize-
ring history. It does not argue that, because
Rooke was beaten by him, Rooke can be
beaten easily; for there is no doubt
that Rockey Moore, when he fought at Isle of
Shoals, novice 2s he was, could have stood his
band with any man in the world at that time,
middle-weight, and that he could haye held
to his _ beat work any heavy
weight, barring Mace or Tom King. He
wus doubt'ess at that moment as good a man
as Tom Allen and a better man than Joe Co-
burn or Ned Price. At ail events, if Rooke
fighis Allen we shall be better able to judge
how much credit Moore deserves for whipping
him.
ROOKE’S ADVANTAGES.

An effort was inadle by Rooke’s friends to set
up the theory that he was sick and weak when
he confronted Moore, but it failed and the fact
was that he never saw a better day in his life.
He was beaten in as faira tight as was ever
waged, simply because his antagonist was his
superior. It was generally admitted by the
most competent judges that this was the best
fight ever foughton American soil and that
young Moore was the best man at middle-weight
this country has produced. The contest gained
very little notoriety at the time owing to the
strenuous efurts made by Moore’s friends to
keep it quiet, 2nd the immediate retirement of
the victor from the ring naturally tended to
prevent subsequent refereuce toit. The ad-
mirers of the fistic art who witnessed Rockey’ s
behavior in the ring were much disgusted at
his immediate retirement and steady refusal to
engage in any more combats, for they
saw in him the hero of the
American ring if he would but
follow up his success. His own disposition,
doubtiess, was to keep on fighting, and he de-
sired to meet Joe Coburn when that worthy
returned from England, but he yieided to fam-
iy influences, and kept his hands clean of
pugilistic gore thereaiter. His style of fight-
ing was mugnificent, except that in this in-
stunce the bad feeling displayed by Rooke
provoked him into an exhibition of ferocity
thathas always been held to be a blemish
upon ring behavior. Once or twice he went
so far as $

TO TAUNT ROOKE
With his inazhility to stand against an antag-
onist whom Rooke, prior to the fight, bad con-
temptuously called ‘*his ma’s boy.’’ But for
cool, deliberate courage, steady and unfug-
sing nerve, avd keen, judicious acience in
parrying, hitting and selecting occasions ahi
places for the delivery of his blows, he has
never been surpassed. The novice, no matter
how game. or how well versed he may be in
boxing, usually stands in more or less
dread of an experienced fighter,
but Moore fought with all the
assurance ofa veteran. He began to force
the fighting in the frst round and forced it 2
the way through, knocking Roake down sev- |
eral times in his own curner, and once or twice |
forcing Nim aloost entirely through tbe ropes.
Rooke is a man of immense atreugth in the
arms and shoulders, and an extraordinary
hard hitter. His ‘‘reach’’ was at least three
inches longer than Moore’s. But Moore was
about three times as quick as Rooke was, and
quicker than any man fhat has fought im the
American ring, excepting, possibly, Yankee
Sullivan. As to general bodily strength, there
is no doubt that Moore was superior to his
swarthy foe. His straight, symmetrical limbs
were ridged, corded and knotted with thews,
BSinews anid muscles until his skin looked as if
it were drawn over a network of small ropes;
while as to wind, his breathing, within five
niinutes after the termination of his sixty-four
minutes of close, incessant fighting, was as
regular as if he had just eaten his dinner.
NOTA SOFT SNAP.

It may be taken for granted that, if Rooke
and Alien fzht, Allen will not chop him up, as
he did McCoole, in a dozen minutes, nor
weaken his buck, as he did Gallagher's, inthe
first two or three rounds. At the very best he
can do; Allen cannot whip Rooke im less than
three-quarters of an hour. It must be remeim-
bered that Rooke’s fights with Hussey and Col-
lins did not amount to enough to try his mettle
atall. The only real trial to which his quali-
ties have ever been subjected was in his fight
with Moore, and we have shown that Moore
could test the qualities of the best of men.
Experiencec men who saw Moore tight at Isle
of Shoals were anxious to back him against
Joe Coburn, though Coburn was then in his
very prime, in the finest condition, and
nearly thirty pounds heavier than
Moore, at his lightest, and at
Moore’s heaviest fighting weight. And
few will question that, in 1867-68, Joe Coburn
Was at least the equal of Tom Allen the best
day he eversaw. Fromall of which it may
be concluded that Rooke isa man every way
worthy of Allen’s muscle, and that if he was
whipped by a middie-weight, anda novice at
that, there is no reason to suppose that he is
therefore Allen’s inferior; for if Allen had
stood in Rooke’s shoes at Isie of Shoals that
day, his fate, in all probability,

WOULD HAVE BEEN THE SAMR.

Rooke has improved in science a great deal
since he fought Moore, and when he went
down to Wilkesbarre to fight Jem Coyne a year
ago last winter, was ina condition like cast
iron. His constitution has never been enfeebled
by excesses as Coburn’s has, while he bas not
become stale and fiabby as Allen has through
oft-repeated training down and fattening up
again. When he and Allen go into the ring
together no judicious man will offer odds on
either of them. Meafirhile, we presume the
authorities of Pennsylvania, Chio and West
Virginia will have something to say about the
mutter.

title: A Card From Tom Allen
text:
A CARD FROM TOM ALLEN.

Some Interesting Reminiscences of the Prize Ring, and a Little Gratuitous Information for the Duffer who Writes Sporting Notes for the Republican.

St. Louis, March 23, 1875.

To the Editor—My attention has been called to an article in the Republican, about which I wish to make a few remarks.

The person who wrote the article must surely be a stranger to the history of prize fighters. I have fought some of the longest battles of any man in the world, as my record will show. I will here mention a few fights. Charlie Gallagher and Bill Davis fought one hour and fifty minutes. Gallagher and Elliott fought one hour and thirty minutes and both men were strong at the finish. McCoole and Coburn fought sixty-seven rounds in one hour and twenty minutes. Now these men did not last above twenty minutes when they met me, and I suppose that is why I cannot stand a long fight.

And as regards my fights in England, my records will show that I stand unrivaled as champion of the middle weights. I have fought nineteen battles in the ring, and I have fought for more money than any man living. My last five fights in England were with Posh Price and George Iles, the former lasting two hours and five minutes and the latter two hours. And my fight with Bob Smith (the black) lasted three hours, and my last fight with Joe Goss was one hour and fifty-seven minutes, when darkness came on; the next morning the doctors advised us to agree to a draw which we did. I have merely made mention of these facts to enlighten this would-be-reporter of sporting articles. And speaking of this, Rooke who is seeking for fame—the reporter has made a grand mistake in the fight between Rocky Moore and Rooke. It was Rooke that got first blood and knock down and it was Moore that lost the teeth and not Rooke, as the reporter said—and if Rooke could have won they would not let him, for he is too big a coward to whip any man. As for Rocky Moore being such a good fighter and so clever, he was the first man I sparred with in the country, and I made a child of him with the gloves, and because I hit him so hard and so often they came on the stage and attempted to mob me, and they stopped the sparring.

Perhaps this man knows more about Rocky Moore than any one else, and since he has got to be a politician it is a pity he has not got some good office. I am sorry he is not better posted in ring matters.

Respectfully yours,
TOM ALLEN, Champion.
summary: In a letter to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, Tom Allen answered a Republican reporter who said he could not stand a long fight. He listed his long English battles with Posh Price, George Iles, Bob Smith and Joe Goss, called himself champion of the middleweights, and disputed the paper's account of the Rocky Moore and Rooke fight.

title: Allen and Rooke Match Ends in Fizzle
text:
ALLEN AND ROOKE.
All About the Big Fight that
Did Not Take Place.

An Insight Into the Peculiar Workings of the
Rough Elemeni of America.

It is only necessary to announce_that the much-
talked-of pugilistic encounter between Allen and
Rooke has proved a fizzleto convince law-abiding
citizens that what was ence recognized a3 the
manly art by the nobility and aristocracy of the
Old World is a defunct institutior, In olden times,
when such clever gladiators as Tom Cribb, Tom

Spring, Sayers, Hyer and Heenan fought for glo-

ry, and made the money involved a secondary

| consideration, the sport was countenanced by the
law, and all attempts at interference were cried

“down by men in high places. In America, since

the day that Morrissey’s mob swindled Heenan out

of his fight with the New York Congressman, a
fistic encounter decided fairly and squarely on the
merits of the men has been a rarity. ,Pugil-
ists made matches for the purpose of
robbing their opponents, and the roughest
gang at the ring side invariably gained
the day. Each section of the country has
its representative mob of roughs, and each mob a
representative leader. As an instance of how
‘¢mills,’? in late years, have been conducted,
reference to the Coburn-Mace meeting at New Or-
leans may be made. Coburn, who is recognized
as a ‘‘duffer,’’ and Mace, the most skillful man
that ever put up his hands, faced each other for

four hours and not a blow was struck. Mace

could have disfigured Coburn out of recognition in

avery few minutes, but knew he could not whip :

the pet of the New York fancy and live in America.
He, therefore, acted entirely on the defense, and
could not prevent the New Yorker from gaining
the reputation of fighting a draw with a man who
could have annihilated him in short order, All of
which has very little to do with Thursday’s fizzle,
except that it will lustrate, to a certain extent,
what follows.

\. Jn January of this year, George Rooke, of New-

aue.g2,500a side, The task of defeating a man

WHAT CAUSED THE MATCH,

Rooke knew that Allen had retired from the

title: Wrestler Bauer Seeks Match Arranged by Tom Allen
text:
2 ee he ee ee ;

Monsieur Theobaud Bauer, the champion
wrestler, is still in the city, but nothing definite
has yet been heard from Christol, who expressed a
willingness to have a bout with any man whom
Tom Allen could produce. Allen left for Louis-—
ville yesterday, and last night gave a sparring ex-
hibition in that city, assisted by his trainers, young
Donnelly and Jack Madden, as well as local box-
ers. He will be back this morning, when the
following communication from Christol, received

at this office yesterday, will doubtless receive his
| attention:
To the Editor of the Globe-Democrat:

CnicaGo, March 10, 1875.—Dear Sir: I have
seen in your honorable journal the conversation
with Mr. Tom Allen, in which he desires to back
Bauer to wrestle against me. If M. Bauer is will-
ing to come to Chicago, lam ready to meet him.
I will be in Chicago for six weeks, and itis beter
for me to wrentie bere than to go to St. Louis.

Yours respectfully. ANDRE CHRISTOL,

Champion of France.

In view of the fact that Allen brought Baner out

here from Boston, on the assertion of a Well-

_ known Chicago friend that Christol would wrestle

| him here, the above epistle looks very much as
though Andre wanted to back out. He doubtless
appreciates the fact that Bauer is neither a Car-
teron nora Rigal, but the most scientific wrestler
in the world, as his record proves. Bauer has
never suffered defeat in this country, but has in
turn defeated Miller, Vanderdecken, Christol,
Regnierand Heyster. InChristol’s late match
with Rigal at Chicago, the latter claims that he
was very unfairly treated, and that he lost the
match through the ignorance of the referee, who
did not understand the rules of Greco-Roman
wrestling. Can this be the reason why Christol is
so anxious to wrestle there? :

After the receipt of Christol’s letter a reporter
hunted up Bauer and notified him of its contents.
Bauer appeared surprised, but stated that he
would take no action in the matter until Allen ar-
rives to-day. Whatthat action will be remains to
be seen.

In connection with Greco-Roman wrestling in
this country a great deal has been said in regard
to hippodroming, and much of it is doubless just.
Bauer has, however, a clear record, and his
friends are legion from the Atlantic to the Pacific,
for the reason that he prefers reputation to
money. This is demonstrated by the fact that he
has never lost a match, and as he has never
met his equal, and thousands of dollars have been
put up on the result of these contests in San Fran-
cisco, Boston and New York, had he been willing
to sell out to the clique of gamblers that controls
each of those cities, he could now be possessed of
a large fortune.

Since the above was written atelegram has been
received at <Allen’s, stating that Chicago men
have been found who will back Christol to wrestle
here, and that one of them will arrive in a day or
twe to bind the match, if Bauer and Allen are
willing to have it goon. To this a reply was sent |
that Allen would send a definite answer to-mor- |
row, which will doubtless be in the affirmative. |

title: Tom Allen Boxing Exhibition Announced
text:
AGAIN VICTORIOUS.
———__
Prof. Bauer Beats the German Champion
! .
| at His Own Game.

A Splendid Exhibition of Strength and
Skill at the Temple Last Evening.
——

The second wrestling match between Prof.
Bauer and Herr Heygster for $250 aside came
off last night at the Temple before a crowded
house. There was considerable excitement
Manitest on accountot the terms of the match,
which were thatthe first fallssould be wres-
tled for according to German andthe second
according to Greco-Roman rules. It was be-
lieved that this would give Heyysterthe ad-
‘Vantage, because the German style is mainly
anu exhibition of strength, und there is no
coubt regarding his superiority in this respect
to Bauer, who relics in a great measure upon
| his skill ane activity. 4
| Tom Allen,the champion pugilist, introduced
the men to the audience at twenty-three min-
utes past § o’clock. Leon Schuler appearing as
umpire’ for Bauer and Carl Boehm tor Heyg-
ster.
| Atthe start the contestants forget that the
first bout was uccording to German rules, and
| had to make afreshstart. They began by a
series of wrist grips, which were continued tun-
til Heygster got a left arm body hold on Baner,
when he tried hard to get both arms around
his body and secure a lock, but Bauer turned
the tables on him, and gained the very lock
Heygster was striving for. He lost it, how-
ever, and some very clever marncuvring wus
done, Heygster at length setting
2 very good body hoid, which
Bauer broke by main strength = aiter
a hard struggle. Quick changes and inter-
aster of holds followed, Bauer being com-
pelled to wipe his hands frequently on his
trunks, owing to the perspiration which flowed
so treely from the ponderous Gerinan. The
bout throughout was fought desperately.
Heygster at one time had a body grip, side
hold, but lost it. He then forced Bauer to his
knees, but it was only fora part of a second,
‘the latter gaining his feet with the agility of a
eat. Heygster on several occasions also secured
good — shoulder locks, but Bauer
invariabiy fought until he treed
himself. At length the bout was_ ended
by Bauer getting a fair body-grip and forcing
Heygster to the carpet on his side, when he
rolled him over, threw his weight across his
chest and the shoulders of the German gave
way and touched the carpet. Bauer was loud-
ly cheered. This bout lasted 18 minutes.

An interinission ot twenty minutes was then
taken. During the recess Tom Allen an-
nounced that at the close of the performance a
silver belt, which Bauer's friends had gotten
uptor bim as the champion Greco-Roman
ga of America, would be presented to

iim.

When time was caHed for_the second bout,
which wus wrestled according to Grwco-RKo-
man rules, Bauer bounded upon the stage
looking as rosy as a girl. Heyyster followed,
but with anything but an elastic step. This
bout was fierce trom the start, and jno time
was lost by either man. Ali the tricks known
were practised by each wrestler. Bauer got
his favorite neck-lock, baving his left arm
around Heygster’s ueck and beth hands
clasped under his chin. It can easily be seen
that this is a terrible grip and # mun
can easily be choked while in such
a position, yet Bauer held his burly antag-
onist thus securely locked for seveyal minutes
and finally forced him to his kneés, wheu he
took a good back hold and raised the 300
pounds of fiesh off the stage in
his arms, but lost his grip,
when MHeygster gained his feet. In en-
dedvoring ‘ulterwards to get another good
hold, Bauer received an ugly knock in the
head, just between the eyes from Heygster’s
left shoulder, but instead of unnerving him it
seemed to madden himand he swiftly gained
a side hold, made Heygster tall to his
knees, and then secured a body
grip and ended the bout by rolling
Heygster over on the stage until both shoul-
ders touched the carpet. This decided the
contest in Bauer’s favor, andthe audience at
once set up a tremendous roar.

Bauer was called out, when the silver belt
alluded to above was presented to him. '

It is not likely that Heygster will again essay
to tackle such a man as Bauer, who is vastly
his superior. as a wrestler. Bauer leaves
soon for California, unlessa match is arranged
between him and Maj. McLaughlin of Detroit.

title: Tom Allen and Joe Goss Championship Fight Set for September
text:
THE THUMPERS.
Joe Goss and Tom Allen at Thoir Train-
ing Quarters.
‘
Current Gossip Concerning the Fight for
the Championship.

The fight which isto take place in September
for a big bundle anu the championship of Amer-
ica, between those noted exponents of the fistic
art, Tom Allen and Joe Goss, continues to create
much comment in sporting circles, and opinion is
pretty evenly dividea as to whether the ‘‘mill’’ is
to be decided on its merits, or whether it-is a
neatly put-up job to lure the unwary into paying
steep prices for excarsion tickets to witness a
sham battle in which one or the other of the prin-
cipals will at the proper moment acknowledge
himself vanquished.

The match was broughtabout in a rather peculiar
way. It appears that wigile Mace was sojourning
in England, prior to.his last visit to America, the
report gained credence that Allen was so very fat
that it would be an utter impossibility for him to
again get in condition to fight. Mace, who is as
shrewd as he is clever with his fists, thought that
it would be a good idea to match Goss against
Allen, and as Joe had never been to this country,
should the match be made he would ‘prove a pay-
ing card in the way of sparring exhibitions.

NEGOTATIONS
were entered into, and as Allen was anxious to
have ashy at his old antagonist, with whom he
had fought a draw in three rings, there was very
little difficalty in coming to terms, and when the
men met at Cincinnati, for the purpose of draw- |
ing up articles, the documents were signed in
short order. At that meeting Goss was very |
much surprised to find that Allen was the picture |
of health,.and not at all corpulent. Shortly after
the making of the match, Goss and Mace dis-
solved partnership. The men were filling a spar- |
ring engagement with Howe's circus, and the
cause of the quarrel was a ‘‘kick’’ made by Joo
because he did not receive as much money for his
services asthe ‘‘gvpsy.’’ Mace tlien declined
furnishing any more of the buttle money, and
Goss was thrown on his own resources. He was
astranger in a country where Allen is looked
upon as almost invincible, had ten weeks training
before him, which necessarily would entail a
heavy cxpense, and half of his share of the stakes
stullto produce. Where this money is to come
from is what gives the match
A FISHY LOOK. -

Bir Joseph, immediately after severing his con-
nection with Mace, went into training at Forest
Home, a delightful retreat a few miles outside of
Cincinnati, which is presided over by Eph Hol-
land, the Mike McDonald of Cincinnati. A great
deal of work had to be accomplished in the way
of ridding himself of superfluous flesh, as nine
year’s idleness had caused the pugilist to assume
aldermanic proportions. When the match was
made Joe weightd 210 pounds. To-day, under
the mentorship of Jimmy Cusick, who prepared
Heenan for his fight with Sayers, Goss pulls the
beam at 175, having reduced himself two anda
half stone by the hardest kind of work. This re-
sult has been brought about by judicious dieting,
long walks, dumb-bell exercise and cold baths.
He bas experienced no annoyance whatever from
the change of climate or strange water, and since
his arrival in America has enjoyed the best of
health. Mrs. Goss is residing with her husband
at Forest Home, which doubtless adds to his
comfort, although her presence would not be
relished by a trainer who meant for his

. MAN TO WIN. =

Allen, it may be said, is never out of condition,
and while Goss requires ten weeks to prepare for
the fray, his opponent needs but x orsix. Al- |
len and Jack Madden left for Cincinnati at the
close of their engagement at the Comique ten
days ago, and a letter from Tomsatates that he has
begun work in earnest, and thathe never was in
better trim in his life. Madden is to attena to his
physical condition until the fight. While here,
Tom was interviewed by a GLOBE-DEMUCRAT re-
porter in hia room at the Olive Street Hotel, and
swore by all that was holy, as only a prize-fighter
can, that the match was onthe ‘‘dead level,’’
that it would come off without the shadow ofa
doubt, and that the best man would win. Me
stated that the fighting ground had already been
selected, that the wale 18 was an admirer of the
manly art, and that h : had given them permis-
sion to slug each other on his farm for the sake.of

witnessing the mill. Allen was very. confident
that he would win, basing his conclusions on
A NOMBRE OF FACTS.

In the first place, he claimed to have had all the
best of the previous fight, and to have been con-
stantly atit, and improved greatly since then,
while Goss had been idle. _He asserted that it
would be almost impossible ror Goss to get into
proper condition, owing to bis mode of life and
the change of climate, but was compelled to con-
cede that Joe had taken time by the forelock, and
was working like a Trojan to.step into the ring a
perfect man.

‘*It will be the liveliest scrap you ever saw for
the first twenty minutes,’’ said the champion.
‘*He's a game ’un, and clever, but a little slow.
He'll stand punishment like a bull-dog, and the
only way you can lick himisto blind him. He
will fight for all that’s out until his frame gives
way, as it is bound to, and then will have to quit.
A man may be as brave asa lion, but it all goes
for nothing when he finds his strength leaving
him, He has the will to keep thumping, but not
the strength to carry it out, and is merely a chop-
ping block for his antagonist.’’

THE MEN AND THEIR CHANCES, —

By this it will be seen that Alien does not by
any means underratW the ability of ‘‘the other
man,’’ but imagines that he wil break down be-
fore the fight is fairly started. On the other band,
Joe's admirers assert that this is all bogh, and
that when Tom discovers that he has made a mis-
pc and that the man opposed vag at 1s fully as
strong and equally clever, he will stiow the white.
ea le which his enemies claim he is liable to
exhibit if worsted, but which he has never yet
done in any of his score of battles.

An ardent admirer of the champion’s, and one
who has been his stanch friend at all stages, was
asked whether he thought the fight on the seventh
of September was to be decided on its merits. His
reply was to the point: ‘‘If these men,’’ said he,
**mean to fight, and I haye no reason to suppose
that they do not, there is nothing on earth that
can stop them, and if the mill is interrupted in
any way, and if the fight is not decided on its
merits, it’s a d—n barney, gotten up for the pro-
ceeds of the excursion andthe mouey to be made
out of sparring exhibitions. Allen, at least,
ought to know better than to cut his own throat
in that way, and I think he intends to lick Goss,

if he can, from the word go.’’
| TWO MORE FIGHTS TO TAKE PLACE.
The approaching mill seems to haye stirred up
| pugilists throughout the country. Fiddler Neary
and Mike Gillespie also intend settling an old
- grudge in the squared circie, and Johnny Hickey
is out with a challenge to fight any 112-pound
man in the country for the feather weight cham-
pionship and $1,000 a side within two months after
| signing articles.

title: Mace and Allen Championship Contest
text:
| a CIRCLE. .
The Chaaision of America vs. the Cham-
| pion of England.

Something About the Mon, Their Train-
ers, Etec., Etc,
: TFrom the Cincinnat! Times. |

The big heavy-weight fight, for the cham-
pionship of the world and $2,500 a side, be-
Frean tim Allen, the recognized champion
of América, and Joe Goss, who, since the re-
tirement of Mace, holds the champion belt of
England, is just now the all absorbing topic

The fight will take place within 100 miles

Both men are now 1n_ active training, Goss

Before giving the records of the men, a de-

bave a word or two to say in regard to pugil-
ism in general. .

THE ORIGIN OF ‘*THE RING.’?’

The art of boxing, as now practiced, may
be said to date from the iniiiding in London
of atheater for exhfbition#of the ‘‘manly
art of self-defense’’ about 1740, A one
Broughton, who, for eighteen years held the
title of Lime og gia of si and is said to
have invented boxing-gloves. He held exhi-
bitions in his theater, and established rules
for fighting, which are quite similar to those
recognized by the London Prize Ring at the

resent day. For many years previous to that
att, however, pugilistic encounters had been
common at fairs and festivals, “in England.
The encounters at Broughton’s were wit-
nessed by the best blood of the land, includ-
ing the Prince of Wales.

Among _ most skillful ;professors of the
art was Jackson, who was champion of ing-
land in 1795. Ile gave instructions to many
of the aristocracy, among whom were Lord
Byron and Shaw, the Lifeguardsman,

In 1817 the future Emperor, Nicholas, of
Russia| witnessed a prizo fight in England,
and shook hands with the victor.

At the present day prize fighting is prac-
ticed only in Great Britain and America} and
{tis thought thit very few of the fights that
have occurred in the past few years haye been
honestly conducted.

The first prize fight in the United States
took place in 1816, between Jacob ar»
father of the famous Tom Ilyer, and Tom
Beasley, the result of which. was a draw.
The rules of the ring were observed during
the first part of this tight, but it soon degene-
rated into rough and tumble, and friends of
the men interfered, after one of Hyer’s arms
had been broken.

This was followed by numerous v; ofa
more scientific character. Among them re |
be mentioned a contest between Hyer an
Yankee Sullivan in 1848; that between Mor-
rissey aud Sullivan; between Morrissey and
Heenan in 1858; Australian Kelly and Ned
Price, of Boston, in 1859; Collier and Ed-
wards, who fought three times, Edwards
winning each fight; Allen and Davis; Keating
and Hollingwood; Alien and McCoole; Cham-
bers and Seddons, etc.

The grgef fights in England during thé last
twenty fears were that between Sayers and
Hee . fought April 17, 1860; Sayers and
Mace, Sayers and Goss, Heenan and Tom
King, etc.

During the last five years or so there have
been few Jights of great interest or conse-—
quence, pth |haay the fatrthat oar who
eee the g have lost all confidénce in

ts favorites, and the manly art of self-defense
has been confined mostiy,to exhibitions of
skill upon the stages of theaters.
CLASSIFICATION OF WEIGHTS. |

A pen of 115 pounds weight or under is
ealied a feather weight. ; |

Between 115 and 1 pounds a light weight.

Between 130 and 150, a middle weight.

_ One hundred and fifty pounds, or over, a
heavy weight.

Asa general rule a beary--walawt fighter
never enters the ring ata less weight than 165
pounds, while a Yexther-weight fighter sel-
dom weighs over 106 to 109.

THK RULES.

The rules under which battles are now
fought in this country are those recently
agreed upon dn England, and which are
known as the ‘‘Rules of the London Prize
Ring.’’ They may be given, in brief, as fol-
lows: «

The ring shal] be on turf formed of a square
of twenty-four feet, bounded by a double
line of. ropes attached to eight stakes. The
lower rope is twe feet, and the upper four
feet from the ground. The choice of corners
is determined by the toss of a coin, the win-
ner of the choice er egen | his corner accord-
ing tothe state of the wind and a
of the sun, it bene considered an “om
to have the sun in his opponent’s face. The
loser takes the Nip corner, aud a space
is provided. in each corner mine enough to ac-
commodate the principal, his seconds, and
his botile“holder, who are allowed to remain
inside the eo when their principals are
waiting the thirty seconds which is allowed be-
tween rounds, atall other times the ring must
ye nonred of all persons except the two prin-
cipals.

As soon as the men také their respective
corners their friends and backers get as pear
to them as the outer ropes will permit, and
the colors of the men.are then displayed. The
custom of tying the colors to the stake in the
corner chosen by the respective principals,
which was in yogue some years since, has
been abrogated, and the colors are now very
seldoin seen attached to the posts or ropes
forming the ring. i

Each of the pemeteeh either by himself or-
through friends, announces his seconds,
bottle holder and smyse: Then comes the
work of choosing a referce; and this is, as a
general rule, the sparred et ne The choice
of the man is, of course,left toeach principal,
who takes the advice of his seconds, umpire
and backers. If no referee can be agreed upon,
the final stakeholger, who in the present in-
stance is Mr. A. B. Edwards, will be forced
to hame a man or aet himself.

The referee decides the |fizht, watebes all
points, decides all .claims|of what is called
foul fighting, and his decision is considered

final. There is no appeal! from it, and who-
ever he declares the winner takes the stakes,
and the other considerations for which he has
a:

The reforee, according to the rules, must
withhold all expressions of opinion until he
is appealed to by the umpires, or until the
close of the fight.

The umpires and the referee are so placed
as to be able to watch the fight, and the judg-
ment of the latter is final.

THE PRESENT MATCH

was made by Goss and Allen through their
soepeoiire friends, and was consummated at
Eph. Holland’s Empire Saloon, on Fifth
street, near Ve, onthe 12th of May last.
At that time the principals met, and attaehed
their names to the following articles of agree-
merit:

Joseph Goss, mnake this joint agreementat the
city of Cincinnati, in the presence of the wit-

sum of five thousand dollars ($5,000), of
which two thousand five hundred ‘dollars
($2,500) is to be staked by Joseph Gos, and

atere meneeerd. ;

In deference to the request of the Society
for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals,
Prosecuting Attorney Baker has made Joe
Goss and Tom Allen give good and sufiicient
bonds to keep the peace inthe state of Ohio
for one year. The law against prize-tighting
is very stringent in this state, and neither
Goss nor Alien ever had any idea of violating
it. It is now authoritatively an-
nounced that it has been determined
to place the price of tickets to the
pugilistic excursion at seven dollars each
instead of ten dollars, as at firstintended. As
but a limited number willbe sold, and those
to proper parties, those who wish to see the
big mili will do well to make early applica-
tion for their pasteboard to Eph. Holland.
The fizhting ground has been selected, and
is surrounded by a2 natural amphitheatre that
will enable all to have a full view of the ring
without any crowding.

summary: The St. Louis Republic reported that Joe Goss and Tom Allen were required to post bonds by the Prosecuting Attorney in Ohio to keep the peace. Ticket prices for the pugilistic excursion were set at seven dollars.

Dad Ryan of St. Louis has been agreed

Jack Looney of St. Louis, and a party

will be seen Kelly is a little anxious

Crxcrxwati, September 6.—There is
& rumor here this morning that Allen
will not get fair play in the fight to-mor-
row. Theysay the best he cangetis a
‘sdraw.’* Allen thinks differently, how-
ever. —

Will write you full particulars to-
night. Publish this in evening papers.

t Tom KELLY.

Crncrynati, Sept. 7.—The point
chosen for the tight between Allen and
Goss is Cloverfield, near Walton, Ken-
tucky, on the Louisville Short Line

Railroad, eighteen miles from Cincin-
nati. Acrowd of some 500 were ir at-
tendance. Goss and Allen take their |
places

In the Ring
At seven o'clock. The fight begins at
7:35. Goss first steps to the middle of
the ring.

First Round—Both men spar cauti-
ously, Goss falling into Allen’s corner.
The sparring is rather tiresome for the
crowd.

First Blood for Allen,
And a clinch and a fall, Goss on top.
Time, seven minutes.

Second Round—Allen strikes Goss on
the lips and slightly staggers him. Goss
has given Allen some heavy body
blows. Goss’ mouth bleeding. A fall
for Alien.

Third Round—Close fighting. Allen
winning.

At this point

The Militia Appeared,
But the fighting goes on.

Capt. Frank Wood, with the Coving-
ton Light Guards, reached the point
north of Walton at 7 o’clock, having
been carried past the fighting grounds
by the conductor. Capt. Wood stopped
the train three miles past the point, and
the militia marched back, arriving at 8
o'clock.

Fourth Round—Exchanges fast and
heavy. Allen, by a terrible blow on
Goss’ neck, knocked him down. Time,
three minutes.

Fifth Rounc—After considerable spar-

ring, Allen struck out and fell short on
Goss’ face. In return he received a blow
in the stomach. This did net
appear to worry Allen, and he returned
heavily on Goss’ body, and a fearful one
on the damaged eye. Goss retaliated,
and, after sharp half-arm fighting, Goss
went down to avoid punishment.

Sixth Round—Both men promptly to
the scratch, Allen leading off, getting in
on Goss’ face. He repeated this, get-
ting in another blow on Goss’ damaged

»right eye. Allen finally fizhts Goss
down.

Seventh Round—When time was
called the Covington Light Guards ap-
peared ard the fight ceased.

W.G. Lobban, aidto the Governor,

Sent for Eph Holland,
And advised that the fight immediately
cease. Hoiland stated he wasa law
abiding man, opposed to blood-shed,
and accordingly stopped the fight, after
seven rounds had been fought.

Holland declares he will make the
men fight out the tight before they reach
Cincinnati to-night. Neither of the
men is mucb punished.

After being dispersed by the militia a
second ring was formed a short distance
below Walton, in Boone County. The
Sheriff was present, but had not sufi-_
cient posse to interfere.

Kighth Round—Goss threw Allen,
though the former was severely pua-
ished.

Ninth Round—Goss forced fighting.
Allen finished round for himself with
heavy blows on Goss’ face.

Tenth Round—Heavy blows exchanged.
Goss forced on the ropes, The fighters
were parted by seconds.

Eleventh Round—Goss leads the fight-
ing—the hardest fighting in this round.

Twelfth Round—Both of Goss’ eyes
badly swolien. Allen knocks Goss
down,

Thirteenth Round—Terrific blow on
Goss’ mouth. Goss on his knees.

Fourteenth Round—Goss threw Allen
by clinching. Foul claimed, but not
allowed.

Fifteenth Round—Heavy, close
figiting; both badly punished.

Sixteenth Round—In chasing Allen
about the ring Goss slips ard falls.

Seventeenth lNound—Goss knocked
over the repes.

Kighteenth Round—Goss plants a
stinger on Allen’s body. Close fizht-

-ing. Foul claimed by Guss, but not al-
lowed,

Nineteenth Round—Goss slips and
falis. Close fighting.

Twenticth Round—Both fall.

Twenty-first Round—In close fighting
Goss falls and is struck by Allen while
cn his knees. A foul claimed and al-
lowed. Fight decided in favor of Goss
at11:50a. m. Alien shows little orno
injury about the face; Goss terribly
beaten, almost blind. Time of fizht—
Cne hour and fifty-two minutes.

Allen Arrested,

CINCINNATI, O., Sept. 7.—Two trains
from the tight to-dey arrived at Newport
at 2:40, and were siopped by the author-
ities, and Tom Allen arrested.
summary: The St. Louis Post-Dispatch provided round-by-round coverage of the Allen-Goss fight at Cloverfield near Walton, Kentucky on September 7, 1876, noting Allen scored first blood and knocked down Goss multiple times before the controversial decision.
