title: Tom Allen Returns to St. Louis After Goss Fight
text:
s THOMAS ALLEN.
His Arrival in St. Louis and Reception
by Friends.
— -
How He Looks and Talks--No More P. R.
for Him.

Tom Allen is back. The man who licked Joe
Goss, and who was cheated out of a fair fight by

the New York delegation that bet on Goss, ar-

rived in our city yesterday morning, and, from all
accounts, will make his home here henceforward.
During the day he visited his many friends, who
were anxiously awaiting. his return. Those who
baunt Tom Kelly's saw him first, and after that
he looked in at Jim Gayin’s, at Charley Henry’s,
and one or two other places, taking his dinner at
the Olive Street, where he isa registered, by the
way. In the evening he visited the Comique, and
was waited on by all the boys. It was a shake of
the hand with this one, a little chat with another,
8 drink with the third, a private confab with the
next, and a square talk with the GLoBE-DEMoO-
CRAT reporter.

. HOW DOES ALLEN LOOK?

He looked the very picture of physical health.
Hair just cropping out again, showing the gray,
however, a fact noticed by his friends. Nota
sign of punishment on his face, which is just be-
ginning to show the ‘‘moss’’ of a mustache, and
the first outgrowths of whiskers and beard. Lips
enregle. Hands O. K., the mght one holding a
gold-headed cane. Tom wore a dark hat, dark
frock-coat, light pants, cut close. You couldn’t
help noticing his small feet. Present weight, 180
ponnas.

There was little about him to betray the pugilist.
A certain sans souct alr indicated the man who
had, by dint of physical prowess, won a moral
regard from his fellows. He was evidentiy at
home, and made others feel so in his presence.
If he has ever been accused of rough talk, it didn’t
show last night. His accent told his nationality, |
but the choice of his words did him credit. He
had apparently forgotten that any newspaper had
ever spoken of him derogatively. No, not quite |
that, for the sting of the New York Clipper wasn’t |

quite gone yet; but, anyhow, the peer of Mace
and King was firmly convinced of the ability and |
disposition of the GLOBE-DEMOCRAT man to tell
the truth. !
THE TALK.

**Tfow about the stakes?’’ was the first question
asked.

‘‘Well, I attached the stakes the night of the
fight. They are all right.’’

‘*‘ButI saw in some paper or other that Goss
was showing the money he received from the
stakeholder and the money he giined as bets.
How's that?’’ r

‘*All he got was $500 and his expenses to Fn-
gland. He was to have left New York for England
on Saturday. Iguess he’s gone now. Stakes are
all right in Edwards’ hands.”

**Who’s your attornéy in the suit?’’

‘‘A man named Root and Gov. Carlisle, of Cov-
ington.’’

**Will you sue in Ohio or Kentucky?’’

‘*In Ohio, of course (with a sly twinkle). I
wouldn't stand much show in Kentucky.’’

**And the suit comes off when?’’

** About the 25th of this month. I'm going over
again to eee to it.”” .

**Now, that you are out of the ring—I suppose
hat’s'so, isn’t it? (Tom nodded assent)—what are
your intentions as to the future?’’

**I’m going to settle down—going to look out
some place—Il've been looking round all day to-
day—and stick to business.’’

‘*You can’t get @ square deal in the ring, can
you?’’

**Oh, no. It isn’t possible now.”

And then Tom looked across the parquette,and,
seeing a man sitting by a pillar who resembled
McCoole in facial outline, he said; ‘‘l guess
that’s Mike; no, it ain’thim either. Well, I'l
goand see anyhow.’’ But it wasn't Mike; he
wasn't in town, so Cool Herbert said, and the br-
standers echoed-that remark.

As to the actual

FIGHT WITH GOsA,

Allen volunteered no remark. It seemed as if the
matter had lost all interest for him, except as the
stakes are concerned. He casually remarked that
on Thursday night Miller, the champion wrestier
of the world, would engage 1n a fencing bout with
Mons. Schuler, while Regnier had volunteered to
perform his great cannon-ball feat. Bauer will
be there, but takes no active part in the even-
ing’s programme, the grand attraction of which
is, of course, the boxing between Allen and
Kelly.

* Tom expects a rousing house, in which, in all
probability, he will not be disippointed. When
his benefit is over, he will be a private citizen for
all future time.

AMUSEMENTS.
Olympic Tireatre-.

_ The presentation of ‘‘Pique’’ in this city is
one of the leading dramatic events of the sea-
son. We have heard of ‘‘Pigque’’ fora long
while. The name has been continually in the
newspapers fora year. It has been abundantly
advertised in the prints, and our citizens who
have seen it in all the glory of Daly's
Fifth avenue setting in New York
have sounded its praises in their
several circles. Our public was well pre-
pared forit, and the fashionable exhibition
in the auditorium of the Olympic last night
was an intelligent response to the fame of
both the attractions of the play, and its prin-
cipal figure, Miss Fanny Davenport. It was
soon after Miss Davenport’s visit here Inst
season, (which was her first acquuintance
with our prilic) that ‘*Pique’’ was pro-
duced in New York. Miss Davenport
had already made herself very sirong
in St. Louis. and her success in the new picce
Was a2 matter of keen interest to her St. Louis
friends. Now she comes with the piece itseli,
and the general interest in the actress and the
play, which showed itself when the box-oftice
was opened for the sale of seats a few days
ago, and again in the large attendance upon
the initial performance last night, was nata-
rally to be expected. ‘‘Pique’’ had been in
rehearsal ror a week at the Olympic.
Noxon and his forces lad been
busy a still longer time preparing
for it a new outfit of scenery. The company
had become ‘‘letter’’ perfect in their parts
and thoroughly drilled inthe business of the
play. Every possible preparation had been
made for the brilliant theatrical event, and it
might as well be stated now that the result last
evening fully answered the promisemade and
public expectation raised. The response in
numbers was full, the appreciation hearty,
and the enjoyment general.

Itis unnecessary ut present to tell the story
or dwell upon the plot of **Pique.’’ It is an
American society play, in which there is sutti-
cient friction between various classes to strike
fire and kindle interest. The clash comes be-
tween a New York society belle and an old
New England Puritan tamily, into which she
has married for pique. A child is born to her
and stolen, and the piot turns
upon the search for the child. The play is
full of incident, and compact with character,
and its dramatic effects are very ingeniously
contrived. They were all brought out, too, in
fine style, fora first presentation last night.
The lines were ali spoken, the dialogue was
rapid, and the perftormunce was over before
twelve o'clock. Hereafter the closing
time will be about half-past elev-
en. The sets are elaborate.
The first cannot be excelled for scenic beauty.
The curtain rises upon a conservatory of real
plants and garden trees; which mingling with
the artist’s colors makes a verfect Ulusion of
green and flowery iInxury. The second and
third (the same) presents a vivid picture of a
severe old Puritan home. The fourth is a
front street and snow scene, which opens into
the interior ofa hovel. The fiftn is a druwing-
room scene. The scenic efiects are brilliant
beyond anything heretofore done for a play in
this theatre.

Of the acting too much praise cannot be
pes Of course Miss Davenport’s Mabel

nfrew is superb in embodiment and cos-
tume and all the dramatic graces. The char-
acter is a frivolous woman redeemed by a
great sorrow, and elevated to the height of a
loving wife and mother. It comes a
glowing picture from Miss Davenport’s hands.

Matthew Standish (Frank Weston) is a splen-
aid character part, and Weston does it spien-
didly. His muke-upis severe, and the em-
bodiment is of tine breadth. We have seldom
seen a purer or more effective
bit of pathos, than his recon-
ciliation with his daughter-in-law. There are
few words, but his face is a volume of feeling.
Charles Rockwell, from Daly’s Fifth Avenue
theatre, does Capt. Arthur Standishin a very
sensible style. Without creat force he is care—
ful and correct. Dr. Gossitt, by_ Ferd.
Hight, is good. Raymond Lessinz
(L. R. Warwick) jacks vim. He
willimprove. Dymple and Gyll by the come-
dians, Chas. Plunkett and Harry Harwood,
respectively are excellent. Rag Money Jim,
by Hand, is welldone. The ladies of the com-
pany all do well, and are peculiarly notted for
the several roles that fall to their share.
The most conspicuous is Rachel—Miss Libbie
Noxon—who has a character part exactly fit-
ted to her, and she made a hit in it. Her
earlier scenes were probably a trifie over-
acted last evening, but she will doubtless
guard against this in future. The play inade a
hit, and it couldn’t Lbeipit. It will be repeated
until further notice.

De Bar’s Opera-House.

The oid style of Irish pieces has gone out of
vogue, and the stage Imshman, as a dramatic
attraction, isu figureof the past. He wasa
very funny fellow, but as a comic, did great
injustice to his class. He really did nothing
but burlesgue Irish character, and manners
and customs, and even therich brogue. He is
gone with the old styie ot delinea-
tors. Boucicauilt has done much
towards cultivating a better understanding cf
Irish character, by givingtruertyvpes. Others
have been at workin the same field with iike
objects. ‘‘Willy Reilly*’ isan example of the
tendency to truth in the later Irisn drama.
Dominick Murray is au actorin perfect bar-
mony with the object above set forth. An
Ttristuman born, an actor by nature and an art-
ist by culture, he is a worthy exponent of the
character, theught and feeling of Ireland.
Dowinick Murray is a genuine Irishman, and
no mere mouther of the brogue and burlesquer
of the character on the stage. When he pre-
sents an Irishman he appreciates the dra-
matic situation and feels the responsibility.
He is true to both his national and artistic in-
a und trusts to the integrity of his work
for effects. Thisis the groundwork of Mur-
ray’s treatment of Ivish subjects, and veing so
founded it cannot tail of its purpose. He
brings intimate kuowiedge, strong dramatic
forces and symputhizing nature to the task,
and these suarantee its masteriy performance.
 **Willy Reilly’’ was produced in excellent
style at De Bar’s, and was played weli. Itis
almost needless to say that Dominick Murray
made a superb character performance of Wii-
ly Rejlly. The churacter gave the actor scope
tor bis best Qualities, and he putthem to the
best use. Miss Florence Chase as
Helen Frolliardg, made a tine figure und truly
embodied this lovely character. Miss
Emnia Maddern as Yom thetIniuocent did
an excelent piece of churacter actiny. Mr.
oO. W. Blake as Andy wus true to the life,
and in fact the whole support wus good.
The play went of with sreat
spirit, and met with a generous
response from the audience, ‘*Willy Reilly’’
will be repeated every evening until Thursazy
inclusive, when Alr. Murray will introduce
**Innocent;or, The Gumbier’s Crime,’’ for
his benefit, and repeat it for Saturday matinee
and evening, which will close his engugement.

The German Drama.

Miss Marie Schaumberg, a noted German
soubrette, made her first appearance at De
Bar’s Opera-house on Sunduy evening and
was weil received. The play wus ‘‘Dear
Fatherland’’—paitriotic und popular and iuii
of merry music. lt wus thoroughly enjoyed by

Episcopal Orphans’? Home Benefit.

The notice of the public has been drawn to

This worthy Institution is in need of mouey to

Class talent will appeur in the comedy offered.
**Caste,’’ always ucceptabie to the public, will |

tertainment on the stage to interest and

title: Arthur Chambers interview on English prize ring conditions
text:
f The English Prize Ring.
[From the Philadetphia Sunday Item.1

As itis a matterof much interest to the sporting
fraternity of the United States to know what is )
goingon in prize ring matters in England (the
mother of the art of self-iefense), a reporter was
sent tothe Champion's Rest, 922 Ridge avenue,
to interview Arthur Chambers on his recent
es the ‘‘old country,’’ with the following
result:

Reporter. What is the condition of the prize
ring at the present time in England?

Chambers. No fighting at all, sir; @ man’s
lucky if he can be backed for £10 a side.

Rep. What is the reason for this radical
change?

Clambers, The license law; for the men who
— wantto make a match, micht took all day
and not get 4 publican either to back them or be
stakeholder, as it would result in the seizure of
his license atence. Thus the strictness of the
ae Operates against any ambition the men may

ve.

Pablic houses are closed on week nights at 11
o'clock, while on Sunday they are only permitted
woopen at 12:30 p. m., forced to close at 2:30,
permitted to open at 6, and forced to close again
at 10 o'clock, just as the business is becoming
or: If dominoes or cards are played even for
drinks, you musi do it with locked doors, fora
discovery by the police would result in a loss of
license. Even it I had a house presented to me
in London I Wouldn’t hare it there, to keep it in
— line, That is what has killed prize-fignt-

te. What has followed this result?

Chambers. Public and private exhibitions of
sparring; occasionally professionals, but fre-
quently among gentlemen amateurs; striculy am-
atcurs, as tlicy will not spar for money, but for
prizes, such as cups, belts, medals, etc.. Many
of these amateurs are equal to wie best profes-
sionals, and there is one gendeman amateur I
could name who could enter the ring with any
professional in England; indeed, he is able to
stand up with any boxer i know.

Rep. Is there any dJikelibood of the sport re-—
turning to its old popularitys

Chambers, No, sir, not while the present Li-
cense Law exists.

Rep. Whatisthe feeling amongthe peovle? _

Chambers, The feeling with the public, for a_
fair, square, up-and-up fight, is jost the same as
of old. The interest in the sport is unchanged. |

Rep. Many of the best men have left Soqeee? |

Chambers. Yes, sir. Tom Allen, Bill Ryall, |
Peter Morrissey, Abe Hicken (who is now in Aus-—
eee i Hicken, Jem Mace, Pooley, Ned |
O'Ba dwin, oe Goss, myself and nearly all the :
men of any importance have come to the United |
States, and I think itis due to these men to say
that their presence here has created and fostered
an interest in sporting matters of all kinds.

Rep. Who are the most prominent professional
men in London at the poser time?

Chambers, Charley vis, middle weight, and
Bat Mullins, light weight, both of London, are
the two best in England at the present time.

Rep. How were you received during your recent _
visit to England?

Chambers. With the greatest nape J and
kindness on ail sides, and ary camer mang at Oldbam
and Manchester. At the latter town, January 8,
at Owen Conroy's house, **The Three Legs of

Man,’’ on Portland street, I was tendered a com-

| ey dinner, at which I was presented with

a diamond badge, worth 50 sovereigns. Previous

to this 1 was tendered a testimonial benefit at

Free Trade Hall, which the people toid me was

the biggest event in the town for many years. I
wound — oung Nixey, of Liverpool:

Rep. ad yoR no fault to find with anything?

_ Chambers. » the Custom House officers,
contrary to law, charged me £5 10s duty on my
belt, which, although I did not wear it at a
times, was, nevertheless, person roperty.
They promised to restore the money, Bue have
not done it.

Rep. Who are the leading eparrers in Man-

Our representative, knowing Chambers’ inter-

tion of dogs by the Oldham Canine Society, on

Thanking the brilliant apende ‘or his politeness,

help hesitating for a moment to glance around at

hand, under a giaes; a cast of Jem Mace's

ent; a stuffed champion bulldog, and endless

How the Allen-Hogan Prize Fight Fiz-

en. iS

In his answer, however, to the petition of Capt.

Capt. McCloy testified that the Looney-tica on

office by storm and carried off a valuable field

title: Gambler mentions Eph Holland Tom Allen Goss fight
text:
@ .
St. Ronis Duly 6
A ROBBER’S REMORSE.
A Reformed Cracksman Tells the Story of
His Singular Career of Crime.

His Adventures by Sea and Land as
Soldier, Gambler, Bank-Robber,
Convict and Tramp.

Ten Years in the Ohio Penitentiary—Pardoned
by Gov. Hayes—He Wants to Ge
to Sing Sing.

[From the New York Times, March 19.]

As Justice Kilbreth was about to adjourn
the session of the Tombs Police Court at 11
o’clock yesterday morning, Officer Kennedy,
of the Twenty-seventh Precinct, entered the
court-room, having in custody a most forlorn-
looking man. At the first glance he appeared
to be an ordinary member of the great army
of tramps, but when he had removed the
misshapen piece of felt that did him service
as ahat, he exposed a face bearing none of
the marks ‘that are impressed upon
the countenance of a whining, shuf-
fling beggar. It was a face present-
ing strange contrasts of fat and lear.
The cheek-bones were covered with swollen,
pulpy flesh, but the lower jaws were lean as

the Joins of a greyhound, and were girt about

with a stubby, dirty-looking beard, that was

-onee perhaps clean and flaxen. Notwith-
standing these strange contrasts and the fact

that the upper lip was weak and protruding,

| the face of the prisoner had a resolute look,

to which the steel-blue eyes, well set beneath
ahigh and rounding forehead, contributed
not a little. Patrolman Kennedy made an
affidavit that his prisoner, Christian Hansen,
bad made about twenty attempts to enter
forcibly as many different stores on Broad-
way. When the

HUNGRY-LOOKING MAN

was arraigned before Justice Kilbreth, his
captor testified that shortly before 10 o’ clock
in the morning he noticed Hansen standing on
Broadway, near Warren street. He appeared
to be watching the witness, and when he
seemed satisfied that the latter saw him, he
walked to the door ofa small fancy goods
store, and made a deliberate altempt to force
it open. a to do this, he walked down
Broadway, ap made at Iecast a score
of attempts at burglary. The oflicer fol-
lowed him, but thinking he was simply in-
dulging in a drunken freak, and was too weak
to do any harm, did not attempttoarrest him,
At last, Hansen, apparently becoming des-
perate, worked with determination at the door
of No. 155 Broadway, and had partly moved
it from its fastenings when the officer laid his
hand upon his shoulder and arrested him.
He made no citemet to escape. but, turning
around, told the officer he was starving, and
had deliberately set about committing a felo-
af in order that he might be sent to Sing Slug

prison.

id Justice Kilbreth was greatly suprised when
he learned that the prisoner

WANTED TO GO TO SING SING,

and questioned him as to his reasous for de-

-siring to go to such a place. Ilansen replied,

in broken English, and with a German ac-

cent, ‘*I am poor, and in the gutter; I bave
been only a few weeks out of the Columbus
(O.) State Prison, and though 1 haye tried to
get honest labor I have been unable. People
will do nothing for me; but Tdon’t want to go
back to my old way. I thought I would do
something that would make the Judges seud
me to Sing Sing.’’ ‘*So,’’ said the Justice,
**you do not want to go back to the old crim-
{nal course you say you once followed?’’ **No,
sir. I might do som@ting that would make
me more miserable.’’ Ald. Morris and Dr.
Elisha G. Harris, who were on the bench
with the justice, became intensely interested
in the case of the frank fellow at the bar,
and urged the Justice to examine into his
ease thoroughiy, so that something might be
done for him if his statements proved true.
Justice Kilbreth then asked Hansen ywhat he
was sent to the Columbus prison for” He re-
pee: **In 1866, Land three others robbed a
ank in Cincinnati, and got $400,000 in cash,
bonds, stocks, ete. We started for St. Louis,
and on our way robbed a mail-car safe of

35,000. Twas caught and sent to prison for
twenty years. About five weeks ago

GOV. HAYES PARDONED ME
because lL had behaved myself well for ten
years. WhenlTleft the prisonI was given
3S. «have used that all up, and since Fri-
day night haven’t had anythingtoeat. No-
body would help me, and I made up my mind
to go to prison again.’’ Thinking to pose
the prisoner, Justice Kilbreth asked him if
he sould opena aafe. ‘*Yes, sir, I can,
and without tools, I think.’’ ~**Well,’’ said
the Justice, ‘‘there is a safe in the back room
that no one connected with.this Court can
open.’’ ‘*Showit to me,’’ said Hansen, ea-
gerly. ‘*T will show you how I would
try to break it.’’ He was led into the exam-
ination-room, at the rear of the Court-room,
and shown a small office safe, which looked
sturdy enough to resist almost any pressure.
Justice Kilbreth, Dr. Harris, Aldersien Mor-
ris, Sergt. Woodruff, and several policemen
gathered in a knot around the prisoner, aud
earnestly watched his actions.. First he gave
the knob of the safe door a twitch with a pe-
euliar movement of his right hand, as
if to test the character of the lock.

Then he knelt down and examined the
safe critically. After a moment’s pauso
he said rapidly: ‘‘I would take putty and put
it all round the rim of the door; but I would
leave a hole here [the base of the door, near
the left-hand corner], and another one here
{the right-hand side of the door, near its up-
per corner]. Then I would put some powder
at this bottom hole, and would put the pump
atthe upper hole. As soon as I began to
work the pump the air would be drawn out
of the safe atthe top, and at the same tiine
fhe powder would be pushed into it by thé air
rushing in below.’’ ‘The explanation of the
burglarious process was perfectly clear. The
spectators) marveling at the simplicity of
the method, began a conversation among
themselves, which prevented Hansen from
telling how he would fire the powder when he
had got it into the safe. He said he was very
weak, and asked permission to sit down while
the party talked, After they had satisiled
themselves that the foree of the exploding
powder, exerted along a diagonal line from
the top to the bottom of the safe door, would
blow the door open, Hansen was again asked
questions about his career. Little by little
the story of his life was drawn from him. It
proved to be exceedingly iutcrestiug, and in
some respects instructive.

A MELANCHOLY DANE.

He was born, he eaid, in Copenhagen,
Denmark, in 1834, and in now forty-three
years old. He received a fair education in
an academy in his native place, and learned
to speak German, Norwegian and Swedish.
H{e came to this country in 1863, landing in
New York. ‘The day after his arrival he
enlisted in Company K of the 7th New York
Volunteers (the Steuben Regiment), com-
manded by Col. Schack. With that regiment
he served at Petersburg, and in one of the
battles was wounded in the left shoulder.
When the war was over his regiment was
mustered out of service on Ward’s Island,
and he came to New York. He did not stay
here long; but went to Cincinnati, where he
procured work as a railroad laborer. He was
paid #2 a day, which satisfied his wants and
enabled him to et by a sum fora ‘rainy
day.’’ It was his habit to frequent at yee
asaloon known as ‘*The Buckeye.’’ In this
place he made a number of acquaintances,
some of whom were fellows who lived with-
out working. He did not suspect, however,
that ir ge criminals. One night he was
invited some of these fellows to walk with
them. He accepted the invitation, and, after
walking a short time, he was asked to go into
a house on Fifth street. He went with the
party, and they ascended a flight of steps and
came to a green door, on which one of his
friends knocked several times. The door was
opened, and Hansen and his conductors en-
tered a gambling saloon. ‘*Oh, that was the
time I began to go down, ’’ said he, excitedly.
**The place was hept by those fellows that
made that fight between Tom Allen and
Goss. Hochheimer & Co. were the proprie-
tors named, but Eph. Holland was with
them. He is a scoundrel, that Eph. Hol-
land.’?

FROM GAMBLING TO ROBBERY.

To be brief, Hansen was induced to gamble
away his savings in Holland’s piace. He be-
eame infatuated with gaming, and, besides
losing his money, lost his work. When he
became destitute it was proposed that he
should take part in the robbery of the First
National Bank of Cincinnati, situated at the
corner of Walnut and Fourth streets, which
three of the men he had become ac-
guntacee with in Holland’s had planned.

e accepted the offer. The pe hired a
basement next door to the bank building, and
started what appeared to the pubie to be a
mean kind of a drinking place. At np, Hd
they spent their time breaking through the
foundations of the bank edifice. After about
ten days | were fully prepared for the
robbery, and early on the morning of Febru-
ary 3, 1866, made their way into the cellar
beneath the bank. Thence they broke
through the flooring of the banking-
room. The watchman apparently did
not hearthem at work,and when they a ber ge
in the bank they frightened him into silence.
They then blew open the vault in the manner
described. Hansen said he would break the
sinall safe inthe judicial examination room.
As stated before, they procured in plunder
$400,000, including bonds aud stocks, and
$5,000 in currency. Upon leaving the bank
the money was divided among the burglars,
and Hansen was given $1,000. The entire
party spent the day afier in drinking and in

| gaming in Hochheimer & Co.’s, or Eph
Hfolland’s saloon. ‘They thus spent $1,000.

| Hansen lost the greater part of this sum, be-
cause he was pitted agaiust what gamblers
teria
A ‘*SKIN DEAL.’”

Having recovered from their carousal, the
thieves determined to leave Cincinnati. They
tirst.weut to Richmond, [ud., where they re-
mained for several weeks. Thinking St.
Louis a more congenial place, they deter-
mined togo thither, and, to pay traveling ex-
penses and keep them in spending money for
atime, they prepared to rob the safe of the
mail car of a train on the Vandalia Railway.

| Their plan for the robbery turned out

| Successfully. When the train stopped
at a watering station on the morning of
March 7, 18titi, and all the employes on it had
sgathered about the water tank, leaving the
mail and bageage cars deserted, the four
thieves broke into the mal car, tumbled the
safe out, and, when the train had gone. car-
ried ita mile away, Where they broke it opeu
and secured $5,000. Afterthis exploit they
continued on their way to St. Louis. Hansen
got drunk aud faiicd to tuke the same
measures for sufety taken by his com-
rades. Those three sharp criminals,
whose names Hansen will not reveal,
left the train about three miles east of
the Mississippi River. Lansen siaied in the
car, and was arrested by St. Louis detectives,
He was at tirst suspected of being one of the
gang led by the James brothers, for it was as-
sumed that those despermioes robbed the
mail-car which Hansen ana his comrades had
ee It was so assumed because the
umes boys had a short time before boldly
robbed a train running between Kansas
City and St. Louis. The St. Louis authori-
ties were unable to fasten upon Ilansen the
crime of robbing the mail-car, but from a de-
seription from Cincinnati they recognized
him as one of the burglars of the First Na-
‘tional Bank of that city. He was accordingly
sent back to Cincinnati, where he was tried
before Judge ‘Taft, lately Secretary of War,
who, upon his conviction, sentenced him to
imprisoument for twenty years. His com-
rades in the Ourglary did not desert him, but,
through confederates in Cincinnati, retained
Judge Cox and Emil Roedei to defend him.
This is one reason for his unwillingness to
disclose their names at the preseut time.
PARDONED BY HAYES.

Hansen passed ten years in the Columbus,
~O., State Penitentiary without once being
punished for disregard of discipline. It was
this good record that induced Governor, now

President Hayes, to pardon himin the first
week of February last. When Hansen
deft the prison he was handed $5, $20
of which was his share of gate money
set apart for well-disciplined prisoners,
and $45 of which were due him from the
contractors for machine work, under whom
he worked in the Pe itee ary « With this sum
he determined to begin the world anew, vow-
ing positively he would uever again commit a
criminal act for the sake of money. He was
given arailway pass to Cincinnat!l, where he
inade a short stay, going thence to Pittsburg.
It was his intention to preevure work as a farin
or railway laborer iu Pennsyivania. He
left the cars’ at Pittsburg and = walked
to Philadelphia. His treatment on his
pedestrian tour, «as he describes it,
would embitter the mind of a less unfortunate
man, and make him rejoice to tura bis band
ageiust humanity. He was either scorned as
a miserable tramp, or when he frankly told
the story of his life was driven oif as if he
were the embodiment of a playue. In Phila-
deiphia Hansen could procure no aid, so he
walked on, ina miserable plight, to this city.
In New Jersey he met with no Good Samari-
tan, and was not more fortunate” in
his search for one in this city.
People scouted him, and even the
Danish Consul, to whom he told
his story, he says, dismissed him witha pres-

-entof four cents. Since he has been in this
city Liansen has slept at niyhtina five+cent
lodgiog-house at No. 107 Greenwich street.
On Friday last he spent his last cent, and
from that time until noon yesterday he ate
nothing. ‘The fact that he was famishing was
proven by his rapid consumption of a tin dish
of soup and an immense loaf of bread given
him in the Lombs prison. :

| PROMISES.

-_ Hansen promised Dr. Harris, Justice Kil-
breth and Alderman Morris that if they st
cure him labor he will henceforward lead an
honest life. Alderman Morris gave him a
small sum of money, and promised to send
him a suit of clothes this morning. He was
“deeply moyed by his syinpathetic treatment,
and returned thanks with his eyes full of
tears. lis case is to be brought to the no-
tice of the Prisoners’ Aid Society by Df. Har-
ris to-day. He was committed to the Tombs
ona charge of disorderly conduct, but will be
released if his tale proves to be true, and aid
will theasbe given hjim to avoid crime in the
future,
summary: The St. Louis Globe-Democrat reported an anecdotal story about a criminal who recalled that Eph Holland operated a gambling saloon where the Tom Allen versus Goss prize fight had been arranged.

title: Donovan and McClellan Fight in New York
text:
THE FIGHT
was finally fixed for to-night, and tickets were
sold at $10 each. About 200 brokers, aldermen
and sporting men gathered in Monstrey’s sport-
ing establishment. There were three rows of
benches. Neura stage about fifteen by twenty
feet, at sides and rear of the stage, were foils,
masks, armor, boxing-gloves, etc. On the left
of the room was a row of closets, and on top of
them was a single row of benches. There were
but two professional fighters in the audience,
and they were adenitted with regular $10 tickets.
| THR PRINCIPALS APPEAR.
-— At 8:25 the applause was begun, and MeClel-
Ian and Donovan stepped on the stage. Johnny
| Dwyer, who-is soon to fight Ryan, of Troy,
for the championship of the “world, and
Ned Mallahan, one of Joe Colburn's old-
time friends, were seconds for McClellan. Joe
Goss, who fought Tom Allen in Kentucky, and
who won the fight through a foul invented by
himself, and Jerry Donovan were seconds for
Donovan. Jim Coburn, Joe's brother, was
umpire for McClellan, and Andy Sheehan, for
whom .
JOHN MORRISSEY
had a hearty dislike, was umpire for Don-
ovan. Billy Borst, the horseman, was chosen
referee. All things being in readiness, time
was called, and the principals and seconds ad-
vanced to the center of the stage and shook
hands. Donovan was unquestionably in better
condition than McClellan, but the odds
in the betting were in favor of the latter; the
sudience were hushed for a moment, and then
bang! bang! bang! and McClellan, driven by
Donovan's terrific raps, dashed against tne
wall. Both were in full ring costume, bare to
their waists and wearing knee breeches, long
stockings and henvy shoes. They- wore
hard gloves and meant to do harm.
| THE FIRST ROUND.
It wasat once apparent that there was no
\humbug about the set to, that somebody wes to
be whipped. When Donovan battered Me-
Clellan’s head ugainst the wall, the latter suc-
ceeded in clinching with his desperate antag-
onist, and fora moment seemed to have the
advantage of him. Donovan freed himself,
end gave McClellan a terrific neck blow, and
followed this up by forcing the tavorite to his
corner, pounding him terribly all the way.
There was a gash in McClellan's head, and his
fuce was covered with blood when he ieil into
his chair, as his friends crieql ‘‘Time’s up.
First blood for Donovan.’’
THE SECOND ROUND
lasted about one minute. McClellan seemed to
cast aside the science which he boasted of, and
began to claw and make frantic dashes at Don-
ovan, who saw his opportunity, and knocked
him sprawling on the floor. The first knock-
down was ‘of course claimed sand allowed for
Donovan. By this time those who had bet their
money on McClellan began to see their favorite
wasno match for Donovan. He was almost
winded. The wound on his head and the bard
knocks on his ribs were quickly telliag, and
miuny were satisfied he was doomed. Dwyer
and Mallahan sponged and fanned him. Dono-
van smiled and sat upright in his chair.
THE THIKD ROUND,
When time was-called for the third round
both men were cautious. It was ‘thought that.
McCiellan’s Ione reach would scientifically fin- |
ish Donovan. fe began to torce the fighting,
and Donovan stopped bim with an iron-like
grip. McClellan's seconds looked at the roof of
the closets, where sat the referee and umpire,
and sereamed, ‘*What are you doing, Jim (Co-
burn)? They are fixing things over there. Why
don’t you attend to your man?’’ Donovan
broke away at this, and with a rush like a but-
tering rain, floored MeClellan, who was picked
up limp and bleeding and carried to his corner, |
THE FOURTH
round opened with Donovan glistening with
sweat and as lively asx could be. McClellan was
seemingly usedup. He clinched with Donovan
aud succeeded in feebly pounding him on the
ribs; he tripped Donovan and both fell. Mec-
Clellan wis ingeniously fanned and rubbed,and
although apparently more dend than alive,
arose when time was called and plunged at
Donovan, hitting him square in the fades: This
excited Donovan, who ground his teeth and
bounded towards McClellan, almost crushing
him against the wall, and throwing him, limp,
bleeding and nearly breathless, to the floor.
Again McClellan's seconds put bim on_ his
feet to meet Donovan, who was as fresh
wpparently as when he began the tight.
MeClellan made two or three desperate
efforts to show that there was yet some fight
in him, but Donovan haminered his face and
drove him to his corner. McClellan dropped
into his chair, and Donovan centinued to pound
him in the face and on the body, until Meclel-
lun’s frieuds sent up a great shout of
‘*FOUL!’” ‘*FOUL.’’ |
The room was in an_=uproar. Donovan |
backed uway, glaring at McClellan and his sec- |
onds. The latter shook their fists at the ref- |
eree, and Dwyer, the Brooklyn bruiser, louder —
than the rest, Claimed the fight for Mc-
Clellan. The referee decided that
the fight should go on, but in
the mid-t of confusion McClellan put on dis
jucket, und stepping over the ropes staggercd
away. The reicree at this decided the fight in
favor of Donovan, and while everybody shook
lis fists and yelled ‘‘police,’’ Capt. Williams
dashed into the hall,

MOUNTING THE STAGE, TE SHOUTED,
‘‘Gentlemen, this must stop instantly; clear
the hall.’’ It was cleared with celerity. Mc-
Clellan and Donevan were paid for their ser-
vices out of the gate money. There were many
private bets on MecOlellan, and his friends
were disconsolate. It had been rumored that
Billy Edwards was backed to fight the winner
of last night's battle, bnt he said that snch was
not the fact, that he had been two years out of
training, and that he does not cure to engage
ina prize fight. The man who most

FEROCTOUSLY RESISTED M*CLELLAN'S CLAIM
that he had won the fight was Joe Goss. The
tight, wiich was one of thesharpest and fierc-
est of hard ylove contests on record, lasted
oily twenty minutes. Donovan walked briskly |
to his home without a scratch, while McClellan,
wilh blackened eyes and chopped scalp and
bruised ribs, wen" inournfully away in a coach.
summary: The St. Louis Globe-Democrat reported on a New York fight between Mike Donovan and McClellan. Among Donovan's seconds was Joe Goss, "who fought Tom Allen in Kentucky, and who won the fight through a foul invented by himself."

title: Jimmy Carroll Wins Bare Knuckle Fight
text:
A Promising Fighter.

_ Jimmy Carroll, who disputes the light weight
championship of New England with Billy Frazier,
has whipped a two hundred pounder named Mike
Scully,in a bare knuckle fight near Chicopee,
Mass. A Holyoke, Mass., eye-witness of the *‘mili”

I saw Joe Goss and Tom Allen do battie and was at
Farnsborough and saw Heenan fight Sayers and
have seen some of the best ones. I never have
seena little man however, that with the bare
knuckles could fight cooler or punish quicker than
Carroll. I have seen hiny with the gloves on but he
is a hundred per cent better with the bare knuck-
les. A gamerandcleverer man than he proved
himeeif against Scully I have never seen. To
whip him you’ve got to send him to sleep.’
Carroll is a Londoner by birth, thirty

ears cf age, and in condition weighs 130 pounds.

He bas an old country record of four winning prize
ring fights, one of them of 102 rounds avainst Ned
Moore of Sheffield, England,}in August, 1875. Moore
weighed 176 pounds and Carroll 122 pounds. Moore
fought till his eyes closed and he couldn't see. Car-
roll landed in this country July 22, 1877. He has had
two glove fights with Bil:y Frazier—one of eigat
rounds at FE» omwdy Mass., and another, a six-round
draw, atthe Cribb Club, Boston. He claims that

denies this, but when Carroil posted $100 for. a con-
test to be decisive of the New Englaud champuion-
ship. Frazier made no response. Carroll desires it
stated that hestilj holds himself ready to meet for
money any man who disputes that he is the light-
weight champion of New England.

ticulars, but the yg was probably off the reel and
a development of the recent fight in which Demp-

next day Jack Hallinane, the variety theater man-

Tr, came to blows, at the Baidwin Hotel, with
arty and Jack Maynard. The Maynards are said

a collision between the factions Jack mm pssy,
in the letter I ished jast week, said: “I’m
afraid there'll be le, as feeling runs very high,
Carr eee 9 th sympathy of some — of
the mischief makers, who boast that
ag a cannot win” Jack Hallinan = is

mer in five and the latter in nine rounds. Dempsey

for $250,4 side and all the gate money, The

A

raphed account says that at the end of the eigh-

Special Correspondence ofthe POst-DISPATCH.
PHILADELPHIA, April 1.—Sporting men here-

abouts do not view with favor the report that

made to ‘‘gammon” the “big fellow” into fight-

their skill in making matches. They have a

half won,’’ and itis evident that in yielding
to Sullivan the amount of the stakes,
they intend to exact from him a con-
cession as to the battle place, which will
give himlittle or no chance to win them.

This is plain from the fact that they say that

Smith would haye no chanoe to win in Amer-

ica, astatement which has no foundation in

fact. English fighters, asarule, have been

exceedingly well treated inthis country. I

know of but one exception, that of ‘‘Deaf’’

Burke, at New Orleans, where he was chased

out of the ring when he was besting one

O’Connell. That was over forty years ago.

Since then Ben Caunt, Bob Caunt, Tom Allen,

Joe Goss, George Ryall, Ned O’Baldwin, Jem

Mace, Charley Mitchell, Jack Burke, - Alf

Greenfield and dozens of other English pugs

have visited the country, fought in it, and re-

ceived the squarest of treatment. No Ameri-
can has ever received justice in England,
who attempted to wrest the cham-
pionship from one of its sons. I have
but to pointto the caseof Heenan to justify
what Ihave said. However, the machinations
of the tricksters will come to naught, for Sul-
livan told me that under no circumstances
would he consent to fight anywhere but in Ire-
land or America. He is the butcher, and if
they don’t like his price they need not buy his
meat. He has the butt of the whip in his hand,
and if he lets it go he has no one to blame buat

Hardly a week passes that I do not receive
letters from parties in different parts of the

tween fighters who are dead and gone and

those of the present day. Of course I cannot

timers by tradition or by what is told of them
in Boxiana or Pugilistica. The other day an
old ‘Hibernian of 70’’ wrote me a long epistie

Dublin, and Donnelly not only had the back-

pentry, but of what would now be called ‘‘the
gang’’as well. The old song tells us that

‘*In eleven rounds there was nine

jawbone.’’ The rounds and the

fer as to the amount of injury Cooper's jaw-

not bear out the report that it was fractured.
Cooper was a good man, however, and in
whipping him Donnelly convinced the En-
glish that he was a tip-topper and fit to fight
most anyone they had. While on alittle jam-

was matched against Tom Oliver, the trial

think by that time John would have him lymg

in a corner as dead, almost, for the time bein

as he is now in reality. But in saying this I

wish to be clearly understood as being guilty

of no treason to Ireland.

title: Tom Allen Cheated Out of Title by Goss Gang Says Correspondent
text:
] 664 99
PADDY RYAN’S “GUFE.
. a
HE BLOWS ABOUT CROSSING THE ATLANTIC
TO FIGHT JEM SMITH.

Plenty of Chances for Him at Home—Arthur
Chambers’ Fistic and Other Attractions—
The Dumb-Bell Exercise—Jack Fogarty
and Joe Illingsworth—Sporting Gossip.

Special Correspondence of the PosT-DIsPATCH.

PHILADELPHIA, May 27.—It is reported that
Paddy Ryan thinks of crossing the briny to
make a match with Jem Smith, to come off in
Ireland. I don’t think Paddy has any such
idea but if he has he should dismiss it from his
mind. Apart from the fact that it is extremely
doubtful if he could fight Smith in Ireland,
there remains another back of it which should
restrain him, and that is that he is physically
incapable of fighting any fairly good man with
any hopes of success. When he became rupt-
ured he should have retired from the ring.
He then could have done so with something of
areputation. He had outlasted Joe Goss, who
had been dubbed Champion of America be-
cause the gang back of him had robbed Tom
Allen out of the fight he had with him at
Walton, Ky., and so had obtained the title for
him. He never had a ghostof a show with
Sullivan at Mississippi City, and the flurry he
made with him at Madison Square Garden was
all bounce. He was informed that the instant
there was ashow of slugging the fight would
be stopped and the affair lasted just thirty-
four seconds.

PADDY’S CHANCES HERE.

He need not go across the water to obtain a
fight. Dominick McCaffrey is very peacefully
inclined toward the generality of mankind, but
he thinks Paddy treated him like a hog at the
picnic ofthe Hibernians at Troy, @ couple
summers ago, and he is just aching to get a
chance athim. Hecan have a four, six or
eight round contest. Dominick don’t think it
worth while to make itjany longer as he be-
lieves that he can do Ryan up in the shorter
number of rounds. My advice to Paddy
is, do not fight at all, but if he will
not take it, it well for him to know
that he can ‘get one nearer home
than Ireland. If he wants to demonstrate that
he can scrapa bit, perhaps he had better
tackle Jack Ashton. Ashton, like himself, is
not very scientific, and if he can get away with
Madden’s — in mepeite like good style
poeete will believe that peng there is
stuif in him yet, and then there will be some
sensein his talkingof fighting “Suen tee
Parson Davies told me that Bill Shereff, the
Prussian, went around Paddy like a cooper
| round a barrel, and most any of the second-
raters can do the Prussian. ~ private opin-
| ion publicly expressed is that Ryan is merely
| blowing for advertising purposes.
| THE DUMB-BELL EXERCISE.

‘*There are no real good heavy weights in
England now,’’ said Arthur Chambers to me
the other day. ‘‘Jem Smith is about the best
they have and he is no match for Sullivan.
Without doubt, I think the best of the English
fighters who came to this country was George
ites mig the Nottingham slasher. Why didn’t
he do better with Alf Greenfield? ‘I’ll tell
you. Simply because he wasn’t in condition
for one thing, but principally because |]
couldn’t get him to exercise with dumb bells.
Do I consider them good thingsto use? The
best things in the world to teach a man how ta
hit fast and paecnen. They must not weigh
more than a pound and a quarter, ora pound
and a nalf, and they should be used three times
aday. The best times are when you get up tn
the morning before you wash, in the middle
of the day ana just before you go to bed. Take
them firmly in your hands, spread your legs
welland square yourself just as eu y you
were going to fight. Then hit out left and
Tight as fast and as hard as you can fora minute
or two by the watch—three if zoe can. Then
goatitagain. Then take another rest—you'll
wantit—and then try the bells a third time.
After that be rubbed down and you’ll find that
if you do this three times a day fora month it
will give your blows more speed and force
than anything else that you cando. A man
who fights needs all the strength he can get in
hisarms. If — are tirea he can neither hit
nor stop, and if he can’t do these he can’t
keep on. He must quit.’’

ARTHUR CHAMBERS’ PROPOSITION.

Arthur tells me that he has not a made the
match between Jimmy Mitchell and Harry
Gilmore, but he is willing to and he will back
Mitchell, not oniy against Gilmore but against
Jack McAuliffe or Billy Frazer of Boston, at
from 126 to 130 pounds, for $1,000, the fight to
be ten rounds and to take place in private in
New York. Chambers declares that he will
not go to Canada for any matches. He thinks
Gotham a good enough place for anybody to
scrap in, and I quite agree with him. He is
also willing to back Joe Acton to wrestle any
man in the world—Muldoon or Evan Lewis,
the Strangler, preferred—either catch-as-
catch-can or Greco-Roman fashion, for $1,006
aside. Here is a chance for handsome William
or for ie me Davies’ man. A match
of this ind in Cincinnati, where
Muldoon is so popular and  deserv-
edly so, or in Chicago, where Lewis is wel!
known, ought to draw like a blister plaster.
He has still another proposition to make. He
saw Tommy Warren fight in Cincinnati and at
Chicago, and he thinks him a etc my good
little man, but in view of the difficulty he has
in getting anyone of his size to ye him, he
thinks Tommy might give away afew pounds
and have a go with Jimmy Mitchell for a purse
or share of the weed money. He says that for
such a match Jimmy would get down to 124
pounds, and he thinks that ten rounds would
about tell which was the top sawyer. I think
so too.

M’CAFFREY AND SULLIVAN.

As yet McCaffrey has received no response
to his offer to fight the champion to a finish at
the Polo Gioonta, in New York,on the Fourth
of July. Now that the authorities have put a
stop to boxing in Chicago, I doubt if anything
will come of it. I presume the Sullivan-
Mitchell affair will be deciared off. What a
pity that sporting men cannot actin harmony.
Their dissensions kill the geese that eo theixz
golden eggs. I don’t know who is right o1
wrongin the matter, but I do know that the
places in which glove fights can eeoase in
public are yearly becoming fewer and fewer.
Of course ‘‘slugging’’ is the chief cause o:
this, but staaning is what the populace
wants. A pre ers of Queensberry fight in En-
gland is an entirely different thing, I am told,
from a contest of the same name in this cqun.
try. There men really spar for scientific
points, while here the ‘‘points’’ are merely
‘*blinds’’ to enable the police to wink at the
affair. The men do the best and hardest they
ean to knock each other senseless, and the
man who accomplishes this feat, or comes the
nearest to it, isthe victor, even if he has not
scored another point in the match. I don’t
think a genuine Marguis of Queensberry con-
test between, even say Burke and Mitchell,
would attract a paying audiencein any city in
the country. Sullivan has taught the people
that science, unaccompanied by hard blows, is
not worth cen ag and they seem to have
gotten the lesson by heart.

FOGARTY AND ILLINGSWORTH.

There is a bare at agen sey 4 that Jack Fogarty
and Joe Ilingsworth may be permitted to bo3
in public in New York, but if the priv Soge is
accorded them I opine it will be with the ee
itive promise that there will be no knocking
out. ny of this character nnn them
would be like the oft talked of but never real.
ized performance of the play of ‘‘Hamlet,’'
with the part of the melancholy Dane omitted
—the nearest approach to which
I ever saw was when an ex-cleric
of Mlinois was the prince and te 4
proposed star of the evening. Jack would
all right in such a contest, but where would
Illingsworth be? Itistrue he might stamp on
the stage and make a noise, to say nothing o:
raising a dust—but Chinese warfare is not ef.
fective in conquering men like Fogarty. I
takes hard knocks and plenty of them to
make him see the error of his way, and so fa!
no one but Dempse; has been able to adminis.
ter the dose that he ‘equires. He is daily get.
ting bigger and tougaer, and I hardly believe
that in a friendly th match Joe can give him
enough knuckle oll to make any impression on
him. MACON.

The recent freedom with which challenges
for championships have been issued has pro-
yoxed considerable discussion affecting the
standing ef championships in general. In a
conversation touching the championships of
pugilism and how they have been won, the
veteran Tom Kelly said: ‘‘Thereis the alleged
qpampionship for middle-weights. You hear
agreat deal  f talk about itand you see how
this and that fighter is matched tofight some-
pody else for it. Well, the ‘middle-
weight championship’ means nothing.
It is an empty title; has no belt attached to it
and it has never been foughtfor. Jack Demp-
acy is called the middle-weight champion but
he is no more 80 than Burke who can fight at
middle-weight or Mitchell who can do the
same thing. Sullivan can be properly be
called the heavy-weight champion of Amer-
tea, for the reason that he whipped Ryan at
Mississippi City when Ryan held that title and
the fight was for the title. The belts that fly
ground the country for the middle-weight
jight-weight and heavy-weight cham-
pionships are mo more worthy than

any pelt that anybody can go out and buy and

offer. All fights for the championship must be
according to London geogptes. 3 rules, with
pare fists, and any fight for a championship
under any other rules will not legally entitle
the winner toit. The Queensberry rules were
made for gentlemen amateurs, and not for
professionals. A man may fight for three
minutes in order to get his opponent in a cer-
tgin position, and just when he gets him there
he is called away and all his tactics os for
nothing. That isnot what I call fair fighting.
A round should never end until one man
js knocked down. That is the legitimate end
ofaround, andit was in this manner that
Sullivan fought Ryan. Forthat reason I says
that Sullivan’s only fight was at Mississippi
City. The title to any championship must be
won under London prize ring rules.

“[f Jem Smith of England fights Sullivan,’’
said Tom Allen, ‘*he must fight him under
London prize-ring rules, with bare fists, of
course. A — between Smith and |
fullivan wouid be for the championship
gui no championship could be won under
gor other rules. No gloves can be used at all.
Jem in correspondence with Smith and he
telis me that he will not fight Sullivan east of
Qmaha. He doesn’t think he would be given
afair show in any city in the Eastern country
and if he fights he’s got to fight fair. You can
announce it positively that Smith will fight no
other way but under London prize-ring rules,
where around only ends with a knock-down,
where wrestling is allowed, and where one
man can throw another, and fall on him, too,
if he knows how to do it.’” |

————
summary: The St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported on January 4, 1887 that Tom Allen stated Jem Smith would only fight Sullivan under London Prize Ring rules with bare fists, as Smith would not accept a fair show fighting east of Omaha.

text:

“OLD SHERMAN THURSTON.”
[| |
Incidents in the Life of the Rough-
} :
and-Tumble Champion.
A Man Who| Was Never Whipped in a
Fight, Yet Was, Withal, as Mild-
Mannersd as a Parson—Some
Staries About “Old -
|* Sherm.’’ |

Yesterday afternoon, at Fremont, Neb.,
Sherman Thurston was given his 6 feet of
earth. He was the most fearless man that
ever lived. He was not given to ‘‘sclence,’’
and never stood up in a ‘‘ring’’ to pound
another man’s/face into a jelly, and aspire to
a ‘*knock-out. 1 Yet he never was whipped.
He fought like the man of old, with his
hands, feet, body and teeth. He was a
adie or enka te fighter,’’ and held the
title of ‘‘chief’’ during a |stormy career,
which ended last Tuesday in a Chicago hos-
pital, when he, Nke all men who have been
phenomenally |developed, went to pieces ail
at once, like ‘‘the Deacon’s one-horse shay.’’
He died of paralysis, the fate of most ab-
normal athletes, |

From St. Paul to New Orleans Thurston will
be remembered asa man built on the oval,
form. From the top of the head, a dis--
tinguishing feature of which’ was a broad and
pleasant smile, giving a good-natured air to
a face, sadly sdamed by small-pox, he shaped
down to a pair of shoulders that were any-
thing but square. Across the hips he was
very broad, and from that line he tapered to
a pair of feet that were small enough for a
dandy of the old days of tight boots and high
heeis. |

Had it not hp ee for @ habit he had of carry-
ing his hands free fromi his body and hanging
down as if supporting great weights, he
would have been mistaken for an race Hae ge D
good-natured | business man, inclined to
patronizing sport.

There was asuggestion of danger in ‘‘Old
Thurston’s’’ Gemeanor, but he never ob-
truded it. i Ds :

The ‘‘sporti & world’’ has had its idols,
but it is doubtful if ge: Gage tn heroes! 4 is heid
in higher regard by that element which ad-
mires pluck, endurance and fidelity to its
own craft than that of ‘‘Old Sherm.’’

‘*He is right up along side of old Jack
Looney,’’ said Jim Egan when he heard of
Thurston’s — and then continuing, ‘‘Old
Jack was a an who thought more of his
word than he did of his life.’”

A ad OF ADVENTURE.

Sherman Thurston was in his 64th year
when he died » Chicago the otherday. His
life was, one of adventure from youth. He
had been a ‘*roustabout,’’ ‘‘safe-blower,’’
‘*monte man,’’ ‘‘cross-roader,’’ had ‘‘done
his bit,’’ was at all times a fighter, but in the
language of his old friend, John: Scott, ‘‘the
squarest man that ever lived, bar none.’’

When his déath was announced from Chi-
cago more or) less notice of his career was
made by newspapers East and West. The
romancer gotin his work. Five newspapers
gaye as many accounts of ‘‘his first fight.’’
They located it all the way from Boston to.
San Francisco, and none of them got itright.
He had been written up as the trainer of
Tom Allen. He never was. Allen was always
afraidjof him. Héhad little to do with pro-
fessional pugilists, except to scare them.
Mike McCoole lived in holy terror of him, and
he made Hogan, the professor of the manly
art, who afterwards ‘‘squared himself’’ and
became a revivalist, Jump out of a window at
Leavenworth.

The handsomest pugilist thatever lived was
Shel Fairchild. He always believed.that he
could whip Thurston, but he avoided him as
he would a pestilence. >

ion don’t you whip him, you can doit,’’
said Billy Carroll to Fairchild one day. .

‘*Of course I can, but I don’t guess I'll give
up an ear forthe satisfaction. They say I’m
purty, and I don’t want to fb Sherman
rhurston a chance tomake my friends liars.’’

Now that the old fellow is dead, the ‘‘old.
timers,’’ men like Ed. Dowling, John Scott,
Jim Egan, Jake Powell, Mike Hines, Charley
Dieht and Abe Steeples, recall. stories of his
career. i

‘<Hre was a biter,’’ said John Scott, ‘‘if you
don’t think so, go ask Jake Powell, he bit his
finger off.’’ | ‘ :

When Jake' was hunted up, he said no,
Thurston did not bite his finger off.

‘<In the days of the Loonéys—'‘The Priest,’
‘The Rat’ and ‘Jack.’ and there you have all
the Looneys’’—said an old timer, ‘‘the Priest
had a saloon called the Clipper. Powell had
never been bested on Almond street. Ile had
been licking soldiers and lovers down there
without losing, and he felt like traveling out.

*«So he makes up his mind that he will do

andsowas gid Sherm. Jake offs with his
coat.and declared himself. They went at it,
both of seeps 2 pretty chuck, but they com-
menced to er up as soon as they clinched;
you can’t describe a rough and-tumble if you
was to try, nD morethan you can descrihea
dogfight. Anyhow, Sherman got his teeth
into Powell’s left hand; Jake fs right, Sher-
man did not bite off his finger, but he gnawed
away at the hand until he broke every bone
between the wrist and the first knuckle of the
little finger, find they had to cut off the finger
to save the arm; so yousee how people gets
things wrong.’’

The second and last performance of ‘‘Nero’’

ings of the week.

title: Prize Ring History Lists Tom Allen Among American Champions
text:
SS ee
INTERNATIONAL PUGILISM,
Big Men of the Past Who Crossed the Water
and Fought Well.
T. P. Evans in Boston Globe.

Never in the nistory of the prize-ring has
Great Britain been invaded with such an array
of foreign pugilists as at present. From the
time when pugilism first obtained a foothold
in the United States, champions not content
with victories on their own soil, went abroad
to do battle with the sons of Britain. The
greatest of these upheld the dignity of the con-
tinent with unparalleled success.

Mollineux, the colored champion, did battle
with the redoubtable Tom Cribb, and the
history of the prize ring tells us that had the
warrior been shown fair play the undefeated
Cribb would have been worsted. Charley
Freeman, on British ground, upheld his own
until he met with an at 2 death.

Yankee Sullivan braved the perils of the At-
lantic to meet the gailant Hammer Lane, and
he succeeded in placing the stars and stripes
above the union jack. All judges of pugilism
who witnessed the contest pronounced him
the greatest phenomenon that ever put
up a hand. Charley Lynch met the
best men of his weight, and encountered
such shining lights of the prize-ring as Simon
Finighty and Young Shaw. Bob Smith, the
colored wonder, rurely ever talked about, was,
in the writer’s opinion, one of the greatest
fighters thet ever lived. His decisive victories
over Tom and Harry Allen remain as two of
the hardest figets ever recorded in the history
of the prize-ring.

Ot the number who have crossed the
ebannel George Roake was perhaps the
most unlucky, being very easily defeated
by Denny Harrington. John C. Heenan’s
memorable battle with Tom Sayers still
lives fresh within the memory of ring-goers.
The whole history of fistiana does not furnish
us with a pugilist so unfortunate as the brave,
kind-hearted and gentlemanly Heenan. His
two contests in England were wrested from
him unfairly. After the Heenan and Sayers
and the Heenan and King fights American
pugilists remained at home until Joe Coburn
crossed to do battle with Jem Mace. The pro-
——_ contest, however, endedina complete

zle.

After this America was invaded by British
pugilists, who found that the rigorous arm of
the law prevented them from getting a living
athome. They, too, found the new continent
cer more lucrative for their business than the
old. .

According to the records, we have had nine-
teen champions of the American prize ring up
to the present, viz.: Tom Hyer, Yankee Sulli-
van, Dominick Bradley, John Morrissey,
John C. Heenan, Joe Coburn, Mike McCoole,
Jim Dunn, Bill Davis, Aaron Jones, Tom
Allen, Ned O’Baldwin, Joe Wormald, Jem
Mace, Joe Goss, Jim Elliott, Johnny Dwyer,
Paddy Ryan and Jobn L. Sullivan.

The last named opened a new era in the
posewee world by offering any man a stipu-

ated sum who would stand before him three
or four rounds. The men who have gone down
before him prove that he is the greatest fighter
that has lived since Jas. Figg boasted of being
the first champion. For several years John
L. has been contemplating a teur to Europe,
but not until the fall of ’87 were his plans car-
ried out.
summary: The St. Louis Post-Dispatch published a history of international pugilism, listing Tom Allen among nineteen American champions and noting Bob Smith's victories over Tom and Harry Allen.

title: Hogan's Old Trainer Recalls the Allen-Hogan Fight
text:
BEN HOGAN’S OLD TRAINER. |
John Sweeney, an old boxer and the man |
who brought out Ben Hogan, is stopping over
in the city forafew days. ‘ ‘Hogan was per- |
forming feats of strength when I first met.
him,’’ said Sweeney. ‘‘He was a good,
strong man, but lacked cleverness. J taught
him how to use his hands, and he fought two.
heavy-weights and defeated them. Then |
he made the match with Tom Allen,
He put up $1,000 of his own money and I |
trained him forthe fight. It is true that the
toughest gang that ever surrounded aring |
was at the Allen-Hogan fight. They were
cutters and shooters and they were deter- |
mined to give Allen the worst of it. Thenl
wanted to save Hogan’s $1,000 and I watched
close for fouls. Allen was a great body-flghter
anda man who fights continually for the
body will get below the belt. There were two
rounds of red hot fighting. Then Hogan,who
was forcing things, led for Allen, who ducked
and sent hisright into Hogan’s stomach. I
claimed ‘‘foul’’ and appealed to Bill Riley,
the referee. The crowd cut In the ring and
pulled knives and revolvers on Alen and his
his seconds. The referee declared ita draw.
That was Hogan’s last fight. Hie is now
preaching and Is sincere in his work. I hada
talk with bim in Chicago not long ago and he
is Just as enthusiastic in his religious work as
he was ten years ago.’”’
summary: John Sweeney, who trained Ben Hogan, told The St. Louis Republic about Hogan's fight with Tom Allen. He described the armed crowd, his claim of a foul when Allen hit Hogan low, and the referee's draw after the crowd cut into the ring with knives and revolvers.

title: Tom Allen Gives Opinion of Prize Fight
text:
M’MANUS-FLINT MILL.
SE
TOM ALLEN GIVES HIS OPINION OF ‘THE
PRIZE FIGHT YESTERDAY.

Flint Failed to Take His Second’s Advice and
Lost the Battle Thereby—Incidents of the
Trip—Kilrain and Mitchell Versus the
American Exchange—Base Ball News and
Gossip—Sporting Matters. ° ;

The result of the prize fight between Mo-
Manus and Flint near St. Clair, Mo., yester-
day, was disoussed pro and con to-day among
the sports about town. The general opinion
seemed to be that the St. Louis man had the
best of the battle and would undoubtedly have
won it had he not given up at the merest show
of rally on the part of McManus.

TOM ALLEN, )
who seconded Flintin the fight, sald to-day
that his man inflicted more punishment on |
McManus than the latter served to Flint and
that, although not beaten much about tbe
head and face beyond aswollen cheek and a
cut lip, he sustained severe punishment about
the body. ‘‘If you noticed it,’’ said Allen,
*‘all the fighting was done over in the other
man’s corner. Four biows were not struck
outside that corner, and if Flint had taken)
my advice and waited for his man
to face him as he should have done the result
would be different. I kepttelling him to stay
in his corner, not to go out over to the other
man’s and that he’d win but, no, he knew
more about it thanI did and he got licked.
Flint is a more acientific fighter than McManus
and he should have walked on that line, If
science is your hold you ought to make science
your play. Itold himto go at his man, hit
him a <1p and then come away and
go at im again as before, but he
wouldn’, and he paid the penalty.
Instead of taking my advice he would rush
over to the opposite corner and hug the man
bythe neck. This gave the man as much ofa
chance to hit him as he had to hit the man,
andthe consequence was that the man gave
him enough. When it comes to tn-fighting,
adummy hagas much show to whip a scien-
tiflo man as a scientific man has to whip him.
No, sir, Flint showed himself to bea quitter,
and I had to throw up the sponge.’’

KELLY'S SaGE COUNSEL.

In addition to the advantage which came
from wa gpa refusal to take the ad-
vice of hisolder andable second, McManus
had the benefit of Tom Kelly’s sage instruc-
tions. Kelly handled his man in iine style,
and McManus absorbed his advice without a
word of protest. Kelly told Mack not to worry
Flint at all, but let him indulge his tendency
to visit him every round in his own corner
and not to <o out of it except when necessary.
McManus followed his instructions, and much
of the credit attaching to the victory rightly
belongs to the veteran trainer and coach,

**Well, we won the fight,’’ said Tom when
the battle. was over, ‘‘butI teil you that we,
pulled it right out of the fire.’’ The Kelly—
Sweeney—McManus crowd won considerabie
money on the battle, probably somewhere in.
the neighborhood of $800, and counting the
stake and the purse in with this roll they had
about $1,500 to divide. Flint was presented |
with a purse of $100 subscribed and gathered |
by McManus on the train returning to the city#

INCIDENTS OF THE FIGBT.

Whether decency of conduct Is the exact
thing to be observed by people who go to
prize fights is probably a question open to dis-
cussion, but it is most certain that the crowd
who attended the McManus—Flint affair yes-
terday never knew what decency in any of its
departments meant, or else they completely
forgot what little they ever did know about
the matter. It had been stated ‘‘that several
very nice gentlemen’’ would be at the fight, but
a close examination failed to develop them.
The majority of these present were in a
state of beastly intoxication before the train
left, on the way, during the progress ofthe
mill and even afterit. Onthe way down one
of the ‘‘spectators,’’ a well-known, fat at-
torney, was eminently unfitted to take care of
himself, and as all his friends were as drunk
as he was and the sopver people inthe party
didn’t care, the said attorney managed to
make things very lively.

At w point about thirty miles west of the
city the fat attorney marched to the rear end
of the rear carand announced in tones thick
from whisky, that ‘‘he would now proceed to
demolish the windowinan abrupt and dia-
bolical manner,’’ and followed up his an-
nouncement by putting his foot through it.

But little attention, however, was paid
either to him or tothe window, and for the
rest of the trip the attorney was conspicuous
for his general ubiquity. The rest of the
passengers demonstrated the elegance of
their manners to everybody’s satisfaction
by falling over one another pell mell and
throwing chicken and ham sandwiches and
hard boiledeggs at one another. One man
cameon board loaded down with a basket
fuil of whisky (in bottles) and this goodly
supply was supplemented withtwo jugs fuil
of the same liquor, carried by a friend.
About the time the fight had finished the
liquor was nearly gone, but the men were so
thoroughly soaked with alcohol that the ef-
fects had not been wornoff even after the
train had reached Grand avenue.

On the return trip a number of the party In-
dulged in the refinedand elevating game of
**‘craps,’’ over which there were several
fignts, without loss of blood, however. Short-
ly after the train had pulied ont of St. Clair
some festive drunkard inthe crowd thought
be would amuse himself by emptying the
chambers of his revolver without scrupulous
attention astothe direction he aimed at, and
the veces oy played hide andseek with their
heads until the firing ceased.

Flint, all battered up, lay on the floor of the
baggage car and was viewed as though he
were a curiosity by the ‘‘gentiemen’’ who
found a delight in

FEASTING THEIR GAZE

with the sight of his fearfully swollen, black-

ened and bruised face and distorted features.

McManus did not appear to be suffering in-

tense pain from the punishment he hud re-

ceived, and discussed the fight intelligently
as he walked through the train collecting the
purse for his defeated adversary.

Altogether the atfair was about as disgust-
Ing an exhibition as anyone would care to
see and the brutality, naturalto all prize
fights, wasemphasized by the remarks and
the comments made upon the various plays
bythe men around thering. It was one con-
tinuous howl without rhyme or reason.
Several ‘‘inhabitants’’ about the locality ar-
rived on coGarem pee! poe as the men were about
to enter the ring and the crowd became terribly
alarmed when someone get the rumor
afioat that they were none other than the
Sheriff ofthe county and his posse. These
fears were dissipated when it became known
that the new arrivals were a country doctor,
who wanted to see blood, and a few railroad
hands. The country ‘‘blokies,’’ as they
were called, seemed to gloat over the bisod.
letting and bellowed themselves hoarse at the
fight, which, as they said, was the greatest
thing on earth.

ele Se oe
summary: St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported Tom Allen's commentary on a recent prize fight, noting that Flint failed to follow his second's advice and lost the battle.

title: Tom Allen Arrested Under Prize-Fighting Warrant
text:
Arresting the Fighters.

In the arrests under the prize-fighting warrants
for the McManus#Flint fight, mentiondd elsewhere,
the veteran Tom Allen was the first to be caught in
the net, as he expressed it. Mewasarrested a few
minutes before noon, —_ as he was about to sit down
to breakfast. The sheriff took him to the Four
Courts, where he gave bond for his —— at
Union, Frankiin Co., in the court of Justice ay |
Frazee at 10 o'clock to-morrow morning. The bond
wasinthe sum of $500. Next came Jim, or Rusty
Evans, who keeps ascaloon on Market street. After
the bond had been drawn up he sald he guessed a
mistake had been made, and tliat Jim Evans of Kan-
ses City, trainer of McManus, was the party
wanted. He was held noti] the matter
could be examined and it could be
definitely ascertained whether he was the man
wanted, he having been merely a spectator, Jake
Esher was the next to be broughtin. He frrnished
bond immediately. After ‘‘Rusty’’ Evans had been
held about an hour Deputy Sheriff ay concluded
he was not the oy wanted, and let_ him go, Evaus
promising to be at his saloon if needed.

Tom Kelly and FP. J. Tucker were brought in at
2 o'clock this afternoon, and were immediately re-
leased on bond,

Union, Mo., the seat of Franklin County, is on the
St. Louis, Kansas City & Colorado Road, and to
reach there at 10a. m. to-morrow the men al have
to leave on that road at 5 o’clock this evening.

THE ORIGIN OF INN SIGNS,

QUEER OLD HOSTELRIES THAT NESTLE IN

THE ROMANTIC MOUNTAINS ACCOUNT FOR

IT,

What is the origin of signs? The earliest
signs are ceftainly heraldic. We have still in
many Willages the ‘‘So-and-so Arms,’’ with
the shi¢id of the lord of the manor em-
biazoned upon it, with all its quarterings. |
or we have the Red Lion, or
the White Hart, or the Swan, all either crests
or cognizances of a family, or of a sovereign |
or queen. The Swan sign is said to date from
Anne of Cleves; the White Hart was the badge |
of Richard Il., and inns with this sign proba-
bly were erected in that reign, and have kept.
this sign unchanged since. We know of inns
under the name of the Rose, whichthere can
be little question came into life as hostelries |
in the time of the Yorkists and Lancastrians. |
The Wheat Sheaf was the Burleigh badge, the
Elephant that of Beaumont, the Bull’s
Head was a Boleyn cognizance, the
Blue Boar the badge of the De
Veres, earls of Oxford, the Green Dragon
of the earls of Pembroke, the Falcon of the |
Marquis of Winchester. It does not, however, |
follow that the inns that have these signs date
from the periods when, let us say, Anne
Boleyn was queen, because they bear the
token of the bull’s head, or from the reign of
Queen Elizabeth, when Burleigh was in
power, because of the wheat sheaf, for it

| will not infrequently be found that they take
their titles and signs from a much more local
origin, the coatior cognizance of the squire
| who holds the manor,
There was a reason for this—the inn was
originally the place where the true
landiord—that is, the lord of the
-manor—received his guests, and
every traveller was his guest. In Iceland at
| the present day there is but one inn at Reyk-
| javik, the capital, and that is kept by a Dane.
The traveller on the island goes to any
farmhouse or parsonage and is taken
‘in. Indeed, by law a traveller can-
not be refused hospitality. When
he leaves he either makes a present of money
or something else that will be valued, but
this isapresentand nota payment. Inmany
parts of Tyrol, it is much thesame. ‘he
excursionist is put up at the priest’s house.
The writer has been thus received, among
! — places, at Heiligkreutz, in the Oetz
hal.
In the evening the room—the cure’s parlor—
was filled with peasants who asked for wine,
and were supplicd. When they left they put
| money in the hand of the pastor’s sister,
while he, smoking his pipe, looked out of the
window. When the writer left next morn-
ing the same farce was enacted. Farther up
the same valley is Vent, where again
the cure receives travellers and his sister re-
ceives the payment, but there a definite
charge is made, but at Helligkreutz what was
given was rt age as a present.
|. The priests who entertain do not, of course,
hang up signs over their doors. The pastor is
supposed to be given to hospitality and would
give of his all freely and cheerfully if he could
afford it, but of late years, as travellers have
become more numerous, his pittance has be-
come smaller, sothat his hospitality can no
longer be gratuitous. In the old romances of
Chivalry we read of travellers always seeking
the castle of some knight, and asking, almost
demanding, lodging and entertaiument.—
(Cornhill Magazine,

evil IN ONE ROUND-
Tom Allen, Ex-Champion, Knocked
| Out by Dan Daly.
- Tom A lien, the ex-champion of the world
was knocked out in one round (rules barred)
by Dan Daly, champion middle weight of
Missouri, at an early hour yesterday morn-
ing. From statements made by a number of
spectators it appears that about 1:30 o’clock
yesterday morning Dan Daly was sitting
in front of his saloon on Seventh
street between Market and Chestnut streets
trying keep cool with the aid of a fan when
three men ran by, followed by Tom Allen,
Dutch Neil, Steve Hearn and Jack Ryan.
The fugitive disappeared around the corner
of Seventh and Chestnut streets and the
pursuers approached Mr. Daly. Allen, who
appeared to be very mad, claimed that one of
the three men who had been calling him vile
names, was in Daly’s saloon. Dan arose
from his chair and told Allen that he must be
| mistaken, as he neyer saw the men _ before,
and most certainly was not hid-
ing them. Allen became infuriated,
and, it is said, accused Dan
of doing things to hurt his (Allen’s) business.
| Charley Daly, Dan’s brother, who was in the
house, heard the loud talking, joined those on
the outside and tried to pacify the irate ex-
champion. AJlon was not to be quieted, how-
ever, and it is alleged that as soon as Charley
interfered he tried to strike him. Dan, who
is much heayier than -his brother, became
riled and threw off his coat and made for Allen.
while Charley paid close attention to Neal
| Hearn and Ryan, who were crowding rather
close upon the principals of the meeting.
Allen retreated into the street and declared
that he did not want to fight, to which Dan
Daly replied: ‘You came here looking for
trouble, Tom, and youshan’t depart in peace,”’
and with this he struck Tom a terrible blow
in the stomach. Allen put up his armsand tried
to ward off the blows aimed at him by the
younger pugilist, but he might just as well
have tried to escape a pile-driver. Daly fur-
ther added insult to injury by telling him that
perhaps he could fight at one time, but that
now he was
A CHESTNUT.
Allen retreated to the middle of the street
and Dan, not desiring to have a repetition of
the Sullivan and Mitchell runaway battle,
closed in on his adversary and struck him a
terrific blow under the chin, felling him to
the ground. The victor calmily surveyed his
work and waited for his victim to rise, but
Allen was done up and he cried out “‘enougk..”’
About this time Officers Pat Scully and Eck-
hard appeared in the distance and Dan retired
inside of his saloon, leavi#§g the ex-champion
to be gobbled.
__ While Dan was fighting with Allen, his
‘brother Charley was not idle. He made’ for
Dutch Neil and Steve Hearn whom he de-
clared he could whip in two minutes, but
they managed to get out of his way before
being séricusly injured. Jack Ryan hada
base ball bat which he swung around his head
in a dangerous manner and came near strik-
ing several spectators. Johnny Gaiten’s bar-
tender threw himself upon Ryan and inflicted
several bruises on the latter’s physiognomy.
Charley Daly gave himself up to the police
and was taken to the Chestnut Street station
incompany with Allen, where they were
both released on bond.
