title: Tom Allen Appeals to Law to Recover Stake Money Dispute
text:
THE WORLD OF SPORT.
TOM ALLEN GOES TO LAW TO RECOVER
STAKE MONEY,

Annual Meeting of the Scorers’ League
—Sullivan Challenges Kilrain—The
Association Delegates Home-
ward Bound—Miscellany.

For more than 80 years Tom Allen has not
been on speaking terms with law. During
the greater part of that period the law has
had Tom on the run, and he was compelled to
step around pretty lively to keep out of its
clutches. Therefore, the very edifying spec-
tacle of Tom Allen appealing to the law for
protection shows that prize-fighting as well
as politics makes strange bed-fellows.

Allen yesterday entered suit against Bill
Clark, the final stakeholder in the Daly-Mce-
Manus match, and gave his grounds for ac-
tion in the following petition:

The plaintiff states that on the 16th day of Octo-
ber, 188k, he and one Dan Daly enteredintoa
wager depending upon the result of a boxin
match with gloves between Dan Daly and Hugh
McManus, which was to take place on the lith
day of December, 1888. That while the event
upon whichthe said wager was made was still
contingent and unknown the plaintiff deposited in
the hands of the defendant, as stakeholder, the
sum of $1,000, to abide the result of such wager,
That afterwards, to-wit on December 5, 1888. plain-
tiff demanded from said defendant the said sum
of $1,009 and payment was refused, wherefore he
prays judgment for said sum of $1,000, interest
and costs. :

For another and criees cause of action the
plaintiff says that on the 5th of December, 1888, at
the City of St. Louis, the defendant received from
the Globe Printing Co. the sum of $75) to the use
of plaintiff. That thereafter and before this action
the plaintiff Gemanded payment thereof from de-
fendant, and that no part has been paid, where-
fore plaintiff prays judgment for $75), interest and
costs. Rowe & MORRIS,

Attorneys for Plaintiff.

Last night Allen called at Tue REPUBLIC
office and submitted the following card for
publication:

To the Editor of The Republic.

I wish in a few words to explain to
the public the character of articles of
agreement in a match for money. Dan
Daly and Hugh McManus made a match ‘and drew
up articles of agreement by which both’ were
bound, These articles say that if either man fails
te live up te them the one so failing is to forfeit
allthe money. The last deposit of $250 a side was
due December 4. I put up ef money in
the Globe- Democrat office according tb the articles,
and received a receipt. I heard the next morning
that Daly’s #250 was not up so I went to the oflice
and at 12 o'clock claimed a forfeit. On December
5 Chas. Daly called at the office and posted the
final deposit of #250. I met Mr. Murphy and asked
him why he had not acknowledged my deposit in
the paper and he said Daly's moncy was not up.
Itold him that I had been there at noon and
claimed forfeit. He then said he had been at
Daly’s the night before and they haa offered
him the money. All deposits were, according
to the articles, to be made at the office of the pa-
per, and as Murphy’s name does not appear in the
articles, he had no power to receive money out-
side the office. Iam willing to leave the matter
to the Clipper, the Spirit of the Times or the Police
Gazetie, and will abide by their decision on my
claim for $750 forfeit for Hugh McManus.

TOM ALLEN,

The temporary stakeholder who ought to
know takes issue with Allen and says Daly’s
money was up on time and thatthe money
was turned over to Clark, the final stake-
holder.
summary: The St. Louis Republic reported that Tom Allen sued Bill Clark, the final stakeholder in a Daly-McManus boxing match, to recover $1,000 in disputed stakes, marking an unusual instance of the former prize-fighter seeking legal remedy.

title: Jem Mace Defeats Tom Allen
text:
VERY FEW OF THEM WEALTHY,
iow the Champion Pugilists Made
Money and Lost it.

From the New York Herald, .

More reckless with his suddenly a
wealth than the gambler is the successful pu-
gilist, The profession, especially at present,
is a lucrative one, but the fighters who have
retained fortunes after making them can
readily be counted on the fingers, while the
spendthrift gladiators are numberless. Sud-.
den relaxation from severe training periods
may account for much of this profligacy, Cer-
tain it is that no class of men are more thor-
oughly satisfied’ to let the morrow look out for
itself than champion pugiliSts.

No better example of an extravagant

pugilist exists than John L. Sullivan, It
was he who developed the knock-out blow,
and by making 4, 6 and 10 round contests as

full of uncertainty and danger as tho old

‘fitish fights mado pugilism the remunera-

| tive profession that it now is. ‘hough

grossly overestimated the “Big Fellow’s”’

"earnings have been treble those of any fighter
who came before him, yet Sullivan now has
little or no money. Jake Kilrain is said to be

as extravagant as was John L,

- Joe Coburn, whoin his old age has had to
hustle for dollars in match making
with other old _ timers, is another
warning example. Jem Mace, whose
benefit in Londen the other day was noted,
is another. Mace and Coburn were the won-
ders of their day, and though they didn’t
make as much money in fights or exhibitions
as the latter}day champions they made more

in other ways. Both these great fighters of

the past are now working hard for dollars.

Old Sam Collyer,,.whose three tremendous

battles with Billy Edwards for the light-
weight championship will long be remem-
bered, has not been a Sunday-school-boy, and
his effort to make money by engaging in a
six-round contest with the young champion
of the 133-pound class (Jack McAuliffe) ex-

cited much sympathy. Dooney Harris, |
another clever old timer and once champion

of the middle-weights, is about town locking

out for odd jobs. ais SBA -

Jem Ward,one of England’s greatest heavy-
weights, died not long ago at the age of 86,
in the semi-charitable Licensed Victuallers’ |
Institution. ‘om Sayers, another famed
champion of England, would have died in >
want but for a life pension presented him |
after his memorable drawn battle with John
C. Heenan, Old Tom Allen, who met defeat |
at the hands of Jem Mace not far from the
svot where John L. Sullivan beat Paddy
Ryan, is living after a fashion in St. Louis.
Yankee Sullivan, one of the most famous of
the old-timers, made and spent big ,»money, |
but died, it is said, at the hands of: vigilantes |
in San Francisco. Australian Kelly, who.
fought the longest battle on record with Jon-
athan Smith in Australia, and was then
beaten in this country in 30 minutes by
Ned Price, lives in New Jersey. .He has
very little property. And soitis with many
of the pugilists who do not set up in saloons,
Mike Donovan, Jim O’ Neil, who fought the
longest battle on record in’‘this country, and
Billy McClean are teaching the young of
this city how to put up their hands. »

Tom King, the heavy-weight who beat and
was beaten by Jem Mace, acquired a splendid
fortune og a book-maker in England and heads
the list of pugilists who did not let swollen
heads run away with business sense. Two
hundred and fifty thousand dollars is what
the late waterman, wrestler, pugilist, painter
and book-maker left as the fruit of his indus-
try and wisdom. Charley Mitchell is almost
penurious and is said to be worth
$50,000. Jack Dempsey didn’t have any
money when he began work this year, but |
the contests with McCaffrey and Mike Dono--
van paid well and he has made a good salary |
most of the time in sparring in variety thea-
tres, besides doing well with his saloon. |
McCaffrey was very careful with his money
when he made it, but as he has been idle so
long he is getting desperate now. |

John C. Heenan made money also, though |
not’ by fighting, for he never had the good
fortune to hear a referee pronounce his name—
as winner of:a prize fight. He becamea
gambler and died in Wyoming Territory,
while on a Western trip, fairly well off.
John Morrissey, though the winner of every
prize tight he ever engaged in, made his |
money, not from pugilism, but as a gambler
and politician. A pugilistic champion whocan
make money and keep it is Arthur Chambers.
Arthur was light-weight champion of Eng-
land and America, and, starting a saloon with
a little money, he is now rated worth $60,000.
Billy Edwards, the efficient sergeant-at-arms
of the Hoffman House cafe, who swept all
before him years ago, is said to hold consid-
erable property. |

Dublin Trieks, who got his start in busi-
ness life by beating Orville (“Awful’’) Gard-_
ner, became worth $500,000. Tricks had a
hard time to beat Gardner and his gang, but
he did it. Once in this battle Gardner, when
hit very hard on the nose, declared that his
shoulder blade was broken. Gardner after-
ward turned revivalist. Tom Kelly is sup-
posed to*have $10,000 worth of real estate in
St. Louis, where he does a prosperous saloon
business. His coming set-to with Joe
Coburn, who recently met Prof. Bill Clarke
ina blackened glove contest, was arranged
only because he feels the need of excitement.
Ed Price, who fought a draw at Spy Pond in
Massachusetts with Coburn years ago and
was one of the best men.in America, is a
lawyer in this city now.

Perhaps the richest of the old time cham-
pions is Barney Aaron, son of the famous
Star of the East, who fought and beat the
best light weights of his day. Barney made
most of his money after leaving the ring, and
is now in the employ of the book-makers on
the big Eastern tracks.

Rare exceptions were the old time battles
that could compare in the amount of stakes
with those of the present day. The only
ones 1 call to mind are the $10,000 Hyer-
Yankee Sullivan battle and the one for $10,000
betaveen Heenan and King at Wadhurst,
England. Heenan and Sayers fought fora
paltry $1,000 a side, which was equalled by
the amount at staké in the jug handled fight
between Reagan and Dempsey. How the
old timers would have opened their eyes at
the “big fellow’s’”? forfeit and challenge the

other day !—85,000 slapped down for a fight-

-er’s first deposit, as was done by Sullivan

and his backers.

title: Boxing Critic Compares Historical Pugilists Including Tom Allen to Modern Fighters
text:
CONCERNING “SLUGGERS.’’
Charlie Sails for ‘‘Lunnon’’—John ELE, Not
Drunk—Fighting Tips.

By Telegraph to the PosT-DISPATCH.

NEw York, January 19.—‘‘Charlie is over
the water and Charlie is over the sea,’’ that
is, he ison the ‘‘briny’’ and will soon again
be in dear old ‘’Lunnon.’’ The »vdoxing
champion of England got a glorious send-off,
too, Jack Dempsey’s farewell address being &
lively one. I saw ‘‘Mister’’ Mitchell two
nights previous to his departure, he being
with Al Smith and ‘‘Parson’’ Davies in Bang’s
Broadway palace. I do not remember having
seen Mitchell look so well on any By y
occasion as he did then, and my wo: for it,
he looked big enough and able to
whip almost any man who wears
shoe leather. Of course I know he won’t
make the attempt. He has declared himself
averse to fighting and pleads bad hands as ap
excuse. Doubtiess he has bad fists, but Ido
not think thatis allthatails him, and I think
that if the truth was known Charlie is fearful
of meeting Dempsey. Not that he would be
afraid to fight Jack, but he knows the —
idolize Dempsey and detest him. He willnot,
I believe,ever meet Dempsey in the ring and all
that Jack can say or do will not induce him to
go in fora finish fight. Itis useless for Jack
to make any more proposalsto him, and the
best thing he can do is to ignore the English -
man.

JOHN L.’S JAMBOREE.

According to reports from Boston Jobn L.
was quietly indulging in intoxicants the past
week, notwithstanding his vows to remain an
abstainer. The news caused much sur-
prise here. and John’s — were
greatly chagrinned. I investigated the
case fully, and the result was I
learned the report was greatly exaggerated.
John doubtless took a few drinks and was
thereby made rather jovisl. But it was not
true, as reported, that he was agg drunk.
It seems very strange that only in Boston is
John found to behave so. He invariably be-
haves well here and also in other cities.
There, however, bis every action {is noted and
every drink taken nz him commented upon.
Just why this is I donotknow. Idothink,
however, that it is an evidence that the big
eg is not without enemies in the city of his

irth.

It takes a’man who knows nothing at all
about pugilism to write intelligently about it,
or, at least that would seem to be the idea of
the man who wrote an article on the subject
published in the January number ofthe Man-
hattan Athletic Club Chronicle. The individual
in question did not mean to touch on the fistic
art in a general way, but startedin with the
evident intention of criticising the recent con-
test between Dempsey and Donovan. But like
all who know little or nothing of a subject. he
was soon beyond his depth, and floundered
about in a helpless way until he finally found
something to wind upon. Of course, as the
article in question would fill a column of the
Post-DisPpatcu, I will not reproduce it. I
will, however, quote from it, andI believe
that all who know what fighting is will sce
how puerile is the work in question.

AN OPINION ON DEMPSEY.

In criticising Dempsey’s form he says:

**He bears so much resemblance to the won-
derwe have been led tosuppose him asthe
building In which he boxed does to a palace.
In the first place he is shaped anythieg but
artistically, holding his left hand too low, his
right too high; his left shoulder and —_ el-
bow too far forward, suggesting that his dis-
position was more to parry blows than to
strike them. His boxing was not first-class,
particularly in the use ofhis left, which he
swung with a stiff elbow, from his thigh to, or
rather somewherein the direction of, his ad-
versary’s face or body.’’

Shades of Tom Cribb. Wasthereever such
an idiotic criticism as the above? In the name
of all that is good on earth, have professors of
the artof boxing, critics with years of ex-
perience been crazy in believing that Demp-
sey’s left hand is his best andthat by reason
of his attitude his length of reach was in-
creased to his advantage and disadvantage of
his opponent? But let that goand follow the
article in question.

**Donovan, who hasavery fairly straight
delivery, strikes with precision and fate:
ment and is, altogether, a fair rep-
resentative of a good, old-fashioned
fighter. * * * Although many blows were
struck during the contest, neither man landed
one well-timed, clean, positive hit. * * *

**Donovan’s straight hitting and good judg-
ment gave him a decided advantage all
through, and proved, or rather re-proyeda,
what was conclusively proved generations
ago, that the straighterthe hitter the better
the boxer.’’

Now, of course we all know whatthe writer
ofthe above means. It must be apparent to
allthat if Donovan ‘‘strikes with precision
and judgment,’’ but did not ‘‘iand one well-
timed, clean, positive hit,’’ his ‘‘straight hit-
ting and good judgment gave him a decided
advantage.’’ The above also proves what

. A COMICAL CUSS

the writer must be. limagine that he did not
meanto prove anything as to the respective
merits of the style of attack and defense of
Dempsey and Donovan, but that he merely
desired to gain renown as ahumorist. Surely
he has succeeded and it is agreat pity that his
name is not known.

Another paragraph of the article which will
be read with interest is the foliowing:

‘*We had noticed an improvement in Demp-
sey’s hitting when he boxed with
Joe Coburn a few months ago,
but it seems that his form ieft him
when engaged in an actual contest with a
better boxer than himseif.’’

And still another: ‘‘We would also suggest
that it would be more to the benefit of the
public if those who write up boxing forthe
press were men who had seen such first-class
pugilists as we mentioned in our April num-
ber. Then their readers would not be misied
into erroneous impressions, through favorit-
ism or wantof knowledge.’’

It will, of course, be a surprise to some
people to learn that Dempsey out-

pointed Coburn, but was BO
match for Donovan, although it is
known that with Joe and Mike at their best the
latter was not in the same class as the former.
It will also please the able critics of pugilism
to learn that this know-nothing of the game,
because they did not, presumably, witness
the work of the men, mentioned in a previous
issues of the Comical. I suppose, like myself,
they are ignorant or tne identity of the men
previously mentioned by the writer quoted.
SOME OF THE OLD ’UNS.

But I am confident, like myself, they believe
he alluded to Nat Langham, Tom Sayers, John
C. Heenan, Jem Mace and Tom Allen.
Admitting that he did, I fail to see how he can
hope to teibs that those men were superior
to the fighters of to-day. Heenan never won
afight, although he should have gained a de-
cision over Tom Sayers, who had previously
been whipped by Nat Langham, whom Harry
Orme defeated. Then, too, Heenan was
whipped by Morrissey and King, the lattex
being beaten by Mace, with whom Coburn
fought two drawn battles. Mace also
beat Allen, who was whipped by
Goss, whom Ryan defeated. Paddy in
turn being knocked silly in short order by
John L. Sullivan. So of all those whom]
suppose this able (?) writer mentioned not
one was an ‘‘undefeated.’” Whereas Demp-
sey never sustained a defeat in the ring.
Donovan won and held the middle- weight
championship, and Sullivan never had an op-
ponent who tried him until good fortune on
Mitchell's part enabled the latter to obtain a
verdict of ‘‘draw’’ with the ‘‘big feliow.’’

New Orteans, La., July 7.—There is noth-

ators at prices ranging from $25 to $0. Sey-

way between these figures, but in one or two
~ases outside price was paid.

Col R. B. Garrett, general southern ar

road Company, estimates that there will be
2,500 people on the eroence, and that gate

;mount the railroad company only receives

The St. Charles Hotel, which is directly o

celebrities. Tom Allen, Joe pangs ME
St. Joe Kid, Joe Murphy, ike
Cleary and a multitude of other fistic
heroes were prominent figures in the vicin-
ity of the hotel during the progress of the
day. To-morrow’s fight was of course the
prevailing topic of discussion. Sullivan con-
tinues the favorite of the talent, but —
sentiment, that is to say, a public sentiment
which is backed by pa and not money,
is all in favor of Kilrain. The genteel element
of the community are almost unanimously
in favor of Kilrain. They consider the
Boston man nothing better than 4
brute, and want to see him whipped.
but they are notinclined to back their pref.
erence. At the clubs to-day the genera.
sentiment was: “We hoped Kilrain will
win,” but when abet was offered the clut
men wanted 2to1. Even the ladies are simi
larly inclined and their sympathies are with
the Baltimore man.

AT SULLIVAN'S HEADQUARTERS,

At Sullivan’s headquarters to-day there
was no departure from the usual air of quiet
confidence. Among the visitors were
Sheriff Malloy, Chief of Police
Hughes of Louisville; Jake Bar
nett of New York and Charles yi
Johnson, one of Suilivan’s backers. They
were entertained in the parlors by Muldoon
while Sullivan remained in seclusion on the
floor above. Sullivan passed a lazy, luxurious
day. His appetite is enormous. For break.
fast he ate a good-sized bass, five soft-broiled
eggs, a half loaf Graham bread ja half dozen
sliced tomatoes. The only liquid he took was
acupoftea. After breakfast Muldoon oh
him a shave, during the course of which
he fell asleep, and while in that condition
Muldoon left him. At 1 o’clock he dined,
consuming his usual quota of three chickens
with rice und chicken broth, anda balf loaf
of bread.

There is still some conflict of opinion as to
Kilrain’s condition. Some think he is too
fat; others too lean. A reporter surprised
Tom Allen, the famous pugilist, taking a
lemonade inthe rotunda of the St. Charles
Hotel. He was asked for his opinion. He
said, ‘I am for Kilrain.”

The reporter requested an opinion as to Kil
rain’s condition. Allen replied;

“It is good, bat | would iike him better if
he were not so fat. I like to seé the cheek.
bones sticking out.”

So there you are. The talent generally con.
sider Kilrain too light and Tom thinks him
too heavy. Everybody is at sea and the bet-
ting is taking curious shoots. Bets are being
made that Sullivan will win in less than six
rounds, and so it goes. Thus far little money
has been wagered here. The Kilrain men in.
sist on odds of two to one. The other side ure
willing to concede $100 to 875, but there is nc
disposition to close at these figures.

also says Kilrainis better than Ryan he will
lick him just the same.’’ Sullivan is only
drinking Bass’ ale. Kilrain is using cham-

A notable trio of the past age of pugilists

The Daly brothers, who are here, were

THE MONEY FOUGHT FOR.

The money involved inthe fight was very
much greater than in any battle known in tne
b story ofthe prize ring, The stakes were
$10.000 a side, making $20,000 altogether.
About 800 inner ring tickets were soid at $15

nooa. {

ago, when he sustained a relapse and was
compelled to return to bed.

—For writing up the Weir-Murphy fight
1s a fake, engineered by bookmakers, the
California Athletic club has expelled M. J.
Geary of the San Francisco Call, and M. J.
Daily of the Illustrated World, from all future
meetings of the club. The main charge was
fhat Weir had thrown the fight for $5,000,
put the reporters were evidently wrong, 4s
Weir was flat broke after the fight.

—A dispatch from England announces the
jeatt of the veteran starter of sprint races,
fom Wilkinson, whose name has been so lon
indelibly associated with Sheffield handy
caps and other prominent race meetings. It
will be remembered that some months ago he
was struck down suddenly with paralysis,
but eventually recovered 80 far as to be able
to get about. He, however, had another
stroke on January 16, and, getting gradually
worse, ne expired at his residence, Hungary
street, Sheffield, three days later.

The Kansas Conference to Be Held To-

Day—Insurance Companies Sue the

[ron Mountain for Cotton Losses ;
—Central Traffic Association.

Special to The Republic,

Cuicaco, IL, Feb. 7.—The reduction of
Nebraska grain rates complicates the West.
ern freight problem more than the announced
reduction of the Burlington anc Northern.
The reduction is not enough to even furnish
an object lesson to the farmers in the way 0!
a break in the market for it amounts to only
from 4¢ cents to2cents a bushel. On the
other hand the reduction, being on through
business only, will work greatly tc
the detriment of lines ending &t
the Missouri River. Instead of breaking
bulk at the river as has been the case
heretofore, all grain at the reduced rate will
be carried to Chicago or the seaboard on
through bills of lading. The St. Paul, Chicago,
St. Paul and Kansas City and the Alton are
thus deprived of their shares of what has
heretofore been competitive business. Vice-
President McMullin of the Alton says his road
will meet the rate vd shrinking the local the
amount of the reduction in the throagh rate
if the- reduction cuts much of a figure in
changing the © routin of grain.
President Stickney of the Chicago, St. Paul
and Kansas City is also prepared to make the
same reduction, but in any event the farmers
wil! not get the benefit of the reduction, the
price of corn already having gone down to an
amount equal to the reduction in rates.

Chairman Walker headed last night a dele-
gation of railroad men who went to Topeka to
consider to-morrow the lowering of grain rates
in Kansas. Aconferénce will be held with
the Kansas Railroad Commission, which has
made a demand on the Transmissouri Asso-
ciation for a reduction of grain rates in Kan-
sas. From the strictures 9 Nebraska on the
board of transportation of that State for
accepting such a small reduction in rates, it
is the general opinion that the roads must
concede a greater Yeduction in Kansas,
although a determined attempt will be made
to use the Nebraska reduction asa precedent.

THE KANSAS CONFERENCE.

Special to The Repubile.

Topexa, Kas.,Feb. 7.—The representatives
of all the railroads will meet with Gov. Hum-
phrey to-morrow to discuss the question of
an emergency corn rate. The conference is
in ip to a letter in which he stated that
the situation demanded a reduction of the
rates oncorn. At present it cost nearly as
mutch to — itto market as the corn is
worth. It will be poor gy | to have united
action by the lines east of the Missouri River
as well as in Kansas.

Freight Traffic Complications.

Special to The Republic.

Curcaco, Feb. 7.—Two additional compli-
cations in the Western situation developed
to-day. The Milwaukee and Northern, con-
necting with the Sooand Canadian Pacific
at Pembina, notified their competitors that
they would put in force between Fort
Howard and Green Bay, Wis., and New
York and Boston rates on grain and other
freight much less than the present rates.
Some of the new tariffs have been issued but
none have as yet reached Chicago. The old
roads heretofore participating in this traffic
will have to meet the Northern competition
by rates from Chicago and Milwaukee, which
will cause a general reduction to all points in
Northern Michigan and Northern Wisconsin
and a consequent rearrangement of through
rates. The other complication is notice from
the Manitoba, or Great Northern, thatif the
Burlington and Northern puts in its proposed
reduction it will meet at the Missouri River
at Sioux City the through rate over the
Burlington and Northern to St. Paul. This
would wipe out the tariffs of the Chicago-
Missouri River lines, and it is hardly thought
matters will come to such a crisis.

Edwin Gould’s Progress.

Special to The Republic.

Datuas, Tex., Feb. 7.—Messrs. Edwin
Gould, W. B. Doddridge, H. G. Fleming and
A. H. Swanson and other prominent railway
officials spent the day in Dallas, In a confer-
ence with leading citizens it was decided to
bring the Cotton Pe 3 road into Dallas with-
out delay. Col. at ‘Meek and_ President
Morgan Jones of the Fort Worth and
Denver are also here, and it is understood
that this road has secured entrance into Dal-
las also.

HE SHINES ON SHERMAN,

Special to The Republic,

Superman, Tex., Feb. 7,—Edwin Gould,
Receiver Swanson and General Manager
Doddridge of the Cotton Belt route arrived
here to-night on atour of inspection of their
lines. The citizens will entertain the party
to-morrow and will show them over the city.
They wilt leave here for St. Louis to-morrow
evening.

Gone Up in Smoke.

Special to The Republic.

Livre Rock, Ark., Feb. 7.—Just $6,103,900
worth of railroad bonds went up in smoke to-
day in the big stove of the State Treasurer’s
office while the Governor and his staff gazed
on officially. This burnt offering consisted
of $160,000 Arkansas Central Railroad
bonds with $836,000 coupons at-
tached ; $498,000 Little Rock and
Fort Smith, with $1,045,500 coupons attached.
These bonds were made under an act ap-
proved July 21, 1568. fois 4 were deposited in
the Treasurer's office, but never issued.
Other bonds of this same series are still in
existence, bearing the date of April 1, 1869,
and signed by P. C. and J.R. Berry. These
bonds, it will be remembered, bad their origin
in a private scheme of Gov. Clayton’s admin-
istration to encourage railroad building in
Arkansas by means of State aid.

The Cotton {nsurance Case.

Special to The Republic.

Litrie Rock, Ark., Feb. 7.—The mucb
postponed and celebrated suit of the Marine
Insurance Co. of London vs. the St. Louis,
Tron Mountain and Southern Railway Com-
pany was begun in the United States Court
here to-day. Twelve of the most prominent
business menof Little Rock compose the
jury. This is one of the many cases that
arose from the great cotton fire
in. this city in i877, at which several
thdusand bales of cotton were destroyed.
The insurance companies, 80 in all, paid the
losses, and afe now claiming damages from
the [ron Mountain people, alleging that the
fire originated from @ passing engine on the
river bank, near where the cotton was etored.
Eight hundred thousand dollars is the aggre.
gate amount of damages to the insurance
companies. The present case will continue
for several days.

A Costa Rica Kailroad.

Cuicaco, Feb. 7.—Senor Manual Aragon,
delegate to the Pan-American congress from
Costa Rica, now in this city, yesterday re-
ceived acablegram from home stating that
his government had just issued a grant to an
English company tobuild a railroad from Sau
Jose to Esperda. “That is excellent news,”
he remarked. ‘“‘When that division is com-
pleted Costa Rica will have an interoceanic
railway, and one can go across the peninsula
in 10 hours. The road will be 36 miles long.
Although it will be built across the Andes,
there are no difficult feats of engineering and
the line ought to be finished in a year. With
the Nicaragua canal and a railway from the
Pacific to the Atlantic, Costa Rica will have
a regular American boom.”

They Want Less Work.

One of the sections of a bill prepared bj
the Federation of Railway Men to be pre
sented to the different State Legislatures
calls for the employment of one brakeman
for each 10 freight cars while en route
Another section of the bill reads as follows:
“The regular day for train service and fo
persons employed for such purposes shall be
eight hours out of each 24, and no man shal
be required or compelled to work for any
longer time or any more hours within each
24 hours.” The 100,000 members of the fed.
eration in support of this measure assert
that railroad accidents occur more frequently
because trainmen are overworked than from
any other cause.

More Ives-Staynor Trouble.

Batrmore, Md., Feb. 7.—An attachment
under the act of 1888 against non-residents
was issued from the Court of Common Pleas
to-day at the suit of the Mineral Range
Railroad Company of Michigan against
Henry S. Ives, Geo, B. Staynor and Thos.
C. Doremus, who compose the firm of Henry
S. Ives & Co. of New York. The claim of the
Mineral Range Co. against Ives & Co. is for
$450,968. It is represented that Ives & Co.
were the financial agents in New York of the
Mineral Range Co., and are indebted to it for
securities, property and money received. The
object of bringing the attachment
in this judicial foriadiction is
to summon Mr. bert Garrett
as garnishee to the amount of ge This
was paid to him by Ives nearly three years
ago asapartof the consideration tor the
purchase of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad
stock held and controlled by Mr. Garrett and
as a guarantee of good faith in the transac-
tion, The vatiroet company claims that Mr.
Garrett 1s not entitled to retain the money
paid him by Ives, ona that it is subject to
attachment in his hands by the creditors of
Ives & Co. Mr. Garrett holds that the mon
was forfeited to him vy Ives’ failure to carry
out his ae of the contract and purchase the
stock. Ives was to have paid $225 a share for
it, the par value being $100. He found he
could not raise the money, although the time
was extended a month. Mr. Garrett sailed
for Europe soon after the expiration of the )
time. |

Battimoreg, Md., Aug. §.—All the members
of Mr. Thomas H. Coakley’s family were
ebloroformed by burglars last night. At
4 o'clock this morning Mrs. Coakley
awoke feeling sick. She staggered along

, until the bath-room door was reached and
she found it locked. She thought this was
strange, asthe door was always left open.
With difficulty she awoke the rest of the
occupants of the house. All of them were
very sick and Thomas H. Coakley was suffer-
ing severe pain from a large knot on his
head. The bath-room door was
forced open and then it was evident
that burglars had done the mischief.
A large trunk in the apartment had been
broken into and the contents were scatterec
overthe floor. An investigation revealed the
fact that alot of valuable silverware and
$100 in cash had been stolen. On going
down stairs the family were treated to an
otber surprise. On the table in the
dining-room were the romuants of a midnigh?
meal. The burglars bad gone about thei:
workinthe most daring manner. A clear
white cloth had been spread over the table
and plates, knives and forks iaid upon it
The edibles were taken from the refrig
erator apd consisted of roast beef
ham, cantaloupe, potatoes, milk, bread
butter, watermelon and various dishe
of dessert. The contents of a bottle contain
ing whiskey and sulphur, which was used b:
the family for medicinal purposes, had als
disappeared.

It is believed that the robbers had secrete:
themselves in the dwelling before the occu
pants retired, and began their work when a)
were asleep.

title: St. Louis Sporting Men Head to the Dempsey-Fitzsimmons Fight
text:
THE RING.

Tem McGregor,the St. Joe Kid, who has
spent so much of his time in St. Louis for the
past year or so, is now in Galveston and has
put up $100 with E. T. Dodds, manager. of the
Gaiveston Athletic Club, io fight either
Arthur Upham or P.J.Pitzlin. It is ex-
pected the club will offer a purse for the
fight in case a match ismade. McGregor
has sent to the Police Gazette the following
characteristic letter:

GALVESTON, Tex., Jan. 1, 1891.
Richard K. Fox: ;

I see that Prof. P. J. Pitzlin is itching for a
go with Jack Dempsey. I Know it is all to
swell Pitzlin, but I will bet a thousand to a
hundred that he will itch for many days after
if he ever should be so unfortunate as to run
against Dempsey. I have one hundred up
with E. T. Dodds, manager of the club, to’
fight Pitzlin for any amount from a broken |
Cigarette up to any amount he can rake,
scrape, beg or borrow. He claimed he fought
and defeated me in three rounds, which
everyone in St. Louis knows is _ the biggest
untruth he ever told in his life. The only way
he would fight was for me to split the money
with him, win or lose, so lI think itis no more
than right for meto be heard in the Police
Gazette. Respectfully yours, .

| L. S. MCGREGOR, St. Joe Kid.
- The Philadelphia papers passed over with
-twoorthree lines of commenta four-round
bout that took place atthe Philadelphia A.
C. last Wednesday night between Billy Dacey
of this city and Waiter Campbell, the boxing
instructor of the Athletic Club of the Schuyl-
kill Navy and universally the idol of all
Quaker City lovers of sparring, says the
New York Sun. ANew York drummer who
was atthe bout told a Sun reporter on Satur-
day, however, that the go was oneof the
liveliest and, at the same time,most interest-
ingly scientific he had ever seen. As this
criticism was made by one who has followed
athletics from youth, and who never misses
a good scrap that comes off within twenty
miles of wherever he may be, ftis worth re-
cording. The gentleman who has no per-
sonal interest in eit her man, added that per-
haps the papers didn’t make much of the go
because the Philadelphia Adonis got the
worst of it.

The men boxed with two-ounce gloves, an
unusually small glove fora public show. Im-.

mediately aiter they shook hands Campbell
stepped back. and bang! bang! went one fist
afterthe other con Dacey’s right cheek. The
blows landed like lightning, and cut the New
Yorker’s cheek a little under the eye, besides
raising something of acushion. Dacey was
taken by surprise, not having expected to
take part in more than an ordinary peer
bout, ae the size of the gloves shoul
have warned him that something unusual
was up.

He rallied inan instant, however, and it
could be seen that he realized that he was up
against something. He measured the situa-
tion correctly and promptiy proceeded to
hammer the -handsonie Campbell, who ranks
asa boxer with any instructor in the coun-
try. Dacey couldn’t reach his face, as Camp-
bell was tootall, but he gotin some of the
wickedest kind of punches on the Philadel-
phian’s stomach and continued fast work on
Campbell’s wind throughout the four rounds
without receiving another blow that hurt.
According tothe Sun reporter’s informant if
the bout had lasted another round Campbell
would have had to give up or be knocked out.

GOING TO THE FIGHT.

Quite a number of people from this city are
going to the Dempsey-Fitzsimmons fight,
whic takes place at New Orleans next
Wednesday night. Tom Allen, Tom Kelly,
the. Daly brothers, the McManus brothers,
Bob Farrell and other local lights of the pu-
geome firmament are making preparations

or the trip,while several other Lome od also at-
tend. Ed Rothey of Omaha has written to the
Daly brothers, stating that he, Jacoby, and
others leave on Saturday for New Orleans. He
says they will probably stop Overin St. Lonis
for a few hours, and wants to know whether
any delegation is to leave from here and
whether special rates to the Crescent City can
be obtained from here. W. J. Elliott tele-
graphs the Daly bros. from Evansville, Ind.,
inquiring whether there will be any delega-
tion from St. Louis.

title: Jack King Puts Up Money With Allen to Fight Boden
text:
PENDRAGON ON COBURN.
<= Se :
THE ENGLISH SPORTING WRITER DIS-
CUSSES THE DECEASED PUGILIST.
Jack McAuliffe and Billy Myer Matched—
The Association Again Put Into the
Soup by the National League—Sporting
News in General.

Henry Sampson, whoas Pendragon of the
London Referee has a world-wide reputation
as a writer in pugilism, reviews the late Joe
Coburn as follows:

**In the course of last week two old-time
fighting men passed away, Harry Poulson
and Joe Coburn, the one an Englishman and
the other an American. Isuppose it is cor-
rect to say that Joe Coburn was an American.
He was always an American, and very much
an American, asa fighting man; as a matter
of absolute nationality he was born at
Armagh, in the now more than ever
distressful country, somewhere about fifty-
six or fifty-seven years ago, and was, at the
beginning of the hegira which took place
shortly afterward, transported to the land of
the star-spangled banner. Thereis not much
opportunity of knowing exactly what class of
fighter Coburn was, and whenhe came over
here with the expressed intention of fighting
Mace, who was then champion, the men did
not get into the ring, and, sofar as I know,
Coburn never showed his form even with the
gloves in this country. The conditions
of the match with Mace were
that it should be for £500 a side, the
battie to be fought in Ireland, and Coburn
was to receive £100 for traveling and other
expenses. Coburn received his £100, but on
his arrival in Dublin, where the high con-
tracting parties all met, he would not consent
to enter the ring or take off his clothes unless
his mother or his aunt, or some other near
and dear relation, was appointed referee.
The affair ended in one ofthe hollowest and
most lamentable failures that even the prize
ring has been able tobringabout. To say
this is to say a great deal, as some of the
worst and most ludicrous flascos this world
has ever known must, one way or another,
have come in connection with prize fight-
ing. But it was so, and there is no
use attempting to disguise or deny it. Ire-
member the circumstances (just over twenty-
six years ago) perfectly well, and don’t know
where their equal could be found for blatant
false pretense and arrant humbug. Till this
day what class of man Coburn really was re-
mains a mystery. If he could fight Mace for
three hours 2nd a half, even in a swamp, and
our old man really meant fighting, he must
have been abit of a goodone. But ourold
man didn’t always mean fighting; and it
might have happened besides that any undue
desire on his part to punch Coburn’s head
would have ended in his own being riddled
with a score or so of bullets.

MYER AND M’AULIFFE MATCHED.

Jack McAuliffe of Brooklyn,the light-weight
champion of America, and Billy Myer, the
Streator Cyclone, have been matched to fight
with gloves for a stake of $,000a side and the
largest purse that can be secured. James
Colville of Boston is McAuliffe’s backer and
Alf Kennedy of Streator, Ill., is Myer’s. A
deposit of $250 a side has been made with Bud
Renaud of New Orleans. A purse of $7,000
has been offered for the contest by the
Olympic Club, but McAuliffe hopes to receive
an offer of $10,000 from the Puritan Club of
Long Island City. If the latter organization
secures the contest there will not be any
stake or side bet, the purse only being fought
for. This is because the officers of the club
are friends of McAuliffe, and while Myer is
willing to fight the New Yorker even before
that organization, he and his backer do not
feel disposed to risk any stake money to the
decision of men who are Known to sympathize
with and favor his antagonist. The match
between Jimmy Carrell and Jack McAullife,
for which the Olympic Club offered $10,000 and
the Puritans $11,000, willnot be made, Fitz-
simmons’ trainer declaring that there is
more money in managing the New Zealander.
It would appear from this that despite all his
howling and talk Carroll was not very anxious
for a return battle with the New Yorker, but
was satified to stand pat on his defeat al-
ready sustained. McAuliffe’s friends
always declared that the news-
paper reports of the fight before the
California Club were all highly coiored in
Carroll’s favor, and that there was notruth
in the assertion that the crafty little English-
man hadthe best of the contest up tothe
time that McAuliffe delivered the knock-out
blow. The McAuliffe men say that Carroll
never had achanceto win, the New Yorker
outclassing him from the star Billy Myer
has been anxious fora go with either of the
men,and McAuliffe in particular. He has
agreed to fight the New Yorker even before
the latter’s favorite ciub, the Puritan, and
has also agreed to the champion’s conditions
as to weight, 135 pounds, give or take two
pounds. This permits the men to weigh in
ati37 pounds, four pounds above the gen-
erally accepted light-weight limit, which is
133 pounds. The Queensbury rules limit,
however, ts 140 pounds and McAuliffe has
been standing on this fact. He is getting too
heavy to train down to i133 pounds without
weakening himself. Dick Roche, the head of
the Puritan Club, was McaAuliffe’s backer
when the latter fought Myer a draw, and
only the Streator boy’s great desire to have
another go at the champion would induce
him to fight before that club.

JACK FOGHRTY TO RETIRE.

Pringle in the Pittsbug Dispetch has always
been a friend and admirer of Jack Fogarty,
the Pennsylvania middle-weight. He has
held that Fogarty was a mere boy when he
fought and was defeated by Jack Dempsey
and that he had not fully developed, and
therefore not the fighter he should be now
that he has reached maturity. Hereis what
Pringle has to say of his favorite:

Jack Fogarty, after vainly trying to se-
cure a battle with any middle-weight in
America, or any other country, for that mat-
ter, has decided to retire from all pugilistic
business. His judgment in this instance may
be wisest, certainly he will in the long run
be the gainer. I have always held the
opinion that Fogarty. wouid be a
dangerous opponent for any man his weight.
Apparently champions and aspiring cham-
plons have held a similar opinion, because
they have steadily declined to meet him, I
Know personally that all Kinds of efforts have
been made in behalf of Fogarty to secure him
a contest with eitherLa Blanche, Dempsey,
Young Mitchell, in short, any middle-weight
inthe world. Theclubs or ‘‘pub-clubs,’’ as
somebody calis them, have strictly adhered
to their custom of keeping their favorites busy
and asa result some ofthe veriest pugilistic
frauds have been put into these pub-club
rings to fight for big purses, real or alleged.
It is a pity that Fogarty has not hada chance
since he became a man to tackle one ofthe
very best ofthe champions. He may, how-
ever, change hismind. He says he won’t.

JACK KING TO MIKE BODEN.
_ Jack King writes to this paper as follows:
 *Thave $50in Tom Allen’s hands to fight
Mike Boden, any style he may mention. He
has been talking about fighting anybody in
St. Louls. Now, ifhe means fight let him
cover this money and arrange a match for a
purse and stake. He will please answer this
as soon as possible if he means business.
Now, Mr. Boden, put up or shut up.
| **JACK KING.’’
summary: In a letter to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, Jack King said he had $50 in Tom Allen's hands to fight Mike Boden in any style Boden chose.

title: Tom Allen in Prize Fight
text:
THE RING.

Many champions have falien hard and suad-
den, but few with the severity and speed of
Jack Dempsey, writes Macon. His skill and
quickness were so great that, though he was
never more thana good ten-stone man, his.
Many victims were men bigger, stronger and
heavier than himself, and finally deceived
him and his admirers into the belief that,bar-
ring the champion of allchampions, he was_
virtually invincible. |

His defeat by La Blanche did not naturally
change this opinion, forit was looked upon
asanunilucky fluke due to a chance blow,
put the pitiable exhibition he made with Bob
Fitzsimmons emphasizes in the most marked
manner the old sporting proverb: ‘‘A good
little man cannot whip a good big one.’’

Now let me say right here that, though
there was less than five pounds difference in
the weight of the Australian and Dempsey,
in reality Jack was at least two sizes smaller
than his opponent. This difference was so
apparent when they faced each other for the
first round that a gentleman who sat inthe
box immediately behind my seat exclaimed:
“*Why,this man Fitzsimmons is big enough
to fight Sullivan!’’ and so he was. Dempsey
looked like a pigmy in front of him.

The Australianisthe biggest man for his
weight leversaw, with one exception, and
that was the late Tom Ryan, the sporting |
printer. Tom was five feet ten inches tall, if
Iremember rightly, and could fight well and |
strong at 108 pounds. Ihave seen him spar
with Joe Coburn, Tom Allienand Jem Mace,
and make a rattling good showing with them,
too. In fact, they could do nothing with him
as longas they Wayed lightly. They had to
put steam to their blows to keep him from
being all over them.

Well, Fitzsimmons is better than Jake Kil-
rain, Jack Ashton, Joe Lannon or George
Godfrey, and his frame is as large as either’s.
Up tothe time that he defeated Billy Mc-
Carthy in California he was as poor as a
church mouse. He didn’t have the money
to pay for even a steerage passage from Mel-
bourne to this country, and he came here asa
stowaway, and worked his passage after his
discovery on the ship by washing down the
decks and such like employment. A pint of
porter or a dram of grog was the extent of his
liquid refreshment a year ago. Now he is
drinking champagne, and by the time he has
devoured the tenderloins of a score of Amer-
ican beeves he will have the meat on his
frame that nature designed it tocarry. Then
he willbe in his proper class, and he will
have to <o up against the Choyinskis and the
Peter Noians of the ring, and not the 154-
pounders.

SULLIVAN AND SLAVIN.

ed rumor’’ that John L. Sullivan has been
matched to fight Frank P. Slavin next sum-

mer, forthe heavy weight championship of
the world. Jimmy Wekely and Phil Lynch of
New York are alleged to have got the big fel-
low to consent to the match and to sign
articles, but ikfmoet ‘*well-authenticated

MRS. WOODWORTH’S TEMPLE.
The Lady Evangelist Again Agitates the
Raising of Money.

- Last night Mrs. Woodworth announced
from the pulpit her intention of building her
proposed temple in this city, and urged those

having made donations to pay in the
amounts, as she desired to purchase the lot
as soon as possible.

‘*We must havea house of worship in St.
Louis at all hazards,’’ said Mrs. Woodworth,
‘‘and when we get a lot the securing of funds
to erect a permanent structure will be more
easy, as the people will see that we are thor-
oughly in earnest, and be more willing to
make donations.

| Rev. Wm. Jones, pastor of the Floating
Bethel of Cincinnati, a reformed sport and
sailor, preached for Mrs. Woodworth last
night and will do soagain. Mr. Jones tellsa
story of his Mfe that rivals that of Francis
Murphy. At the age of 16 he was
a prize fighter, being backed as
a boy wonder inthe ring by Tom Allen of St.
Louis. Heafterwards became a sailor and
developed the usual tendency of people so
employed for strong drink. He was arrested
and locked up thirty-nine times by the police
on various offenses. Several years ago he
reformed and has since been working among
the poorer classes in Cincinnati. Rev. Jones
is a forceful, though not learned talker, and
thinks that Mrs. Woodworth is a wonderful
worker. He will probably go back to Cincin-
nati Tuesday.

Rev. H. H. Spiherof Springfield, Ill., who
hadso much success in preaching for Mrs.
Woodworth last week, is expected to return
the latter partof this week and again get
down to work. Rev. Spiher regards St. Louis
one of the best flelds in which he has yet been
engaged with Mrs. Woodworth, and says
that he expects to see a magnificent temple
erected here for the glorification of the
**power.’*’ Mrs. Woodworth promises to soon
give out a list of late cures, which, she says,
are growing more numerous at each meeting.

SPORTING NOTES. |

Peter Jackson, under Parson Davies’ man-
agement, is drawing crowded houses in Lon-|
don.

Charley Mitchell isnot anxious for a try at
Peter Jackson. A boastful challenge made |
by Mitchell was not accompanied with money
to uphold it.

Peter Maher, the Irish champion, is coming |
back to this country in August, and says that.
he willchallenge George Godfrey to fight
him in the Coney Island Athletic Club for a |
purse, |

The Pritchard-O’Brien match has been de-
clared off. The Welchman isill, and Pritch-
ard can now lie on his oars until the time
comes for him to begin training for his battle
with Jim Hall. |

Kibblewhite, the English runner, stands 5
feet 912 inches In height, and weighs, in run- |
ning costume, ten stone. Heis still the one- |
mile amateur champion, and during his ca-.
reer has secured more than £1,000 in prizes.

Peter Maher, who received sucha severe
drubbing at the hands of Bob Fitzsimmons,
has returned to ‘*the ould sod.’’ He received
an enthusiastic reception at Dublinand was
treated more like a conqueror than a con-
quered one.

Tom Alien is keeping very quiet overin St.
Louis..It was Tom that discovered before the
Jackson-Siavin fight that Peter Jackson’s—
lungs were gone and that every time he
coughed he iet goa little of hisliver. Tom’s—
diagnosis was not remarkably successful.
—[Chicago Mail, |

A representative of the Pastime Club of Los |
Angeles is in San Francisco trying to match ©
wae Dawson and Billy Maher. The latter .
has chalienged Dawson. At present Dawson |
and Needham are trying to get a match in the |
California Club, and it is thought they will be |
brought together. If not, Dawson says he
will meet Maher.

The bookmakers at Latonia are not walkin
on velvet if the hee which was clipped
from Wednesday’s issues of the ew can
be taken as acriterion: A half dozen more
books a off in the new drawing yester-
day and there are now only twenty-three
books onthe line. When the meeting opened
thirty-elgnth pencilers hag up their slates to
the route at Latonia. The fact that fifteen of
them have thrown up the sponge since the
meeting began shows that the public must
have been eating up the books’ rolls. A
great many of the pencilers will go from here
to Chicago and put up their slates at Garfield.

The Doe’s Origin.
{From Harper’s Young People.)

Dogs belong to the species that naturalist
call Canide. Thisis a family of carnivorou:
mammals, to be found in nearly every part of
the globe. The dog existed ina domesticated
state during prehistoric times, and therefore
we are unable to solve the question of its ori-
gin. Baron Georges Cuvier, the gréat French
naturalist, who could, it is said, ary ae single
bone of an animal, even though it longed
to an extinct race, consfruct the complete
skeleton of the animal and determine to what
species it belonged, said that the dog is ‘‘the
completest, the most singular, and the most
useful conquest ever made by man.’’ The
naturalists ‘do not agree in their theories in
regard to the origin of the dog.

Some suppose that allthe breeds of modern
dogs have sprung from.a single source, while
others maintain thatthey are the product of
the ee of several distinct species. Of
those who favor the first idea, the majority
think that the parent of the Gog is the wolf;
some others favor the jackal, while a few are
inclined to believe that dogs are descended

.from an extinct species. These latter point to
the fossil remains of alarge dog found in the

d aan tertiary deposits as the probable wild
stock.

Those who think the wolf to have been the
parent base their theory on the general re-
semblance of the wild wolf to some modern
dogs, and to the further fact that) the tao aod
Maux frequently capture and tame wolves
and cross them with their dogs, so as toim-
prove the breed. The jackal theorists use the
same arguments as those who favor the wolf
idea, and they hayeas many facts to warrant
the supposition. fe ,

But the prevalent idea to-day is that the doz
is a mixture of several species, living and ex-
tinct. This opinion is founded upon the con-
sideration that irom the earliest historic times
there have existed many different ph of
aogs, totally distinct from each other and yet
closely resembling modern forms. |

And then wild hate ee of dogs have existed
in all quarters of the globe, and savages of all
races have been fond of heme | these. It is
unlikely, as Darwin has poin out, that any

one of these breeds should: have

selected for domestication. The fear of

man in wild animals is a gradually acquired

instinct, and before this was developed a race

ofanimals could have becn much more easily
tamed than later. iid

When the Fatkland Islands were first vis-
ited by man. the wild dogs found there ap-
proached him withouteither fear or aversion.

Special Dispatch to the Globe-Democrat.

ALBUQUERQUE, N. M., September 16.—Some
three months ago, at the request of numerous
parties interested in the matter, the Governor
of this Territory issued a proclamation call-
ing a general Convention of all those inter-
ested in the sheep and wool industry in all the
States and Territories west of the Mississippi,

hibition of the Territorial Fair. Responses to
that invitation were received by the Commit-
tee of Arrangements from the authorities of
Arizona, Texas, Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa,both
the Dakotas, Montana, wyoming. Colorado
and Idaho, which, including New Mexito,
make twelve States and Territories repre-
sented in the present Convention, The
men who came as delegates are all prac-
tically engaged in the wool business, either as
growers or dealers, and therefore bring to the

iscussion of the subjects coming before the
meeting a snow iodge gainea by Ch eg A
large number of subjects of much interest to

vention, and the most cap Saget of these are
probably a resolution in favor of an effort to
secure uniform legislation in all the sheep-
growlng States upon several important points,
such as a genera scab law and laws to Fa
phe the spread of ate rh gy diseases, laws
for the general protection of sheep, an at-
tempt to secure better railway accommoda-
tions, silly net more favorable freight itn 8
and better facilities for the handling ang ng
ping of shéep and wool; the best means to h
adopted to improve the grade of wools: ques-
tions in relation to sorting and handling, and
various other hooks of interest to those en-
gaged in the business. :

ov. Prince called the Convention to order
and delivered the opening address. He re-
fev¥ed to the fact that the delegates were here
in response to his invitation, and he felt grat-
ified to see in attendance such a large number
of intelligent and brogressiye business men,
represcs Sing Roatiy all sections of that great
divéeion of the country west of the Mississippi
River, and feltconfident from the character
of the men he saw before him that their delib-
érations could not fail to result in much good
to the important cause in which they were as-
sembled. . ‘

At the conclusion of his remarks Dr. G, 8.
Easterday, Mayor of the city, welcomed the
delegates to Albuquerque ina tew timely and
pe fold pen remarks, in which he proved
himself as much at home in woo! as in politics
er medicine. The Convention then proceeded
to organize by the election of officers.

Corbett’s Alleged Shabby Treatment of

<5 Mike Donovan.

HE SENDS THE PROFESSOR A CHECK
THAT WAS PROMPTLY RETURNED.
The Man Who Risked Everything for Him

Gets $250 for His Pains—Starter
Jimmy Rowe’s Career—An Eastern
Writer Scores Von Der Ahe—Gossip

From Turf, Ring and Diamond.

New York, Sept. 20.—Taking up Jim Cor-
bett asa protege turns out a very unsatis-
factory experiment for veteran Mike bono-
van, the boxing instructor of the New York
Athletic Club. Whenthe Californian made
his first visitto the metropolis three years
ago Donovan took a fancy to him and
through his influence Corbett was made a
guest of the New York Athletic Club, an
honor that has fallen to no other pugilist.
The professor was also largely instrumental
in getting on the Corbett-McCaffrey match
and in other ways rendered invaluable ser-
vices to the young stranger,

When Corbett returned to the city after his
battle with Peter Jackson in San Francisco,
the courtesies of the New York Athletic Club
were again extended to htm. Prof. Donovan
proposed the challenge to Sullivan and got
Ed Kearny and other New York Athletic Club
members to put up a large share of Corbett’s
§1,000 . stake. Mike took a prominent
share in making the big match, and
since then has looked after Corbett’s
interests faithfully. It was against the
wishes of prominent officials of the New
York Athletic Club that Donovan went to
New Orleans to act as adviser in Corbett’s
corner, and the matter may yet result unfor-
tunately for him.

After Corbett’s victory Donovan was the
most jubilant man inthe country, for he felt
that he was an especially important factor to
the new champion’s greatness. Corbett won
something like $35,000, and as Donovan had
been in a measure instrumental in obtaining
that money he naturally expected a hand-
some remembrance. Saturday Mike received
a letter from Corbett. There was a familiar
looking narrow slipinthe envelope andthe
professor’s faceexpanded. But ashe read
the figures on the check, the smile
faded. The piece of paper called for $250,
and was so far from Donovan’s expectations
that he immediately returned the check to
Corbett with a few remarks. In reply the
pugilist- asked him what he thought his
services was worth. There was some sur-
prise at Corbett’s action in the matter. Even
those who bear no good will toward the New
York boxing instructor opined that the least
Corbett might have sent would be double the
amount of the check, and that $1,000 would
be nearer the proper caper.

GODDARD ON HIS MUSCLE.
’ PHILADELPHIA, Pa., Sept. 20.—Joe Goddard,
the Australian, bested Dick Wiley of Fair-
mount in three rounds, at the Ariel Athletic
Club, lastnight. The challenger of Corbett
had his man ‘‘out’’ inthe first round when
time was called. The other rounds were
lighter, but Wiley was very groggy at the
end of the third. On Wednesday night at the
Arie] Club Goddard wiil meet Jim McVey,
who helped to train Corbett,
A WELL KNOWN 8ST. LOUIS PUGILIST.

An important omission in Sunday’s article
descriptive of prize fighters who have made
St. Louis their home was the dismissal with a
passing reference of ‘‘Dubiin Tricks,’’ one of
the best Known prize ring characters in this
city in the "60s.

Wm. Blake, or as he was then better
known, Dublin Tricks, was a pugilist of
more than ordinary reputation, who after
his battle with Mike McCoole trained and
handled that worthyin all his subsequent
battles. He also trained Charlie
Gallagher, who met Tom Allen twice,
fefeating him the first time. After
McCoole’s retirement Mr. Blake forsook his
prize-r.ng associations and has followed out
his trade ofshipcarpentering. Throughatyp- |
ographical error Mr. Blake was mentioned
AS a notorious pugiiist instead of a noted one.
Contrary to general opinion he is a native
American. and not of foreign birth. He
boards at the St. Louls House, on Main and
Locust streets, and works for the Anchor
Line and other steamboat companies,

THE ‘‘TERRIBLE BLACKSMITH’’ AFTER FIGHT.

Jim Burge, the Australian Iightweight,
who was known as the ‘‘terrible blacksmith’’
in the Antipodes, and who is now in San
Francisco, is anxious to fight either Billy
Gallagher or George Dawson at 140 pounds,
pr Eilly Dacey, the New York lightweight, or.
any man in America at from 128 to_ 138
pounds. Burge says he fought Dawson three
draws at home and is ready to settle the
— of superiority with him any time he

esires. The ‘‘terridDle blacksmith’’ also
states that his proper fighting weight is from
128 to 130pounds, but he professes to be will-
ing toconcede either Gallagher or Dawson
ten pounds. Ifeitherof the latter accepts
Burge says the conditions must cali
for a weigh-in at the ring side.

Billy Dacey, the New York Hght-
weight, is in San Francisco just at
present, having arrived there with George
Siddons, who is matched to fight Solly Smith
of Los Angeles the latter aps of the present
month, last week. Dacey is always ready or,
atleast, has doneensugh of challenging in
eg years, to lead the public to believe that

eis reomgys be fight anyone at his weight in
America. e now has an opportunity to
demonstrate whether he really is as anxious
to fight as a good many Of his friends believe.

PUGILISTIC POINTERS.

Alarge audience welcomed Jchn L. Sulll-
Van and his new play, entitled ‘‘The Man
from Boston,’’ at Providence, R. 1., last
night.

Since Jim Corbett has become champion he
has recived a number of letters from ladies
and friends in Brooklyn asking him to appear
in that city. Corbett has concluded to oblige
them and will appear Thursday afternoon
and evening in a glovecontest at the Star
Theater.

Tom O’Rourke, George Dixon’s manager,
is making arrangements for a reception the
colored teatherweight champion’s New York
friends will tender him towards the latter
part of the present month in Madison Square
Garden. O’RKourke says that Dixon will meet
JohnnyGrifin for $10,000 a side after next June
when his theatrical contracts expire.

Two local pugilists who are more prone to
ight with their hands than their mouths,a
yuite uncommon proclivity among the local |
fraternity, are going to settle a much-mooted |
jyuestion of superiority. The men referred to
are Johnnie Daly and Frank, alias ‘‘Dutch,’’
Nell. The fightis the outcome of a spirit of
rivairy between the two Market street pugi-
istic resorts. Neil, by iis recent vic-
tories, has become the pride of
tom Kelly’s, and Johonte Daly is
the hero of the habitues of his brother’s re-
sort. There is no personal animosity be-
[weenthe men, but Neil’s recent victories
have led him to belleve that he is the best
manofhis welghtinthecity. Johnnie Daiy
happens to tip the scales in Neil’s neighbor-
hood and, as aconsequence, thinks Dutch is
a littie offon hisjudgment. Both are willing
to put the matter toa test and will glve each
other a bot argument.

Charley Daly announces that he will put up
$500 on behalf of his brother fora finish fight
at catch weights with skin or two-ounce
gloves. Hels willing that the fight should
come off in a room with only five people to a
side witnessing ithe encouter, or he is willing
to have the affair pulled off at Neil’s selec-
tion. Nellis not only willing but anxious
for a go with Johnnie and said yesterday that
jom Allen would see that his $590 was forth-
coming.

Time and place will be decided upon when
the stake money is posted.

Both Dalv and Nell are well known mem-
bers of the local pugilistic fraternity and are
notable more fora willingness to fight than
toissue chaNenges and carry on war in the
newspapers. Both men weigh about 140
pounds. Neilis short and stockily built and
isasureand hardhitter. Daly is taller and
has the advantage of his opponent in reach.
Acontest between the two means a test of
gameness. .

title: Charley Mitchell Writes Tom Allen About Corbett Fight Plans
text:
CRIMSON AND BLUE.

CHARLEY MITCHELL WRITES TOM ALLEN
A CHARACTERISTIC LETTER.
He Says Corbett Will Strike a Surprise
Party Before the Tenth Round—Char-
ley’s Version of His Troubles—Gossip
ofthe Pugilists—Turf Topics—General
Sporting News.
NEw York, Nov. 19.—The sixty days’ reign
of foot-ballas king of sports is nearing Its
end. Foot-ball enthusiasts have no eye
just now for anything but the great game to-
day in Hampden Park, when Yale and Har.
vard will lock horns. The game will be o!
extraordinary interest to the Princeton
eleven, who will tackle the blues on Man-
hattan Field Thanksgiving Day. The tigers
are practicing with a vengeance for the fray,
and they meanto wipe out Pennsylvania’s
defeat If it is withinthe bounds of possibility.
The Princeton boys will attend the Yale-
Harvard match, and then return to Nassau’s
cam pus and see if they can master the tricks
which they may have seen the Yales work.
Yale will probably not use the same signals
in her game with Harvard that she has pre-
pared for the Princeton game, as there might
be a chance to block some of their combina-
tions.
The Greggains-Costello battle, which will
occur on Monday,Nov. 28,at the Co_ey Island
Athietic Cinb, promises to bs one of the
most famous that hasever been decided in
the stakeless ring of the club by the sea.
Both men are masters of the art of boxing
and each aspires to the middle-weight cham-
pionship of the world. The winner will with-
out doubt be matched to fight the victor of
the Hall-Fitzsimmons contest. The future of
Costello and Greggains depenjis upon the out-
come of their meeting on the 28th, and they
are carefully preparing for it—Costello at the
Navesink Highlands with Peter Maher and
Joe McGrath, and Greggains at Saus, Mass.,
uncer the direction of his manager, Martin
Murphy, and Howte Hodgkins. It would
|be difficult to imagine a _ place better
j;suited for a training ground for ath-
| letes than the spot at the Highlands of Nave-

sink where Maher, Costelloand McGrath are

getting in form for their mills. The men are

domiciled ata comfortable hotel just below
| the turreted tuwers inclosing the twin Hghts

of the Highlands. Costelio is training ear-
| nestly, honest!y and ungerudgingly. He fairly
|}loves his work and revels In it all day.
| He means to get in the finest possible condi-
| tlon for his ight with Gregzains on the 28th,
| and if conscientious, preliminary work will
put him there he will be all righton that
; night. His right hand bothers him some
stulll, and heis favoring it considerably. It
| will be remembered that he injured it se-
| verely by falling over a chain fence at Coney
| Island the night of the Choynski-Godfrey

mill. Buffalo now weighs 157!2 pounds, and

} will go Into the ring at 15s or 159 pounds.
| Maher is going it slow in his work and the
casual visitor would say he was indolent
and averse to genuine training. He looks
| very Wellandsays he feels Al, but the me-
| dium of work he did yesterday was a poor
criterion to judge him by. Histrainer, Tom
| Clark, says he is doing all that is necessary
| and that he will be in winning form on Dec.
| 8, when Goddard faces him.
| MeGrath is extremely lazy for a little fellow
| who is going up against such a crack as Billy
Pliimmer, but he may buckle to his work
after awbile and put some ginger into his
gait by the time he meets Plimmer, Dec. 23.

Maher did a little unlooked for sprinting the

| other day to get out of the way of a Long

Branch express on the Shrewsbury River

bridge, and he showed a fine burst of speed

| which possibly saved his life. Sports who

| have a fine eye for ‘‘lines’’ on pugiilsts, say

| Greggains will win his fight with Costello.

| And now for another batch of caloric fight-

}ingtalk. Jimmy Carroll has put up $1,000 to

| bind a match between his clever feather-
weight, Johnny Griffin of Braintree, and the
little Senegambian champion, George Dixon.

Carroll insists, however,that he will not per-

| mit Griffin to fight at less than 120 pounds and
this he adds is two pounds lighter than the
| legitimate avoirdupois of featherwelghts. As
‘Tom O’ Rourke insists just as empratically
| that George shall not scrapat over lis and
| demands the same weight from Griffin, it is
; easy to see thata muss is assured in the near
| future. After Dixon, Carroll says the match
| 1s open to young Griffo of Australia, Billy
| Murphy, Ike Weir or any man in the feather-
weight class. Meanwhile O’Rourke says
there 1s $1,000 for Billy Murphy to cover and
takeon a mill with Dixon at 118 pounds, but
not an ounce heavier. Something tangible
in the fighting line surely ought to come out
of allthis conversation.

Phil Dwyer has denied that he is Corbett’s
backer and says that he never backed a
fighter in his life. What is more, he does
not intend to. Headds, however, that he is
willing to advance him any reasonable
amount. He hasannounced that he will not
in the future hold any more stakes.

The several committees of the New York
Press Club’s proposed athletic carnival at
Madison Square Garden on the afternoon and
evening of Dec. 17 are wouping hard to make
the affair a success. TNe Entertainment
Committee is arranging an athletic pro-
gramme that will eclipse anything of Its kind
ever givenin thecity. Foot-racing, hurdle-
jumping, bicycling, lacrosse, tug-of-war,
foot-bali, wrestling on horseback, fencing on
horseback and other equestrian perform-
ances are some of the sports already decided
upon. Thecommittee will aim to make the
afternoon performance particularly attract-
ive to women and children.

Sporting men are excited over a report
that Al Smith, the well-known sporting man,
had bucked the tiger and won $22,400 in cold
cash. Of this amount he is said to have
won $20,000 at one sitting. If all accounts be
true, this is the way Smith has won his
small fortune. Overa year agoa friend bet
him $600 that he would not abstain from
Mquor a year. smith took the bet and jis
year expired last Sunday. On the day _ fol-
lowing, he went toa gambling resort in West
Twenty-eighth street and began to play faro.
He stayed there two days and two nights,
eating and drinking atthe table and taking
short naps at intervals. When he arose
from the table he was $20,000 richer and
pretty well filled with champagne. He went
home, according tothe story, but returned
next day and played an hour ‘‘for car fare.’’
He won $2,4004n that time. Al Smith has been
a backer of walking matches and of John L,
Sullivan, owns a half interest in the White
Elephant pool room, and has made money in
all these ventures. . fhe only game he never
could beat was theups and downs of stocks
in Wall street.

California Athletic Club Champion Corbett
and Peter Jackson, the colored heavyweight,
stood face to face yesterday in a hotel office
in Philadelphia. The meeting was friendly.
Peter extended his hand, saying to the
champion: ‘‘Mr. Corbett, I congratulate you
on your splenaid victory.’’

Corbett replied in a quiet way, thanking
Peter.: No fighting taik was induiged in.

make a tour of the Pacific Coast. The ‘‘Par-

Zz) oy \"h Yacht Club for an in-

A fies been brought to a satisfac-
age tory conclusion at last,
smal is and now there is a scram-
ble of yachtmen to Bristo), R. I., where the

been organized in New York for the
purpose ef yacht buildiag. Mr.

terday. Another syudicate will send arep-

gether the men who have been sleeping over

Joe Godaard is as conceited as a new-born
kangaroo. His victory over Peter Maher
has increased the size of his hat at least 100
per cent and itis still on the swell. God-
dard is very much cut up because Corbett
refuses to abandon his theatrical engage-
ments and meet him in the ring at once. The
champion has intimated to Maher's
conqueror that it would not be
a bad idea for him to get
ona match with Peter Jackson or Charley
Mitchell and defeat one or both of them
before setting up as a champion killor. This
is a very clever move on Corbett’s part. Hoe
would prefer to have Goddard and Jackson
settle their little difficulty and leave
Mitchell for himtodeal with. In the mean
while he can goon with his theatrical busi-
ness and Mitchell, being in jail, is not
likely to worry him for a while. (Goddard,
however, thinks Jackson is a little below
him in his class. It would be fun to see
Peter get after the Australian in the ring.
Goddard is no more of a prize fighter in the
modern sense of the word than Tom Allen
is. Hoeis allarms and legs in the ring and
fights like an automatic windmill. A care-
ful man like Jackson would make short
work ot him, and I venture the prediction
that if they ever come together Goddard
will not last over five rounds.

They say thatit is extremely doubful if
George Dixon will ever figure asa principal
inthe ring again. Men who have seen him
lately say he shows signs of staleness and
Shenae distress. Dixon is very young, but

e has trained oftener and fought harder
than most pugilists twice his age, and the
ordeal of *‘meeting all comers in four-round
bouts’? is beginning toteli on him. A
member of the Schuylkill Navy Athletic Club
of Philadelphia, who saw Dixon in that city
last week, says of him: ‘‘I don’t think
Dixon’s hands would stand along fight. He
has used them so much in these four-round
bouts that they are no longer the weapons
they were. I think that is the reason Tom
0’ Rourke will not let him make a match with
Griffin at anything-above 118 pounds. ’’

If Dixon has gone back in his work so far
as this, he must have been faring very badly
of late and gone to pieces very suddenly. He
was here some six weeks ago, and although
hard pressed in a four-round bout at Miner’s
Theater, appeared to be taking things rather
easily as though he had a heap up his sleeve.
He is one of the few fighters that can afford
to retiro fromthe squared arena. In the
past five years he has put by about $30,000,
pnd itis said he bas won nearlyas much
More recently in speculation,

An attempt willbe made at the forthcom-
ing session of the New York Legislature to
have the jaw governing racing in this State
amended so thst the season will begin on
April 15 and continue until November 15. A
poweriul lobby has been organized to push
the amendmert in the Legislature, and
no expense will be spared, we are told, to
have it passed. The powers that be in
the Board of Control are said to be the moy-
ing spirits behind the scheme. There is no
doubt that such an amendment would be re-
ceived with delight by those interested in the
race tracks, but there will be strong opposi-
tion to it from other quarters. An effort will
be made, itis said, to have the racing laws
entirely reconstructed and made more favor-
able to the racing associations. Whether
this broad plan will go through is another
question, We shall see.
